India, Re-30511. – Jīrṇoddhāraḥ (according to the Kāmika).
Total pictures: 261. (Last two folios are blank.)
The dimensions of the folio are 40 × 4 cm. (p = picture; f = folio [number as mentioned on the folio]).
There are seven lines per folio.
c = column.

The worship of Vighneśvara: The preceptor, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, washes the vessel for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) with the Astra-mantra; places it upon the support (*ādhāra*) with the Hṛdaya-mantra; and fills it with scented water while reciting the Mūla-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. (l2)

Having placed flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) there, having worshipped with the six-limbed root mantras, having consecrated [them] seven times with the *praṇava* (OM), having protected them, having sprinkled [them], and having rendered them nectar with the *dhenumudrā*, he should sprinkle himself—the substance and his own self—with that water using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*). Then he should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). The preceptor (*ācārya*), taking *darbha* grass in both hands and having prayed to Vighneśvara...

Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by the ritual striking of the head, [he proclaims]: "By the command of Śiva, Śiva, Śambhu, on this auspicious lunar day, for the bipeds and quadrupeds dwelling in this place, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas..."

For the purpose of attaining all desired goals through the gateway of the cessation of all misfortunes, in the rite of the restoration of the ruins and the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of the venerable Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara— who is accompanied by the Mother Kāntimatī, joined with the venerable Mūla-liṅga, together with his retinue from Saura up to Caṇḍa, and endowed with the venerable Mūla-liṅga— according to the method prescribed in the *Kāmikāgama*.

From the permission of Vighnarāja until the end of the three fortnights of worship, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa as a constituent part of the collection of materials for the sādhana; I shall also perform its constituent parts, such as the recitation of the Puṇyāha. For the sake of the Puṇyāha—

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, and having strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should sprinkle the mound with water while reciting the Śiva-Gāyatrī. Having worshipped Ramā, one should wash the *vardhanī* vessel—which is encircled by the *kumbha*—with the Astra-mantra. Having placed it in the center of the lotus with the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should fill it with scented water while reciting "āpo vā idam."
Having adorned it with mango sprouts and other such items:
(l3) "Obeisance to Brahmā at the base; obeisance to Viṣṇu in the middle; obeisance to Rudra on the lip; obeisance to Nandin on the two sides; obeisance to Mahākāla;
[at the cardinal directions] starting from the east—obeisance to Gaṅgā; obeisance to Yamunā" (l4).

Salutations! Salutations to the Godāvarī; salutations to the Sarasvatī; salutations to the Narmadā; salutations to the Sindhu; salutations to the Kāverī; salutations to the Tāmraparṇī—having thus worshipped them. [At] the nose: salutations to Vighneśvara; in the center: salutations to Varuṇāsana.

One should meditate upon Varuṇa, seated upon a sea-monster (makara), the Lord of the Tīrthas, a treasury of nectar, and the Sovereign of the Western Quarter, standing facing the east during the festival. (6) Having worshipped with "Salutation to the Form of Varuṇa," having applied collyrium to the eyes, and having filled the hollowed palms with flowers, one should [worship] with the mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa" and with his root-mantra.
Having invoked with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], having established with the *sthāpinī*,

having brought into proximity with the *sannidhānī*, and having restrained with the *niṣṭhurī* [or *rayā*], and having offered a welcome; then, perceiving that the Lord has said, "Welcome, my child," one should [place the mantras] in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands, such as the heart and so forth.

(l1) Having performed the placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*), having established identity with the root mantra (*mūla*), having protected and concealed [the deity], and having offered the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*); [saying] "Salutation to Varuṇa," one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the mantra ending in *svadhā* and *svāhā*. (l2)

Having worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, *dūrvā* grass, and flowers, [reciting]: "Obeisance to Varuṇa; obeisance to him who holds a noose in his hand; obeisance to him whose vehicle is a crocodile; obeisance to him adorned with priceless jewels; obeisance to the Lord of the Western Quarter. Having thus worshipped, one should offer incense and a lamp with the *kavaca* mantra, present fruits and other offerings with the root mantra (*mūla*), offer the *ārātrika* ceremony with the *kavaca* mantra, and complete the worship up to the end of the recitation (*japa*).

Having worshipped the movable seat (*calāsana*), then having placed [the materials] upon the pedestal (*sthalikā*)—having deposited the thick [substances], and having arranged the betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) and the large *āmuka* fruits—[he should worship with] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Candra; obeisance to the heart. Having thus worshipped, [he should invite] four Brāhmaṇas.

"We request from you for the sake of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). With these words, [the officiant] should take *darbha* grass... "Oṃ, being permitted by you, I shall cause the auspicious day to be proclaimed. Thus the *ācārya* should say. "Oṃ, let it be proclaimed... [The response of the priests]: "Oṃ, let it be proclaimed.
(l6) The response of the priests is: "Oṃ, water! He should place the *tīrtha* [water] into their hands. "Auspicious are the waters, continuous... ... "Oṃ, the *anvāhārya* [oblation]."
Thus [is performed] the *āhārya* offering. They should say: "Oṃ, let the *āhārya* be well-considered.

He should give betel-leaves with the words: "Oṃ, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). They should say: "May the *svasti-dakṣiṇās* protect [us]. He should pray: "May there be much to be given. They should say: "So be it. [Then he recites: "The *iḍā* is the invocation of the gods..."

Having performed the recitation (*japa*), the preceptor takes the *vardhanī* vessel, places his right knee upon the ground, holds the *vardhanī* with his right hand, and resting it in his left hand, touches the top with his right palm.
Having requested, "May your minds be concentrated," they respond, "Our minds are concentrated. [He says,] "May you be gracious," and they reply, "We are gracious."

This is the response. The teacher should request of the Brāhmaṇas: "May there be peace; may there be prosperity," and so forth, ending with "May the rite be auspicious. Having worshipped the firm seat, their response shall be: "May Mahādeva be pleased, may Mahādeva be pleased."

"Let the auspicious time be proclaimed. [The recitation continues] up to: "Whatever merit lies in the lunar mansion, he makes that very day auspicious. Having performed the *puṇyāha* rite, [the officiant says]: "May you all declare it auspicious! The response is: "Om, it is auspicious. [Then follows the recitation of: "The golden-hued, pure, purifying ones"; "Pavamāna"; "The Śiva weapon"; "The Pāśupata weapon"; "The Kṣurikā weapon."

The Aghora-weapon. The Vyoma-weapon. ...and having been seated upon their thrones, they recite the *Sūkta* beginning with "śī indra" (RV 8.91). They chant these three times; they rejoice together four times. Chant the *Sāman* hymn "pavasva. The waters indeed... hā.

Having likewise recited the *sūkta* and the *varuṇa-mantra*, and having thus performed the recitation and offered the fruit of that recitation, he dismisses Varuṇa from this jar with the mantra "tat tvā yāmi," saying: "I dismiss Varuṇa. Having thus dismissed him...

Having offered the *arghya* with its face turned away, one should sprinkle all [the materials] with the mantra "vāstoṣpate". Thus ends the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and the dismissal of the deities of the auspicious day;
this should be observed elsewhere.
[Now follows] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Now, the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is described. In the southwest of the *navaka* [mandala], having prepared a nine-square grid on ground smeared with cow dung using powders of turmeric paste;

and having prepared a nine-square grid on a sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) containing a *droṇa* measure of rice; having spread *darbha* grass upon it with its tips pointing east and north; and having sprinkled it with the water of the general *arghya* while reciting the *astra-mantra*, [one should offer] flowers and parched grain.

(l4) Having strewn [the sacrificial ground], [one says] "Obeisance to the Śiva-tattva... (ko)ṣṭha" in the center; "Obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva-koṣṭha" in the east; "Obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva-koṣṭha" in the south;
"Obeisance to the Puruṣa-tattva... in the north. (l5)

Salutation to Koṣṭha. In the west: salutation to Kālatattvakoṣṭha. In the southeast: salutation to Pṛthivītattvakoṣṭha. In the southwest: salutation to Aptattvakoṣṭha. In the northwest: salutation to Vāyutattvakoṣṭha. In the northeast: salutation to Prakṛtitattvakoṣṭha. Having thus worshipped the compartments (koṣṭhas), [one worships] in their midst: salutation to Kauśika. In the east...

Homage to Kaśyapa. To the south, homage to Bharadvāja. To the north, homage to Gautama. To the west, homage to Atri. Again, [homage] to Āśija; again, homage to Kauśika. To the southwest, homage to Kāśyapa. To the northwest, homage to Bhāradvāja. To the northeast, homage to Gautama. Thus... here.

... having worshipped the sages; among those [offerings], five vessels made of gold and other materials measuring one *prastha* or half a *prastha*, wrapped in thread, washed, polished, and inspected—having placed these five vessels in the center, the east, south, north, and west, as well as in the corners beginning with the southeast—from one *prastha*, half a *prastha*, a quarter of a *prastha*, and a *kuḍuba*.

Having set out the prescribed number of bowls possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, and having gathered cow’s milk and other [substances], and having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*), [one should offer]: in the center—“Homage to Supratiṣṭhapātra”; in the east—“To Suśānta” (l4).

Salutation to the Vessel. To the south—salutation to the Vessel of Radiance (*tejovat*). To the north—salutation to the Vessel of Jewel-Water (*ratnodaka*). To the west—salutation to the Vessel of the Principle of Nectar (*amṛtatattva*). To the southeast—salutation to the Vessel of the Principle of Water (*aptattva*). (L5) To the southwest—salutation to the Vessel of the Principle of Necessity (*niyatitattva*). To the northwest—salutation to the Vessel of the Principle of Time (*kālatattva*). To the northeast—salutation to the Vessel of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). Thus.

Having worshipped the vessels, having placed a *kūrca* grass-bundle separately in each of them, one should pour the milk of Kṛṣṇā into the central vessel with [the mantras] addressed to Īśāna and Aghora; the curd of Sitā into the eastern [vessel] with [the mantras] addressed to Tatpuruṣa and Vāmadeva;
and the ghee of Dhūmrā into the southern [vessel].

"Thou art semen, thou art light, thou art splendor. [With these words] from the Aghora [mantra], [he places] cow-urine in the southeast. To the north, [he places] cow-dung with the Gāyatrī and Vāmadeva [mantras]. "Homage to the Red One. [He places] cow-dung in the west. [He recites] "Gandhadvārā... and the Sadyojāta [mantra].

With those two [substances], [the area] the size of an axle; purified with cow-dung, water, and cloth; measured according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior; a *prastha* of fragrant oil and flour in the fire; with the verse "agnim īle" and the *Hṛdaya* [mantra]. In the southwest—*iṣetva* with this mantra, an *āmalaka* fruit; having consecrated half a *prastha* with the *Śiras* [mantra]; with the mantra "agna āyāhi."

Having placed half a *prastha* of powdered *rajanī* with the *śikhā* [mantra], and having consecrated it; in the northeast, having consecrated water from *kuśa* grass mixed with fragrance—half a *prastha*—with the mantras “*śanno devīḥ*” and “*devasya tvā*”;
and then, having worshipped Sadāśiva in milk.

Having worshipped thus: "Obeisance to Īśvara in the east; obeisance to Rudra in the south; obeisance to Viṣṇu in the north; obeisance to Brahmā in the west; obeisance to the Heart in the southeast; obeisance to the Head in the southwest; obeisance to the Tuft in the northwest; obeisance to the Armor in the northeast. [Then one worships] the presiding deities of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as the seat and other articles.
Having offered the oblation and performed worship with the mantras beginning with Īśāna,
[reciting them] once, twice, three, four, or five times, one should consecrate each of the substances situated in the southeast and other directions individually with the heart-mantra and the others.
Then, having protected them, poured water over them, and rendered them nectar-like, [one should proceed].

Having combined the cow-dung and other materials with their respective mantras and the root mantra in a vessel—others [using] water with *kuśa* grass—and having stirred them clockwise three times with the root mantra, the *tryambaka* mantra, and the weapon (*astra*) mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; then, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times; having performed the expiation by reciting the weapon mantra one hundred times; and having worshipped Śiva with the root mantra and completed the worship at the conclusion of the recitation.

Having performed the protection (*rakṣā*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should cover it with *darbha* grass. Thus ends the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Now follows the procedure for the installation of the nine jars.

On a ground surface smeared with cow dung and adorned with powdered turmeric paste, one should arrange nine [vessels] in the center and so forth. Having placed [the offerings] in due order with the six-limbed mantras of Gaṇeśa, [the vessel] is wrapped with thread and surrounded by a *droṇa* measure of water; it is a new cloth.

It has been washed and consecrated. Taking the pitcher (*kumbha*) with his heart, he places it in the center with the root mantra. Around it, having placed two *prastha* measures [of grain] possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, he places them with their respective root mantras. ... Is it austerity?

With the mantra beginning "bhūmyā," he fills the pitcher with the root mantra. Having adorned it with mango sprouts, coconut, perfumes, flowers, and bundles of *kūrca* grass, each with its respective mantra.

Having placed cardamom, cloves, camphor, sandalwood, and ushira root at the base with the mantra "sahi ratne," and having deposited gold, one should worship as in the case of the tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana). Sitting facing north, one should purify oneself, the site, the materials, and the mantra-substances in their proper sequence, like Śiva, and apply a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste.

Having taken [the flower], having placed the flower upon one's own head, and having meditated upon oneself in the form of Gaṇapati, one should worship externally. [One should worship] the jar and so forth, from Śakti up to Padmā, worshipping each in its respective place. Then, one should worship the powers of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*): *namaḥ* to Tīvrā; *namaḥ* to Jvālinī; *namaḥ* to Narmadā; *namaḥ* to Bhogadā.

Salutation to Kāmarūpiṇī; salutation to Ugrā; salutation to Tejovatī; salutation to Satyā; salutation to Vighnanāśinī—having thus worshipped, one should then worship the three mandalas: "Salutation to the seat of Gaṇapati. [This is] the form of the Lord of the Gaṇas: saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, with the face of an elephant... [wearing] a crown and a casket, holding a goad, a *laḍḍuka* sweetmeat, and beautiful teeth, intensely radiant like fire.

Having placed the image with the mantra "Salutation to the form of Gaṇapati," having bestowed the eyes with "Salutation to the eyes," and having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should meditate upon the image as being of the nature of light while reciting the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā" and the root mantra,
for a moment fixed upon the target.

Having invoked [the deity] with the *āvāhinī* mantra using the *mūla-mantra*, and having performed the worship from the installation (*sthāpana*) up to the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should worship Vighnanāśinī in the northeast. Then, in the pitchers starting from the east, one should worship:
salutations to Gaṇādhipa; salutations to Gaṇeśa; salutations to Gaṇanāyaka; salutations to Gaṇakrīḍa; salutations to Lambodara; salutations to Ekadanta; salutations to Heramba.
Homage to Vighnanāyaka!
Having meditated thus: "All [the deities] are richly adorned with the ornaments of the lords of serpents, their trunks decorated with offerings of food;
they have four arms and three eyes, and possess the complexions of the guardians of the directions..."

Having performed the worship from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the end of the recitation (*japa*) with the respective root-mantras, and having caused the Brahmins to perform the recitation from the *Śrī Rudra* up to the *Gaṇapati Sūkta*, one should then worship the door of Gaṇapati. Having sprinkled it with water from the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) while reciting the *astra-mantra*, [one worships] above the door: on the right—*glauṃ vikaṭāya namaḥ*; on the left—*su*...
"Salutation to Bāhu on the right; salutation to Vimala in the middle; salutation to Bhīma on the southern branch; salutation to Devadatta on the northern branch.

Having thus worshipped the door-keepers, and having worshipped [the threshold] with "Salutation to the Weapon (Astra) on the threshold," one should enter within, leading with the right foot. Then, in the southwest, having worshipped and fully honored Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhipati), with "Salutation to Brahmā."

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the root mantra of Gaṇeśa ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*; having worshipped the seat for the bath; and having removed the remains of previous offerings (*nirmālya*) with the Gaṇeśa-gāyatrī;
[one performs] the ritual up to the bathing with fragrant oil and other substances.

Having consecrated him with the respective mantra, having offered the mantra-food, and having wiped him with a fine cloth, one should adorn him with a loincloth, a waist-thread, a lower garment, an upper garment, a sacred thread, ornaments, unbroken grains, scents, flowers, and garlands of *dūrvā* grass; then one should worship Gaṇapati: "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti; salutation to the Praṇava; salutation to Dharma; salutation to Jñāna."

Homage to Vairāgya. Homage to Aiśvarya. Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Ā... up to Padmānta, [one should worship]: Homage to Dīvrā. Homage to Jvālinī. Homage to Nandā. Homage to Bhogadā. Homage to Kāmarūpiṇī. Homage to Ugrā. Homage to Tejovatī.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to Śakti" and "Salutation to Vighnanāśinī," and having fully honored the maṇḍala, [one should worship] with "Salutation to the seat of Gaṇapati.
[He is] of the color of saffron, endowed with four arms, having the face of an elephant, and wearing a crown together with a casket.
He who holds a hook, a sweetmeat, and a noose in his hands, whose tusk is like fire, and who is the very embodiment of Gaṇanātha.

Salutation to the form of Gaṇapati. May the Blessed Lord Vighnarāja come hither. Then, having performed the placement of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*) in the locations of the Mothers (*mātṛkāsthāna*), one should then place the thirty-one digits (*kalā*).
"Īśāna, the lord of all sciences... Sadāśiva"—with these [mantras], one places [the digit] upon the head as Īśāna. 1.
"May we know that Tatpuruṣa; salutations to the elephant-faced one"—thus at the face.
"Salutations to Aghora-Vināyaka"—at the heart. 3.
Then, "Salutation to the Terrible Vināyakas" at the belly;
(4) "Salutation to the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Terrible Ones" at the neck. 5.
Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the four-armed one—on the right arm. 6. Salutation to Sadyojāta, the lord of the Gaṇas—on the left arm. 7.
To the one who agitates all living beings.
Homage!
To the one devoid of beginning and end, to Vakratuṇḍa, homage! On the trunk: 9.
To the foremost, to Heramba, homage! On the navel: 10.
Salutation to the one of white complexion and protruding belly; on the abdomen. 11. (l7.
Salutation to you, O King of Obstacles; on the back. 12.
Salutation to the one fond of food and with ears like winnowing baskets; on the right ear. 13.
Salutation to the one in the form of a child with ears like an elephant’s; on the left ear. 14. Salutation to the one with a rat as a vehicle, the formidable one; on the right hand. 15.

Salutation to the one who holds a sugarcane stalk and has ears like chowries; on the left thigh. 16. Salutation to Vighnarāja in the field of the arts of knowledge (*vidyākalā*); on the right knee. 17. Salutation to the wielder of the mace (*gadādhara*) who is moon-colored; on the [left knee]. (l2)
Homage! At the left knee: 18.
Homage to Bhīma, the son of the Unsteady One (Calācalā). At the right hip: 19.
Homage to Lalita, whose nature is the Guṇas (Prakṛtiguṇa). At the left hip: 20.
Salutation to Akṣaya, who holds a staff in his hand; [at] the waist. 21.
Salutation to Śaktikalā, the left one; at the right side. 22.
Salutation to the one with noose in hand and a curved beak; on the left side: 23.
Salutation to the one with a beautiful face, [from the mantra] "I take refuge in Sadyojāta..."; on the right foot: 24.
Homage to the eternal one, who resembles the moon; [this is] on the left foot. 25.
Homage to the one whose entire body is suspended by a thread; [this is] on the right hand. 26.
(L5) Homage to the inexhaustible Lakṣmī; [this is] on the left hand. 27.
Salutation to Anādibhava in the form of Yama; [this is] on the nose. 28. Bhajasva mā... lāya, salutation; [this is] on the head. 29. Bhavāya, salutation; (l6) [this is] on the forehead.
"Salutation to Svadhā" on the right arm; 30.
"Salutation to Udbhava," "Salutation to Dhṛti" on the left arm. 31.
Having thus performed the placement of the thirty-one kalās and having filled the joined palms with flowers, [one recites] "gaṇānāṃ tvā... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.1.1).

Having visualized with the root mantra a splendor possessing the radiance of ten million suns upon the object at the auspicious moment, having invoked it with the invocation-mantra, having established it on a lotus seat with the stabilization-mantra, and having brought it into close presence with the proximity-mantra.

Having restrained [the deity] with the *niṣṭhurya* (or *raśmī*) mantra, having offered the welcoming *arghya* with the root mantra (*mūla*), and having announced, "Welcome to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas," one should contemplate that the words "Child, welcome" have been spoken by the Deity. Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantras in the locations from the heart to the hands, having established oneness with the root mantra, and having protected and bound [the deity], one should perform the rites of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) and form the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).
Having offered [the offerings] with the endings *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*,

having given the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, having presented three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra, having consecrated [the deity] with pure water through meditative visualization, and finally having wiped [the deity] with a drop of water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and a fine cloth; (l4)

Having offered the waist-thread, loincloth, garment, sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and garlands of dūrvā grass with the root mantra, and having presented incense and lamps with the armor mantra; then, having worshipped again with the heart mantra and with the nine or seven names, and having worshipped the limbs of dissolution, he should pray for the worship of the limbs of enjoyment in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the directions beginning with Īśāna and the East.

*Hṛdayāya namaḥ* (to the heart), *śirase namaḥ* (to the head), *śikhāyai namaḥ* (to the crest-lock), *kavacāya namaḥ* (to the armor), *netrebhyo namaḥ* (to the eyes), *astrāya namaḥ* (to the weapon)— having thus worshipped,
[one should worship] with "Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇādhipa together with the deities of the first enclosure" in the middle of the petals.
In the east and other directions: *Namaḥ* to Hastavaktra; *namaḥ* to Vighnarūpa; *namaḥ* to Viśālākṣa; *namaḥ* to Akṣa; *namaḥ* to Vidruma;

*namaḥ* to Unmatta; *namaḥ* to Lalita; *namaḥ* to Kumbhodara. Having thus worshipped, [one pays homage] to the illustrious Gaṇādhipa together with the deities of the second enclosure: *namaḥ* to Āmoda at the tip of the petal; *namaḥ* to Pramoda; *namaḥ* to Sumukha.
Homage! Homage to Durmukha! Homage to Avighna!

(l2) Having worshipped with "Homage to Vighnarāja," [one worships] "Homage to the illustrious Gaṇādhipa together with the deities of the third enclosure. Outside the petals—having worshipped Indra and the other world-protectors—together with the deities of the fourth enclosure (l3).

Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇādhipa. Outside of that—having worshipped the ten weapons beginning with the Vajra and ending with the Lotus—one offers salutation to the illustrious Gaṇādhipa, the deity of the five enclosures. Again, having offered incense and lamps, and having consecrated the offerings—from mung-bean rice, jaggery-rice, sweetmeats, plantains, coconuts, and so forth, up to betel—with the four purificatory rites, [one places them] in his presence.

Having placed [the offering], having sprinkled [it] and rendered it immortal, having given the *āpośana* water, and having recited the mantras beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *svāhā*, one should announce: "I offer this to you;
may you accept it, O Lord of the Gaṇas. Thus he announces.

Having offered three drops of water from the *culika* in the center with the root mantra, and having again offered the *uttarāpośana*, one should satisfy [the deity] with hand-washing, foot-washing, sipping water, the *arghya*, betel, incense, lamps, worship, the *rātrika*, the sacred thread (*pavitra*), and offerings of song, dance, and other services; then one should pray: "O Vighneśvara, who has a beautiful face, and so forth; salutations to you, O you who are ever fond of modakas."
Having dispelled the obstacles that have arisen— be gracious to me so that I may be free from hindrances.
O curved-tusked one of massive body, with a radiance equal to ten million suns,
O God, grant me freedom from obstacles in this rite of the eightfold binding.

"Salutation to that illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired goals, and who cuts through all obstacles. Having thus prayed, one should recite the root mantra of Gaṇapati one hundred times with a rosary of beads. [Then follows] the food offering (*naivedya*).

Again, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) at the heart and the feet, water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the faces with the root mantra followed by *svadhā*, and the respectful offering (*arghya*) on the head with the *Īśāna* mantra; and having recited the root mantra of Gaṇapati one hundred and eight times for the sake of the fire-oblation (*homa*), and having made the offering; he should offer it into the hand of Gaṇeśa held in his own hand, using the root mantra and the "Secret from the Secret" (*guhyādiguhya*) mantra.

"Gaṇagāyatryā-vakuṇṭhāya vidmahe, hastivaktrāya dhīmahi; tanno dantiḥ pracodayāt. Having recited this Gāyatrī and offered three handfuls of flowers, [one should pray for] the absence of obstacles for the rite that has been commenced.

Having first brought [the rite] to completion, one should pray for the desired object. This is the worship of Gaṇapati as taught in the *Kāmikāgama*. Both [of these acts] begin with the performance of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*). Now, the gathering of materials: Then the preceptor, having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), should again worship Gaṇapati with the root mantra, preceded by the striking of his head.

Having prayed to Vighneśvara, having prostrated before the Guru, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "O Śiva, Śiva, by the command of Śambhu, on this auspicious lunar day, for this God of gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, together with the venerable Mūlaliṅga, including the entire retinue from Saura up to Caṇḍa— the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva— [this is] the restoration of the ruins..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the sake of this rite, beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati and ending with the sacrifice after three fortnights, I shall collect the materials required for the performance of the eight binding rites," he then says: "As a constituent part of that, I shall perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*)."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) to be recited according to the previously mentioned procedure, and having sprinkled the gold and other materials with that water, one should place the three-legged stands (*tripādī*) on a pure spot adorned with turmeric paste and powder in the presence of the Lord (*Īśvara*). Upon them, one should worship [the elements], saying: *Aṃ*—salutation to the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*); *Yaṃ*—salutation to the sun-mandala (*sūryamaṇḍala*); *Maṃ*...

Having worshipped with "Oṃ, salutation to the Soma-maṇḍala," and having placed a copper vessel upon that [maṇḍala]— [the vessel] whose heart...— he should place the washed property of the deity within it. Then the preceptor,
having brought together his own [attendants] as well as the multitude of devotees, even though they were covered by [the vessel], he should wash them.

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the Astra-mantra, one should worship it. Having worshipped with "Salutation to Ananta" and "Salutation to Padma," one should perform the ritual service with the mantra "Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having invoked Brahmā, who consists of gold, [one should proceed].

Having performed the worship from the offering of the seat (*āsana*) up to the final food offering (*naivedya*), one should then, for the sake of completing the commenced rite without obstacles through the grace of Vighneśvara, for the sake of obtaining benefits in many places, and by the favor of the Lord for the attainment of all desired goals, offer a thousand, five hundred, or three hundred coconuts together with fruit and betel-leaf. Then, having presented the *ārātrika* lamp-waving ceremony:
Having offered sandalwood paste, betel, food offerings, coconuts, and pieces of fruit to the Brahmins and others, the Ācārya, together with all the devotees, should pray to Gaṇapati and the Lord:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the world, worshipped by gods, asuras, and men!"
In that matter, you should pacify the union with the servant of action.
"O Lord, free from greed for wealth, grant me abundant means for the performance of rites;
may this entire web of rituals be complete and devoid of deficiency. Having thus prayed—
The collection of substances. This, however, has been accomplished through another statement consistent with the words prescribing the eight types of binding found in the *Kāmikāgama*. (l6.
Now, the purification of substances:

Then the preceptor, having purified his hands, having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, having prayed to Vighneśvara, having prostrated before the Guru, and having restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), [performs] the *saṅkalpa*...
One should perform [the rites] for this very deity,
the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva, together with his mother the illustrious Kāntimatī, accompanied by the illustrious Mūlaliṅga,
for the purpose of the restoration and eightfold binding of the dilapidated [temple], beginning with the worship of Gaṇeśa.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the purification of the materials—consisting of recitation (*japa*), oblation (*havana*), and sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—for the sake of establishing the fitness for performing the rite of Śiva regarding the substance prepared for the purpose of accomplishing the act of generating the three fortnights"; and having further resolved: "As a limb of that [rite], I shall perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*"); one should prepare the auspicious day and the *pañcagavya* according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having sprinkled the ground with water empowered by the Astra-mantra, and having fashioned a grid of nine squares using powders of turmeric paste, one should place three-legged stools upon it. On the first stool: "Salutation to Brahmā.
On the second: "Salutation to Viṣṇu."

In the third [position]—*namaḥ* to Rudra. In the center—having worshipped with "Homage to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*)," "Homage to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*)," and "Homage to the fiery disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*"); having placed a copper vessel upon that; having placed gold within it;

having sprinkled it with the *puṇyāha*, *pañcagavya*, and *arghya* waters while reciting the *astra-mantra*; having removed that water and wiped it clean; [one should place] everything prepared therein.
Having placed gold [therein], one should worship:

"Salutation to Ananta; salutation to Praṇava; salutation to Padma; salutation to Astrāsana. Having invoked that deity while reciting the root mantra of Śivāstra, and having fully worshipped [Him] from the seat up to the end of the *japa*, together with the Brahmins—(l7)

At the conclusion of the recitation of the *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* and the *pavamāna-durgā-mantra*, one should separately recite the mantras of the Śivāstra, Aghorāstra, Kṣurikāstra, and Vyomāstra one thousand times,
five hundred times, or one hundred times.

Or, having recited [the mantra] and offered [it], on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the east of that— having performed the rites of tracing (*ullekhana*) and so forth as for the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*), having sprinkled [water], having established the fire, having swept around it, having sprinkled water around it, and having strewn grass around it—

one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*). Then, having spread *darbha* grass to the north, upon those [blades] one should place the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the small ladle (*sruva*), the large ladle (*sruc*), and the sprinkling-vessel (*prokṣaṇī*).

Having performed the *sādhana*, having prepared the two strainers (*pavitras*), having sprinkled [the materials] thoroughly, and having placed the strainers within the vessel for the purpose of the *prokṣaṇī* water; having filled it with water, having turned the vessels face upwards, and having sprinkled them with the *astra-mantra*; having taken cow’s clarified butter (*gavyājya*), [one performs] the purification beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*).

Having performed the ritual disposal of the implements, taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles along with the *kūrca* grass-bundle, heating them in the fire, wiping them clean with the tips, middles, and bases [of the *darbha* blades], casting the *darbha* blades into the fire, placing them upon the *kuśa* grass on his left side with their bases facing inward, arranging them with the *śambara* mantras, performing the sprinkling of water and other rites while worshipping the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s), and having offered oblations into the fire with the *vyāhṛti*s;

Having installed the image of the seat and having invoked the weapon of Śiva with the root mantra, while holding gold, one should offer it separately with fruits, cooked rice (*caru*), honey, and *dūrvā* grass— each soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*)— repeating the root mantra a thousand times;
[then] the gold [is offered] with clarified butter.

Having sprinkled [the materials] with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having projected the form residing in the fire onto the heart and other centers, and having completed the remainder of the fire sacrifice up to the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), one should dismiss the fire. By this, the purification of the substances is accomplished; this, however, is according to the *Makuṭa*.
Now, the division of the pure substance:

having thus offered the mantra-purification which is of the nature of Śiva, the preceptor, with palms joined in reverence and recollecting Śiva, should divide it in the presence of the eleven [deities] and utter: "Three parts for the sake of the Śiva-sacrifice; one part for the consecration of Śiva; one part for the officiating priests; one part for the two preceptors."

"One portion for the purpose of feeding Brahmins, a second portion for the purpose of recitation and giving, and two portions for the purpose of sacrifice every three fortnights; thus shall I employ [the wealth] in all cases. Having said this, [he worshipped] Īśvara with the eightfold offering of flowers.
Having performed worship and offered the *ārātrika* lamp, one should pray. Thus ends the section on the ritual substances according to the *Kāmikāgama-sutrantra*.
Now, the determination of the auspicious moment (*muhūrta-niścaya*)—thereupon the Preceptor (*ācārya*).

Having sat down in the tortoise posture (*kūrmāsana*) in the presence of the Lord, and having performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should prepare the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*) with red sandalwood, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other materials. Then the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is made: "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of gods, Sadāśiva, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, accompanied by the venerable Mūlaliṅga, [for] the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara..."

Together with Brāhmaṇas and astrologers, I shall determine the auspicious moment for the consecration of the jar for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple] and its eightfold binding. For that purpose, I shall perform the worship of the nine planets, beginning with the Sun. In the presence of the Lord, [I shall perform this] with white pigment and powder. On the eight-petaled [lotus]...

(l1) Having drawn a lotus, [one should place] the Sun in its center; the Moon in the east; Mercury in the south; Jupiter in the west; Venus in the north; Mars in the southeast; Saturn in the southwest; and Rāhu in the northwest. (l2)

Having worshipped the banner in the northeast with the *āsana*, *mūrti*, and *mūlamantra* mantras, using water for the *arghya* offering, perfumes, flowers, and other articles; having presented the food offering (*naivedya*), and having made prayers;
having summoned the devotees who know the ancient dharma, the Vajras, and the Naigamas, as well as the artisans, craftsmen, and others;
and having given them sandalwood paste and betel—especially those who know the dharma of the scriptures, O Śiva (l4).

Having gratified the astrologers with sacrificial fees and other gifts; having thoroughly examined the *jyotiḥśāstra* and *śilpaśāstra* treatises concerning the *kāmyaka* rites and so forth; and having determined an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), [he undertook] the restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*) of this God of Gods in this year, during the month beginning and ending with Aries, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day conjoined with a favorable lunar date, weekday, and asterism, at his own ascendant (*svalagna*).

Saying that the *muhūrta* for the sacrifice of the eightfold bonds (*aṣṭabandhana-yāga*) and the vase-consecration (*kumbhābhiṣeka*) must be performed, one should offer the night-vigil (*ārātrika*) preceded by an announcement to the Lord, the Blessed One, and then pray for blessings. Thus ends the *Kāmikasvatantra-muhūrta*.

The determination: these four—namely, the collection of materials, the purification of materials, the distribution of materials, and the determination of the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*)—should be performed either on the day preceding the eightfold ritual actions of binding, or on a single day. (p15a, l1) Now, the construction of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*):

Then the teacher, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having washed the vessel for the general offering (sāmānyārghya-pātra) with the Astra-mantra, having placed it upon its support with the Hṛdaya-mantra, having filled it with scented water using the Mūla-mantra ending in vauṣaṭ, having deposited flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), having worshipped it with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Mūla-mantra, and having consecrated it seven times with the Praṇava;

Having protected and veiled [the site], having performed the rites of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules, and having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking the head [of the image], one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*):
"On this auspicious lunar day, of this God of gods..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the purpose of the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*), including its primary and secondary limbs (*sāṅgopāṅga*), for the restoration of the ruins and the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of the venerable Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara— accompanied by the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, together with the venerable Mūla-liṅga and his retinue— I shall have a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) constructed," he shall then perform the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of auspiciousness) as an ancillary part of that rite, as previously described.

Having performed the *puṇyāha* rite and having sprinkled [the ground], one should— either in the presence of the Lord, on the two sides, in the northeast, in the southeast, or in another pleasant location— purify the ground down to the knees with the *astra-mantra*,
level it, and smear it [with cow dung].
The preceptor, having constructed a Śiva-yāga pavilion— measuring from five cubits up to fourteen cubits as appropriate, square on all sides, level, and resembling the surface of a mirror—
[should place] therein [the sacrificial threads] with their tips pointing eastward.

Having laid out twelve lines at the top, one obtains one hundred and twenty-one squares. In the center of that, in the divine square for the principal Śiva and the *vardhanī*, there is a group of eight pitchers (*kumbha*).

In the sixteen squares of the *paiśāca* [region], there are [pitchers] in the intermediate directions. For the sake of the pillars, there are [squares] in the cardinal directions starting with the east; for the sake of worship, there are the remaining eight squares; and for the sake of the eight auspicious signs (*maṅgala*), there is that square.

In the fifty-six outer squares consisting of the human [mandala], there are two paths (*vīthi*) in the corners; in the center of the nine [squares] starting from the east, there are the eight square-shaped sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and others; and between Indra and Śaṅkara, there is the primary circular sacrificial pit.
Outside of that, at the site for the Rākṣasas, there are forty Ghaṭa-toranas; the remaining space is suitable for the teacher to move about with his disciples.

(L5) Outside the pavilion, there should be a location for sixteen pillars. Having thus prepared the pavilion of this form, in one-third of its center, a square altar (*vedikā*) [should be made] with a width of— (L6)

Having constructed the primary altar with a height of one *rdho* [half-a-handspan], and outside of that, a secondary altar (*upaveśa*) twelve finger-breadths high and six finger-breadths wide, resembling the interior of a mirror; and having further established it on the human plane (*mānuṣapada*), one should construct around it, starting from the east, sacrificial fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) characterized by excellent features, shaped as a quadrangle, a triangle, a half-moon, an equilateral triangle, a circle, a hexagon, a lotus, an octagon, and a circle.

If it is endowed with the proper characteristics, one should have it constructed for the purpose of sacrifice. This is the procedure for the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) as taught in the *Kāmikāgama*. However, this should be undertaken preceded by the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*);
it should be performed prior to the commencement of the ritual action (*kriyā*).

Now, the purification of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*): the Preceptor, having performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkṛtya*), prepares the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having worshipped Vighneśvara, he should pray to him. [He makes] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of Gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, accompanied by the venerable Mūlaliṅga and his retinue... Śrī...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of achieving the fitness required for the sacrificial rite of the sacrificial pavilion of Sadāśiva, the Lord of Veṇuvana, which has been renovated and bound with eight supports, I shall perform the purification of the sacrificial pavilion," [he should first,
with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), using a spade]...

Having dug the ground and raised it up with that same [mantra], having kindled the pit with dry *darbha* grass using the *astra-mantra*, having filled it with pure earth using that same [mantra], and having sprinkled it with cow-dung water using the *astra-mantra*,

one should join the staff and other implements together with the *astra-mantra*, polish them with that same [mantra], and smear them with that same [mantra] according to the previously stated procedure.

Having performed the *puṇyāha* and the *pañcagavya* rites, having sprinkled the sacrificial ground with those two using the *astra-mantra*, having fed twenty-four Brahmins with various kinds of food, having removed the remnants, and having caused a cow-pen to be constructed, one should again cause the *puṇyāha* to be proclaimed. Thus [it is done]. (p16b, f13a)

1) The purification of the sacrificial hall for the Svatantra-yāga as taught in the Kāmika-āgama must be performed prior to the commencement of the eightfold binding rites. Next is the selection of the patron (yajamāna).

The king, having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), completed all his daily obligatory rites (*nityānuṣṭhāna*) and others; then, having approached the presence of Śiva preceded by a prayer to Sāmbaśiva, [he addressed] a brahmin of noble lineage, who was like Indra, distinguished by virtuous conduct, and proficient in the rituals of the Vedas and Āgamas.

Having invited an excellent Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to Śiva, righteous, accompanied by his wife, and distinguished by such qualities; having seated him upon a pedestal and performed worship; and having himself taken two coconut fruits together with flowers and *darbha* grass, [he should offer them] to this God of gods, accompanied by the venerable Mother Kāntimatī and joined with the venerable *mūlaliṅga*.

In the Śivayāga, accompanied by its ancillaries (upāṅgas), for the restoration and eightfold binding of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva together with his retinue, [he offered] to the Blessed One, the witness of the entire network of Vedic and Āgamic rites.
In the Śivayāga...

Having chosen the best of Brahmins—who has been requested by the sacrificer with the words, "I choose you [to serve as officiant] for the sake of abandoning this place for the deity mentioned in the mantra"—and having given that excellent Brahmin, who has responded with "Oṃ, I shall do so," garments, ornaments, and other items as mentally intended and in limited measure, one should pray [to him]. This is the selection of the sacrificer (or officiant). Alternatively, if there is a need for duties such as knowing the Dharma, the performer of the rite (the officiant) himself may perform it. Thus.
This selection of the patron (*yajamānavaraṇa*) is indeed established by logic.

Likewise, [there is] the *madhuparka* and the selection of the preceptor (*ācāryavaraṇa*). Then, the patron, having performed the ritual purification of all parts (*sakalīkṛtya*), having duly prepared the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking his head [with his hand], and having prostrated before the Guru—
Having restrained the breaths, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*):

"On this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the sacrifice of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana-yāga*) of this goddess, the venerable Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā, preceded by the offering of *madhuparka*, I shall perform the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the other officiants. Having thus resolved, [one should proceed] with the ordinary water (*sāmānyodaka*).

Having sprinkled the materials with the Astra mantra, having spread there ten pairs of blades pointing northward, and having spread Darbha grass over them with their tips pointing east, he should cause the preceptor and the others to sit facing him, bow to them, and then, in the northeast of these, having spread east-pointing Darbha grass for the purpose of placing the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), he should place the vessels upon them.
A water-pot for the purpose of placing the vessels for the *madhuparka* offering;
vessels for the *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya*; vessels for the *madhuparka* with their lids; pairs of garments; pairs of earrings; finger-rings and other ornaments;
a turban; a sacred thread; and a rosary of beads.

Having prepared the ash-receptacle and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, having silently fashioned the two *pavitra* strainers, having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī*, and having placed the *pavitra* strainers face upwards; having sprinkled [them] with the *astra-mantra*, having taken up the *pādyapātra* vessel and placed a *kūrca* grass-bundle therein, and having poured water into it; he should consecrate it with the *tryambaka* mantra and the three-fold *śivayāga* mantra. In that [vessel]...

Having placed rice grains [into the vessel], having purified them, having worshipped with the primary and secondary ingredients, having touched [the vessel], and having covered it with a lid—thus is the *ācamana* water; thus is the *arghya* offering. Having placed the strainer across the *madhuparka* vessel, having first poured in the honey...

The second [offering] is curd; the third is ghee; the fourth is milk; the fifth is water. Having worshipped with the root-mantra and having covered it with a lid, one should likewise perform the rites for all the presiding deities (*mūrtipās*) using the mantras of the limbs (*aṅga-mantras*) of the forms beginning with Śarva.
Then, having prostrated before the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the others, [one should worship] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ*. One should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) with [the mantra] ending in *śirase svāhā*. Having offered the respectful offering (*arghya*) with [the mantra] for the crest-lock (*śikhā*) ending in *svāhā*, one should give a pair of garments with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). With the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should offer sandals, finger-rings, and ornaments. Having offered a new golden or other sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) at the root [of the deity] with the sacred-thread mantra, one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having offered incense and flowers with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and likewise having offered them to the individual forms of the guardians (*mūrtipā*) with their respective form-mantras (*mūrtimantra*) and limb-mantras (*aṅga*), and having bowed again, one should pray while grasping their feet:
"By me, [they] have been fully worshipped."
"O Goddess, let the sacrifice for my petition be performed by those who have been gratified with sacrificial fees;

may it be propitious, free from defects, devoid of all calamities, and pleasing to the face of the Goddess Īśānī, whose essence is all the gods. O Guru, together with the guardians of the forms, [the success of] all depends upon your pleasure. Thus he should pray.

Taking darbha grass in his hand, [the petitioner says]: "We choose you, O Ācārya, to perform all the rites for this lady, the noble mother Śrī Kāntimatī, beginning from the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) and the formal authorization (*anujñā*), up until the three-fortnightly sacrifice (*tripakṣayajana*). Thus is the choosing of the Ācārya. [The Ācārya replies]: "Oṃ, so be it; I shall do all that."

The words of the preceptor: "Just as Gīṣpati [Bṛhaspati] is to the gods in Indra’s Amarāvatī, so may you always be the preceptor in this Śiva-sacrifice. Thus are the words of the preceptor. (L3) Having thus requested, such is the selection of the preceptor.

The Selection of the Mūrtipas: The Sacrificer, having taken darbha grass, says: "In this divine Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā, for the eight-fold binding Śiva-sacrifice, I choose you as the Earth-mūrtipa. [The Mūrtipa replies: "Oṃ, so be it. This is the speech of the Mūrtipa. Then the speech of the Sacrificer: "The Earth indeed sustains the worlds; the worlds consist of the Earth."
[You] are remembered [as such]. O you whose form is the earth, whose nature is all-pervading—homage be to you! In this Śiva-sacrifice, we choose you as the embodiment of water.
Indeed, water sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of water.
O you whose form is water, who pervade all things; salutations be unto you.
Thus ends the selection of the supreme embodiment of water. In this Śiva-sacrifice, we choose you in the form of fire.
Fire indeed leads the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of fire.
O you whose form is fire, obeisance to you, the all-pervading embodiment of fire.
The selection of the image of Agni: "In this Śiva-sacrifice, we choose you as the image of Vāyu. (p18b, l1) Regarding the worship of Vighneśvara:
the Ācārya, having duly prepared the *sakalīkaraṇa* and the general *arghya*, and having fully worshipped Vighneśvara, should perform the *saṅkalpa* for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord.

Of this Lord of the Gods, the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, accompanied by his consort Kāntimatī, for the rite of restoration and the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) to be performed according to the method prescribed in the *Kāmikāgama*,
[the presence of] Vighnarāja...

I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa as a constituent part of receiving the materials for the practice, beginning with the worship and ending with the sacrifice performed every three fortnights. As a constituent part of that, I shall perform the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*).

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the purpose of the auspicious day, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, and having strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, I shall sprinkle the mound with the Śiva-Gāyatrī and worship Ramā.

Having washed the *vardhanī* vessel with thread encircled by the *astra-mantra*, having established it in the center of a lotus with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, having filled it with scented water while reciting "āpo vā idam," and having adorned it with mango sprouts and other ornaments— at its base...

Salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Viṣṇu in the center; salutation to Rudra on the lip; salutation to Nandin on the two sides; salutation to Mahākāla. Having worshipped [the rivers] starting from the east: salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Yamunā; salutation to Godāvarī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Narmadā; salutation to Sindhu; salutation to Kāverī; salutation to Tāmraparṇī. In the nose: salutation to Vighneśvara.
In the center, [one should offer] "Salutation to the seat of Varuṇa.

One should meditate upon Varuṇa, seated upon a sea-monster (*makara*), the lord of the sacred ford (*tīrthanātha*), the treasury of nectar, the sovereign of the western quarter, standing facing east during the festival.

Having worshipped with "Salutation to the form of Varuṇa," having applied collyrium to the eyes, and having filled the joined palms with flowers, one should invoke [the deity] with the mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa" and its root-mantra using the invocation mudrā; establish [him] with the establishment mudrā; bring [him] into close proximity with the proximity mudrā; and bind [him] firmly with the binding mudrā. [Then offer] the welcoming arghya.

Having offered [the water], and perceiving that the Lord has said, "Welcome, my child," one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *hṛdaya* and other mantras in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands.

Having established oneness by means of the root mantra, having protected and concealed [the deity], and having displayed the *mahāmudrā*, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth, ending with "Salutation to Varuṇa! Svadhā! Svāhā! followed by "Salutation! (*namaḥ*).

Having worshipped him with *rākṣata* and *dūrvā* flowers: "Salutation to Varuṇa; salutation to the one who holds a noose in his hand; salutation to the one whose vehicle is a sea-monster (*makara*); salutation to the one adorned with priceless jewels; salutation to the Lord of the western quarter. Having worshipped thus and offered incense and a lamp with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), he should proceed.

Having offered fruits and other items with the *mūla-mantra*, having presented the *ārātrika* lamp with the *kavaca-mantra*, having performed worship up to the end of the recitation (*japa*), and having worshipped the movable seat (*calāsana*), one should then place purified rice grains upon the pedestal (*sthalikā*). Having arranged betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) along with pieces of areca nut (*kramuka*) and *bṛhatī* fruit, one should worship them with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Candra; obeisance to the Heart. Then, [one should invite] four Brahmins.
"O sirs, we choose [you] for the sake of the auspicious day. With darbha grass...

"Permitted by you, I shall cause the auspicious day to be proclaimed. The teacher should say: "Om, let it be proclaimed. This is the response of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). May there be welfare for the four-footed.

The preceptor, taking up the *vardhanī* vessel, should sprinkle all the ritual substances. This concludes the *puṇyāha* rite. Now follows the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having prepared a surface smeared with cow dung and divided it into nine squares using turmeric paste and powder;

having prepared nine squares on a mound of rice measuring one *droṇa*; having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing east and north; having sprinkled [the area] with the general *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*;
[and] with clusters of flowers...

Having strewn [the sacrificial ground], [one should offer salutations]: in the center—salutation to the square of the Śiva-tattva; in the east—salutation to the square of the Sadāśiva-tattva; in the south—salutation to the square of the Vidyā-tattva;
in the north—salutation to the square of the Puruṣa-tattva; in the west—salutation to the square of the Kāla-tattva; in the northwest—salutation to the square of the Vāyu-tattva.
"Īśe—salutation to the storehouse of the *prakṛti*-tattva. Having thus worshipped the storehouses, [he worships] in their midst:

(l7) "Salutation to Kauśika. In the east—"Salutation to Kāśyapa. In the south—"Salutation to Bharadvāja. In the north—"Salutation to Gautama. In the west—"Salutation to Atri. Again, in the southwest (dagnau)—"Salutation to Kauśika. In the southwest (naiṛtyām)—(p20a, l1)

Salutation to Kāśyapa. In the northwest—salutation to Bharadvāja. In the northeast—salutation to Gautama. Having thus worshipped the sages who carry the vessels, one prepares five vessels made of gold or other materials, measuring one *kalā*, *agni*, *vāyu*, and *prastha* respectively; these are wrapped with thread, washed, fumigated with incense, and consecrated with sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). These five vessels are placed in the center, the east, and the south.

Having placed [them] in the north-western [directions] and in the [four] corners beginning with the south-east, one should set down vessels of the previously described characteristics, measuring half a *prastha*, one *prastha*, a quarter *prastha*, and half a *kuḍava*.

Having gathered the products of the cow, such as milk and so forth, and having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), [one should place them] in the center: "Homage to the well-established vessel" (*supratiṣṭhapātrāya namaḥ*). In the east: "Homage to the well-pacified vessel" (*suśāntapātrāya namaḥ*).

In the south: "Homage to the radiant vessel" (*tejovatpātrāya namaḥ*). In the north: "Homage to the vessel of jewel-water" (*ratnodakapātrāya namaḥ*). In the west: "Homage to the vessel of nectar" (*amṛtapātrāya namaḥ*). In the southeast: "Homage to the vessel of the nature of water" (*aptattvapātrāya namaḥ*).

Homage! To the southwest—(l6) homage to the vessel of the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*). To the northwest—homage to the vessel of the principle of time (*kālatattva*). To the northeast—homage to the vessel of the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Having thus worshipped the vessels, place a *kūrca* grass-bundle separately within each of them. (l7)

The milk of a black cow, having been drawn into the middle vessel and placed upon a level surface; the curd of a white cow, in the east—with the two [mantras] *Dadhikrāvṇas* and *Tatpuruṣa*; the ghee of a smoke-colored cow, in the south—with *Śukram asi* and *Aghora*, and with *Namaḥ Kapilāyai*; the cow-urine, in the north—with *Gāyatrī* and *Vāmadeva*; the cow-dung of a red cow, in the west—

Having purified [the vessel] with *gandhadvāra*, *sadyojāta*, cow-dung water, and cloth, each to the size of an *akṣa* fruit, one should pour in the measured amounts according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior. In the southeast—scented oil and a *prastha* of flour—with the *agnim īle* verse and the *hṛdaya* mantra. In the southwest—with the *iṣe tvā* mantra.

Half a *prastha* of *āmalaka* [fruit] at the head, having consecrated it with the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*) and the *śikhā*-mantra; half a *prastha* of turmeric powder, having placed it and consecrated it; in the northeast—half a *prastha* of *kuśa*-water mixed with fragrance, having consecrated it with the mantras "May the goddesses be auspicious to us" (*śanno devīḥ*) and "Of the god, let there be" (*devasya tvā*); then, having worshipped Sadāśiva in the milk; in the east—
Salutation to Īśvara. To the south—salutation to Rudra.

To the north—salutation to Viṣṇu. To the west—salutation to Brahmā. To the southeast—salutation to the Heart. To the southwest—salutation to the Head. To the northwest—salutation to the Crest-lock. To the northeast—salutation to the Armor. Having thus worshipped—

Having worshipped the presiding deities of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, from the seat (*āsana*) up to the food offering (*naivedya*); having consecrated each [substance] individually one, two, three, four, or five times with the *Īśāna* mantras; having consecrated the substances situated in the southeast and other directions with the *Hṛdaya* and other [mantras] one by one, and having protected, veiled, and rendered them nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛtya*); [one should place] the cow dung and the other [substances] into the central vessel with their respective mantras.

Having joined [the vessel] with the *mūla-mantra*, [he places] water with *kuśa* grass at the end. Having churned it three times clockwise with the *tryambaka* mantra and the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having recited the *mūla-mantra* one hundred and eight times, he recites the *astra-mantra* one hundred times for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Having worshipped with the root mantra (*mūla*), having performed worship up to the point of recitation (*japa*), and having performed the rites of protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should cover it with *darbha* grass. This is the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
[The remainder of the folio is blank. (p21b, l1) No continuity.
"Indeed, Vāyu sustains these worlds which are known;
O you whose form is Vāyu, omnipresent, salutations be to you, O Vāyumūrti! Thus is the selection of Vāyumūrti. In this Śivayāga, we choose you as Ākāśamūrti. (L2.)
He indeed upholds the worlds; the worlds are known to be composed of space.

"O you who are all-pervading, whose form is the span [of the universe], O you whose body is space, salutations be unto you! Thus is the invocation of the Supreme Space-form. (3) In this Śiva-sacrifice, I choose you, who are the very form of the sacrificer;
for the sacrifice indeed sustains the three worlds, and we are remembered as being composed of sacrifice.
"O you who are all-pervading, whose form is sacrifice, O embodiment of sacrifice, salutations unto you!
(l4) Thus is the selection of the Sacrificer-form. In this Śiva-sacrifice, I choose you as the Soma-form.
"Soma indeed sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of Soma. (l5)
"O you whose form is the moon, who pervade all, O Soma-formed one, salutations be unto you! Thus is the invitation to the Soma-formed deity.
In this Śiva-sacrifice, I invite you, the Sun-formed deity;
for the Sun indeed sustains the worlds, and the worlds are remembered as being composed of the Sun.

"O you whose form is the sun, who are all-pervading, salutations to you, O Sun-embodiment!"—thus is the selection of the Sun-embodiment. ... "I choose you for the office of the officiating priests—you who are born of noble lineage, full of devotion, intent upon worship, and skilled in the sacrifices to Śiva."
Indeed, you gods and sages, led by Bṛhaspati,
who are equal to Brahmā, as well as the seven beginning with Vasiṣṭha, [reside] in the heavenly world.
The sages, beginning with Agastya, who are experts in the performance of Śiva’s sacrifice, declare:
"A sacrifice free from defects bestows the desired fruit, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Let this be performed by those who are skillful, vigilant, and composed."

The Selection of the Preceptor and Others—this [section] has been written following the *Bodhāyana-sūtra* related to the Krama ritual. Now, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipa*), having performed the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkṛtya*) and having taken up *darbha* grass, should perform the selection of the Brahmins. As follows, in this...
"O assembly, we choose you for this rite"— having thus chosen four Brahmins, having placed sacrificial fees and betel in their presence,
and having honored them, [he should proceed] without remainder...
Having said, "The assembly is present," and having accepted the nine [offerings] with the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [he says]:

"For the sake of accomplishing the fitness for performing the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) consisting of the eight bindings (*aṣṭabandhana*) of this venerable Veṇuvaneśvara and the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, may there be the accomplishment of the fitness to perform the tonsure (*vapana*) together with the image-guardians (*mūrtipa*); please grant your grace, O you who are purified by the conduct of the Vedas and the Smṛtis."

"Having performed the shaving for the sake of purifying the body, you shall grant me permission. Having thus obtained permission, [he makes] the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for this venerable Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In order to achieve the fitness for performing all the rites, beginning with the permission (*anujñā*) and so forth, in the ritual of the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) for the restoration of a ruined temple (*jīrṇoddhāra*) and the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), I shall have the tonsure performed together with the image-guardians (*mūrtipa*s)," the Preceptor (*ācārya*) then takes three bundles of seven *darbha* blades each. With the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), he [cleans] those [blades] three times, starting from the neck up to the head.

Having wiped [it] and discarded [it], taking up another [piece], one should wipe [the body] three times with the *astra* mantra from the navel up to the neck; taking up the remaining single [piece], one should wipe [the body] three times with the *astra* mantra from the navel down to the feet; having discarded that as well—
In this manner, having sprinkled the image-protectors along with them, one should recite the mantra:
"Various sins, equal to Mount Meru and Mandara, reside taking refuge in the hair; therefore, I shave [the head] to be hairless. (l5)
Taking the materials required for the ritual bath along with the idols, he should depart from the village toward the east or the north,
carrying a bamboo staff, a purifier (*pavitra*), a new cloth,
a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a lump of clay, cow dung, flowers, sesame seeds, myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and *kuśa* grass.

Having taken turmeric, *uśīra* root, and the six types of bathing substances, [one should take] water from a river flowing to the ocean... (l7) ...having purified it, on a clean spot—having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, having set out the materials for the bath, and having protected them, one goes elsewhere; sitting facing east, having first shaved the beard and hair... (p23a, l1)

Having performed a pure bath by immersing himself thirty-two times in the Mahānadī river; having put on dry clothes; having applied sacred ash (*vibhūti*); with *darbha* grass in hand, having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

"On this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the restoration of the dilapidated [temple] and the eight-fold binding of this deity, Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva, as a limb of the personal Śiva-sacrifice (*ātmaśivayāga*), preceded by the sixfold ablution..."
Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I shall perform the ritual bath (*kriyāsnāna*)," [one performs] the Varuṇa-bath (*vāruṇasnāna*).

Standing in water reaching up to the navel, having paid homage to the deity of the sacred ford and offered prayers: "Whatever meritorious sacred fords exist throughout the three worlds, may they all be present for me at the time of my bath. Having spoken thus, [he should bathe] with mantras containing the word *surabhi*, with those addressed to the waters (*vāruṇa*), and with the *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* and *pāvamānī* verses.
Or, having sprinkled oneself with other Varuṇa mantras, one should bathe; this is the Varuṇa bath.

(The Earth-clay Bath: Then, having taken earth and reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should rub all the limbs seven times; having rubbed them in water, [one should recite] "ava... (l6). Taking another portion of earth and placing it in the left hand, one should divide that also into three parts. Facing the current of the water or facing the sun, one should [recite the *astra-mantra*] seven times.

Having recited [the mantra] over it; having recited the remaining portion seven times with the *netra* [mantra]; having recited the third portion ten times with the *mūla* [mantra]; having cast the portion of earth consecrated by the *astra* [mantra] in the eastern and other directions with the *astra* [mantra]; and having placed it in water consecrated by the *netra* mantra—[then], having smeared all the limbs, beginning from the head, with the earth consecrated by the *mūla* [mantra].

Having wiped [the hands] twelve times, and again the two hands which consist of the nature of the Sun and Moon, one should perform... (l2) ...with water. One should bathe once with scented *āmalaka* fruit and other substances; this is the "earth-bath" (*mṛttikā-snāna*). The "five-product-of-the-cow bath" (*pañcagavya-snāna*)—
Having bathed on the bank of the water... (l3) ...one should bathe with the Ṣaṇmukha-mudrā; this is the Pañcagavya-bath. Now follows the royal ceremonial bath:
On the bank of a body of water,
having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with ground turmeric and so forth, one should place five golden jars wrapped with thread upon it; [then] the waters...

Having placed the sacrificial ground (*raṇya*) and adorned it with mango sprouts and other offerings; having invoked [the deities] starting from the center and ending at the west, and starting from Īśāna; having worshipped them;

having caused the recitation of the *pāvamāna*, the *Durgā-mantra*, and the *pañcabrahma-mantras*; and at the conclusion of the recitation, having placed [the deity] in the western part of the water-pot (*kumbha*)... having sipped water (*ācamya*), having applied ashes, and having taken the *vibhūti* with the right hand and placed it in the left hand with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, [one should perform] the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

Having performed the consecration (*saṃskṛtya*)... [broken folio] ... having empowered it with mantras, one should sprinkle it with [water from] the Īśāna and other directions, and bathe preceded by twelve immersions. Thus [is the procedure for] the Agneya bath...
[line 2].
(Mantra-bath—?
Taking water with both hands and standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite the Sadyojāta and other mantras separately five times each, and then sprinkle [it] upon the head...
The mantra-bath. Now, the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*): again, taking water with the hollowed palms (*añjali*), preceded by the recollection of the *praṇava*, [recite it] ten times... (l4)
"Having sprinkled [oneself], one should bathe"—this is the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*).
Now, the Vāyavya bath:
[one should bathe] with the dust from the faces of herds of cows produced from [their] fluids... (l5)
The bath.
Now, the Māhendra-bath:
one should bathe during a shower accompanied by sunshine. In the absence of that, having collected water from a shower accompanied by sunshine... (l6.)
Now, the ritual bath (*kriyā-snāna*):
standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should contemplate Śiva and Śakti in the right and left hands respectively, take up water, and wipe the head with it.

Having bathed with mantras associated with water and the *liṅgas*, accompanied by the *ṣaṇmukhī-mudrā*, one should emerge from the water, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and look at the sun.

1) [Those who have passed away] while traveling, let them accept this water from the wringing out of my garment, which has been given by me. Having cast [the water] with the mantra "vastraśikhādagān," and having reached the riverbank,
having moistened [it], being composed— (2)

Wearing clean garments, a crown, and an upper cloth, he should perform the ritual bathing and libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. Then, having performed the ash-bath immediately after the water-bath, he should wash his feet and hands and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with his right side turned toward the east. Previously unattached, he should then salute the Vedic twilight (*sandhyā*) with his hair tied up.

At its conclusion, one should perform the Śaiva [rite] according to the rule, whether it be equal or eight-fold. This is the ritual bath (*kriyā-snāna*). This is a specific type of daily bath according to the *Kāmika-svatantra*.
Now, the daily practice (*nityānuṣṭhāna*):
Sitting on the bank of a body of water facing north,

having purified the water with the Astra-mantra, having fashioned it into a square, having inscribed the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center, and having performed the rites of binding and so forth, [he should perform] the inhalation (*pūraka*) with the Udbhava-mudrā.

Having taken the nectar flowing from the *bindu* and placed it in the midst of water, one offers the *arghya* with "Oṃ hrīṃ gaurīyai svāhā. One performs the sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the *tatva* mantra; touches the ears and other limbs with the *astra* mantra; and, having first struck the head, prays to Vighneśvara. Having prostrated to the Guru and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one places the mantras on the hands and limbs, takes the sacred ash (*bhasman*) in the left hand.

Having cast [the seed] with the *hṛdaya* mantra, [one should place] a sesame-sized [portion] with the *astra* mantra. Having cast the *asura* in the southwest (*naiṛtyāṃ*), and having performed the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and other rites, one should bind the left hand with the right hand,
recite the *saṃhitā* mantra, and [apply it] to the head, face, heart, waist, and feet with the *pañcabrahma* mantras.

Having dusted oneself with ashes, having applied the ashes with the Sadyojāta mantra, having sipped water (ācamana), and having performed the placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should offer the arghya water with the mantra "Khaṣolkāya svāhā" and meditate upon the twilight (sandhyā). In the morning,
one should meditate upon the Brāhmī [Sandhyā] within the lotus of the heart.
She is adorned with jewels, initiation-threads, and precious garments; she wears matted hair and a sacred thread;
she is seated upon a swan and a lotus; she is youthful, four-faced, and four-armed.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī, who has eight eyes, holding a deer-skin and a rosary in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left, at dawn when the sky is filled with stars.
At midday, in the midst of the clouds,
[one should meditate on her] wearing white garments, with a white cloth as a sacred thread,
seated upon Garuḍa in the lotus posture— arise, O you who possess fresh youth!

At midday, one should meditate upon the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, adorned with all ornaments, holding a conch and a discus in her left hands, and a mace along with the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands.
At evening, [one should meditate on her] in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, with youth slightly faded,
four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon;
holding a trident and a third eye on the right, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a spear (*śakti*) on the left.
