Salutation to the form of Amṛteśvara. “O Soma, you whose virility is equal on all sides, come to the assembly of the Unborn. Having thus invoked [him] with the words, “Om, I invoke Amṛteśvara into this jar,” one should perform the invocation.

Having performed the threefold installation with the root mantra, and having offered the welcoming *arghya*, one should assign [the mantras] to the locations from the heart to the hands: *Sāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Siṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *Hrīṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vauṣaṭ*; *Saiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *Sauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Saḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Having thus assigned them, one should protect [the deity].

Having veiled [the deity], having rendered [it] immortal, having worshipped with the offerings from the water for the feet (*pādya*) up to the lamp using the root mantra, having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and having performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and the offering of the recitation (*japa*), one should then worship the *pālikā* vessels and so forth.
(L2) In the *pālikā* situated at the right foot of the eastern door: "Obeisance to the seat of Sahasrādi; obeisance to the form of Sahasrāṅgi; obeisance to Sahasrāṅgī. In this [vessel]:

I invoke and establish [the deity] in the *pālikā* vessel containing a thousand rays... Having performed the rites from the installation (*sthāpana*) up to the lighting of the lamp, and having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), [one offers] "Obeisance to Pūṣan" in the northern *pālikā* at the door, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Having performed the full worship up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), one should worship Puṣṭi with "Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi" in the bowl situated at the eastern step of the southern door. Then, having worshipped Kuṭī with "Oṃ, obeisance to Kuṭī" in the bowl situated at the western step of that same door, one should perform the invocation and worship up to the offering of food. Next, one should worship Trikaṭī with "Obeisance to Trikaṭī" in the bowl situated at the southern step of the western door, and Śāti with "Obeisance to Śāti" to its north.

ĀKHA + JYA. Having worshipped the goddess on the *pālikā* situated at the western step of the northern door with "Salutation to the Goddess," and having worshipped [the deity] to the east of that with "Salutation to Śānti," and thus having worshipped the eight *pālikās*,
one should then worship the *ghaṭikās*.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to Puṣpiṇī" at the hour-vessel situated in the southeast corner; having worshipped with "Salutation to Uṣādevī" at the hour-vessel situated in the northwest corner;

having worshipped with "Salutation to Mahiṣī" at the hour-vessel situated in the southwest corner; and having worshipped with "Salutation to Śaṅkhinī" at the hour-vessel situated in the northeast corner (the Īśāna position).

Having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śruti" at the hour-glass jar situated in the northwest corner; then, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Smṛti" at the hour-glass jar situated in the southeast corner; [and] with "Oṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti" at the hour-glass jar situated in the northeast corner;
[then] in that southwest [corner]...

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Praśāntā in the fixed *ghaṭikā*," one should likewise worship milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the sacrificial offering (*naivedya*) for each of the eight *ghaṭikās* individually;

then, one should worship the bowls (*śarāva*). Having worshipped with "Salutation to Svāhā" in the bowl situated in the northern position of the southeast corner, one should worship with "Salutation to Svadhā" in the bowl situated in that southwest position.

Having worshipped [her], [one should worship] Kṣamāyī with "Oṃ Kṣamāyīṃ Namaḥ" in the bowl situated on the square of the southwest corner (nairṛtikoṇa). Having worshipped [her], [one should worship] Kātyāyī with "Oṃ Kātyāyīṃ Namaḥ" in the bowl situated on the square of the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa). Having worshipped [her], [one should worship] Mohāyī with "Oṃ Mohāyīṃ Namaḥ" in the bowl situated on the southern square of the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa). Having worshipped [her], [one should worship her] in the bowl situated on the northeast square (īśānapada).

Having worshipped [the goddess] Jayā with "Obeisance to Jayā" in the shallow bowl situated at the southern foot of the northeast corner; having worshipped [the goddess] Bhadrā with "Obeisance to Bhadrā" in the shallow bowl situated at the southern foot of that [corner]; having worshipped Kīrti with "Obeisance to Kīrti" in the shallow bowl situated at the northwest foot;

and having worshipped the deities residing in the bowls, beginning with their installation, separately offering milk-rice (pāyasa) up to the final offering (nivedana); then, together with the Brahmins, touching the medicinal herbs (oṣadhī).

Having recited the *Auṣadhisūkta*: "The herbs that were born from the gods in the distant past—of those brown ones, I celebrate a hundred and seven varieties. A hundred are your names, and a thousand are your growths. Therefore, O you who possess a hundred powers, grant me water."

The wounded, the flowering, the nourishing, the most excellent for healing; the fruitful and the fruitless, the swift-moving, the dwelling ones, those that carry across the sick—these plants I have extolled for you, O Goddess, so that they may drive away diseases and bring us prosperity. [Note: The provided text contains fragments of Vedic hymns (Atharvaveda) interspersed with non-Sanskrit phrases and scribal corruptions.
The above translation reflects the intended meaning of the extant Vedic verses.]

This is the power of the manly strength; as I, seeking vigor, strike these plants, you shall perish like the self of a goat, O King, like one who eats at the tip of the stalk. He who harms and he who consorts with the enemies, O King, like those who are blind—he, the sage...

He is called the physician, the healer, the one who drives away disease. His mother is named Niṣkṛti (Remedy), and you, O plants, are the healers. You are flowing, winged [streams]. He who causes illness has been driven away by the remedy. One of you after another, having laid down in the lower vessel, all you plants have returned together. All of you, speak this for me with one voice: "Arise, like cows from the stall! O plants!

The plants shall flow forth from your own self, O Pushan; by that [power], they have crossed over all obstacles. The plants have driven away whatever blemish was in our bodies—those which stood upon us from the north and those which entered limb by limb.

[He should recite] "tā sitaya kṣyaṃ pibāyantamugro madhyama... [and so forth]. May no harm come to me, like a digger who digs for one to whom he has given a gift, or like one who performs a *brāhma* [rite] for another.

Having recited the royal mantra (*rāstra*) one hundred times, while uttering the Heart Mantra, one should sound all musical instruments, especially the conch, and recite the ten seed-syllables. Previously, in the *pālikā* vessels and so forth...

Having cast the seeds mixed with liquid into the heart-mantra, then the sowing of the seeds into the jars is performed with the heart-mantra. Then, the sowing of the seeds into the eight shallow bowls is likewise performed with the heart-mantra alone. Thus, having cast the seeds everywhere, (l. 3) [End]

First, having placed the heart-earthenware (*hṛnmṛd*) from the womb of the Earth-goddess into the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with the Heart-mantra alone; having sprinkled the *pālikā* vessels and others with water from the Moon-pitcher (*candrakumbha*);
having again filled the Moon-pitcher with pure water;

having performed worship according to the *Saṃhitā*; and having worshipped Indra and the other deities along with their respective powers around the pitcher; [one should place] lamps on the southern and western cords of the pavilion.

Having kindled [the fire] and sprinkled the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with pure water, having covered them with powdered cow-dung, one should prepare a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) free from defects such as drafts, which provides non-extinguishing [fire],
until the conclusion of the ritual in the evening.

In the morning, preceded by worship, one should protect [the site] free from defects; thus ends the rite for the auspiciousness of the Goddess in the Kāmikāgama. Now the characteristics of the *pālikā* are stated:
the width of the mouth of the *pālikā*... (l7)
It is declared to be eight finger-breadths [in width];
their circumference is three times that, and the thickness of the base is six finger-breadths.

In this manner, the measurement for the mouth of the water-jar (*ghaṭikā*) and the arrow-receptacle (*śarāba*) should be made with four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*). Then follows the binding of protection by the preceptor and others:

now the instructor, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having prepared the general offering of water (*sāmānyārghya*), and having worshipped Vighneśvara, performs three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by the striking of the head.

Having made this resolve on an auspicious lunar day, [I], together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipas*), shall perform the binding of the sacrificial thread (*rakṣābandhana*) for the protection of the form of the sacrifice, which is a constituent part of the ritual of the goddess consisting of the restoration of the ruins (*jīrṇoddhāra*) of this venerable mother Kāntimatī.

Having thus made this resolve, having duly performed the *puṇyāha* rite and the preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having gathered the materials for worship, one should smear a square area with cow-dung water.

Upon that, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus from ground turmeric powder, and having prepared an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) of rice and other grains upon it, one should strew it around with *darbha* grass, flowers, and parched grain (*lāja*). Upon that...

Having washed with the *astra* mantra a water-pot (*kumbha*) that is wound with thread, fumigated, and worthy of being measured by the auspicious water; having filled it with pure water using the left hand; and having placed it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra, [one should adorn it] with cloth, perfume, mango sprouts, garlands, and tufts of grass (*kūrca*).

Having adorned [the area] and placed gold, one should set down three-legged ritual stands (tripādī) upon a square, smeared surface fashioned into the shape of a lotus in front of the jar. Upon those, one should place a copper vessel filled with pure rice,
distinguished by a coconut with its sprout, a bṛhatī fruit, turmeric, sacred ash, betel, mango, kramuka nut, and a nine-stranded thread, and provided with a golden ring.

Having established [the deity], having sprinkled [it] with the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should worship the jar (*kumbha*). *Oṃ namo ādhāraśaktaye* (Homage to the Support-Power). *Oṃ namo anantāya* (Homage to Ananta). *Oṃ namo dharmāya* (Homage to Dharma). *Oṃ namo jñānāya* (Homage to Knowledge). *Oṃ namo vairāgyāya* (Homage to Dispassion). *Oṃ nama aiśvaryāya* (Homage to Sovereignty). *Oṃ namo padmāya* (Homage to the Lotus).

"Salutation to Vāsukya; salutation to the form of Vāsukī; salutation to Vāsuki. Having thus worshipped, and having placed [the mantra] on the two eyes with "Salutation to the two eyes," and having filled his joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers, he recites:

"Salutation be to the serpents, whoever they may be, who are upon the earth; those who are in the intermediate space, and those who are in heaven—to those serpents, salutation! Those who are in the bright realm of heaven, whose brilliance is like that of the sun..."

In the rays; for them the seat has been prepared in the waters—to those serpents, homage! To those arrows of the Yātudhānas, or those which move within the rays of the sun and within the Vedas—to those serpents, homage!
With this mantra, in this [rite].

Having invoked Vāsuki with the words, "I invoke Vāsuki into the pitcher," and having worshipped until the end of the recitation, and having touched the pitcher together with the Brahmins, one should perform the recitation in sequence: the Sāvitrī, the Śiva-gāyatrī, the beginnings of the Vedas along with their associated mantras, the *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ*, the *brahmasūtra*, the *tryambaka*, and the *śrīsūkta* and *svastisūkta*. Then, having dismissed Vāsuki, [one should sprinkle] the threads with that water.
Having sprinkled water upon the preceptor, the worship of the thread (*sūtra*) should be performed:

"Homage to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*); homage to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*); homage to the fiery disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*). Thus, the three discs are to be prepared. Having worshipped them, [one should offer] to the *māyā-śakti* in the rice, and to the seventy million great mantras in the coconut.

Salutation! Salutation to Lakulīśa in the ashes! [One should worship] the infinite, imperishable Kavya, whose mouth is iron. Having invoked the mantra with the *bhukti-mantra*, and having worshipped up to the lamp, one should take the threads with the *tryambaka-mantra*. Having smeared them three times with ashes taken with the thumb and ring finger, and having consecrated the threads with the *ghṛta-sūkta*, [one should apply them to] one's own right hand.
And the image-bearers [should enter] with rice together with its awns, filling a conch shell;

distinguished by the sound of that conch, they should enter the Brahma-station with the mantra: "O Brahman, Sāman, Kṣatra, Bhr̥gu, Vr̥ṣṇi, Triṣṭubh, Ojas, Śam, O mighty hero! Indra with the fifteen-fold Stoma."

This middle [thread] is protected by the *samara* wind; having tied a knot at the root, it is further protected with ashes using the *ghṛtasūkta* and the *tryambaka* [mantra]. Having circumambulated the village on the right side and having fastened the threads upon the head of the elephant (*mātaṅga*), and having performed the circumambulation, the rite of binding the protective thread is completed; at the conclusion of the binding, [one should worship] the Goddess together with the image-bearers (*mūrtipāḥ*).
One should pray:
"O Goddess, O Goddess, Sovereign of the World, Support of the World, Mistress!"
For the sake of marking the eight bonds and for our protection.
"O Maheśvarī, by your grace I shall hold this [object] in my hand as a token of your favor.
You alone are our refuge; nothing else whatsoever exists [as such].

Having thus prayed, together with the Brahmins, he should offer blessings preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) and accompanied by mantras and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). [Then he should honor] the Brahmins...
On the first day:

worship of the Lord of the Assembly with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); worship with the permission of the Goddess; the permission of Brahmā; the Great Resolve (*mahā-saṅkalpa*); the declaration of the auspicious day (*svasti-puṇyāha-vācana*) and the collection of earth;
the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), and the eightfold binding of protective cords (*rakṣabandhana*).
The junctions of day and night.
Now, the purification of the site:
in the main pavilion of the deities, [the ground] is square and equal on all four sides, provided with four doors, adorned with four archways, and smeared with cow dung. (l3)

Having prepared a pavilion made of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for the purification of the site— measuring two to five cubits and adorned with various flowers— the Preceptor (*ācārya*), having bathed, sipped water (*ācamana*),

and performed the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) and other rites, sprinkles the pavilion with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*). Then, using a cord made of rice-flour paste, he [draws] the eastern line, the transverse line, and likewise the water-line, forming a nine-square grid.
Having prepared [the offerings],

having placed four *prasthas*, two *prasthas*, or half of that amount of rice and other grains in each of the compartments, having adorned himself with earrings and other ornaments, having put on the sacred thread (*pavitra*),
and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having performed the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), and the placement of the thirty-eight energies (*kalānyāsa*), the letters (*lipinyāsa*), the mantras (*mantranyāsa*), and so forth; having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste; preceded by the auspicious sounds of conchs, dundubhi drums, bherī drums, mardala drums, and hymns;

and taking darbha grass, [he says]: "First, I shall perform the worship of Mahāgaṇapati. Having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules.

Having made the request and performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) on this auspicious lunar day for the sake of the destruction of all the sins of ourselves and others, and for the increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth, [this is] the ritual limb of the goddess-worship consisting of the restoration of the ruinous [temple] and the eightfold binding of the image of this Goddess, the venerable Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā.

For the sake of accomplishing the fruits of the four aims of life; for the sake of warding off all diseases; for the sake of warding off all defects; for the sake of destroying all enemies; for the sake of attaining all-knowledge; for the sake of accomplishing the grace of all deities;
for the sake of the abundance of wealth and grain through the cessation of famine; and for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the purpose of removing the faults of killing all living beings, such as the murder of a Brahmin; for the purpose of warding off evil grahas such as Rākṣasas; for the purpose of increasing all powers; and for the purpose of pleasing Śrī, Kānti, and Mati, I shall perform the specialized rite of purifying the site (*vāstuśuddhi*), preceded by the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and the sprinkling of the great five products of the cow (*mahāpañcagavya*). (l5)

Having performed the rite according to the rules by following the previously mentioned path for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should prepare the great five products of the cow (*mahāpañcagavya*). Having strewn [the area] with five-fold *darbha* grass and sprinkled it with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should [assign the mantras]: "Obeisance to the square of the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) in the center; obeisance to the square of the Sadāśiva-principle (*sadāśivatattva*) in the east; obeisance to the square of the Vidyā-principle (*vidyātattva*) in the south."

Homage! To the northern square of the *puruṣa*-principle, homage! To the western square of the *kāla*-principle, homage! To the southeastern square of the *pṛthivī*-principle, homage! To the southwestern square of the *ap-* principle, homage! To the northwestern square of the *vāyu*-principle, homage! To the northeastern [square], homage!

"Salutation to the treasury of the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*). Having thus worshipped the enclosures (*koṣṭha*), one should worship the carriers of the vessels (*pātravāhaka*) therein: in the center—salutation to Kauśika; in the east—salutation to Kāśyapa; in the south—salutation to Bharadvāja; in the north—salutation to Atri; in the west—salutation to Gautama. In the eastern *pāvaka* [quarter]—salutation to Kauśika; in the *rākṣasa* [quarter]—salutation to...

Homage to Kāśyapa. In the northwest—homage to Bharadvāja. In the northeast—homage to Atri. (L3) Having thus worshipped the sages who carry the bowl, [one should prepare] a bowl made of gold, silver, bell-metal, clay, or any other suitable material; it should be eighteen finger-breadths high, twenty-four finger-breadths high, or ninety-six finger-breadths high. (L4)

The neck (*māna*) should be endowed with appropriate circumference, accompanied by the defects of curvature and so forth; the throat (*kaṇṭha*) should be six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long and provided with two finger-breadths for the hollow of the throat (*kukaṇṭha*);

the lip (*uṣṭha*) should be one finger-breadth thick, and the mouth should be of primary importance, possessing a width appropriate to the requirements. Having prepared the central vessel, there are four vessels starting from the east, sixteen finger-breadths in height, and nine finger-breadths—

Having prepared a wide vessel provided with two neck-protrusions (*kaṇṭhaśūla*), measuring four finger-breadths in width and having four feet; having sprinkled the middle and other vessels— those excellent vessels resembling the chest of a horse— and having washed them with the *hṛdaya* mantra, [one should proceed].

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the Astra-mantra, [one should worship] in the principal vessel: "Obeisance to Brahmā" in the center; "Obeisance to Viṣṇu" on the rim; "Obeisance to Rudra" on the right side;

"Obeisance to Vaṇadhī" on the left side; "Obeisance to Mahākāla" on the northern side. In the center: "Obeisance to Gaṅgā," "Obeisance to Yamunā," "Obeisance to Godāvarī," "Obeisance to Sarasvatī," "Obeisance to Narmadā," and "Obeisance to Sindhu."
Salutations! Salutations to the Kāverī! Salutations to the Tāmraparṇī! To the east—salutations to the Ṛgveda!

(l2) To the south—salutations to the Yajurveda! To the north—salutations to the Sāmaveda! To the west—salutations to the Atharvaṇaveda! To the northeast—salutations to Mahālakṣmī! Having thus worshipped the deities of the vessels and so forth, [in] the center—(l3)

Homage to Supratiṣṭhapātra. In the east—homage to Suśāntapātra. In the south—homage to Tejovatpātra. In the north—homage to Ratnodakapātra. In the west—homage to Amṛtapātra. In the southeast (l4)—homage to Niyatikṛtvapātra. In the southwest—homage to Kālatattvapātra. In the northwest—homage to Kālakalatattvapātra.
In the northeast: "Salutation to the vessel of the Unmanifest. Having thus worshipped the vessels:

"Salutation to the one of red color. With the mantra of Īśāna: "O Soma, swell the three-prastha measure of milk in the center; may your virile power be equal on all sides, for the attainment of strength. (l5–l6)

Having placed [the vessel] in the middle: "Homage to the smoke-colored one (*dhūmravarṇa*). Two *prastha*s of curd: "I have performed the *dadhi-krāvaṇa* for Viṣṇu, the vigorous horse; may he make our mouths fragrant, may he prolong our lives"—having placed this in the east with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra. One *prastha* of ghee from a tawny cow (*kapilā*): "Thou art pure, thou art light, thou art splendor. Having poured it into the south with the *aghora* mantra.

Six *prasthas* of cow urine from a blue-colored cow, [recited] with the *brahmagāyatrī* and the *vāmadeva* [sāman]. To the north, for the one who is appointed, water mixed with the dung of a black-colored cow; four *prasthas* of it serve to cleanse the cloth. [Recited with the verse:
"The one whose door is fragrance, who is invincible, ever-nourishing, and full of manure... (l. 2)

"I invoke you here, Śrī, the sovereign of all beings"—with this mantra, and immediately with the *Śivagāyatrī* mantra and the mantra "devasya tvā," [he prepares] a *prastha* of water with *kuśa* grass. Having prepared it thus, [he places it]:
in the center—"Salutation to Sadāśiva"; in the east—"Salutation to Īśvara"; in the south—"Salutation to Rudra"; in the north—"Salutation to Viṣṇu"; in the west—

Salutation to Brahmā. In the southeast—fragrant oil, one *prastha*. Salutation to the Ṛgveda—one *prastha* of flour-powder. In the southwest—three-quarter *pāda* of *āmalaka*. Salutation to the Yajurveda. In the northwest—powder of *rajanī*, half a *prastha*. Salutation to the Sāmaveda.

Having thus worshipped: in the center, having consecrated curd five times with the Īśa mantra; in the east, having consecrated ghee eight times with the Puruṣa mantra; in the south, having consecrated cow-urine once with the Vāmadeva mantra; in the west, having consecrated cow-dung with the Sadyojāta mantra.

Having consecrated it nine times with the *vyāhṛtis* over the fire six times, and having likewise consecrated other offerings such as the sacrificial cakes (*iṣṭa*) with the Heart-mantra alone, one should worship them with incense, lamps, and so forth using the Root-mantra. Then, having mixed curd into the center [of the offering] with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra, [one should proceed] with the Aghora-mantra.

Having added ghee to the center, and having mixed cow-dung water with the *sadyojāta* mantra— others [add] kuśa-water— one should again consecrate it with the mantra "devasya tvā," as well as the *Śivagāyatrī* and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Having offered incense and a lamp with the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) and touched it with *darbha* grass, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times and perform the lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*) and the fragrant gesture (*surabhimudrā*).
Having displayed [it], having protected it, having enveloped it,

and having covered it with *darbha* grass, accompanied by various musical instruments and the proclamation of "Svasti," [he should proceed] from the sacrificial pavilion and other starting points toward the northeast (*īśāna*) with the holy water (*puṇyāha*) and the great five products of the cow (*mahāpañcagavya*).

(The Ritual for the Site) — Now, one should purify the site with the Astra-mantra. Thus, the method of applying the purification of the site in the form of the Great Five Products (mahāpañcagavya) should be employed after understanding it according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal. If performed in this manner, the Five Products indeed increase one's sons and grandsons, bestow nourishment, grant wealth, and bring about the destruction of enemies.

For the sake of purifying the site (*vāstu*), one should have [the rite] performed by an *Ādiśaiva*. The procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) has been declared; now hear the procedure for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the five products of the cow in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* of the *Kāraṇa*.
Now, the seven purifications: (l7.

This, however, should be written down if it is seen in the *Svatantrakāmika*. [Repeated: Now, the seven purifications. Then the preceptor, having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkṛtya*) together with the forms, [prepares] the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*). (p54b, l1)

Having duly prepared for and worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made: "On this auspicious lunar day, for the purpose of purifying the site suitable for the performance of the Goddess-sacrifice—namely, the pavilion, the enclosure, and the Brahma-sthāna, which are ancillary to the rite of the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the restoration and eight-fold binding of this Goddess, the venerable Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā—I shall perform the sevenfold purification. Having thus resolved, [he performs] the Puṇyāha and the Pañcagavya rites.

(13) Having prepared [the site], taken up the spade and other tools, and gathered dry darbha grass, cow-dung, water, and pure clay; first, in the presence of the Lord, the preceptor has drawn [the mandala] with the Astra-mantra using the spade. (14)

Having dug [the ground] with the mantra *bhūmibhūmnā*, one should place the excavated earth elsewhere. Having dug to the depth of a palm tree (*tālamātra*), one should lift [the soil] with the *astra* mantra.

Having burned dry grass in the pit with the *astra* mantra, [one recites]: "Obeisance to the *astra*. Then follows the sprinkling of cow-dung and water, and the filling again with pure earth. With the *astra* mantra, [one performs] the "cow-habitation" (*gonivāsa*); [this includes] the dwelling for cows and so forth, [reciting]: "Obeisance to the *astra*."

Having given [the offering] and dismissed [the deity], one should then [offer] the remains of the priest's portion with "Obeisance to the Weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*). Then, having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*) and sprinkled the ground with water for the weapon (*astodaka*), one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and worship Mahālakṣmī or Brahmā. In this very same manner, [one should do so] in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇṭapa*).

At the site of Brahmā, one performs a tracing with the *astra-mantra* using a wooden peg (*śaṅku*) and digs to the depth of a span (*prādeśa*) with a spade, saying: "Homage to the *astra*. Having removed the earth and cast it elsewhere, saying: "Homage to the *astra*," one burns dry grass in the pit (*avaṭa*). Having removed that ash and sprinkled cow-dung water over it with the *astra-mantra*, one fills it with pure earth using that same mantra.

Having leveled [the ground], having caused a cow-pen to be constructed by means of a mantra, having provided refreshments for the laborers, having dismissed them, having fed the Brahmins, having cleared away the remnants of the meal, having smeared [the site] with [cow-dung],
and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow and water from an auspicious day; ||| l3 ||| by these two [means].

Having sprinkled [the site] with the Astra-mantra, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, and having worshipped the Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the seven purifications in this very order— beginning from the station of Indra and ending at Īśāna— preceded by the sounding of conchs, drums, and auspicious musical instruments. Having worshipped Indra and the other deities in their respective stations and having bid them farewell, one should enter the temple and perform what was commenced at dawn.

One should pray to Gaurī, saying, "May this rite be auspicious. Thus ends the sevenfold purification (*saptaśuddhi*). This [procedure] has been compiled in accordance with the scriptural statements of the *Kāmika-tantra*. Otherwise, if it is seen in the *Svacchanda-tantra*, it should be written down.
Now, the ritual offering to the site-deity (*vāstubali*):
Then the preceptor— whether by night or by day— in houses, temples, and so forth, born into a family of the primary Śaiva tradition, with a mind clear and contented during the day.
Having bathed well, wearing new garments, a turban, and an upper cloth,
and adorned with ornaments on the five limbs by anointing himself with sandalwood and other unguents;

And likewise, one who is devoid of the *uṣṇīṣa* [should be excluded] from the worship and the fire-offering (*homakarma*). Thus distinguished by such qualities, having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) five to ten cubits in size in front of the Goddess, or at her sides, or in the northeast; and having fed the Brahmins therein—

Having smeared the pavilion with cow dung, having sat upon a tortoise-seat facing north, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), and having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules— (l3) the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): on this auspicious lunar day, for this Goddess Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā...

The restoration of ruins, the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), the rites for the limbs of the Goddess, the rites for the limbs of the ritual action, the sacrificial pavilion, the abode of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*), and so forth— these are the requirements for the ritual; for the purpose of purifying the site (*sthalavāstuśuddhi*), there shall be the *puṇyāha* rite, the worship of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the worship of the water-jars, the worship of the maṇḍala, and the offering of oblations to the site (*vāstubalika*) preceded by the *vāstu-homa*.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall perform [this]," and having duly established [the ritual] with the *puṇyāha* and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), [he should proceed] in the decorated pavilion.
In the ritual system (*tantra*) of Śakti and others, however, there is the supreme Vāstu-rite; [it consists of] the nine squares of Nanda and Vinanda.
Having formed nine squares in the center, one should discard them.
Having established a square in the four directions, one should draw two squares from each corner.
There should be a single square surrounding [the center], with a trident at the tip of each corner. One should then draw a circle in the four directions, which is the supreme resting place.

In accordance with this statement, having first laid down ten threads [running] eastward, and likewise ten threads running northward, there arises a grid of eighty-one squares, as stated by the one named Patañjali in the *Paramaśāyin*. In its center is the nine-square Brahma-place; to its east are six squares for Samarya; to the south are six squares for Viśva; and to the west—(line 2).

For Mitra, six squares. To the north—six squares for Pṛthivīdhara. In the southeast—two squares for Āpa. To its west—two squares for Āpavatsa. In the southwest—two squares for Savindra. To its west—two squares for Sāvindra. In the northwest—two squares for Indra. To its east—two squares for Indrajaya. In the northeast—[three squares].
—Two *pada*s for Rudra.
To its east, two *pada*s for Rudradāsa. Thus is the second enclosure (*āvṛti*). The outer *prasthapada*s, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Āditya, are well known. These are indeed well known.

In the positions of Brahmā and the others, there should be an adornment with five powders according to their respective colors and qualities, if it is to be done in any way. In the center—the nine-square position of Brahmā—it is white; Vivasvat is white-colored, Mitra is like gold, Bhūdhara is black-colored, and Āpas is likewise white, [while] Japāpuṣpa is red-colored.

Indra is the color of the rising sun; Sāmindra is blue-colored; Indra is reddish-brown; Indrajaya is white; Rudra is like coral; Rudrajaya is yellow; Īśāna is the color of milk; and Parjanya is likewise.
Mahendra is water-colored and black; Śyāmaka is dark;
Āditya is red; Satyaga is variegated in color;
Bhraṃśa has the luster of the *dhūka* flower; and Kunda is like the sky. (2)
Agni is said to have the color of that [fire]; his worship is like a red lotus;
Vitata has the luster of Indra’s wrath; and Vidyutvarṇa is marked by the planets.
Yama is like black collyrium; Vastugandha is like a ruby;
Mṛgarāja is like a bumblebee; and Mṛga is like a cloud.
Then Nairṛti was like fire, and Dauvārika was white;
Sugrīva had the luster of a pale throat, and Uṣadattaka resembled the half-moon.
Varuṇa was white-complexioned, and the god [Vāyu] was black in color.
Likewise, the attainment of blue lotuses and the [attainment of] verses are like the sapphire of the lord of evil yakṣas.
The wind [element] has the appearance of smoke; in disease, it resembles Mahārudra. Likewise, the Nāga is conch-colored, while the primary one resembles clay.
The white lotus is the radiance of Bhallāṭa; the golden radiance is that of Somakaṭa; and there is the red lotus spoken of by Nṛka.

Then, on the lunar day beginning with Śakha, there is Aditi, who has the luster of kramuda; she is the letter in the thirty-second square. Śarakī has the hue of Kapila, and Vidhāri is like a cloud. The one called Pūtanā has the color of smoke.

Pāpā is a wretched rākṣasī; Skanda has the appearance of jewel-light; Haryamā resembles jewels; Jṛmbha has a shadow like smoke; Balipañcaka has a blackish hue. Thus are their colors described. This description of the colors of the deities of the bali offering is recorded in other Āgamas. [It is located] in the northeast of the bali-maṇḍala.
Having smeared a mandala measuring one cubit with cow dung,

having placed [the vessel] therein, and having strewn it around with *darbha* grass, flowers, and parched grain; having washed with the *astra-mantra* a new jar capable of holding a *droṇa* measure of water,
wrapped with thread, and having filled it with pure water.

Having established [the vessel] upon that mandali, to its north— one should establish a vardhanī vessel, capable of holding a measure of two prasthas of water, marked with thread, washed, and filled with pure water;

having adorned it with cloths and other ornaments, and having sprinkled the articles for worship and the articles for the fire-oblation with the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), as well as one’s own body, using the *astra-mantra*.

Having meditated upon the nature of Brahmā, one should worship: in the center—salutation to Ananta; salutation to Dharma; salutation to Jñāna; salutation to Vairāgya; salutation to Aiśvarya; salutation to the Lotus; salutation to the Brahmā-throne.
The swan saw him— pot-bellied, fair-complexioned, with a frown and crooked eyes,
four-faced and four-armed, holding a water-pot and a rosary.
With his arms raised, adorned with a shining lotus, and endowed with a sacred thread and a topknot;
Sarasvatī stands between his thighs, holding a lute and a book.
He is arrayed in white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes.

Having meditated thus: "Salutation to the form of Brahmā; salutation to the eyes. Having thus applied the eyes, and having filled his joined palms with flowers, he recites the mantra beginning with *brahmajajñāna* and concludes with:
"O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us... be our dwelling, free from disease. Whatever we implore, favor that for us; be auspicious unto us."
May there be well-being for our bipeds and quadrupeds.
O Lord of the Dwelling, may we dwell with your auspicious assembly, which is rich in horses and cattle. Bring us security in times of peace and success in our endeavors.
Do you all protect us always with your blessings. Amīvāha.

"O Vāstoṣpati, entering all forms, you who are a most gracious friend to those who offer oblations—be auspicious, be auspicious! (l4) With this mantra, [one should say]: "I invoke Brahmā, together with his retinue, along with the Vāstu-deity, into this maṇḍala.

Having thus invoked him and worshipped him up to the offering of incense, [one should worship] in the east: "Salutation to Samarya"; in the south: "Salutation to Vivasvat on the six-padded spot"; in the western six-padded spot—

Homage to Mitra. In the northern hexagon—homage to Pṛthivīdhara. (L5) In the southeast double-square—homage to Āpa. To its west—homage to Āpavatsa. In the southwest double-square—homage to Sacīndra. To its west—homage to Sācindra. In the northwest double-square—(L6)

To the two-footed [deity] in the east: *namaḥ* to Indra. To the two-footed [deity] to its north: *namaḥ* to Indrajaya. To the two-footed [deity] situated in the northeast corner: *namaḥ* to Rudra. To the one to its east: *namaḥ* to Rudradāsa. One should worship these deities starting from the northeast corner and ending with the previously mentioned [two-footed] positions: *namaḥ* to Īśa; *namaḥ* to Parjanya; *namaḥ* to Jayanta; *namaḥ* to Mahendra; *namaḥ* to Āditya.

Homage to Satyaga! Homage to Bhṛśaṅka! Homage to Akṣarikṣa! Having thus honored and fully worshipped these, [one proceeds] to the southeast and so forth: homage to Agni; homage to Pūṣan; homage to Vitata; homage to Grahakṣata; homage to Yama; homage to Gandharva; homage to Bhṛṅgarāja; homage to the Ṛṣis; homage to Nirṛti; homage to Dauvārika.

Homage to Puṣpadanta; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Śoṣaroga; homage to Pāpa; homage to Yakṣman; homage to Vāyu; homage to Nāga; homage to Mukhya; homage to Bhallāṭa; homage to Soma; homage to Durga; (l.

3) homage to Diti; homage to Aditi. Having thus invoked these deities in the thirty-two squares beginning with Īśāna, [one should worship them] with the mantras "to the seat" (*āsana*) and "to the form" (*mūrti*), followed by "homage" (*namaḥ*).
Having worshipped the edge of the lamp, [one worships] from the southeast trident onwards:
*namaḥ* to Carakī; *namaḥ* to Vidārī; *namaḥ* to Pūtanā; *namaḥ* to Pāparākṣasī; *namaḥ* to Skandā in the east and other directions; *namaḥ* to Jṛmbhā; *namaḥ* to Aryaman; *namaḥ* to Balipiñcha.

Having worshipped these [deities] with their respective seat-mantras (*āsana-mantra*), form-mantras (*mūrti-mantra*), and root-mantras (*mūla-mantra*), using their own names up to the offering of lamps; at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), [one recites]: "O Brahman, you who desire to know, first from before the boundless, by the light of your own nature, bring hither the seven sisters; such is the likeness of this, the source of the unborn, the All. O Lord of the Dwelling (*Vāstoṣpati*), recognize us, you who are easy of access.

With the mantra: "O you who are without enemies! For this great [offering] of ours, be pleased; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds," and while holding curd-rice mixed with jaggery in his hand, he says: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vārasitā together with her retinue."

"Ye brahmaṇe svāhā!"—this [offering] consisting of *pānasa* (jackfruit), honey, and so forth, for the four [deities], is called the *balī* of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). In the intermediate directions, the *balī* of cooked rice with all its curries (*kṛsara*) is for the four deities beginning with Japa. The *balī* of mung-bean rice (*mudgānna*) is for the eight deities beginning with Īśāna. The *balī* of *gulānna* (rice with molasses) is for the deities beginning with Hutāśana. The *balī* of ghee-rice (*ghṛtānna*) is for the eight deities beginning with Paścimā. In the northwest (*vāyavyā*),...

For the deities of the northern direction, curd-rice is the offering. For the eight external deities, mixed rice is the offering. For the deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Piñcā, [the offering is made] with their respective names in the dative case followed by *svāhā*.
Having thus separately offered the bali-oblation and water for drinking, and having performed worship up to the point of recitation with incense, lamps, and so forth—(Kumbhapūjā):
the worship of the vessel below should be performed: "Homage to Ādhāraśakti; homage to Ananta; homage to Dharma. (l5)

"Salutation to Padma. Having thus worshipped the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), [one says]: "Salutation to Brahmāsana, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*). Haṃ Saṃ Sathaṃ Kundidaṃ Gauram, with knitted brows and a crooked gaze, four-faced and four-armed, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*).
With arms raised, holding a radiant lotus, and endowed with a sacred thread and a topknot.

Having meditated thus: "Sarasvatī is in the middle of the thighs, holding a lute and a book, adorned with white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes," one should say: "Homage to the Lord of the Site, the form of Brahmā. Having thus offered to the two eyes, saying "Homage to the two eyes," and having filled the hollowed palms with flowers:

With the mantra *vāstoṣpate* or the mantra *brahmajajñāna*, he invokes Brahmā together with his retinue of attendants, saying: "I invoke [Brahmā]! Having thus invoked him and performed the worship from the ritual installation (*sthāpana*) up to the recitation (*japa*), [he does] exactly the same on his left.

Having worshipped the six seats, [one offers] "Salutation to the seat of Sarasvatī. [One should meditate on] Sarasvatī, who wears white garments, holds a rosary and a book in her right and left hands respectively, and is most gracious.

Salutation to the form of Sarasvatī. Oṃ hrīṃ suṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Having performed the worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the recitation of mantras, [one should proceed] in the quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) previously prepared in the mandala, preceded by the purification of the pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra).

Having performed the rites up to the end of the mouth-offering according to the procedure prescribed for Vedic fire-rituals, one should invoke Brahmā— the Lord of the Site— into the center of the fire with the mantra *vāstoṣpate* and the mantra *brahmajajñānam*. Having worshipped him with offerings up to incense and lamps, one should offer ten oblations of clarified butter at the place of the food offering (*naivedya*) while reciting the root-mantra of Brahmā.

(The Principal Oblation) — Now follows the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). At the place of the food offering (*naivedya*), one performs an oblation of fuel sticks (*samidh*) at the root of the *brahma* tree—using *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* wood respectively—in separate sets of one hundred each. Then follows the *vyāhṛti* oblations for the four deities beginning with Samarya.

There is a fuel-oblation (*samiddhoma*) for each of the twenty-five [deities] separately; a fuel-oblation of ten [fuel-sticks] for each of the eight deities beginning with Āpādya; and a fuel-oblation of five [fuel-sticks] for each of the external deities beginning with Īśāna.

The *samidh* oblation: for the eight deities beginning with Śaravyā, there is a *samidh* oblation performed once for each, using their respective root-mantras. Then, the *vyāhṛti* oblation. In the same manner, there is an *ājya* oblation for Brahmā and the others. In the same manner, there is a *caru* oblation. [Regarding] the *tilājya-sūkta*, it is the same; likewise, there is a *taṇḍula* oblation. Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* for each substance, one then offers the mixture of all substances with the mantra "Havyavāha."
Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra beginning "vaiśvānara," one should recite the thousand-syllable [mantra] of Aghora a thousand times.
Then, one should offer a thousand roots of śarati for the sviṣṭakṛt oblation.
Having performed the ritual attendance...

(l4) one should offer the *kūṣmāṇḍa* bali. Having worshipped the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*) residing in the fire with incense, lamps, and so forth, having requested [blessings] with the food offering (*naivedya*), and having performed the oblation (*huta*), one should pray with the words "parama... (l5).

Thinking, "I shall unite the invited Vāstunātha Brahmā with the maṇḍala," one unites him with the root mantra. Having likewise worshipped those situated within the maṇḍala, and having made a request, thinking,
"I shall unite the Vāstunātha Brahmā together with his retinue from this maṇḍala into the pitcher," one unites him with the root mantra and offers the *arghya* with the face turned away.

Once again, thinking "I shall dismiss the Vāstunātha residing in the pitcher, together with his Śakti and retinue, into my heart," one should perform the dismissal with the root mantra. Having offered the *arghya* for the one facing away, [one should offer it] to the Ācārya for the sake of attaining the full fruit of the performed rites.
Having given the aforementioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should pray for blessings. Thus ends the Vāstubali offering to the Goddess.
Then follows the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Then the preceptor, having performed the ritual integration of the self (*sakalīkaraṇa*),
makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) on an auspicious lunar day as an ancillary part of the *vāstubali* offering for this goddess, the venerable mother Kāntimatī.

"I shall perform the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) as a subsidiary rite for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple], the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), and the sacrifice to the Goddess. For that purpose, I shall perform the worship of the ankles (*gulphapūjā*) and the selection of the Brahmins. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and having touched water, one should collect dry leaves and the like from trees suitable for sacrifice, as well as dry *darbha* grass together with plantain leaves.
Having had a man made with two balls at his feet, provided with a tail, and adorned with a cloth, flower garlands, and so forth;

having brought the man near the fire, others having spread out auspicious grasses (*udagra*) in front [of him], he should place the man upon them facing west. Then, having sprinkled him with the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having consecrated him with the *astra-mantra*, he should empower him with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Salutation to the seat of Dhūmrākṣa.

(l6) Salutation to the form of Dhūmrākṣa. Salutation to Dhūmrākṣa. *Kṣaṃ ruṃ*, I invoke Dhūmrākṣa into this gulba. Having thus invoked him, and having performed the rites from installation up to the lamp with the Heart-mantra, thereafter (l7)

"For the purpose of purifying the site used for the worship of the goddesses in this sacrificial pavilion and so forth, and for the purpose of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), we choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Having thus chosen him, and having meditated upon the Brāhmaṇa as being the form of the *Vāstu-puruṣa*,

having invoked him and offered a seat and other honors, and having given him two garments and other gifts according to his pleasure, one should adorn him with red sandalwood paste, red unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), red flowers, and so forth.

With that [offering], one should present a bali-offering of red rice accompanied by pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit and provided with *arghya* and flowers. Reciting "Oṃ kṣa ruṃ dra la dhūṃ rākṣāya svāhā," having caused the bali to be offered and having given collyrium, [one should offer] in this [place], preceded by a gift of betel, water, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Having given [the object] with the words, "I bestow this upon you for the purpose of performing the circumambulation with fire," and having sprinkled the remaining portion with *ājya* for the oblation, one should take the *śulba* (cord), give it to a Brāhmaṇa, and with that very same *hṛdaya-mantra*, join the mouth of the site (*vāstumukha*) with the heart of the site-fire (*vāstvanala*). Having kindled it, [it should be performed] accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and bells.
Accompanied by the presiding priests whose voices were endowed with auspicious sounds,

he [performed] together with the recitation for a holy day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and fifty-three *vāstu* jars, preceded by the recitation of the *astra* mantra,
for the purpose of the sacrifice to the goddesses at the site of the Brahmā-sthāna and other locations within the sacrificial pavilion.

Having performed purification, having cast away the cord from afar, having sprinkled [the area] with cow-dung and water, having bathed together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipas*), and having sipped water for ritual purification (*ācamana*), he should enter the temple. Then, having again performed the *puṇyāha* rite according to the rules, the preceptor (*deśika*) should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion and all other areas, including the village, the house of the planets, and the temple of the deity, with the mantra beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*).
One should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) for the prevention of all faults; such is the rule for the independent performance of the circumambulation with fire.
Now follows the procedure for the feeding of the *saṅgraha* Brahmins.

Then the preceptor, having performed the ritual identification (*sakalīkṛtya*), makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, commencing from the previous day’s offering of the medicinal herbs for binding to this Goddess, the venerable Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā, up until this point, by means of performing eight new bindings..."
Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the sake of removing all defects that have arisen,

I shall feed eight Brahmins for each of the eight limbs [of the body], preceded by an oil massage and a bath, followed by various kinds of food— both solid and soft— and accompanied by some sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
numbering one hundred," [he should then proceed with] the one hundred Brahmins.

Having seated them upon the ritual seats (*pīṭha*) and others, and having worshipped them with the thought that they are the Lord (*Īśa*), one should feed them, beginning with solid and soft foods. Thus ends the procedure for feeding the Brāhmaṇas according to the *Kāmikasvatantrasaṅgraha*. (L5. Now follows the offering to the ego (*ahaṅkārabali*).

Then the preceptor, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), and having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules, made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day,

for the purpose of removing the fever, afflictions such as *māryā*, and other calamities that have befallen [this person] due to the decay and loosening of the eightfold bonds of the Goddess Kāntimatīmbā— "

By the grace of fierce deities such as the *vetālas*, for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects, I shall cause the *ahaṅkārabali*—which is an ancillary rite of the *jīrṇoddhāra*, the *aṣṭabandhana*, and the *śivayāga*—to be performed by a Pāśupata Śaiva. For that purpose, [the rites of] the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the nine... [are required].

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the worship of Bhadrakālī, preceded by the offerings of bathing substances, the invocation of Bhadrakālī, and the consecration with oils and other materials";

and having duly established the *puṇyāha* water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—in a decorated pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) adorned with various flowers, fruits such as sugarcane stalks, coconuts, and betel nuts, or elsewhere in a pleasing location in front of the Goddess... [the rite is performed].
In a pavilion fragrant with the incense of black agallochum, camphor, wicks, and other perfumes, adorned with many lamps burning together, beautified by uśīra roots, betel leaves, and jambīra fruits,
[he sits] upon a tortoise-seat.

Having sat down facing east, north, or toward the Goddess; having performed the purification of the seat (*pīṭhaśuddhi*); having carried out the purification of the self and the purification of the mantras; and having prepared a nine-square grid before the Goddess; within that, having constructed five altars (*sthaṇḍila*) beginning with [the one for] Prahlāda and ending with the water-vessel; and having spread *darbha* grass upon them; [one should place] the principal *vardhanī* vessel measuring one *droṇa*, and [another] measuring one *āḍhaka*.
Having brought eight *vardhanī* vessels, each measuring two *prastha*s, and having filled them with water purified by straining through cloth and by inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*),
one should grind cardamom, cloves, camphor, *uśīra*, and *campaka* buds into powder.

Having cast [the offerings] into those waters, having adorned them with the ends of a cloth, tufts of *kūrca* grass, mango sprouts, coconut flowers, and garlands, having made a *tilaka* mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste, and having placed a flower upon one’s own head while reciting the root mantra; and having contemplated one’s own body as being of the nature of *Śakti*, one should worship externally: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti*. [This continues] until the end of the devotion.
Having worshipped the lotus and so forth, one should then worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*).
(l2) Homage to Durgā; homage to Bhadrā; homage to Bhadrakālī; homage to Ambikā; homage to Kṣamā; homage to Padmagarbhā; homage to Āryā; homage to Kṣemaṅkarī. Of these— (l3)
General meditation:

Having meditated thus: "They resemble collyrium applied at different times, holding swords and shields in their hands, with hair standing erect, possessing deformed faces, and adorned with all ornaments."

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Śubhaṅkarī" in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should place the *mātṛkās* in the pitcher and assign their respective digits (*kalās*) to those locations: "Obeisance to the digit Nivṛtti" at the feet; "at the navel, [to the digit] Pṛthvī... (line 5).
*Oṃ* *Kalāyai* *namaḥ* (Salutation to Kalā). At the heart: *Vidyākalāyai namaḥ*. At the forehead: *Śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. At the crown of the head: *Śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*.
Having thus performed the placement of the *kalās*, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
One should meditate on her seated upon a corpse-throne, holding a pestle, an arrow, a club, and a sword in her hands.

I worship Bhadrakālī, who removes all enemies, whose dark limbs are adorned with a garland of severed heads, who possesses a face as serene as the moon and sun, whose form is composed of the letters of the alphabet, and whose hands— adorned with bracelets and water-pots— bear a skull-topped staff and a boon-granting gesture, while her attendants carry a shield and a thunderbolt.

"Salutation to the form of Bhadrakālī! Salutation to the eyes! Having thus assigned the eyes, and having filled his joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers, he should recite the root mantra of the Goddess. Visualizing the incomparable splendor consisting of manifold lights within his joined palms, and again reciting the root mantra of the Goddess up until its dissolution, he should say: "I invoke the Goddess into this jar."

Having performed the invocation, the ritual of installation (*sthāpanā*), and so forth; having offered the guest-water (*svāgatārghya*); having prayed, "O Goddess, [reside] in the Lord of the Entire World"; and having applied the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs] to the locations of the heart and so on, preceded by the root mantra of the Goddess; having displayed the *mahāmudrā*; having rendered [the deity] completely one with oneself (*paramīkṛtya*); and having displayed the *padmamudrā*, the *yonimudrā*, and the *surabhimudrā*—[this constitutes the sequence] from the seat (*āsana*) up to the end of the recitation (*japa*).

Having performed worship, and having likewise worshipped Caṇḍikā upon the *vardhanī* vessel preceded by the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), [he says]: "In the east, obeisance to the seat of Brāhmī. [He visualizes] Brāhmī as red, four-faced, seated upon a swan, and four-armed.
Holding the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a rosary (*akṣamālā*) and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) in her hands;
salutation to Brāhmī during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā. Having worshipped her with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), [one proceeds] to the southeast corner:
the white goddess Maheśvarī, seated upon a bull and possessing four arms.
Adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, along with an axe, he is the protector of the world.

Salutation to the form of Maheśvarī. Having worshipped her with all rites from invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), [one worships] on the right: Kaumārī, mounted upon a peacock, adorned with all ornaments, holding a spear, a thunderbolt, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, her lotus-like face being exceedingly gracious.
Salutation to the form of Kaumārī. Having invoked Kaumārī, [one proceeds] to the southwest: salutation to the seat of Vaiṣṇavī.
O Tārkṣya, that Vaiṣṇavī is peaceful, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
She has four arms and is adorned with all ornaments.
Salutation to the Vaiṣṇava form.
(l2) Having invoked and worshipped [it], [one proceeds] to the west: salutation to the seat of Vārāhī.
Vārāhī is black in color, with long tusks, and terrifying.
[She holds] the thunderbolt (*kula*) and the mace (*musala*), and [bestows] the boons and fearlessness. Homage!
(3) Homage to the one in the form of Varāhi. Having invoked and worshipped her, [one should worship] in the northwest corner: "Homage to the seat of Mahendra.
[One should meditate on] Mahendrī, who has a red body, is seated upon a goat, holds a thunderbolt in her hand, and possesses great strength.

[One should worship] her who has four arms, a thousand eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments—homage to the form of Mahendra! Having invoked and fully worshipped [her], [one should proceed] to the north: "Homage to the seat of Cāmuṇḍā!
[One should meditate on her] as being in a state of wrath, with beautiful dark limbs, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a trident and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in the right hands, and a staff and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in the left;
homage to the form of Cāmuṇḍī. Having invoked and worshipped [her], [one should likewise worship] right there: "Homage to the seat of Gaṇapati.
[One should visualize] that red Gaṇapati as having an elephant's face, with a tusk, a noose, a goad, and a fruit.
And [he saw] the elephant-faced Lord of the Gaṇas, holding [the moon] with his curved trunks.

Salutation to the form of Gaṇapati. Having invoked Gaṇapati and worshipped him, [one places] the girdle in the northeast: "Salutation to the seat of Vīrabhadra. Vīrabhadra is seated upon a bull, cloud-colored, wearing a garland of skulls, holding a sword and an axe in his right hands, and a hand-drum and a shield in his left.

Salutation to the form of Vīrabhadra. Then, those initiated as knowers of the mantra, having recited the root-mantra of the Goddess one thousand times and the [mantras] of the limbs ten times that amount (one hundred each), and having offered the oblation, they shall prepare the fire— preceded by the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)— either in the pit to the east of the water-pot (*kumbha*) or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), beginning with the *ādhāra* [mantras].

Up to the conclusion of the marriage rite, according to the procedure for the Śiva-homa, one should worship Agni, Hṛt, Padma, the Preceptor (Deśika), and Bhadrakālī in sequence. Having performed the worship from invocation (āvāhana) up to the lamps, one performs the primary oblation (pradhāna-homa) with Palāśa fuel-sticks (samidh) numbering one hundred, using the root-mantra of the Goddess. There is also an oblation of clarified butter (ājya-homa) in that same number, with [the quantity] the size of a fresh Āmalaka fruit.

The *caru* oblation: one hundred times, with a handful [of grain] and its root-mantra; the *lāja* oblation: again one hundred times, with a handful and its root-mantra; the oblation of new grain (*navadhānya*): that same number of times, with its root-mantra and in its own measure.

The oblation of cakes (*apūpa-homa*). According to that same method, there is the oblation of plantain fruit (*kadali-phala-homa*) preceded by five offerings of a single plantain fruit. There is the oblation of *śrī* leaves numbering one hundred. There is the oblation of lotuses (*padma-homa*) numbering one hundred according to their own measure. There is the oblation of the three types of *uśīra* with each offering accompanied by the root-mantra (*mūla*) numbering one hundred. With the root-mantra numbering one hundred...
For a single coconut,

one performs a hundred oblations preceded by ten preliminary offerings (*daśāhuti*). Having offered in this manner, one then dismisses the fire according to the Śaiva ritual procedure for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings, and without concluding the rite,
[proceeds to] the *balipīṭha*.

Having washed [the area] and fashioned a triangle with red powder, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of food mixed with sandalwood and the remains of the *homa* sacrifice, saying: "Homage to the many-formed ones (*bahuberāḥ*); homage to the hosts (*gaṇāḥ*); homage to the spirits (*bhūtāḥ*); homage to the departed (*pretāḥ*); homage to the *piśācas*. Having thus worshipped, one should offer the oblation ending with the word *svāhā*. Then..."

Homage to the Mothers! Homage to the Yoginīs! Homage to the Ḍākinīs! Homage to the Mothers! (L3) Homage to Gaṇeśa! Homage to Vīrabhadra! Homage to the Mothers of Space! Homage to the Mothers of the Gods! Homage to the Mothers of Beings! Homage to the Mothers of the Ancestors! Homage to all the Mothers! Having thus worshipped:
May all the goddesses of the host of Mothers, holding weapons and observing their vows,
remain pervading the world for the sake of the rising power of one who desires strength.
"May the Mothers, having been worshipped, constantly grant security.

Having meditated thus, and taking the remnants of the oblation consisting of red substances together with red flowers and water for honor (*arghya*), one should offer the *bali* at that very spot where the previous name was sown, using [the deity's name] in the dative case followed by "svāhā."
Moreover: Having performed the collective offering (samaṣṭibali) after worship— those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce places,
as well as those who are gentle and dwell in gentle places.
Those who dwell in the heavens, on earth, and in the depths of the netherworld;
the Mothers, both fierce and gentle, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas.
Likewise, may all others who have become obstacles and who dwell in the ten directions,
with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering;
may they always nourish our success and protect us with constant peace.

Having uttered this mantra, one should offer the *bali* in the center of a red triangular mandala accompanied by red flowers, saying: "To all, svāhā! To all [goddesses], svāhā! Then, having washed the feet, sipped water (*ācamana*), and applied ashes, one should pray: "I worship the Goddess. Having consecrated her with the root mantra through the rites beginning with the application of oil and ending with the installation, [one should offer] a new red cloth.

Having smeared [the deity] from the feet up to the face with red sandalwood, red flowers, vermilion, saffron, and divine fragrances; having adorned [the deity] with ornaments using the root mantra; and having decorated [the deity] with *ketakī*, jasmine (*mallikā*), red oleander (*karavīra*), and other fragrant flowers, one should worship. *Ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. *Anantāya namaḥ*. *Dharmāya namaḥ*. *Jñānāya namaḥ*.
Homage! Homage to dispassion! (l5) Homage to sovereignty! Homage to non-dharma! Homage to ignorance! Homage to non-dispassion! Homage to non-sovereignty!
Homage to the lower covering! Homage to the upper covering! Homage to the bulbous root! Homage to the seed! Homage to the stalk! (l6)

Homage to the sprout! Homage to the thorns! Homage to the petals! Homage to the filaments! Homage to the pericarp! Homage to the lotus! Homage to Durgā! Homage to Bhadrā! Homage to Bhadrakālī! Homage to Ambikā! (l7) Homage to Kṣamā! Homage to Padmagarbha! Homage to Āryā! Homage to Keśakārī!
Resembling powdered collyrium, with swords and shields in their hands,

with hair standing erect, possessing deformed limbs, and adorned with all ornaments— having meditated thus, one should worship [the goddess] Śubhaṅkarī in the pericarp with the mantra "Namaḥ". Then follows the meditation on the Mātṛkās in the previously mentioned locations beginning with the forehead.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, one should then place the *kalās*: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā; at the feet. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalā; at the navel. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Vidyākalā; at the heart. Oṃ haiṃ... [at the head].

*Śāntikalāyai namaḥ* | On the forehead. *Oṃ haṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ* | On the head. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), then follows the placement of the goddesses (*devīnyāsa*). *Oṃ hrīṃ bhadrakālyai namaḥ* | On the head. *Oṃ hraṃ karālyai namaḥ* | On the mouth. *Oṃ hrīṃ kaṅkālyai namaḥ* | On the heart. *Oṃ hrīṃ vikarālyai* [namaḥ] | On the private parts.

*Namaḥ* at the navel. *Oṃ hrīṃ kālyai namaḥ* at the feet. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner and having meditated upon the Goddess accordingly, one should place the form with the mantra: *Namaḥ bhadrakālīmūrtaye*. Then, having placed the eyes with the mantra: *Netrābhyāṃ namaḥ*.

Having filled his joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers, having visualized within his palms a mass of manifold lights, having uttered the mantra corresponding to the form [of the deity], and having invoked her with the words, "I invoke the goddess Bhadrakālī," and having performed the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth,

having offered the *svāgatārghya* with the root mantra, and having made supplication, he should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs preceded by the mantras according to the root mantra of the goddess in the locations from the heart to the ends of the hands; then, with the root mantra...

Having performed the rites of unification (*ekatva*), protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*); having displayed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), the image mudrā (*bimbamudrā*), the womb mudrā (*yonimudrā*), and the fragrant mudrā (*surabhimudrā*); and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, as well as incense and lamps; [and having offered] rice with jujube (*gulānna*) and rice with mung beans (*mudgānna*).

Having prepared milk-rice, flour-based sweets, edible pastes, black gram cakes, fried cakes, small meat-balls, sesame cakes, coconut, various fruits, and pieces of sugarcane; having sprinkled them with water; having perfumed them; having offered them with the root mantra; and having presented betel nut along with betel leaves for the sake of refreshing the mouth.

Having performed the worship up to the end of the recitation (*japa*), accompanied by incense, lamps, offerings, hymns of praise, auspicious benedictions, dance, song, and instrumental music; having sprinkled the triangular *balipīṭha* with red sandalwood water; having honored it with flowers and offered the oblation (*naivedya*); [he should offer] the remaining food along with red powder.

Offered upon the triangular sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*): *svāhā* to the many forms (*bahuberāḥ*), *svāhā* to the single forms (*ekaberāḥ*), *svāhā* to the seven Mothers (*saptamātaraḥ*), *svāhā* to Vīrabhadra, *svāhā* to Gaṇeśa, *svāhā* to the Yoginīs,
*svāhā* to all the hosts of spirits (*bhūtagaṇāḥ*), *svāhā* to the Yoginīs, *svāhā* to Brahmā, *svāhā* to Vighneśa.
Svāhā! To the Piśāca, svāhā!

To the hosts of Koṭarākṣasīs, svāhā! To the Rudras, svāhā! To all [the males], svāhā! To all [the females], svāhā! Thus, [he offers] water mixed with red flowers accompanied by the five musical instruments.

One should offer the *bali* oblation endowed with flames and accompanied by [the appropriate substances]. In a place without space, one should offer the *bali* with the fist closed. One should offer the *bali* with the previously mentioned mantra. That night, having spread a mat fashioned from coconut leaves in the presence of Bhadrakālī by means of the *pāraśava* [method], and having strewn red sandalwood and red flowers upon it, one should scatter them there that night.

With the Pāraśaiva [mantra], one offers an oblation of red rice, mung-bean rice, and the flesh of goats and chickens, etc., reciting "Oṃ hrīḥ" followed by the root mantra and "bhadrakālyai svāhā. "I give these offerings; having given them, this is for your satisfaction. (l4)

"Drink!"—this [is said] five times. Having gratified [the deity] with the meat of a goat and a cock, blood, and water, [one should say]: "This plow-blade, accompanied by black-gram cakes, is for you as a noose. All this must be performed by a Pāraśava. When Kālī is to be satisfied, if the Ācārya has not performed the living-sacrifice (*jīvabali*), a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to a Brāhmaṇa woman.
It perishes during terrible fear for the king and the kingdom,
when afflicted by a great plague.
Likewise, during the fear of epidemics among people, and in such occasions as the restoration of dilapidated structures.
In this very way, O Kālī, you bring about your presence through the bali-offering;
for the mortal who performs it thus, his prosperity increases. This "bali of the ego" has been compiled from other Āgamas in accordance with the words of the *Kāmika-vidhāyaka*.
If [the deity] is seen in the independent [mandala], then it must be written at that very moment; this is the offering of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkārabali*).
The entry offering (*praveśabali*)—
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the time for the offering at the time of entry,
as well as during the consecration and festivals, upon entering a new dwelling,
at the time of entering a village, and when a great disease breaks out.
And likewise during the fear of great pestilence, at the end of the eon, and even during the fear of famine.
For the sake of their satisfaction and pacification, one should perform the entry-offering (*praveśabali*).
If the entry-offering is omitted, that village shall perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the entry-offering.
Listen now to the characteristics of the altar (vedikā) situated in the center of the site, in each of the eight directions.
Four finger-breadths in height and twice that in width,
resembling the surface of a mirror, one should draw a wheel in the center.
First comes the worship of Vighnarāja, and second, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having worshipped the third jar, one should perform the worship of the sword as the fourth;
having worshipped the fifth weapon, one should fully worship the sixth, which is food.
The seventh [rite] is the striking of the drum; the eighth is the offering of the bali;
the ninth is the offering of the bali, and the tenth is the fire-oblation (*homa*).
These ten rites have been declared; thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.

Then another preceptor— firm of limb, a knower of mantras, a twice-born devotee of Śiva— having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the sake of the entry-offering on a night endowed with an auspicious moment, during the bright or dark fortnight, under a fixed and auspicious lunar mansion, a favorable conjunction, and a favorable karana; adorned with the five ornaments and wearing red garments.

Wearing a blue turban and upper garment, having smeared all his limbs with white ashes, the knower of mantras should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark according to the sequence of the ritual stages. Having adorned himself with red sandalwood paste, red flowers, and rudrākṣa beads, and having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, he should duly prepare the general *arghya* offering. Then, having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules, [he should proceed] preceded by the striking of his head.

Having prayed to Vighneśvara, having prostrated before the Guru, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the removal of all calamities for all [people], beginning with Brāhmaṇas, who reside in this place..."

For the sake of accomplishing all desired aims through this goddess, Śrī Kāntimatyambā, and by means of the cessation of the afflictions that have befallen most living beings due to the entry of seven types of beings— namely, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, kālikās, śaralyas, and bhairavas— caused by the decay of her previously performed eightfold binding (aṣṭabandhana), [this is done] for the purpose of protecting that goddess.
Specifically, for the protection of the village, for the accomplishment of all desired aims, and for the protection of the village folk preceded by the expulsion of malevolent grahas such as yakṣas,
[this consists of] the tenfold rites, the restoration of the dilapidated, and the eightfold binding rituals.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the rite of the offering for entry," and having touched water; having duly prepared the *puṇyāha* and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) according to the previously mentioned method;

having worshipped Śiva in the form of a seat within the water-pot (*kumbha*) intended for the *rākṣoghna* oblation, using the root-mantras; and having completed the worship; having worshipped Rudra, known by the name Rāvaṇa, in the sword (*khaḍga*), and having completed that worship.

Having consecrated the Goddess of the Astras with the essence of the *likuca* fruit and other substances, having adorned her, and having worshipped her by means of its root, as well as the roots of the seat and the image; having fully honored her with *śāli* rice measured at one *āḍhaka*,
along with cow’s fresh butter, cardamom, and other fragrant substances—

Having prepared food characterized by the auspicious signs of food and endowed with various substances, and having adorned it; having worshipped and fully honored [the deity] with the root-mantra of the Pāśupata weapon, preceded by the seat-mantra and the image-mantra;

and having collected turmeric water together with pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit for the sake of the offering (*bali*), [one should prepare] well-husked *śāli* rice grains, measured in the quantity of a *bhāra*.

Having gathered various condiments together, and having worshipped the drum with the *āditya* [mantra]... having struck it with the mantra; likewise, having gathered all substances such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, preceded by a prayer to Īśvara, [he placed] the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) upon a palanquin.
Having mounted [the platform] and taken up a sword with his right hand, preceded by the sound of all musical instruments, he goes out from the temple; [there he prepares] brick powder,
turmeric powder, conch powder, flour powder, the general *arghya* offering, the *puṇyāha* water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the sacrificial oblation (*havir*).

Earthenware vessels, pieces of pumpkin, turmeric-colored drinks, fragrant flowers, incense, and so forth; coconut blossoms, *pūka* flowers, young coconut fruits, *jaṃbhīra* fruits, plantain fruits, *laḍḍuka* sweets, *modaka* sweets, cakes, *vaṭaka* balls, coconut-based preparations, lamps fed with the five oils and burning with flames, parched grain flour, incense-lamps, and other such articles for worship.

Having gathered these, and having brought the other offerings for the lamps of goats and so forth, one should go to the Brahma-sthāna. There, having washed with cow-dung water a square altar (*vedikā*) that is four finger-breadths high and two *tāla*s in width and length, and having sprinkled it with the *puṇyāha* water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the *arghya* water while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with powdered turmeric from conch-shell powder and the like.

Having prepared [the site] with two verses, having scattered parched grain and flowers, and having supplicated the Lord of the Weapon (Astra-īśvara), one should place a five-fold bundle of *darbha* grass endowed with the proper characteristics in the center of that mandala;
then, sitting upon a tortoise-seat (*kūrma-āsana*) facing north—

One should worship: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Mahālakṣmī; obeisance to the form of Mahālakṣmī; Oṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.
