Having invoked her with the words, "In this installation, I invoke Mahālakṣmī," and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, one should worship her with white cloth, white perfumes, fragrant flowers, lotuses, and saffron. Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should display the lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*). To its east and so forth: "Obeisance to Śarākī."

Salutation to Mahāvīreśvarī; salutation to Vijayī; salutation to Jayī; salutation to Mahāmātra; salutation to Pāṇī; salutation to Vāgvādinī. Having thus invoked these [deities] and worshipped them, one should take pure food—the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consisting of rice grains equal in measure to a *śivataṇḍula*—mixed with curd and clarified butter. Oṃ Śrīṃ.

Having offered the *bali* with the mantra "Mahālakṣmyai svāhā" upon the coconut husk over the spread *darbha* grass, and having satiated [the deity] eighteen times with the *bali* while reciting "idaṃ te vānam" eighteen times;
(L3) then, taking pieces of black sugarcane, plantains, sweetmeats (*modaka*), parched rice flour (*lāja-saktu*), coconut flowers, and betel nut flowers from atop the husk.

O Mahālakṣmī, you who reside in this village, protect, protect us and those like us! Having taken five lamps fed with five kinds of oil, five-flamed, along with citron fruits, betel leaves, and fragrant substances,
[grant us] the cessation of our misdeeds.

Having prayed, "Protect! Protect! and having prayed, "Be attentive," and having completed the worship and restrained [the senses], one should proceed to the station of Indra, preceded by the King of Weapons (Astrarāja). This is the worship of Mahālakṣmī. Then, having arrived at the station of Indra, one should construct there an altar two cubits in measure and four finger-breadths high; having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and water while reciting the Astra-mantra, upon that—

Having drawn an eight-cornered maṇḍala mixed with conch powder and other powders, having scattered sandalwood, saffron, and fragrant flowers upon it, and having placed a tuft made of five *darbha* grasses therein,
[one should say]: "Homage to the seat for all sacrifices."

"Salutations to all who are of the form of the senses! I invoke all the Yakṣas. Having worshipped them with the ritual services beginning with invocation, having honored them with Karavīra flowers accompanied by dark-colored garments, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and fragrant substances, and having offered incense and lamps, one should take milk-rice (pāyasa) measured by Śiva, along with all kinds of side dishes, fruits, and so forth, accompanied by all musical instruments such as the kettledrum (bherī).

Oṃ hāṃ! To the flaming-eyed ones; to those with upward-pointing hair; to the yakṣas who are greatly terrifying, manifold, and possessed of great strength and prowess—svāhā! Having thus offered the bali-oblation upon the darbha grass spread over the mat... this is for you.

Having offered a drink with the words "pānam" (drink), and having satiated [the deities] ten times with handfuls of turmeric-water while reciting, "I satisfy those worthy of all sacrifices," he should take these— pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, plantain fruit, pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa*, sweetmeats (*modaka*), parched rice flour (*lāja-saktu*), coconut, flowers, and betel nut— and offer them to the Yakṣas upon the mat.

Having made this request: "O Yakṣas, protect, protect this village-dwelling worthy one, myself and others! Having taken these five lamps smeared with five oils, rice, fruit, betel, and red karavīra flowers and so forth, grant protection preceded by the removal of our misfortunes," and having caused the offering of a goat and other victims, [one says]: "O Yakṣas, leave this place!"
"By the command of Śiva, you Yakṣas Veśaku and Deśika, quickly vacate Indra’s abode and go to the mountain peak! Having thus dismissed them and completed the worship,
he should proceed to the fire-pit together with the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).

In the place of the fire, upon an altar measuring two cubits in length and four finger-breadths in height, which has been consecrated with the *puṇyāha* rite, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and sprinkled with water empowered by the *astra-mantra*, one should prepare a mixture of turmeric powder combined with the dust of bricks and other materials; having placed a bundle of grass (*kūrca*) therein and adorned it with fragrant substances such as perfumes and flowers, [one should recite]: "Salutation to the seat of all *rākṣasas*."
Salutation to the form of all *rākṣasas*; salutation to all *rāk�sasa*s.

(l4) Having worshipped with red sandalwood, red *akṣata*, fragrant flowers, and *japā* flowers, [reciting] "I invoke all *rākṣasas* into this," and having offered incense and lamps, [he recites] the *śivaparimita*... (l5)

Taking auspicious items—namely parched rice flour, turmeric powder, hibiscus flowers, honey, cakes, curd, ghee, and the five products of the cow—one should say: "Oṃ, salutation to you, the fierce-angry ones; to those of terrible form;

to those with fanged teeth; to the fearsome ones; salutation to those of great strength and prowess! O Rākṣasas, please accept this worship along with its condiments and this sacrificial offering. Thus [one should offer] upon the *darbha* grass.

Having set it down and offered the beverage with the words, "This drink is for you," and having gratified all the *rākṣasas* ten times by pouring water from a turmeric-infused vessel with joined palms while saying, "I satisfy [you]," he should place upon a mat all the fruits such as pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa*, as well as flowers, into a coconut jar. Then, with a *pāraśava* [officiant], he should offer a red ram and a cock, which have been sprinkled with the five oils and placed upon the five flames and so forth.

Having cut [the thread], and having taken these offerings, one should pray: "Protect me from this! "O you protectors, O hosts, you who are fierce in anger and possessed of great strength, quickly [act] by the command of Śiva! (l3)

"O you who are without Rakshasas, who move within the domain of fire, leave the southeast corner and go to the mountain forest. Having thus dismissed them, they proceeded with the sound of all musical instruments to the region of Dharmarāja.

There, upon an altar sprinkled with *pañcagavya*, unhusked rice, and water consecrated by the *puṇyāha* rite—resembling the surface of a mirror two cubits in measure and four fingers high—they [applied] powders of the night.

Having drawn a nine- or ten-cornered figure mixed with brick powder, having scattered fragrant flowers and perfumed substances, and having placed a bundle of grass (*kūrca*), one should invoke [the deity] with: "Obeisance to the seat of all beings; obeisance to the form of all beings; obeisance to all beings. Then, having worshipped [the deity] with a seat and so forth, with black cloth, black incense, and *pāṭala* flowers.

Having offered incense and lamps, and having placed a coconut-pitcher before that [deity], and having laid darbha grass upon it, one should take an oblation measured for Śiva— saturated with ghee, milk, and curd,
and mixed with sesame, cakes, *tulasī*, and lotus flowers— and recite: "Oṃ, salutation to you all."

"To the beings of great strength and prowess, equal to Maghavan, with cruel fangs, and terrifying—svāhā! Having offered the *bali* accompanied by the sound of all musical instruments such as kettledrums (*bherī*), and having presented this drink (*pānaka*) to them, one should satisfy all the beings ten times with handfuls of turmeric-water, saying, "I satisfy all the beings. Then, [one should place] all the flowers upon the mat (*kaṭa*).

Having offered all fruits, all perfumes, (l3) and jambīra fruits; having offered pieces of kūśmāṇḍa gourd; [to those] spirits who [accept] this worship, these substances, and this black ram sacrifice (*bali*) sprinkled with the five oils and consisting of the five fires and so forth—(l4)

Having taken [the offerings] and prayed, "Protect us!", one should say: "O spirits, you who are satisfied by the bali-offerings and you who are swift-moving, all of you, by the command of Śiva, go quickly toward the southern direction; having released the southern quarter, proceed to the mountain peak. Having thus offered the worship, one should depart preceded by the King of Weapons (Astrarāja). Thus [it is said].
Born from the maṇḍala of the elements;

(l6) then, having gone to the region of Nairṛti, one should scatter fragrant substances and flowers upon a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, using powders of bricks and other materials, while drawing the solar diagram (*sūryakoṇabali*). (l7)

Having placed a *kūrca* [seat-grass bundle] and invoked [the deity] with: "Obeisance to the seat of all *piśācas*; obeisance to the form of all *piśācas*; obeisance to all *piśācas*; I invoke all *piśācas*," one should perform the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth.

Then, having worshipped with saffron-colored cloth, red sandalwood paste, red unbroken rice (*akṣata*), blue *arka* flowers, incense, and lamps, one should offer *kṛsarā* rice mixed with ghee and honey.

Taking an offering mixed with cakes, sweets, red flowers, black *yoni*-flowers, and *śrī*-flowers, one should say: "Oṃ, homage to all you piśācas—those with thin bellies, those of long form, those of cloud-like form—to all piśācas, svāhā! Having thus offered the oblation upon *darbha* grass, (l. 3).

Having offered the drink with the words, "This is your drink," and having satiated all the piśācas ten times by pouring water from a turmeric decoction with cupped hands while saying, "I satisfy you all," he should place all kinds of edibles,

all flowers, and all fruits upon the mat. Then, he should present this offering, distinguished by a sacrifice of boar, cock, and pig, together with five lamps fed with five oils and possessing five flames.

(15) Having accepted the worship and having prayed, "Protect us!", [he says: "O Piśācas, swift-moving ones, by the command of Śiva, quickly release [him] and go to the southwest corner in the midst of the forest! (16)
One should release [the offering]. This is the bali for Nirṛti and the Piśācas.

(Worship of the Brahma-rākṣasa in the western direction)—Then, having gone to the western region, on a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) with the previously described characteristics, purified with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, [one should draw] with turmeric powder mixed with conch-shell and other materials.

Having drawn a seven-cornered or a universal (viśva) cornered [mandala], having scattered fragrant substances such as saffron, and having placed a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca), one should invoke [the deity] with:
"Obeisance to the seat of the Brahma-rākṣasa; obeisance to the form of all Brahma-rākṣasas; obeisance to all Brahma-rākṣasas; I invoke all the Brahma-rākṣasas. Thus, having invoked them...

Having performed the installation and worshipped with black cloth, white perfumes, *puṇnāga* flowers, and so forth, and having offered incense and lamps; and having taken ghee along with curd-soaked cakes, solid sweetmeats (*modaka*), flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), parched grain (*lāja*), turmeric powder, *rājapuṣpa*, and molasses-rice (*gulānna*); [one recites]: *Oṃ namo bhagavadbhyaḥ dīrghadaṃṣṭrebhyaḥ*.

Having offered the *bali* with the words, "To the great-bellied ones, to the great heroes, to all the *brahmarākṣasas*," and having presented the drink with the words, "This is your drink," one should satisfy all the *brahmarākṣasas* ten times by pouring handfuls of yellow water while saying, "I satisfy [you]. Then, having placed fruits, all ritual substances, and flowers upon the mat, one says: "O *brahmarākṣasas*, accept this worship."

Having accepted the offering consisting of a white ram together with five lamps whose flames are fed by five kinds of oil, and having entreated them, saying, "Protect us!", [one says]: "By the command of Śiva, you obstructing *brahmarākṣasa*s, quickly [depart]!"
"Having been released from the abode of Varuṇa, go to the shore of the ocean. Thus one should dismiss [the deity]. This concludes the worship of the Brahma-rākṣasa in the western direction.
(Worship of Kālī in the northwest corner)—Then, having gone to the northwest corner, on the previously mentioned altar...

Having sprinkled [the ground] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, and having drawn a sixteen-cornered [mandala] with powders of bricks and the like, one should scatter fragrant flowers and perfumed materials and place a bundle of grass (*kūrca*) therein. [One should then recite:
"Salutation to the seat of Sarvakālī; salutation to the form of Sarvakālī; salutation to Sarvakālī. Having thus invoked her, saying, "I invoke Sarvakālī,"...

Having worshipped with yellow garments, *gandharāja* flowers, and incense, and having offered incense and lamps, one should take fragrant rice mixed with this powder—consisting of parched grain, flowers, black gram, mung bean, mustard, and black pepper—along with cakes and excellent pure food smeared with curd and honey. Then [one should recite]: *Oṃ namo bhavadbhyaś caṇḍakopebhyaḥ*.

Having offered [the oblation] upon *darbha* grass with the words: "Svāhā to those who bear spears and skull-bowls; to those of various forms; to those with upraised hair; to the Kulodarīs; to the Vetālas, Muṇḍas, and Kālīs," and having presented it with the words, "This drink is for you," he should satisfy all the Kālīs ten times with handfuls of turmeric water, saying, "With this handful, I satisfy all the Kālīs," while standing upon a mat.
Having offered all kinds of edible foods, all fragrant substances, all flowers, and all fruits, one should pray: "O you who are all-Kālīs, accept this *bali* offering and protect us!
Then, by the command of Śiva, you Kālīs [should depart] quickly.
One should dismiss them by saying, "O harmers of living beings, release the wind-bull and go into the middle of the forest. This is the worship of Kālī in the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa).

(Uttaraśasara-lipūjā) — Now, having gone to a northern region endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, one should draw an eighteen-cornered [mandala] upon a consecrated altar using turmeric powder mixed with the powders of conch-shell and other substances. Then, having strewn all types of fragrant materials and flowers, [one should place] a *kūrca*...
Having placed [the vessel] there, [one should offer]: "Homage to Sarvasaralī, the seat! Homage to Sarvasaralī, the form! Homage to Sarvasaralī! I invoke Sarvasaralī.

Having invoked her and worshipped her with variegated garments and variegated flowers, and having offered incense and lamps, one should take plantain fruit, salt, sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*), curd, ghee, and pure food soaked in honey, and [recite]: "Oṃ, homage to the Śaralīs!"

Having offered [the oblation] with the words: "Svāhā to the long-bodied ones, with curved fangs, black-colored, possessing great strength and prowess, and all the arrows!"—and having presented the drink with the words: "This is your drink"—he satisfies all the arrows with handfuls of turmeric water.

Having thus offered libations ten times; having presented pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and all other flowers and fruits upon the *ṭopa*; and having prayed: "O Śaralī, accept this worship, as well as this *bali* offering consisting of a lamp with five flames fed by oil along with a ram and a cock, and protect us"—[one says]: "By the command of Śiva, you are indeed slayers of living beings."
Having dismissed them with the words, "Leave this gentle place and go to a desolate region," [performs] the worship of the northern arrow-line.
(The Kāmikapraveśabali):

Now, having gone to the northeast corner, one should draw a thirty-six-cornered [mandala] on the sacrificial altar (*vedi*)—which has been sprinkled with water during the *puṇyāha* ceremony according to the previously mentioned characteristics—using a powder mixed with conch-shell and other substances. Then, all flowers and all fragrant materials, leaving none remaining, [should be prepared].

Having scattered [the offerings] and cast down the ritual grass (*kūrca*), [one says]: "Homage to the seat of all Bhairavas! Homage to the form of all Bhairavas! Homage to All! Having thus invoked with the words, "I invoke all the Bhairavas," [one performs] the installation and so forth.

Having worshipped with white garments, white perfumes, and white *arka* flowers; having offered incense and lamps; having spread *darbha* grass upon the ground with *oṃ*; and having taken red food mixed with curd, honey, *vaṭaka* cakes, sesame, *apūpa* cakes, and various side dishes—free from any remaining fragments of other substances—one recites: *Oṃ namaḥ sarvabhairavebhyaḥ krūrebhyaḥ daṃṣṭrebhyaḥ virūpebhyaḥ namaḥ bhayānakebhyaḥ*.

Having offered the *bali* on *darbha* grass with the mantra "Parakādisarvabhairavebhyaḥ svāhā," and having propitiated all the *Bhairavas* ten times with collyrium and water infused with turmeric, saying "I propitiate all the *Bhairavas*," [one offers] this drink.

Having offered the drink, and having placed upon the mat all fragrant flowers, citron and other fruits, all kinds of edibles, and the finest of all musical instruments; [he says: "O Bhairavas, accept this worship—this offering of a black goat whose limbs are free from defects, sprinkled with the five oils, illuminated by the five flames, and provided with all excellent substances."

Having thus entreated them, saying, "Protect us and our many other devotees," he dismissed them, saying: "O Virūpa, Bhairava, and the others, by the command of Śiva, depart quickly from the northeastern quarter and go to the shore of Udaya. Having thus sent them away, [he addressed] the Yakṣas and the others once again.
One should pray:
"O Yakṣas and other malevolent beings dwelling here on this earth, please grant me passage as I travel upon this ground, like a swift current carrying one away. Having prayed thus:

Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and others, and having presented it to the Brahmins, he should quickly go elsewhere, put on fresh garments, and perform his bath. Then, preceded by bathing, he should apply the sacred ash (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) for all the disciples and their attendants.

Having held the Aghora-weapon mantra and having recited it one hundred and fifty times, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should enter the temple after bowing to the Lord and reciting the mantra "sahasrāṇi sahasra" [ten million times]. He should then pray for his desired object. Thus ends the offering of the entry-bali according to the Kāmika-tantra.

Now follows the *rakṣoghnahoma* (the oblation for the destruction of demons): On that night, the preceptor, together with the *mūrtipas*, having performed the bathing and other rites and having donned the sacred ashes (*vibhūti*), shall adorn himself with the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and other ornaments; facing north, he shall sit upon a tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) and perform the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*).

Having prepared the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), having worshipped Vighneśa according to the rules, having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking one's head [in salutation], having prostrated before the Guru, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs,
he makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for this Goddess, the venerable Mother Kāntimatī.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the purpose of warding off evil planets such as *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, and *rākṣasas* that have taken possession [of the village] through the decay and distortion of the eight previous bonds and subsequent characteristics,
and for the increase of the deities who protect the village,
I shall perform the *aṣṭabandhana-aṅgārākṣoghna-homa*," and having touched water, [he should proceed] with the *puṇyāha* and *pañcagavya* according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having prepared [the site] as distinguished by deities who destroy demons, and having consecrated the materials for worship, the materials for the fire-oblation, and the ground itself, one should place eight-petaled lotuses made from flour-powder and turmeric powder before Śiva,
in the center, the south, and the north.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) upon those [sites] with cow dung and other materials, one should take a consecrated jar (*kumbha*) that is filled with one *droṇa* of grain, possesses the proper characteristics, is well-formed, washed, and wrapped with thread.

Having filled the jar with water while reciting the mantra "āpo vā idam" preceded by the ritual tracing (*ullekhana*), and having established it, one should perform the rites up to the offering of flowers within it, using grass-bunches (*kūrca*) and so forth, accompanied by their respective mantras.
Having adorned [it], having placed a wooden pedestal in the form of a tripod upon the sacrificial mound to the south,
and having laid a cloth over it, and having established a coconut together with its husk upon that, and having adorned [it],
one should arrange a wooden pedestal in the form of a tripod upon the sacrificial mound to the north.

Having placed a red cloth upon that [altar], and having established upon it the sword of destruction (*nidhanakhaḍga*), which has been purified by the four refinements (*saṃskāra*) such as washing and inspection, consecrated with the *astra-mantra*, and treated with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), auspicious water, and so forth; and having adorned it— then, having prepared either a triangular or a quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the eastern part of the water-pot (*kumbha*).

Having performed the rites from the purification of oneself up to the purification of the mantra, having applied a *tilaka* on the forehead with sandalwood paste, and having placed a flower on the head, one should worship externally with the words "Homage to the Self of Speech (*girātmane namaḥ*") and honor it with a flower. Below the principal jar (*pradhānakumbha*), one should worship with:
"Homage to Ananta," "Homage to Dharma," and "Homage to Jñāna."
Salutation to Vairāgya. Salutation to Aiśvarya. Salutation to Padma. Salutation to the seat of the deity who destroys Rākṣasas. The Meditation:
[One should meditate upon the Lord] who bears a trident, a skull-bowl, an axe, and likewise a hand-drum;
who possesses a formidable form, has three eyes, and bears the moon upon his crest. (Verse 3)
The great Lord, with fangs bared and his curved brow dancing with a fierce glare,
was devouring spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and other such beings.
Having thus meditated upon Mahādeva, who has the appearance of the submarine fire and is burning the three worlds, one should contemplate him as the destroyer of Rākṣasas.

Thus, "Salutation to the form that slays the Rākṣasas. Having offered the eyes with "Salutation to the eyes," and having filled his joined palms with flowers, he offers the oblation while reciting the mantra: "I sprinkle the slayer of Rākṣasas at night. Then, with the mudrās for invocation and so forth, he says: "I invoke the Supreme Lord, the slayer of Rākṣasas, into this pitcher."

Having requested [the deity] and performed the installation (*sthāpanā*) and other rites, one offers the *arghya* for the welcome. The prayer is: "O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World! Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras upon the locations starting from the heart and ending with the hands, and having established oneness with the root mantra, one should perform protection, the sprinkling of water (*avakuṇṭhana*), the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and offer the *mahāmudrā*. Then: *namaḥ svadhā*.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, ending with *svāhā*, and having presented water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), clothing, fragrance, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), flowers, incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), and the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), while reciting the root mantra; having prayed for one’s desired object, performed the silent recitation (*japa*), and made the formal announcement (*nivedya*); [one should then] worship the seat—beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti—on the coconut situated on the pedestal to the south, while reciting the root mantra; and having applied the five Brahmans, [one should offer] "Salutation to the Seat of Śiva" (*śivāsanāya namaḥ*). Śiva...
Salutation to the Embodiment. One should meditate thus:

"O Śiva, I meditate upon You, seated on a lotus throne, possessing an auspicious body, with five lotus-faces, ten arms, and three eyes; and in each of Your hands, O Auspicious One, You hold a plough, a battle-axe, a sword, and a thunderbolt."

Having meditated thus: "He gradually assumes the bell, lotus, and *jaṅghā-kuśa*, which are smooth and well-polished," one should say: "Homage to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*); homage to the eyes. Having thus bestowed the eyes, one should fill the hollowed palms with flowers and recite: *ākvāhaṃ* (or *kvāvahaṃ*) *tryambakam*.

Reciting the mantra, "We worship the fragrant one who increases nourishment; may I be freed from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, through the immortal," he invokes [the deity] with the *Sadyojāta* face while focusing on the root [of the coconut]. Having invoked, saying, "I invoke the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva in this coconut," and having performed the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth, he offers the welcoming water (*svāgatārghya*) with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, remain present within this image with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship.

Having thus made the request, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras in the locations of the heart and so forth, having established oneness with the root mantra, having protected [the deity], having sprinkled [water] around [the vessel], having rendered it immortal, and having displayed the great mudrā; having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (*arghya*)—ending with *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*—to the five-faced [deity] purified by *māyā*... [he offers] the residence, [and then] to the Blessed One, the consecration, clothing, unguents, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and lamps.

Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) with the root mantra, having performed the *ārātrika* rite, and having recited the mantra, one should pray at the altar (*vedi*). Then, on the northern pedestal (*pīṭha*), having worshipped the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Padmā, one should worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*):
"Salutation to Mahādevī; salutation to Vāgdevī; salutation to Pārvatī; salutation to Kṛttikāyinī; salutation to Maheśinī; salutation to Śaktaśakti."

Salutations! Salutations to Kālikā! Salutations to Caṇḍikā! In the midst of that, salutations to Vīraśakti! Salutations to Khaḍgecchāsanā! Salutations to Khaḍgamūrti! Salutations to Khaḍgeśa! The Meditation (Dhyāna):
[I meditate upon her] whose hands brandish a sword and a skull-cup, and who is clothed in a tiger skin.
Having meditated thus: [on him] with a loud laugh, blazing faces, and all his mouths wide open;
adorned with jewel earrings and armlets, resembling a blazing fire—[one should say]:
"Homage to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*), and having worshipped thus, [one says]: "Homage to the eyes," [and worships] the eyes.

Having offered [these], and having filled his joined palms with flowers, while reciting the *kṣurikā* weapon-mantra of Khaḍgeśa, he should invoke the venerable Rudra named Khaḍgarāvaṇa into this sword.

Having performed the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth, he should offer a welcoming *arghya* with the Heart-mantra. Then, having applied the Heart-mantra and the others to the respective locations such as the heart, and having established oneness [with the deity] by means of the Root-mantra.

Having performed the protections, the binding with the *avakuṇṭhana* [mudrā], and the rites of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and having bound the five-faced [mudrā], one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the *arghya* offering, ending with the utterances *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*. Having offered the services beginning with the fragrant paste (*snānoddhar-tana*) and ending with the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), using the root mantra, and having recited it and presented the food offering (*naivedya*), [one proceeds] to the east— [Fragmentary text from page 76a, line 1]

Salutation to Asitāṅga Bhairava. In the intermediate direction—salutation to Rudra Bhairava. In the south—salutation to Caṇḍa Bhairava. To the Rākṣasa—salutation to Krodha Bhairava. In the west—salutation to Unmatta Bhairava. In the northwest—salutation to Kapāla Bhairava. In the north—salutation to Bhiṣṇa Bhairava. In the northeast—salutation to Saṃhāra Bhairava. These are the eight Bhairavas.

Having performed the worship separately, beginning with the invocation and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*), one should duly establish the fire in the previously situated square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), preceded by the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*). Then, according to the procedure for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*),
[the rites] from the *ādhāna* up to the *vivāha* [are to be performed].

Having performed [the preliminary rites], having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti in the midst of the fire, having invoked Śrī Rudra in the form of the deity who slays the Rākṣasas, and having completed the worship up to the lamps,

one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Kṣurikā weapon mantra; then, offering one oblation each with the heart and other mantras corresponding to those respective [limbs].
Now follows his fire sacrifice (homa): with leaves of the *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, and *bilva* trees,

one should perform [the oblation] twenty-five times for each of these individually— namely, for the *Śivāstra*, the *Pāśupatāstra*, the *Aghorāstra*, the *Vyomāstra*, the *Kṣurikāstra*, and the Root-mantra (*mūla*) respectively.
The oblation (*homa*) is performed with the *savyā* [mantra]; having offered separately ten times each with the previously mentioned mantras,

and having offered separately ten times with the mantra "To Vāstoṣpati," and having offered ten times with the "Brahmajijñāna" mantra, and having offered separately ten times each, one offers *plakṣa* wood fuel sticks with the "Pari no Rudra" mantra.
Having offered ten oblations;
(l2) having offered ten oblations each of *udumbara* and *bilva* fuel-sticks separately with the *tryambaka* mantra; then the *vyāhṛti* oblation; then the *ājya* oblation;
for the principal [rite], one hundred oblations with the *kṣurikāstra* mantra. (l3)

For each of the eight Bhairavas, there are ten oblations. With the *Brahmasūkta*, there are ten oblations. With the *Varuṇasūkta* and clarified butter (*ājya*), there are ten oblations. With the *Viṣṇusūkta* and clarified butter, there are ten oblations. (L4) With the *Tryambaka* mantra and clarified butter, there are ten oblations. Then follows the *vyāhṛti* for the principal deity; with the *Kṣurikāstra* mantra and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), there are one hundred oblations. For the eight Bhairavas...

With each respective mantra, ten oblations are offered individually. There is an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) with the *Brahmasūkta*; an oblation of cooked rice with the *Varuṇasūkta*; an oblation of cooked rice with the *Viṣṇusūkta*; and an oblation of cooked rice with the *Rudrasūkta*.
[The oblation] with the *Brahmasūkta*...

Having offered oblations with each individual mantra, one should offer ten oblations of *caru* with the *tryambaka* mantra. Then follows the *vyāhṛti*-oblation. In the same manner, the *lāja*-oblation is performed.
Then the *vyāhṛti*. The *sarṣapa*-oblation.
Then the *vyāhṛti*. Then the sesame (*tila*) oblation. Then the bamboo-shoot (*vaiṇava*) oblation. Then the *māṣa*-oblation. Then the *mudga*-oblation. Then the *śrī*. Then—

The oblation of plantain fruit: in this manner, having offered all the substances individually ten times each with the Kaṣūrikā mantra, preceded by the Vyāhṛti oblations; thereafter, [the offerings of] sesame oil, coconut oil, Madhūka oil, castor oil, and neem oil.

Having combined [the substances], one hundred oblations are offered with the *kṣurikā* mantra; for each of the eight Bhairavas, one oblation is offered with their respective mantras. Then follows the *vyāhṛti* homa. Black pepper, cumin, and cotton seeds—having combined these, one hundred oblations are offered with the *kṣurikā* mantra; for each of the eight Bhairavas, one oblation is offered with their respective mantras. Then follows the *vyāhṛti* homa. Now...
By means of mustard seeds, honey, clarified butter, parched rice flour, and *sukra*—

thus having combined these seven substances in a quantity measuring two *prasthas*, one should offer them into the fire with the mantra *kuṇṣvapājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthivīm*. One shall not be stained by the dust of the earth.

Entering into these three worlds, you run with the wooden vessel; you are the one who knows the *rakṣases* through the sacrifices. Your flames fly swiftly, reaching out boldly as they blaze. O Agni, let your tongue consume him;
being unrestrained, release your flames in all directions. Release your piercing touches; become most swift against his life-force, for you are the undeceivable protector of us who are far away.
May the one who seeks to harm us be driven away; may he not find a path through our distress.

Rise up, O Agni, and stretch yourself out; burn down another as an enemy, O you of the sharp weapon! He who has brought us misery with his kindling-stick—burn him down, O devouring one, as he lies with his tongue turned downward. Stand upright and strike back at us!

O Agni, manifest your divine powers; let the unsteady ones be cast down. Distinguish between those kin and those who are not kin among our bodies; choose the enemies as your prey. He who is present at the assembly knows the assembly... [he is] most excellent. Like a bird, he utters songs for your sacred prayer (*brahman*). All riches and splendors have settled upon him, the wise one who shines toward the heavens. Let there be sweat for you, O Agni.

Having praised you with the constant oblation, may he prosper in his own home through long life. May all days be auspicious for him; may that vision be ever-present. I praise your benevolence; may our voices resound like the wind. May the winds blow favorably for us.
This is the song: O you with fine horses and a good chariot, crush [the enemy];

let me not cause the kṣatriyas to wither; O son of Dr̥ḍhacyut, may I find you here in many places—O lord of the house, dwelling at night and by day, O you who are mindful. Playing, may your vital breaths be well-disposed toward me; let not your splendors be broken.

They stand firm among the people—those whose horses, O Agni, approach with beautiful bridles as if on a well-constructed chariot. You become the protector of such a one, the friend of him who from the beginning has delighted in this human [path] with upright intent.
I shatter the great [obstacles]. 4.

Let not that [hostility] of my father Gautama follow me through his words of kinship. O Hotṛ, most youthful one, of skillful intellect, take heed of this our speech among all living beings. Sleepless, crossing over, most gracious, not failing in their bounty, nor like wolves—those most excellent ones, your protectors, sitting down unwearied, O Agni, may they guard us with your protection. Those guardians who do not neglect you... what is yours...
O Agni, seeing [the truth], the Aduryas protected it;
they guarded the well-performed deeds from all sides. Let those who desire to harm not reach the world of the virtuous. 5.

O Bhūḥ, we have been made truly fortunate by you; through your guidance, may we obtain dark-hued steeds. May both blessings be granted to us in truth, for you, O Father, perform what is dear to our ears. O Agni, with this fuel we shall worship you; taking up the recited Soma-verse, burn away the malicious ones and protect us from the Rākṣasas and from deceit.
May he, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the vigorous one in the race, the friend, the refuge, come for our protection. May Agni, well-kindled and most firm, grant us fuel by day.
(6) May he protect us from harm at night. With his great light, Agni shines; through his vast power, he makes all things visible. He overcomes the divine illusions of the enemy.
I cast the Rakṣasa into your two sharpened horns.
And the roaring ones, with sharp weapons, shall go to heaven; they slay the Rakṣasa even in his intoxication. His splendors shatter, and the godless obstructors flee away.

Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation; having offered the oblations beginning with the *jaya* and ending with the *vara*; having offered one hundred oblations with the five-weapon mantra (*pañcāstra*); immediately thereafter, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*; having worshipped the fire; having united the deities residing in the fire with those on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*); and having presented the offering (*bali*) into the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should pay homage to Śiva and pray for one’s heart’s desire. Thus concludes the *rakṣoghnahoma*.

The Prasannapūjā— [this is] the worship. Then the preceptor, adorned with the five-fold ornaments, together with the image-protectors, having renounced food, and preceded by the recitation of auspicious blessings, enters the temple of Śiva and [stands] before Śiva.

Having sat in the tortoise posture (*kūrmāsana*), having performed the ritual identification with the deity (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having prayed to Vighneśvara; having washed the vessel for the general offering (*sāmānyārghyapātra*) with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*); having placed it upon the support (*ādhāra*) with the heart mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*); having protected and concealed it; having sprinkled the articles of worship with the weapon mantra; and having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*)—[of the rite] which is about to be performed...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In order to complete [this rite] without obstacles, I shall first perform the worship of Mahāgaṇapati," and having performed the rites from the water-offering up to the recitation (*japa*), he should pray to Vighneśvara and,
having received permission, proceed.

Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), [one should say]: "Śiva, Śiva! By the command of Śambhu, on this auspicious lunar day, in this region, in this kingdom—for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects by means of the cessation of all misfortunes for all devotees, beginning with the primary Śaivas—and especially in this village, for the purpose of preventing famine and unrest from this land."
By the grace of Sāmba-Parameśvara, for the sake of accomplishing all desires of bipeds and quadrupeds, and for the attainment of every fruit— of this God of gods,
together with his consort Kāntimatī.

Today, as a preliminary limb (*saṃkocāṅga*) for the Śiva-sacrifice of the restoration of the ancient bonds (*jīrṇoddhārāṣṭabandhana*), I shall perform the *prasannapūjā* for the sake of removing the defects that arose when [the deity] reached this state through the wearing away of the medicinal herbs applied during the previous eight-fold binding of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, who is Śiva himself, beginning from Saura and ending with Caṇḍa. As a limb of that [rite], preceded by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and preceded by the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)...

(13) I shall perform the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) and the installation of the nine jars (*navakalaśasthāpana*). Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the sake of the auspicious day, and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus there, [I shall proceed] with the *Śivagāyatrī*... (14)

One should worship the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*). With *oṃ hāṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*, one should wash the *vardhanī* vessel, place it in the center of the lotus, and fill it with scented water. *Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
*Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ nandine namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*. [Offering] at the nose.
Salutation to Viśveśvara; salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Yamunā;

salutation to Narmadā; salutation to Kāverī; salutation to Godāvarī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Sindhu. Having thus worshipped, having protected [the area], having sprinkled [it with water], having rendered it nectar-like, [one offers] the seat and so forth.

Having performed the worship with the sixteen-fold offerings, the preceptor should say: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to all the Brahmins! Permitted by you, I shall cause the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. The Brahmins should reply: "Oṃ haṃ, let it be recited. [The preceptor says: "May you, sirs, pronounce 'well-being' for the rite of the propitiatory offering (*prasannapūjā*). "Well-being for the rite of the propitiatory offering! "Oṃ, peace, peace!"

(12) Having sprinkled the articles for worship with water consecrated by the *puṇyāhavācana* rite and with the mantra "vāstoṣpate," [he recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ, [this is] the seat for the Mūlamūrti-mantra; Pṛthivī is the seer, and Merupṛṣṭha is the seer. (13)
The meter is Sītala; the deity is Kūrma. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Self (*ātman*); [this is] for the head. The Seer is Ātman, the meter is Puruṣakakṛt, and the deity is Paramātman.

May those beings who are present, and those beings who dwell upon the earth, depart by the command of Śiva—those beings who are creators of obstacles. Then, having prepared a beautiful seat: *Oṃ hāṃ*.

"Astrāya hūṃ phaṭ. Thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). "Oṃ hrīṃ kavacāya vauṣaṭ. This is the covering (*sañchādana*). "Oṃ hāṃ tejo jvalaprākārāya namaḥ. This is the encircling with the rampart (*prākāraveṣṭana*). Now, one should perform the application of ashes (*bhasmadhāra*).

Just as one takes ash purified according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*), consecrates it with the *saṃhitā* mantra, and then purifies that which is not yet purified by means of the [kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti: *oṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*;
*oṃ hiṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ*.

Having purified [it] with "Oṃ, salutation to Śāntyatītakalā," and having taken up the ashes, one holds them in the left hand with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Heart. Then, with "Oṃ hāṃ, Phaṭ to the Weapon," one expels the quality of sound by means of the upward stroke (*udghāta*),
because of its finality and impurity.

Having abandoned form, one should meditate on the nature of the supreme ether and the elements, characterized by permanence, purity, and pervasiveness. With the mantra *oṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*, having burned away the defects of the elements residing in the body—initiated by the fire arising from the big toes—one should flood it. Then, having contemplated that the bound form is entirely empty, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ sa śivāya*.

*Vauṣaṭ*. Thus, with streams of nectar flowing from the lotus of the mouth situated at the end of the *śikhā*, having entered through the openings of the converging channels (*saṅkalanāḍī*), he completely bathes the entire body, both internal and external, [and focuses] on the stalk in the heart.
Having established the seat consisting of pure *vidyā*— in the form of a lotus with petals and a pericarp, joined with the *praṇava* [OṂ] which possesses the measures of the lotus and crocodile—

and having meditated upon the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) as descended into its pericarp by means of the four-part *praṇava*, one should [unite] the Self, which is of the nature of Śiva and exists in the form of a seed-syllable located at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), with that [seat] by means of the five-part *praṇava* together with the *ātma-mantra*.

Having expelled the portion belonging to the Asuras in the southwest with the *astra* mantra while performing *pūraka* [breathing], having consecrated it with the root *saṃhitā* mantra, protected it with the *astra*, enveloped it with the *kavaca*, and [sprinkled] water from the base of the fingers with the *hṛdaya* mantra— (p80b, f73a).

Having sprinkled [the ashes] with the root mantra and having rubbed them together, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* beginning from the head: *oṃ hāṃ sauṃ sa śivāya namaḥ*. With the five fingers, one applies it on the head:
*oṃ hiṃ śirase namaḥ*.

With three fingers on the forehead: *oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*. With the middle finger on the right ear: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hiṃ śirase namaḥ*. With three fingers on the forehead: *oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*. With the middle finger on the right ear: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. With the middle finger on the left ear: *oṃ huṃ*.

Salutation to Aghora. On the middle finger of the right hand: *oṃ hāṃ* to the heart, salutation. With three fingers on the heart: *oṃ hūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), salutation. On the right arm: *oṃ haiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), salutation.
On the left arm: *oṃ hoṃ*.

*Oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*—at the navel. *Oṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*—on the right knee. *Oṃ hauṃ netrāya namaḥ*—on the left knee. *Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*—on the back. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ saśivāya vauṣaṭ*. With the remainder [of the ashes], one should sprinkle [the body] with water on the head. This is the procedure for the application of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*).
Now, regarding the holding of the *pavitra* and the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*,
one should establish the general *arghya*.
Then follows the sequence of the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*).

1. Now, purification of oneself (*ātmaśuddhi*); 2. purification of the place (*sthānaśuddhi*); 3. purification of the materials (*dravyaśuddhi*); 4. purification of the mantra (*mantraśuddhi*); 5. purification of the *liṅga*. These are the five purifications.

Having performed these in sequence from the purification of oneself up to the purification of the mantra, one then performs the worship of the conch (*śaṅkhapūjā*). [One prepares] the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*).

Having established [the deity], having deposited the respective substances, having filled [the vessel] with scented water, having performed worship along with the ancillary rites (*sāṅga*), having performed the protections, the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste,
and having placed a flower upon one's own head.

One should contemplate one's own body as having the form of Śiva. Having placed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) to the west of the altar, one should worship the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) according to the rules. (l4) Then, having prepared nine compartments and properly fashioned a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with sacred substances and the like, one should place a water-pot (*kumbha*) in the central compartment; therein are the materials for the pot, such as sandalwood and so forth. (l5)

Having placed [the materials] upon the altar; having arranged the nine gems; having filled [the vessel] with fragrant water filtered through cloth; having adorned it with mango sprouts and coconuts; having established the *vardhanī* jar in the northeast (*īśānī*);
having arranged the five gems; and having installed the jars beginning with Ananteśa in the east and other directions—for all of these...

Having adorned it with mango sprouts, one should worship the central jar there. Having recited [the mantra] beginning with *brahmajijñāna* and ending with *yuvāsuvāsā*, [one should offer salutations]: *oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*; *anantāya namaḥ*; *dharmāya namaḥ*; *jñānāya namaḥ*; *vairāgyāya namaḥ*; *aiśvaryāya namaḥ*.
l1) Homage! Homage to Adharma. Homage to Ignorance. Homage to Non-detachment. Homage to Lack of Sovereignty. Homage to the Upper Covering. Homage to the Lower Covering.
Homage to the Kṛta Age. Homage to the Tretā Age. Homage to the Dvāpara [Age]. l2)
Salutation to the Yuga; salutation to the Kali-yuga; salutation to Skanda; salutation to the seed; salutation to the stalk; salutation to the lotus; salutation to the pericarp;

salutation to the filaments; salutation to the petals; salutation to Vāmā; salutation to Jyeṣṭhā; salutation to Raudrī; salutation to Kālī; salutation to Kalavikaraṇī; salutation to Balavikaraṇī; salutation to Balapramathanī.

Salutation to Manonmanī. Salutation to the solar disc. (L4) Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Salutation to the lunar disc. Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc. Salutation to the fiery disc. Salutation to [the lord] of the fiery disc. (L5)

Salutation to Rudra, the Lord; salutation to the circle of Śakti; salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the circle of Śakti; salutation to the seat of Śiva; salutation to the form of Śiva; salutation to Śiva;
salutation to the head of Īśāna; salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa; salutation to the heart of Aghora; salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva; salutation to the two feet of Sadyojāta.

Having thus performed the placement of the form (*mūrtinyāsa*): *oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ haiṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hiṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*. Then...

Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā*, having performed the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*, and having performed the placements beginning with the *śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā-golaka* and ending with the *daṇḍabhaṅgi-muṇḍabhaṅgi-kalānyāsa*, [one should say] "Salutation to the body of knowledge (*vidyādehāya*)," apply the eye, meditate upon the form, invoke [the deity] into the ninefold form at the end of the crooked one starting from earth (*kṣiti*), and fill the joined palms with flowers up to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having led [the light] forth, having meditated upon it as resembling the fierce sun, having brought it down onto the forehead, and having again led it up to the space between the eyebrows, having meditated upon it as consisting of light within the hollowed palms,
[recite] "āt tvā vahantu... and "triyambakaṃ yajāmahe."

Having invoked [the deity] from the nectar [of the heart] into the root-form of the image, having established it with the *sthāpanī* mudrā, having brought it into proximity with the *sannidhānī*, having firmly fixed it with the *sannidhāpanī*, and having restrained it with the *niṣṭhurā* (or *niṣṭhurā*) mudrā, and with the root mantra *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ*, having offered a welcome and the *arghya* water, having bound the five-faced [mudrā], and having entreated the Lord, the Master of the Entire World, one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Then, one should worship Śiva with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
Having offered incense and lamps, having placed the heart-mantra and other mantras in the locations from the heart to the ends of the hands, having established oneness with the root mantra,
and having protected, concealed, and rendered [the deity] nectar-like, [one should display] the lotus mudrā.

Having displayed the *bimbamudrā* and the *manorathamudrā*, and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*; having worshipped the *Manonmanī* in the *vardhanī* vessel; and having invoked and worshipped Ananteśa and the others starting from the east; and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*; and having worshipped them with the services of perfumes, garlands, and so forth; [one offers] incense and a lamp.

Having given [the offerings], having presented the fruit-offering (*phalanaivedya*), betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), coconut, and so forth, having performed the lustration (*nīrājanā*) and other rites, having offered the *ārātrika* and the daily sacred thread (*nityapavitra*), having fully worshipped Śiva, having offered the recitation (*japa*), and having prayed to Śiva,
[the officiant should perform] the Rudra-recitation (*rudrajapa*) with the Brahmins.

Having had [the fire-pit] prepared, and having obtained permission for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), he should pray to Śiva. Then the preceptor (*ācārya*), having performed the four or eighteen consecrations (*saṃskāra*) in the square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) in front of the altar (*vedikā*), and having worshipped the fire from the laying of the kindling wood (*ādhāna*) up to the marriage rite (*vivāha*), and having worshipped Śiva there in that fire with substances beginning with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and ending with parched grains (*lāja*).
Having offered [the oblation], then having offered to Sviṣṭakṛt,

having offered the *janvādi* and the *abhyatāra*, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship Agni. Having drawn three circles in front of Agni, one should place the *bali* offering there in due order.

Having cast [the materials] and having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should unite the Śiva-fire with the Śiva-pitcher. Then, having performed the worship of the Sun, he should perform the worship of the door. Having sprinkled the door with the Astra-mantra: above the door, "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Saṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. I praise Gaṇeśa, who is like a dark cloud, pot-bellied, and holding [his tusk]. Gaṃ.

Salutations to Gaṇapati. (This text is taken from the second folio. (p83a, l1) In the house of the elements, there are sixteen squares for the ground of the gateway; nine squares shall not be [there]. In the center, there is a ninefold altar together with three squares in the middle; there are nine sacrificial pits and five Śiva-maṇḍapas. (l2)

The ritual procedure: the pitcher of Prāgbhūta; likewise the pitcher of Āgneya in the south; the Veda of Dākṣiṇya in the southwest (Niṛti); likewise the pitcher of Agni; then the sixfold [pitchers] of Aruṇī and Aśvinī; the Yuga-pitcher in the north (Soma); and the triple pitcher of Īśa.
In the east, however, it should be square; in the southeast, it has the shape of a vulva;
in the south, it is a half-moon; in the southwest, it is triangular;
(l4) in the west, the sacrificial pit is circular; and in the northwest, it is hexagonal.

To the north, there should be a lotus-shaped pit, while in the northeast, an eight-cornered one; between Indra and Īśāna, one should cause a circular pit to be made. [These are dedicated] to Īśa, Brahmā, Mahākāla, Śānti, Nandin, Indra, and Bhāskara.
Agni, Yama, Vighneśa, Vidyā, Bhṛṅgīśa, and Vāstupati;
Viṣṇu, Nirṛti, Amāskanda, Nivṛtti, Ukṣā, Astra, and Pāśin.
Vāyuvighna and Caṇḍakalā; homage to Sarasvatī!
She is white, wearing white garments, and holding a rosary and a book.
And with her right and left hands, she holds the very gracious Sarasvatī.
Salutation to Sarasvatī. Between those two—
holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus in her left and right hands respectively.
Being flooded by two golden carts with elephant-like forms, she possesses great splendor.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. (L3) To her right—
[is] the red [deity], three-eyed, with matted hair, holding a sword and a lotus in his two left hands.
And [he saw] Nandikeśvara, holding a rosary and a trident.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin. To the north:
Gaṅgā, seated upon a crocodile throne, white in form, holding a blue lotus and a full water-pot in her two right and left hands respectively.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. On the left branch—[one should worship] Mahākāla, who is black, three-eyed, and has four arms; holding a rosary and a trident in his right and left hands, and possessing a fierce countenance.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākāla! To his north, one should visualize Śyāmā, seated upon a tortoise, holding a water-pot in her left hand and a blue lotus in her right hand, and [surrounded] by the Yamyās.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yamunā. Obeisance to all the door-keepers. On the southern door-panel—obeisance to Vimala. On the northern door-panel—obeisance to Subāhu. On the lintel—obeisance to the Śatarudras.
O All-pervading One, whose form is the entire universe known through the Vedāntas, O Virūpākṣa!
Devoid of distinctions, yet possessing the form of all the specific attributes of Viśveśvara;
open the door!
You who fulfill the command of Śiva, the Lord of Time, the Protector of the Field, and the Chief of the Gaṇas.
"O Lord, grant me the instruction for the worship of Mahādeva.
Homage be to the gatekeepers of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
with your favor, I shall commence the worship of Śiva."
"O Lord, Sovereign of the Son of the Mountain, First Overlord, O All-pervading One!
Grant me, O All-pervading One, the command to perform the propitiation of Śaṅkara.
Having thus prayed, [he struck] with three blows of the heel and the whirling of the right index finger.

Having thus reflected on the triad and performed the worship of the doors in this manner, one should enter within with the right foot foremost and worship the triad of powers: "Homage to Icchā-śakti," "Homage to Kriyā-śakti," "Homage to Jñāna-śakti. Having worshipped the three powers, and having worshipped Brahmā in the southwest (niṛti) with the words "Homage to Brahmā," one should go near the *liṅga* with a handful of flowers.

Having worshipped with the three principles (*tatva*): "Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the *ātmatattva*; salutation to Śiva, the lord of the *vidyātattva*; salutation to Śiva, the lord of the *śivatattva*. Having offered incense and lamps, having presented fruits and other offerings, having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, and having prayed to Śiva for the sake of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

One should pray for the permission (*anujñā*) of Śiva. Then follows the purification of the *nirmālya*. Having offered oblations with the root mantra, one should consecrate [the disciple] in due order with substances such as scented oil and so forth.
One should sprinkle him with oil using the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*), and with *likuca* fruit using the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*).
Ground *āmalaka* and *rajanī*, etc., consecrated with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having formed a fist with the base of the *darbha* grass, one should purify the pedestal of the *liṅga*;
[one should perform] the pure bath with the *praṇava* and [wear] a wet garment with the nine-syllable mantra.
Having recited the *gavya-brahmamantra*, one should offer milk with the five weapon-mantras (*pañcāstramantra*);
likewise, curd for the bath with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, and ghee with the *bahurūpa* mantras;
and similarly, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with the *pañcaprāsāda* mantra.
The essence of the fruits with the Rudrasūktas, and the honeys with the Puruṣasūktas.
The wise one, having consecrated sugarcane juice, *pā(pavamāna*, the coconut for Parjanya, and food with the Śiva-gāyatrī;
One should employ the Bilva, Śaṅkha, Ambuja, Gaja, Ambu, Śrīrudra, Camasa, Udakabheda, Māla, and likewise Kṣāya,
at the conclusion of the thousand-stream bath, following the end of the ritual ablution.

Having thus consecrated [the deity] with water from the *kumbha* vessel, sprinkled [it] on the head with *arghya* water, offered the *mantra*-food, and gratified Śiva with collyrium, camphor, and other offerings; having discarded the wet garment and wiped [the deity] with pure cloths while reciting the root mantra; and having adorned [it] with garments, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), ornaments, perfumes, and so forth—one should perform the *prasanna-pūjā*. It is as follows:
"O Lord, permit Gaṇeśa, who is worshipping the sandals of the Teacher of the World,

as well as [the deity] who has accomplished the task accordingly. Having thus informed Śiva, one should worship the Enjoyment Power (Bhoga-śakti) residing in the inner sanctum after having consecrated her, following the proper sequence.
One should worship Gaṇapati. I praise the pot-bellied one who holds [the tusk]. *Gaṃ*, obeisance to Gaṇapati. In the northwest—one should worship Śrī, standing facing south.
In the northeast, one should worship the Seven Gurus.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other honors with their respective names, [one should worship] at the base of the deity’s pedestal: in the center, obeisance to the Support (*Ādhāra-śakti*); to Ananta.

Homage! Homage to Dharma! Homage to Jñāna! Homage to Vairāgya! (l4) Homage to Kanda! Homage to Aṅkura! Homage to Nāla! Homage to Ananta! Homage to Takṣaka! Homage to Kambalaka! Homage to Mahābījaka! Homage to Śaṅkhapāla! Homage to Kārkotaka! (l5)

Homage to the pill (*gulikā*). In the center—homage to the one who has the brilliance of ten million suns, whose form is circular, the *laṃ* syllable, and whose seat is Ananta. Above that—in the southeast corner—homage to the foot of Dharma; homage to the foot of Jñāna; homage to the foot of Vairāgya; homage to the foot of Aiśvarya. In the directions starting from the east—homage to the foot of Adharma; homage to the foot of Ajñāna.

Homage to the one whose feet are non-detachment. Homage to the one whose feet are non-sovereignty. In the center: homage to *saṃ*, the covering of the quality of *sattva*. Homage to *raṃ*, the covering of the quality of *rajas*. Homage to *taṃ*, the covering of the quality of *tamas*. Homage to the one with a face formidable with fangs. To the three-eyed one of terrifying form, [mounted upon] a lion...

Salutation to Vāma-siṃha, who has a white armor (*śvetavarma*) and a square form, for the sake of protection. Above that, in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*): salutation to Bhūtarūpa, whose feet are the Kṛta age; salutation to Tāraṅgapakṣa at the front of Bhūtarūpa; salutation to Bhūtarūpa, whose feet are the Dvāpara age; salutation to Bhūtarūpa, whose feet are the Kali age. In the directions starting from the east: salutation to Bhūtarūpa, whose feet are the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Homage! Homage to the one whose form is the elements, who has Niyati as his feet.

(L3) Homage to the one whose form is the elements, who has Kāla as his feet. Homage to the one whose form is the elements, who has Kalā as his feet. In the center—homage to Keśava, who has the center as his feet.
To the yellow-colored eight-cornered [mandala], to the Lord seated upon the yoga-posture, homage! (L4)

Above that—[or] *pari*?—to the coral-colored seeds, [I offer] homage to Krūrā, who is silver-colored; to the lapis lazuli-colored stalk, [I offer] homage to Vairṇikā, who is reddish-brown colored. (l5) To the eight petals, which are conch-colored, [I offer] homage; to the secondary petals, which are red-colored, [I offer] homage; to the filaments, which are crimson-colored, [I offer] homage.

In the center of the pericarp: oṃ namaḥ | āṃ namaḥ | rāṃ namaḥ | ū namaḥ | vyoṃ namaḥ | maṃ namaḥ | vyāṃ namaḥ | piṃ namaḥ | naṃ namaḥ | maṃ namaḥ | On the tips of the filaments: vāmāyai namaḥ | jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ | raudryai namaḥ | kālyai namaḥ |
Salutation to Kalavikaraṇī. Salutation to Balavikaraṇī. Salutation to Balapramathinī. Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Salutation to Manonmanī.
In the middle of the petals—salutation to Ananta. Salutation to Sūkṣma. Salutation to Śivottama. (p86a, c1. in this folio)
Subject/Matter (in two columns): Ekanetrāya namaḥ | Ekarudrāya namaḥ | Trimūrtaye namaḥ | Śrīkaṇṭhāya namaḥ | Śikhaṇḍine namaḥ | Karṇikāya namaḥ | To the south: Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ.
In the north: *hiṃ*, salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). In the center: *hūṃ*, salutation to the principle of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*).
[Salutation] to the great knot of the principle of Māyā, which is joined with the petals of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), and endowed with the filaments and the powers beginning with Vāmā.

Salutation to the lotus-seat, which is circular in shape, white in color, whose seed-syllable is the letter *ya*, and whose pericarp consists of the reality of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). Above that: salutation to the solar disc; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc; salutation to the lunar disc; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc; salutation to the fiery disc; salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fiery disc; salutation to the disc of power (*śakti-maṇḍala*).

Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala. Salutation to the one whose form is an eight-cornered [figure] and whose color is white. Salutation to the one endowed with three maṇḍalas, possessing the color of the *sahakāra* tree, and seated upon a pure throne. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva. Having formed the *āvāhana-mudrā* with flowers and led [the deity] from the heart up to the middle of the eyebrows, [one visualizes] the light...

Having visualized the form of Śiva as embodied and held within the hollow of one's joined palms, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form with the mantra: *oṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ*. Then, while reciting the temple-mantra beginning with "earth" (*kṣiti*) and ending with "the crooked one" (*kuṭila*), one should invoke [the deity]. Having established [him] with the *sthāpinī* mudrā, made him present with the *sannidhānī*, and restrained him with the *niṣṭhurā* mudrā, one should render him immortal (*amṛtīkṛtya*).

One should perform the rite of vitalization (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), having presented incense and a lamp, and having offered the guest-water of welcome (*svāgatārghya*) with the root mantra, one should pray: "O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World! (l. 2)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands; having established oneness by means of the root mantra; having rendered [the deity] immortal by means of the *mahāmudrā*;
having displayed the *padmamudrā* and the *bimbamudrā*; (l3) having offered incense and lamps; and having worshipped the limbs of absorption (*layāṅga*).

Having requested [the deities] for the sake of worship with offerings of enjoyments and limbs, [one should say]: "Salutation to Manonmanī. Having worshipped Ananteśa and the others, beginning with the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), one should perform, in every instance, the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*). Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*)—ending with the utterances *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*—and having presented fruits and other items, one should satisfy [them] with the ritual services (*upacāra*). [Then one worships] Śiva.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offering of flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),

one should present the *ārātrika* lamp and the perpetual sacred thread (*nityapavitra*). Having performed the worship until the end of the recitation (*japa*), and having made the petition, "O God of gods, Lord of the World," one should go outside and offer incense and a lamp, together with various side dishes.

Having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavi*) consisting of all kinds of edible foods soaked in ghee and accompanied by the five grains according to one's capacity; having performed the worship of the great lamp; having gratified Śiva with the recitation of the Vedas, blessings (*āśīrvāda*), the five-limbed Drāviḍa hymns, pure dance (*nṛtta*), song, and instrumental music; and having paid obeisance—for the sake of the Śiva-sacrifice for the restoration of the dilapidated temple and its eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) which is to be performed...
One should pray to Śiva for the sake of contraction [of the universe]. Thus ends the Prasannapūjā.
The Ritual of the Maṇḍapa: Regarding the ground of the door—on the ground of the door, in the house of the six flavors and elements, there are sixteen squares for the feet;

the center should consist of nine squares. Together with the three middle squares, this is the central ninefold altar. Within it, there are five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and the ninefold Śiva-maṇḍapa arrangement. Likewise, there is one jar (*kumbha*) in the east, and similarly one jar in the south, the southwest, and the southeast.

Likewise for Agni; for Varuṇa, a six-cornered [shape] and an Aśvinī [shape]; for Vāyu, a jar; in the region of Soma, it should be a yoke; for Iṣa, a three-jar [shape]. To the east, however, it should be square; in the south-east, it has the form of Bhaga. In the south, it is a half-moon; in the south-west, it is triangular.
In the west, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular; in the northwest, it is hexagonal;
in the north, it is a lotus-shaped pit; and in the northeast, it is octagonal. Between Indra and Īśāna, one should cause a circular pit to be made.
From Īśa, Brahmā, Mahākāla, Śānti, Nandī, Indra, and Bhāskara;
[then] Agni, Yama, Vighneśa, Vidyā, Bhṛṅgīśa, and Vāstu; Viṣṇu, Nirṛti, Amā, Skanda, Nivṛtti, Ukṣan, Astra, Pāśin, Vāyu, Vighna, Caṇḍa, and Kalā.

One should place Caṇḍakalā and the goddess Soma, and Guru in succession; [then] Saura, Torana-kalā, Ādi-nandin, Śrīdhvaja, Ayudha, Gaja, Astra, Vāstu-bhūpa, Bhūmi-maṅgala, Śarīra-daśakra-yajña, Na-cakra-guṇapa, and Guru. One should install them.
The rainbow is male; red, black, smoky, moon-bright, white-shining, golden-colored, and crystal are female; the flag is female; and the crystal is male.
O Brahmaṇaspati, the [deity] should be placed starting from the east and colored red;
that of Ananta is blue in the southwest, while for Citra in the center, she is yellowish-white.

Having thus prepared these and having installed the eight banners, [he should install] the archways, the gate-keepers, Praśānta, Śaśidhara, and Ghaṭṭa; the archways of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), Vāstu-lakṣmī, Gaṇapati, the Guru, Dharma, and the other Lords of Knowledge (Vidyādhipas). These [vessels], along with the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhanī*, should be endowed with the proper characteristics, provided with lids, accompanied by threads, and covered with cloths.

Having placed the vessels for the oblation— consisting of heaps of mango leaves, gold, jewels, and grains— in their proper positions, and having then gathered the implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
the Guru, having performed his daily ablutions and rites, shall go to the sacrificial hall accompanied by his assistants and the *mūrtipas*, and perform the worship of the Sun.

(Sūryapūjā) — First, between Indra and Pāvaka, he should worship the eternal station of Sūrya in that water-pot. Immediately thereafter, having gone outside, washed his feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should enter again and face north.

Having become [the deity] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, provided with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should recite "Astrāya hūṃ phaṭ" ten times. Beginning from the eastern gate, one should worship in sequence;
the arches (*toraṇa*) should be joined to the arches, and one should worship the lords of the gates (*dvāreśa*) in the pitchers (*kalaśa*).
At the eastern gate: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Peaceful Archway (Śāntitoraṇā).

Salutation to the Ṛgveda. Salutation to the Kṛta Yuga. On the spikes: salutation to Pūṣan; salutation to Dhātṛ; salutation to Vidhātṛ; salutation to the Three Worlds; salutation to the Bhuvarloka; salutation to Soma; salutation to Aṅgāraka; salutation to Pratyūṣa; salutation to Prabhāsa. At the southern door-archway: salutation to the Bhūti archway. Salutation to the Yajurveda.
Homage! Homage to the Tretā Yuga! At the roots: homage to Bhārgava; homage to Parjanya; homage to Indra; homage to Aśoka;
homage to Svarloka; homage to Maharloka; homage to Budha; homage to Bṛhaspati; homage to Ajaghanya.

On the archway of the western gate: *namaḥ* to the archway of Bala; *namaḥ* to the Sāmaveda; *namaḥ* to the Dvāpara Yuga. On the spikes: *namaḥ* to Aryaman; *namaḥ* to Tvaṣṭṛ; *namaḥ* to Bhūtasañjīvana;
*namaḥ* to Ananta; *namaḥ* to Janaloka; *namaḥ* to Tapaloka; *namaḥ* to Śukra; *namaḥ* to Śanaiścara; *namaḥ* to Mitra.
Homage!
At the northern gate-arch: homage to the Arch of Health; homage to the Atharvaveda; homage to the Kali Age.

On the spikes: "Salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Sāvitrī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to the Bestower of Prosperity; salutation to Satyaloka; salutation to Śivaloka; salutation to Rāhu; salutation to Ketu; salutation to Dhanada. Thus, having worshipped with the *pādya* and other offerings using these respective name-mantras.

At the northern pitcher of the eastern gate: *oṃ hāṃ śāntikalādvārāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root mantra: (l2) The meditation—four-faced, four-armed, black in color, and possessed of great strength.
She holds a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; she is peaceful, wears a sacred thread, and is adorned with serpents.
In the eastern jar of the southern gate: *vidyākalādvārāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root mantra, the meditation is as follows:
[She is] red-colored, with a topknot of matted hair, three faces, and four arms.
She holds a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, and resembles a crystal in brilliance.
In the southern jar of the western door: *namaḥ* to the door of the *nivṛtti-kalā*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root [mantra], the meditation is as follows:
She has the appearance of molten gold and is adorned with four arms.
Vajrābhayā and Akṣamālā are proclaimed as those who turn back desire.
In the western jar of the northern gate: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the door of the kalā of Pratiṣṭhā. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root [mantra], the meditation is as follows:
Resembling pure crystal, she has five faces and four arms;
holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is adorned with jewels of stability.

Having offered incense and lamps, having thus performed worship and presented the ritual services (*upacāra*), again at the southern jar of the eastern gate: *oṃ hāṃ namo nandine*. Having worshipped the root-mantra of the seat-form (*āsana-mūrti*), the meditation is as follows: "Nandin is remembered as having four arms and being endowed with matted locks (*jaṭā*) and [an] axe (*akṣa*)."
[He holds] a trident, a sword, a thread, and [two hands] joined in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
*Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Nandin. Having offered incense and lamps, [one should place] the seat and the image in the third jar to the south of Īśāna: *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Mahākāla. The seat and the image...
Having worshipped the root [mantra], the meditation is as follows:
Though three-eyed, he does not have a dark body; his beard and hair are tawny.
Carrying a small sword in his right hand, he holds a shield and a trident in his left.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, having offered incense and lamps, one should worship the seat, the image, and the root mantra at the western pitcher of the southern door with: *oṃ hāṃ bhṛṅgiṇi namaḥ*. Then, the meditation:
Four-armed and three-eyed, Bhṛṅgīśa has a tawny complexion;
he holds the gesture of fearlessness and an axe in his right hands, and displays the gesture of granting boons and a trident in his left hands.

Having meditated thus, having performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root-mantra of Vināyaka in the third jar to the west of the Āgneya jar with: *oṃ hāṃ vināyakāya namaḥ*. The meditation is as follows:

Having meditated upon the elephant-faced one— who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms, holding a noose and a tusk in his right hands, and an elephant-goad and a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*) in his left— and having worshipped him, one should offer incense and lamps.
In the northern jar of the western door: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha*. Having worshipped the root-mantra of the seat-form (*āsana-mūrti*), the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
The Bull is bull-shaped, three-eyed, with the luster of a *kunda* flower, the moon, or snow;
he is the support of all beings, possessed of great strength and sharp horns.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root-mantra of Skanda in the third jar to the north of the Nairṛta-jar with: *oṃ hāṃ skandāya namaḥ*. The meditation is as follows:

Having meditated thus— [on him] who has one face, a serene countenance, red in color, and the appearance of a youth; who is either seated or standing in a stable posture, and is adorned with a basket-shaped crown— and having worshipped him, one should offer incense and a lamp.
At the eastern pitcher of the northern door: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīdevī*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
The goddess has one face and two hands, adorned with all ornaments;
she wears a basket-shaped crown (*karaṇḍamakuṭa*) and is embellished with pearls and other jewels.
Having meditated thus upon the Goddess, whose face is serene and whose hand shines with a white water-lily (kahlāra),
and having worshipped her, one should offer incense and a lamp.
To the east of the Vāyu-pitcher, in the third pitcher: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Caṇḍeśvara has four arms, one face, and three eyes;
he is endowed with a rosary, a trident, a water-vessel, and a crown.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root-mantra in the second jar to the north of the Nirṛti-jar: *oṃ hāṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Seated comfortably in the lotus posture, yellow in color, and possessing two eyes, she—
whose eyes are like lotuses— holds a pair of lotuses with her two hands.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having honored each [deity] individually with water for the feet and other offerings, one should again worship the eight banners in the eight directions beginning with the east:
"She is red in color, has matted hair, two arms, and two eyes."
All of them, adorned with various ornaments, stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Praśāntapatākā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śaśidharapatākā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Parjanyapatākā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jayantapatākā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhūtisañjīvanapatākā. (Oṃ hāṃ) Amṛta...

Salutation to the Banner (*patākā*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Wealth-Banner (*dhanapatākā*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Prosperity-Banner (*śrīpradapatākā*).
