Having thus worshipped and honored [them], [one performs] the worship of the ten weapons (*daśāyudhapūjā*) in the sequence starting from the east.

One should perform the worship: "Homage to Vajra. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root [mantra], the meditation is as follows: Śakti has the form of a woman, is red-limbed, and possesses three eyes.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the root mantra of the seat-form with "Daṇḍāya namaḥ. The meditation is as follows:
Having meditated thus: "The Staff is indeed a man, black in form with red eyes," and having worshipped him, having offered incense and a lamp, [one says]:
"Salutation to the Sword. [This is] the seat. (l. 7)
Having worshipped the root-form of the deity, one should perform the meditation:
"And [he holds] a sword; the person has a dark-blue body and angry eyes. Having meditated thus and worshipped, one should offer incense and a lamp.

*Oṃ pāśāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the root form of the seat (*āsana-mūrti*), one should perform the meditation: "...the seven-headed serpent-man joined with a tail. Having meditated thus and worshipped, one should offer incense and a lamp.

Homage to Aṅkuśa! Having worshipped the root form of the seat, one should perform the meditation: "A man emaciated by his own parts, known as Vyāvṛta, possessed of great strength. Having meditated thus and worshipped, one should offer incense and a lamp.

"Salutation to the Mace. Having worshipped the root-mantra of the seat-form, perform the meditation: "The mace also [protects] that preta, who has very full hips and breasts. (L3) Having meditated thus and worshipped, offer incense and a lamp.
Salutation to the Trident. Having worshipped the root of the form of the seat, the meditation is as follows:
"The divine person of the Trident has white limbs and auspicious eyes.
Having meditated and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat and the root-form with "Obeisance to Padma. The meditation is as follows:
"And the lotus, and the divine person, white-limbed and of auspicious eyes."
Having meditated thus and performed worship,
(l5) having offered incense and a lamp,
[one should say] "Obeisance to the Wheel" (*cakrāya namaḥ*). Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root mantra, the meditation is as follows:
Thinking, "May we, as embodied men, pierce the hundred-spoked wheel with our heads," one should meditate thus, perform worship, offer incense and lamps,
and then again worship the eight elephants starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
(Gaja-aṣṭaka-pūjā) — Homage to Kumuda-gaja. Homage to Kumudākṣa-gaja. Homage to Puṇḍarīka-gaja. Homage to Vāmana-gaja. Homage to Śaṅkhakarṇa-gaja.
Salutation to Śravaṇagaja. Salutation to Sumukhagaja. Salutation to Supratīkagaja.
(Western Door Worship)—Again, having approached the western door and having sprinkled the door with the Astra-mantra, [one worships] Mahālakṣmī on the Udumbara post above the door. (p91a, l1)

On its right side: *Gaṃ*, obeisance to Gaṇapati; on its left side: *Taṃ*, obeisance to Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī. Then, having worshipped the door-keepers in the west as usual, and likewise having dispelled the obstructing spirits (vighnas)—who are fond of divine substances from the celestial realm—by means of casting divine flowers, striking with the heels of the feet, and so forth, one should [secure] the door-leaves of the eastern, southern, and northern gates with the Astra-mantra.
Having taken recourse to the south-eastern direction from the right side of the western door, and having provided space for the obstacles that have emerged there by contracting his left limb,
he touches the threshold with his right foot.

Having entered [the inner sanctum] preceded by [these rites], for the purpose of dispelling obstacles, one should worship the second jar to the north of that door with: *oṃ hāṃ astradvārapālāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
(L5) "The boon-granting [hand], likewise the spear, and the iron trident."
One should worship her who holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her hands and the gateway of weapons (astradvāra).
Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp,
then,

having circumambulated and taken one's place at the location of Nirṛti, one should [offer] to the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhipati) in the third pitcher to the east of the pitcher of Nirṛti: *oṃ hāṃ vāstvadhipataye*.

Salutation to Brahmā. Having worshipped the root seat-form (āsana-mūrti), the meditation is as follows: [One should meditate on] Vāstunātha, the Creator, peaceful, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left.

Having worshipped [him] with the words, "He who was standing there is now seated upon a white lotus throne," and having offered incense and a lamp, one should protect the sacrificial hall equally by means of the *astra-prākāra* (the rampart of weapons) and the *kavaca-avakuṇṭhana* (the armor-binding).
Then, in the jars of the pavilion, [one should offer]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the earth-element (*pṛthivī-tattva*)."

On the grasses: *oṃ hāṃ aptattvāya namaḥ*. On the reeds: *oṃ hāṃ vāyutattvāya namaḥ*. On the bonds: *oṃ hāṃ vahnitattvāya namaḥ*. On the pillars: *oṃ hāṃ ākāśatattvāya namaḥ*. (L3) On the canopy: *oṃ hāṃ candrāya namaḥ*. On the ripples: *oṃ hāṃ jāhnavyai namaḥ*. On the garland of *darbha* grass: *oṃ hāṃ vāsukine namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped— (the worship of the eight auspicious symbols on the altar)—
on the eight auspicious symbols surrounding the altar— (l4)
In the east and so forth: (1) Upon the mirror held by Urvaśī—*namaḥ sūryāya*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Skanda.
(2) Upon the full water-pot held by Menakā—*namaḥ jaleśvarāya*. *Oṃ hāṃ*. (5)
Salutation to Lambodara.
(3) Salutation to Sthāṇu, who has Rambhā holding his bull. Salutation to Vīrabhadra.
(4) Salutation to Mātaṅgī, who has Tilottamā holding a pair of chowries. Salutation to Gaṅgā. (5)
Salutation to Mahālakṣmī, who bears the Śrīvatsa and possesses a beautiful countenance; salutation to the Mother of All.
(6) Salutation to Sarasvatī, who bears the Svastika and is beautiful; salutation to Rudra. (7)

To Vimalā, salutation! To Cakriṇī, salutation! (l7) To Agni, salutation! To Gaurī, salutation! Having worshipped in this sequence, [one should place] upon a seat of black antelope skin to the south of the altar: for the seat of the Self (ātmāsana). (p92a, l1)
Having thus consecrated [the water], sitting with a gentle countenance, and having performed the *karanyāsa*, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the *aṅganyāsa*;

having protected [the area] by means of internal sacrifice, oblation, meditation, the three *tāla*-claps, and so forth; and having sat down, one should then prepare the special *arghya* (offering water). The special *arghya* is provided with barley, white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, water, sesame, tips of *kuśa* grass, milk, and flowers.

Having accomplished that, having sprinkled his own head with that water, having sprinkled the sacrificial implements along with the *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra*, and having performed the purification of his own mantras,
[he should touch] the palm of his right hand...

Having anointed [the palms] with elephant-ointment (*gajendra*), one should worship the palms of the hands with: "Homage to Ananta; homage to Dharma; homage to Jñāna; homage to Vairāgya; homage to Aiśvarya; homage to Padma; homage to Śivāsana; homage to Śivamūrti; homage to Śiva. Then, having invoked Śiva there by means of the root mantra and having visualized the worship of his limbs (*sāṅgapūjā*), one should place the hand of Śiva upon one's own head.
One should cultivate the realization: "I am Śiva, worthy of all commands.

Having prepared a sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) thirty-six finger-breadths long and one palm in height, consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having secured it at the right hip, one should protect oneself with it. [Then] within one's own body, the principles (*tattva*)...

Having installed the forms of the Lords of Reality (*tattveśvara*) and the Lords of Form (*mūrtīśvara*), and having meditated upon Śiva residing in the lotus of one's own heart as pervading all that, and having reflected that [all] is non-dual (*advaita*), one should adorn oneself with the five ornaments of the limbs— namely, the lower garment, the upper garment, the golden sacred thread (*upavīta*), the necklace, the earrings, the ring, and the armlet— and then perform the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Then, in the southwest (*naiṛtyāṃ*):
Facing the direction of Īśāna and so forth,

having placed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having sprinkled them with the Astra-mantra, and having gazed at them while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śiva," one should sprinkle them with kuśa-grass water while reciting "Oṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ."

Having struck [the ground] with a weapon and *kuśa* grass, and having sprinkled [water] while reciting "Oṃ hyaiṃ kavacāya vauṣaṭ," one should recite: "By the earth, through its abundance; by heaven, through its vastness; having heated the atmosphere with water—O Aditi, in your lap, O Agni, eater of food, for the sake of eating food, for the sake of consuming, this cow has stepped forth, the radiant one; she has returned to the mother, and as she goes toward the father, she shines upon the thirty-fold sky. *Āyaṃ gauḥ praśnirakramīdasan mātaraṃ punaḥ | pitaraṃ ca prayanaḥ suvaḥ || triṃśadyāmapi rājati vāk ||*

To the winged bird, for the sake of the infant, he has cast [the oblation] with the swift-moving steeds. From his out-breath, the in-breath moves far away; the Great Bull has looked upon heaven when he, impetuous and supreme, was scattering [the waters].
O Agni, that which you have fashioned is well-ordered and renewed.

We dig up for you that which is sown with wrath upon the earth; may the Ādityas, all the gods, and the Vasus gather it together. Aditi, the gods, the Gandharvas, humans, cattle, and the Suras—of all those beings, the Mother is the Great Earth, the Mighty One, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Jagatī, the Wide One, Pṛthivī, the Abundant One, she who has become the All. Who is she?
For Vasiṣṭha said that Truth is indeed the nectar of immortality. The goddess Medinī is Vasundharā; she is also the goddess Vasudhā and Vāsavī.
She is the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), the hearing and the sight of cattle, and the greatest glory.
The goddess who contains the Golden Germ (*Hiraṇyagarbha*), the goddess who brings forth progeny; she has been led to her seat for the sake of truth.
Sāvitrī, the daughter of the ocean, has brought the goddess Arthakī. She is the great supporter, the great sovereign; she is the terrifying one at every peak and in every sacrifice.
She is the wife of Indra, the pervasive one, the celestial river.

Obeisance to the Goddess Lakṣmī, the beloved friend of Mādhavī, who rests upon the serpent Śeṣa, who dwells in the waters, who is the abode of prosperity, who stands upon the earth, who is supported by the horse, who is the wife of Viṣṇu, the great Goddess, Mādhavī, the beloved of Mādhava.

I bow to the Goddess, the consort of Acyuta. "Let us know the wielder of the bow; let us meditate on the Lord of all perfections; may He inspire us"—having thus sprinkled [the water], [one recites] *oṃ*.

HĀṂ ASTRĀYA HUṂ PHAṬ. Having dug the ground with that [mantra], having removed the earth with that very same [mantra], and having worshipped it with "HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ," having leveled it with that very same [mantra], and having sprinkled it with "HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ."
Having adorned [the deity] with that very [ointment], [one should worship her] in the center of the pavilion:
resembling pure crystal, five-faced, four-armed, holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; she is Śāntyatītā (Beyond Peace), the bestower of boons.

"Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the Kalā Śāntyatītā. Having thus meditated upon the pavilion consisting of the Kalās, [one recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ, to the Weapon, huṃ phaṭ! Having drawn three lines facing east and three lines facing north, one draws a single line above them. Upon that, two blades of *kuśa* grass are placed in the form of a double trident (*triśūla*). This is the "vajrification" (*vajrīkaraṇa*), performed with two blades of *kuśa* grass whose tips point toward the east and the north.

Having placed the four-footed [mantra], for the sake of the success of parched grain and sandalwood, one should worship those *bhasma*, *dūrvā* grass, and *kuśa* blades. These seven should also be mixed together with the *astra* mantra. Having scattered them all around in the form of the weapon with the words "Homage to the Weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*), one says: "Homage to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*).

Thus, having gathered the modified form with bundles of *kuśa* grass, and having placed it upon the northeastern altar of the eastern altar, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) over that,
and having placed the water-pot (*kumbha*) upon that according to the ritual rules,

having arranged the *vardhanī* vessel to its south with its spout facing west, and having worshipped Ananta, Dharma, Jñāna, and the others as the movable seat situated upon a lotus within the pot— [one should proceed].
One should perform the placement of the forms:
(l5) *oṃ śluṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ*.
[He is] three-eyed, four-armed, fierce, with red [complexion], and endowed with matted locks.

Wearing yellow garments, holding a noose, an arrow, a bow, and a trident— this is called the All-Gracious, the means for accomplishing all desired objects. Having meditated thus in the mind, one should worship the Pāśupata weapon.

Having invoked [the deity] with these and other [mantras], and having worshipped [him] together with his limbs (*aṅga*), one should worship the movable seat (*calāsana*) in the *vardhanī* vessel as before, [reciting]: "Oṃ ślīṃ paśū huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the power of the Pāśupata weapon.
[One should visualize the goddess] red in color, with flaming hair, and bearing a sword and a shield.

Having meditated upon the goddess Āstreśvarī, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Then, one should worship the world-protectors, Indra and the others. To the south of the eastern gate, in the second jar—the Indra-jar—one should offer: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya*.
Salutation. Having worshipped the form of the seat, the meditation is as follows:
One should worship Indra, who is mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, who is yellow in color, holds a thunderbolt, possesses a thousand eyes, and is stationed in the eastern quarter.
Laṃ, obeisance to Indra, the lord of the gods. Having worshipped the form of the seat, the meditation is as follows:
[He is] mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, yellow-hued, and holding a vajra.
One should worship Indra, the thousand-eyed, situated in the eastern quarter.

*Laṃ*, obeisance to Indra (*la3*), the lord of the gods, who holds a vajra in his hand, whose vehicle is Airāvata, together with his retinue and weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp into the fire-vessel: *Oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*. (*la4*)
Having worshipped the root-form of the seat, the meditation is as follows:
one should meditate upon Agni mounted on a goat, red-bodied and red-eyed;
if [the fire-altar] is ascending with stones, he is joined by the *śakti*, *sruk*, and *sruva* ladles. (l5)

Salutation to Agni, the lord of splendor, who holds a spear in his hand, whose vehicle is a ram, together with his retinue and weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should offer them] to the jar of Yama:
*Oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
He has a dark complexion, holds a staff in his hand, and is seated upon a buffalo throne;
he carries a palm sprout in his hand and is adorned with all ornaments.

"Obeisance to Yama, the lord of the pretas, who holds a staff in his hand, whose vehicle is a buffalo, who is accompanied by his retinue, and who is armed. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] in the vessel of Nirṛti:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root mantra, the meditation is as follows:
One should visualize Nirṛti as dark-complexioned, holding a sword and a shield,
with a terrifying Rākṣasa form, mounted upon a corpse, and possessing three eyes.

*Kṣaṃ*, obeisance to the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who holds a sword in his hand, whose vehicle is a *preta*, together with his retinue and weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] Varuṇa’s pitcher with: *Oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*.
Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Varuṇa, however, has a noose in his hand, is white in color, and possesses great strength;
he is the god seated upon a crocodile, adorned with all ornaments.

Vaṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, lord of the waters, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a makara, together with his retinue and weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp: at the wind-pole, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root-mantra: the meditation—Vāyu is smoke-colored, mounted upon a deer, and endowed with a banner.
Carrying a goad in his right hand and likewise a banner in his left.
Or [one should offer] to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), who holds a banner in his hand, rides upon a deer, is accompanied by his retinue, and is armed with weapons:

*namaḥ*. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] in the vessel of Soma: *oṃ hāṃ somāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root-mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[One should visualize him] as the lord of the Yakṣas, holding a mace in his hand, white in color, and seated upon a horse.
Having two arms, a red face, lotus-like eyes, and holding a lotus in his hand.

"Oṃ, salutation to Saṃ, the Lord of Yakṣas, who holds a mace in his hand, whose vehicle is a horse, who is accompanied by his retinue, and who is armed with weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] in the Īśāna-pitcher: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra, the meditation is as follows: "One should meditate upon Īśāna as having four arms, three eyes, and wearing matted hair."
Holding a trident in one hand, mounted upon a bull, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his other hands.

Salutation to Īśāna, the Lord of Knowledge, who holds a trident in his hand, whose vehicle is a bull, who is accompanied by his retinue and weapons. Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] in the eastern jar of the Niṛti-jar: *Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the image, and the root-mantra, the meditation is as follows:
[He has] the conch, the discus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; his body is dark-complexioned, and his vehicle is Tārkṣya.
The god who wears yellow garments, has two eyes, and four arms.
Salutation to the infinite Viṣṇu, the lord of the earth, who holds a discus in his hand, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya, together with his retinue and his weapons.

Having offered incense and a lamp, [one should worship] in the pitcher to the south of Īśāna: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra, the meditation is as follows:
Brahmā is four-faced, the creator... wearing a rosary of beads.
Those who are mounted upon swans and endowed with four arms—

*Lāṃ*, obeisance to Lokādhipati, who holds a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand, whose vehicle is a swan, together with his retinue, and accompanied by his weapon. Having offered incense and a lamp, one should then take up the *vardhanī* vessel of the Pāśupata weapon; having had the disciple invoke that jar, one should oneself [pour] from the *vardhanī* into the vessel emerging from the western nozzle.
Having sprinkled those [vessels] with uninterrupted streams of water from the mouths of the jars, moving clockwise all around with the root mantra—
those [waters] which are worthy of the world-protectors— for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the sacrifice; (l2.)

"...until it must remain by the command of Śiva. Having thus proclaimed the command of Śiva, [he should place] the primary pitcher (pūrva-kumbha) in its own place and the *vardhanī* pitcher behind it. Having worshipped the firm seat (*sthirāsana*) for the sake of the lotus [pedestal], representing the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), the attributes (*dharma*), and so forth, he should perform the ritual placement of the form (*mūrtivinyāsa*) in the pitcher: "Oṃ śīṃ paśūṃ huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon."

"Salutation to Śiva and Śakti. Having thus touched the eastern pitcher with the fist for prosperity (*bhūti*) and with the tip of the thumb from behind, and having performed the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* by means of the mudrā of the manifestation of the forms (*mūrti*), [he places] the form in the east and the *vardhanī* vessel in the west.

Having installed the forms of the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvara-mūrti-mūrtīśvaras) within that pitcher, having protected it with the Astra-mantra, and having touched the pitcher, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. One should recite it ten times that number over the *vardhanī* vessel. [Then one should say: "O Lord of this sacrifice, you indeed are the immovable form of these [deities]; take up your sword of wisdom for those who belong to you."
Having placed the sword of gnosis (*jñānakhaḍga*) into the boon-granting hand (*varadahasta*) of the western-faced [deity] with a pure intention, one should pray:
"O Blessed One, this temple of impurity is filled with manifold obstacles."
It must be protected by that weapon for as long as its completion exists here.
Then, one should visualize the sacrificial pavilion with all remaining obstacles dispelled by the splendor of the weapons manifested from the *vardhanī* vessel situated upon its seat.
Then, from the air-vessel into the eastern vessel: *oṃ hāṃ vināyakāya namaḥ*.
Having worshipped the root-mantra of the image on the seat, the meditation is as follows:
[One should meditate on] the elephant-faced one, who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms;
in his right hands he holds a noose and a tusk, while in his left hands he holds a goad and a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka).

Having meditated thus and performed worship, (l3) having offered incense and a lamp, [one worships] Sadāśiva in the western jar of Īśāna: *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra, the meditation is as follows:
The Goddess beheld Sadāśiva, pure as a jasmine flower or the moon, possessing five faces and a massive body,
with ten arms, a serene countenance, and five colors.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root mantra with: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*. (l5) The meditation:
[He is] red in color, two-eyed, and holds a boar’s tusk and a trident.
With four arms, let us fashion Ananta standing and holding [the earth].

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root mantra with: *oṃ hāṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He] holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, carries an axe in his hand, and has a bull for his vehicle.
"I take refuge in the Guru Śrīkaṇṭha, whose radiance is as white as camphor.

Having thus meditated and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root mantra with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Goddess Śrī," and then perform the meditation:
The Goddess stands upon a lion, holding a trident with her two hands;
she is adorned with a jeweled crown and embellished with pearls and other ornaments.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root mantra with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Guha. The meditation is as follows:
[He is] a youth clad in a single garment, radiant, and red in color.
I take refuge in the god Guha, whether he is seated or standing firm.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seat and the root-form with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. (L3) The meditation:
"I take refuge in Viṣṇu, who holds a conch and a curved weapon, who is dark-complexioned, who wears yellow garments,
and who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi. Having thus meditated and worshipped, and having offered incense and a lamp, [recite] Oṃ.

Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Having worshipped the root-form of the seat, the meditation is as follows: Having bowed to the four-faced Creator, the giver of even the worlds, who is endowed with a yellow complexion, one should worship Brahmā. (l5.)

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should worship the seven gurus in sequence. Having worshipped Śiva in the center of the pavilion with the ritual services beginning with invocation,
and having likewise worshipped the Lord of the Maṇḍala, and having offered incense and a lamp— the procedure for the worship of the Maṇḍala is completed.
Salutations to Śrī Kāntimati and Śālivāṭīśvara.
Now, the procedure for contraction (*saṅkoca*) is described:

following the worship of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), at midnight when the moon is conjoined with a movable zodiac sign (*cararāśi*), the preceptor, having first performed the ritual bath according to the water-mantra (*vāruṇasnāna*), shall put on two new garments.

Adorned with two earrings made of gold and gems and other ornaments, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), having worshipped [the deities] beginning with the Sun and ending with the Guru, and having offered a formal request, he should go near the primary *liṅga*. (L2) Having caused the evening protective worship (*sāyarakṣapūjā*) to be performed according to the rules, and having himself worshipped with the "eight flowers" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), he should bow to the God of gods and pray.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, omniscient Destroyer of Tripura,
[speak] regarding the purpose of the eightfold binding rites at the time of the commencement of contraction.
"Grant me permission and ensure that my devotion remains free from obstacles, O Śaṅkara.

Having thus prayed, one should sit upon a seat consisting of a tortoise and other supports, covered with a tiger skin, on the southern side of the ground smeared with cow dung, within the inner sanctum of the womb-chamber (garbhagṛha) in the intermediate pavilion (ardhamaṇṭapa). Having established the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya), one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules preceded by the ritual striking of his own head, and having offered prayers, with the *pavitra* in hand and seated upon *darbha* grass, [he says]: "On this auspicious lunar day,

for the purpose of the restoration and the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of the venerable Veṇvaneśvara Sadāśiva, together with his retinue, along with the venerable *mūlaliṅga*, accompanied by the goddess Śrī Kāntīmbā, of this God of Gods..."
"I shall perform the rite of contraction (*saṅkoca-karman*).

For that purpose, I shall perform the installation of the auspicious jar (*śivakumbha-sthāpana*), the procession (*yātrā*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpya*), and having caused the declaration of the auspicious day distinguished by Mahādeva to be recited according to the rules, [he prepares] the five products of the cow.

Having established [the deity] and sprinkled it with those two [substances] using the Astra-mantra, having performed the rites from "ātma" up to the purification of the mantras, and having performed the nyāsa with the Mātṛkā and other [mantras],
then, in the center of the half-pavilion—

With the two powders of ground turmeric. [The line] pointing eastward. [The line] pointing northward. The four-threaded [cord], the knowledge of the enclosure: "First, from the front, out of the boundless... "Bring hither to me the well-lighted one... "The highest points of this [world] are its foundations; you have disclosed the womb of the existent and the non-existent. "Flying up to the heavenly vault, the golden one... "In the heart, the infinite ones beheld you... "The golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, of Yama..."
In the womb is the power of Śakra and Nambhūriṇa.

O Soma, when your own equal has been made, bestow virility from every side; be present at the gathering of strength. That Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—that Rudra who is in all beings...

"Salutation be to that Rudra! Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; he established his foot in three places; it is gathered in his dust. "All have magnified Indra, the gatherer of the ocean, the best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors, the true lord and master of spoils. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with these mantras in the center of the chest, [one recites]: "O Earth, be pleasant, a protector of beings and a refuge."
"May she who dwells within grant us wide-spreading protection.
Having recited this mantra, [he should offer] thirty-two *prastha* measures of grain, half as much rice, and half as much sesame seed; so it is said.
Half of that [measure] should be for the parched grain (lāja), and above that, one should draw a lotus.
Having spread darbha grass,
the instructor [should know that] rice is said to have Earth as its deity;
sesame has Agni as its deity, and parched grain is traditionally held to have Vāyu as its deity.

Darbha grass and space are said to be known as consisting of the five deities. [Recite: "That by which [you grant] offspring for our small [offspring], like unto other [beings]; that seed, the two-fold grain, the unbroken rice—grant us that! We pray for it—for great wealth, for all-encompassing auspiciousness. This is the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Having placed [the vessel],

having poured rice with the Sadyojāta mantra, sesame seeds with the Vāmadeva mantra, and parched grain with the Aghora mantra; having drawn a lotus with the Tatpuruṣa mantra and having strewn it with *darbha* grass,
[one prepares] the Śiva-vessel measuring one *droṇa*.

Then, having taken a *vardhanī* vessel measured by an *ajala*, along with two *prastha* measures of unbroken rice grains (*viśalya*) in the hundreds of thousands, provided with lids and made of gold, silver, or copper;

and having brought them with the mantra "O mother of progeny, may you enter our protection" and "The one who destroys the enemies of the *droṇa*-vessel," he should establish the surrounding jars (*parivārakumbha*).
The new thread for the *kumbha* should have nine lines, while that of the *vardhanī* has five;
the *kalaśa* should have three threads—this is the declared characteristic.

The best is the size of a sesame seed, the middling is that of a barley grain, and the lowest is that of an elephant’s eye; this is the Rudraveṣṭana. White, red, turmeric-colored, black, and blue—these are the five.
But for one situated in the contraction [of the breath], the best of instructors should envelop the [vital] points.
Spinning out the thread, following the light of the atmosphere,
he watches over the luminous paths that have been prepared; he goes along without entanglement, awakening the vigilant one, and generating the divine people through the thread.

Having wrapped [it], and thereafter having washed the jars with the *astra* mantra, having filled them with incense such as *guggulu* and other substances, and having established the jars and so forth in their respective positions— beginning with the central one— using the previously mentioned mantras,
[one recites]: "The waters indeed pacify this."

"O Vasu, may the god [purify] us again with the flawless purifier, with the rays of the sun. Having thus filled the jars with water, having cast into them cardamom, cloves, camphor, uśīra, saffron, and sandalwood; and having washed a golden blue lotus, a conch shell, a tortoise, and a rhinoceros—these being made of gold—with water from the *gakhya* jar while reciting the root mantra; ... [the text continues].

Having arranged [the materials], and having placed the nine jewels in the center of an eight-petaled lotus made of gold weighing one *niṣka*, and having cast the nine jewels while reciting the mantra "sahira... nidāśuṣe su...",
one should place [the vessel] upon the five-fold *vardhanī*.
Having placed the Three Jewels in the jars; having cast a tuft of grass (*kūrca*) at the bottom with the *marmamantra*; having placed an *aśvattha* leaf together with a mango leaf above the jar;

and having placed young coconut fruits—complete with their crests—into the jars and so forth with the mantra "Born from the coconut, svāhā to the head" (*nālikerasamudbhūta iti śirase svāhā*); and having fashioned a golden image above that, [one places] the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*).

Having written [the mantra] and placed it upon that with the root mantra, thereafter, using *darbha* grasses joined according to the number of the reality (*tattva*), having made the tips four finger-breadths long, having made a knot measuring two finger-breadths,
and having placed a tuft (*kūrca*) together with its tip, [one should visualize] the Rākṣasas at the tip of the tuft.

Having applied a decorative beard-ornament (*alaṅkārakūrca*) with the *kṛti* mantra; then, one should wear a cotton garment or a linen garment with the mantra: "Clad in fresh raiment and girt about, he has come; you become fierce when being born. The sages, possessing that insight, elevate it—the wise one who, with his mind, seeks the gods for us" (RV 3.8.4). Having applied perfume with the mantra "Gandhadvārām" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1), [one should apply] those [plants] which bear fruit...

"May the one born of Bṛhaspati, who is without fruit and without flowers yet possesses flowers, release [us] from sin. With this mantra, one should perform the offering of cloth, whether it be cotton cloth or linen cloth. "Gandhadvārām, durādharṣām, nityapuṣṭām... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.11.4).

I invoke here Śrī, the sovereign mistress of all beings, you who possess the power of action. Having applied fragrant scents, one should perform worship, adorning [the deity] with flower garlands and other ornaments: *oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. [One should worship] those plants which bear fruit, those which are unfruitful, those which have flowers, and those which are flowerless—the great and spreading ones—may they and I and you be one. Having adorned [the deity] with flower garlands and so forth, one should perform worship. *Oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*.

Salutation to the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). Salutation to the primordial tortoise (*ādikūrma*). Salutation to Ananta. (L7) Salutation to Vāsuki. Salutation to Takṣaka. Salutation to Kārkoṭa (or Kaṭaka). Salutation to Padma. Salutation to Mahāpadma. Salutation to Śaṅkha. Salutation to Gulika. Having thus worshipped them:
Yogāsana—having visualized a yellow hexagon:
*namaḥ* to Yogāsana; *namaḥ* to Kṛtayuga; *namaḥ* to Tretāyuga; *namaḥ* to Dvāparayuga; *namaḥ* to Kaliyuga;
*namaḥ* to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); *namaḥ* to Niyati; *namaḥ* to Kalā; *namaḥ* to Kāla—in the center.
Salutation to Keśava.

Regarding the lion-throne: having meditated upon a four-cornered throne of red color—salutation to Dharma; salutation to Jñāna; salutation to Vairāgya; salutation to Aiśvarya; salutation to Adharma; salutation to Ajñāna. (l3)

Salutation to Avairāgya. Salutation to Aneśvaratva (Naiśvaryatva). Salutation to Sat-tva. Salutation to Raṃ-rajas. Salutation to Taṃ-tamas. Salutation to Paṃ-padma. Having displayed the lotus mudrā: salutation to Śivadharmakanda. Salutation to Śivajñānaikanāla. Salutation to the eight Aiśvarya-petals. Salutation to the seed-syllable. Salutation to the stalk. Salutation to the sprout.
Homage to the petals! Homage to the filaments!
(L5) Homage to the pericarp!
On the petals: homage to Vāmā; homage to Jyeṣṭhā; homage to Raudrī; homage to Kālī; homage to Kalavikaraṇī; homage to Balavikaraṇī.

Homage! Homage to Balapramathanī! Homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī! Homage to Manonmanī! On the tips of the petals: *aṃ* homage to the solar disc; homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc; *hiṃ* homage to the lunar disc.

Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar (*soma*) maṇḍala. Salutation to *maṃ*, the fire maṇḍala. Salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire maṇḍala. Salutation to the Śakti beginning with Kuṭilā. Salutation to Īśvara, her lord. Salutation to the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti.

Salutation to Sadāśiva, the presiding deity of that [liṅga]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva. Oṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva. The meditation: The pitcher is to be known as the seat; the wise practitioner should deposit water along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Likewise, he should place the gems, the bones, the thread, and the channels (*nāḍī*).
The garment is declared to be the skin, and the coconut is likewise the head;
the tongue is known as the brush, and the mango leaf is remembered as the matted hair.
The gift of pomegranate fruit—this is the characteristic of the water-pot (*kumbha*).

*Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*, salutation to the one whose body is knowledge (*vidyādeha*). Having invoked [the deity] with the mantra of Sadyojāta, through the meditation: "Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus," and through the meditation: "Peaceful, seated in the lotus posture."

Having established [the deity] with the five-syllable *sthāpinī* mudrā; having performed the confinement (*sannirodhana*) with the two six-syllable *sannidhāna* mudrās; having performed the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the nine-syllable mantra;
and having bound [the deity] with the *kṣurikā* mantra and the *prāsāda* mantra...

Having offered the guest-water (*arghya*) for welcome and performed the *dhenumudrā*, having worshipped with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having recited the Śiva-gāyatrī and the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times,
one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the heart and other locations of the jar,
[saying]: "O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, until the conclusion of the worship..."
For that long, may you remain present within this jar with a spirit of affection.

(L7. Having offered the *svāgata-arghya* with the *sadyojāta* mantra: "With the *sadyojāta* mantra, I offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the feet. Homage to Vāmadeva; I offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the mouth. With the root-mantra of Śiva (*śivamūla*), I offer the *arghya* upon the head. (P100b, L1)

Having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel with its nozzle facing west near the principal jar (*pradhānakumbha*). Having established the eight jars in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should worship the *āsana-mūrti-mūla* [deities]—namely Manonmanī, who is the embodiment of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)—within the *vardhanī*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
His face should be like refined gold, and his eyes like fire;

he possesses four hands holding a lotus, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a blue lotus (*utpala*); his limbs are adorned with various ornaments and a staff.
Whose nature is the state beyond the mind (unmanī), radiant with the pot-shaped crown.

Oṃ Hrīṃ! I invoke Manonmanī. Having offered the food offering, incense, and lamps, one should worship the seats and forms, beginning with Ananta and ending with Ekanetra, in the cardinal directions starting from the east. One should worship the seats and forms, beginning with Ekarudra and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, of the pitchers situated in the intermediate directions. The meditation is as follows:
One should meditate upon Ananteśa, who is red in color, has five faces, ten arms, fifteen eyes,
and wields ten weapons.
Salutation to Ananta. Salutation to Bhūmi. One should meditate upon Śiva as Sūkṣmeśvara—blue in color, with five faces, ten weapons on his five heads, ten arms, and fifteen eyes.
Salutation to Sūkṣmeśa. Salutation to Su...
[I, the worshiper, should meditate upon] Śivottama, who is white, five-faced, five-headed, and possesses fifteen eyes;
who wields ten weapons and has ten arms.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śivottama; obeisance to Kṣānti.
Having meditated upon Śambhu—who has five faces and five crests, who is ruddy, possesses ten hands, holds the weapons of a fisherman, and has but one eye—one should worship him.
Homage to Yekanetra! Homage to Prabhā!
One should meditate upon the pure Ekarudra, who is endowed with five heads, joined with five faces, possessing ten weapons and ten arms. (2)
Salutation to Yekarudra; salutation to Puṣṭi.
[He is] five-headed, five-faced, with blood-red arrows, likewise ten-armed, with a serene countenance, lotus-eyed, and in the full bloom of youth.
One should meditate thus upon the entry into the directions and worship Trimūrtīśa with [the mantra]:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti; obeisance to Śruti.
[He is] glorious, five-headed, and five-faced, [and is] other than white.
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭheśvara, who possesses ten weapons and ten arms.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha; obeisance to Kīrti. One should worship Śambhu Śikhaṇḍīśa, who is red, fivefold, five-faced, endowed with ten faces, and possessing ten weapons.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin; obeisance to Medhāyin. Having worshipped each [deity] with the rites beginning with invocation and ending with the lamp offering, and having caused the Brahmins to recite the *vidādi* mantras, one should go near the Great Liṅga, sit upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*), and perform the purification of the ground (*bhūśuddhi*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), and the salutation to the Guru.

The purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the triple striking with the heels (*pārṣṇighātatraya*), the expulsion of obstructors (*vighnoccāṭana*), the placement of the *ajāpā* mantra (*ajāpānyāsa*), the breaking of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*), the breaking of the head (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*), the breaking of the face (*vaktrabhaṅgi*), the breaking of the digits (*kalābhaṅgi*), the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*), the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters (*mātṛkānyāsa*),

the external *mātṛkā* placement, the *mātṛkā* placement of Śrīkaṇṭha, the placement of the thirty-eight digits (*aṣṭatriṃśatkalānyāsa*), the placement of the twenty-five digits of Gaurī (*gaurīpañcaviṃśatikalānyāsa*), the placement of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvanyāsa*), the ritual of making [the self] complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and the placement of the five-syllable mantra (*pañcākṣaranyāsa*).

One should perform the *golaka-nyāsa*, the *vajra-golaka-nyāsa*, and the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*). Having sprinkled all the implements, such as the *liṅga* and others, with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), [one should worship] with: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti, who sits upon the tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*) below, whose form is white like the Ocean of Milk."
She has the form of a sprout from a seed within a bud, and she bestows boons and fearlessness.
One should worship the Power (Śakti), who holds a noose and a goad and whose form is the foundation (Ādhāra), with the mantra:
"Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Seated Ādhāra-Śakti. Having thus worshipped the seat (āsana) up to the final Śakti, one should fully worship Śiva along with the seat, the image, and the root-mantra.
Having meditated [on the deity] as seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, with the curved edges of the earth and other elements, one says:

"Homage to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādehāya namaḥ*). Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, and having displayed the six mudrās—beginning with invocation and installation—with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and having offered the *surabhi-mudrā*, one presents the welcoming water-offering (*svāgatārghya*) at the locations of the limbs of absorption (*layāṅga*).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart. Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the Head. Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the Tuft of Hair. Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the Armor. Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the Three Eyes. Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the Weapon.

Having honored [it] with "phaṭ," having made a request for the sake of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment, and having honored [it] three times with the root mantra, one should meditate on Śiva in the form of twelve petals; then, taking Īśāna first from among the five heads, one should worship him on the petal of Īśāna.

[He meditated on] the Lord, who has the luster of crystal, who is the cause of the world, three-eyed, moon-crested, gentle, gracious, and holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the form of Īśāna. Having first taken [the mantra] for the five faces, [one places it] on the eastern petal:
[he who is] clad in yellow garments and a sacred thread, three-eyed, and golden-hued.
One should meditate upon the god Tatpuruṣa, who wears a citron and a rosary, bears the moon upon his crest,
and is adorned with all ornaments. *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Tatpuruṣa.* Taking Aghora from the region of the heart, [one places him] on the southern petal.
Three-eyed, wearing a crown with a moon, and gentle, he is adorned with a tortoise;
bearing a beard and matted hair, his face is formidable and marked by fangs.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with all kinds of scorpions,
he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose.
In his four left hands and his four right hands,
one should meditate upon Aghora, who crushes enemies, bestows all desires, and shines like fresh water, holding a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the one whose form is non-terrible (aghoramūrti)! Having taken the secret mantra from the center, [one places it] on the northern petal:
Vāma is red, with a very radiant luster, [wearing] garlands, garments, and a sacred thread.
With a prominent nose-tip and a crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa), holding a sword and a shield in his hands.
Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to the form of Vāmadeva. Beginning from the feet, on the western petal: (l2.
Richly adorned with white blood, perfumes, and ornaments, wearing a cool turban and white garments;
gentle, endowed with a moon upon his crest, having the appearance of a youth, and three-eyed.
One should meditate upon Sadyojāta as white, with hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta. Having taken up the eyes for the eyes, [he places them] in the northern part of Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Having taken up the heart...
On the southeastern petal— on the petal in the direction of fire, which is the form of the heart-manifestation whose nature is the command of true being—
one should invoke and worship the Peaceful One for the sake of attaining omniscience and other perfections.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart that resembles the moon. Taking the head from the region of the head, [place it] on the petal of Īśāna. Indeed, the form of the head-mūrti has the nature of all-pervading whiteness, visible within the range of sight.
The wise one, ever-content, should worship the Self as Śiva for the sake of accomplishment.

To the form of the Head, which has the luster of gold: *aṃ hiṃ*, obeisance! Taking the topknot (*śikhā*), [one offers it] to her who is the color of vermilion in the southwest (*niṛti*). *Oṃ sūṃ*, obeisance to the Topknot! From all the limbs...
Having taken up the armor—
indestructible by others, radiant, the self of all-knowingness, and imperishable—
one should worship the marvelous armor for the sake of attaining complete independence.

*Bhṛṅgabhāsvara* and so forth: *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. Having taken the weapon (*astra*) in his hands, on the eastern petal—in the directions beginning with the east—the wise one should worship the form of Śiva’s vow (*śivavrata*) and the Śiva-weapon of great power for the sake of union with infinite power (*anantaśakti*) in the four directions.

Having thus worshipped these [deities], beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the lamp (*dīpa*), as if they were Śiva himself, one should display the *dhenu*, *padma*, *triśūla*, *makarī*, and *sṛgā* mudrās for Īśāna and the others. Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the root mantra, one should display the *mahāmudrā*. Then, one should perform the worship of Śrīkaṇṭha and the Mātṛkās, as well as the worship of the thirty-eight *kalās*.
Now, the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇārcanā*).
(First enclosure: Homage to Īśāna. Homage to Ambikā. Homage to Tatpuruṣa. Homage to Gaṇāmbikā. Homage to Aghora. Homage to Gaṅgī. Homage to Vāmadeva. Homage to Gaurī. Homage to Sadyojāta. (L5)

Homage! Homage to Umāyī; homage to the Heart; homage to Vāmāyī; homage to the Head; homage to Nīlī; homage to the Crest-lock; homage to Cakrāṅgī; homage to the Armor; homage to Pāśāṅgī; homage to the Eyes; (l6) homage to Khaṭgī; homage to the Weapon; homage to Gambhīkāyī.
The second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*): Salutation to Ananteśa. Salutation to Bhūti. Salutation to Sūkṣma. Salutation to Svāhā. Salutation to Śivottama.
Salutation to Kṣānti. Salutation to Ekanetra. Salutation to Prabhā. Salutation to Ekarudra. Salutation to Puṣṭi. Salutation to Trimūrti. Salutation to Śruti.
Homage! Homage to Śrīkaṇṭha. Homage to Kīrti. Homage to Śikhaṇḍīśa. Homage to Medhā. The third enclosure.
(103b, l1) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nandin. Homage to Gaṅgā. Homage to Mahākāla. Homage to Yamunā. Homage to Bhṛṅgin.

Salutation to Hlādinī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; salutation to Vallabhā; salutation to Siddhi. (L2) Salutation to Vṛṣabha; salutation to Bhadrā; salutation to Skanda; salutation to Vallidevayānā (Senā); Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Devī;
salutation to Caṇḍeśvara; salutation to Rūpiṇī.

Now, the fourth enclosure: Homage to Indra. (3) Homage to Śacī-devī. Homage to Vipula. Homage to Agni. Homage to Svāhā. Homage to Svadhā. Homage to Yama. Homage to Kālī. Homage to Līlā. Homage to Nirṛti. Homage to Jātā. (4)
Salutation to Sukeśī; salutation to Varuṇa; salutation to Hlādinī; salutation to Harṣiṇī; salutation to Vāyu; salutation to Mahiṣī;

salutation to Aṅgadāyī; salutation to Soma; salutation to Ṛddhi; salutation to Nivṛtti; salutation to Īśa; salutation to Jita; salutation to Svarūpiṇī; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Bhūmidevī; salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Sāvitrī.

Salutation to Sarasvatī. Now, the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa): salutation to the Vajra; salutation to the one whose nature is serene; salutation to Śakti; salutation to the one whose nature is wrathful; salutation to the Daṇḍa; salutation to the one whose nature is the qualities (guṇa); salutation to the Khaḍga.
Homage to Komalātmāyī. Homage to Pāśa. Homage to Viṣātmāyī. Homage to Aṅkuśa. (l7) Homage to Vikṛtātmāyī. Homage to Gadāyī. Homage to Mantrātmāyī. Homage to Triśūlāyī. Homage to Padma.
Homage to Mahāpadmāyī (1). Homage to Cakra. Homage to Mahāpadmāyī (2). Homage to Mahāyogapī... (p104a, l1)
Salutations! Salutations to the Seat of Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyāpīṭha*). Salutations to Vibhūti in the region of Nirṛti. Salutations to Mahālakṣmī in the region of Vāyu.

Again, in the northern part, salutations to the seven Gurus beginning with Sadāśiva. At the front of the southern seat, salutations to the form of one’s own Guru. Having thus worshipped, having offered the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) and presented incense and lamps, and having performed the worship from water onwards ending with water, [he requests] permission.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, cause of the world’s joy!
Homage be to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, Sadāśiva, who are ever dear to your devotees.
"O Sadāśiva, remaining within the *kumbha*, contract [the space];
O Śambhu, always grant your grace in the rite of the eightfold binding.
Having thus prayed—"O Śaṅkara, remaining in the five locations, make it free from obstacles"—[one should proceed].

One should perform the *yātrā-homa*: having prepared a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) one cubit (*aratni*) in front of the water-pot; having performed the rites from the drawing of lines up to the end of the marriage ceremony; facing north;
[one should prepare] a space one cubit in size and three finger-breadths high with dry sand.

Having made the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) a perfect square, one should perform either the fivefold or the eighteenfold consecration (*saṃskāra*). Having performed the purification with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, the washing with the *Vāmadeva*, the drying with the *Aghora*, the maturation with the *Puruṣa*, and the sprinkling with the *Īśāna*; and having gazed upon the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *Śiva-mantra*:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva," and so forth, according to the principle [of the respective mantras].

Having laid down six lines with their tips pointing east and north, one should perform the rites up to the offering of oblations. Having established the six lines with [the mantras] beginning with *brahmajñāna*, one should worship Brahmā, Yama, Soma, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Śakra at the center and the other [points] of the six lines.

Having made it adamantine (*vajrīkṛtya*) by means of the vajra-mudrā, and having fashioned a crossroads for oneself, [one should offer] a blade of *kuśa* grass with the mantra: "Haṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śiva."

Having sprinkled [the site] with water, having released [the thread] in the north, and having visualized the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as perfected through the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should—within its center—arrange five compartments separated by two lines. Having worshipped the five digits (*kalā*) beginning with Śāntyatītā and ending with Nivṛtti in the compartments from the center to the western end, [one should worship] with: *oṃ hāṃ kalāmayāya kuṇḍāya*.

Homage! Having encircled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar (*sthaṇḍila*) with a cord tripled [in thickness], one should worship it with: *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. One should perform the ritual of making it adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*) with three blades of *darbha* grass. Having placed [the cord] in the center of the pit with the *Śivāstra* mantra, one should secure the door with the *Pāśupatāstra*: *ślīṃ paśū huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ*. [This is done] in the center with a single blade of *darbha*.

Having rotated [the vessel] with the armor mantra (*kavaca*) and set it down, one should place a bundle of three *darbha* grasses with their tips pointing east within it; then, having likewise cast a seat of three *darbha* blades to its north,
one should visualize Vāgīśvara, who is red in luster, three-eyed, and four-armed,
endowed with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, and holding a noose and a trident.
Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara. Having worshipped him with this, to his north:
Pālīśī, who has the luster of a lotus flower, possesses four arms and full breasts, and holds a book for exposition, a water-pot, and a rosary.
Having reflected thus: "Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī," and having offered water for honor (*arghya*) with both hands;

(l2) having brought fire produced from a forest or other source into a new vessel such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), and having placed it before the officiant (*hotṛ*); [reciting] "Raṃ, phaṭ, obeisance to the weapon (*astra*)," one casts out the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*). Having assigned [the fire] to Nirṛti, one gazes upon the fire with the root-mantra of Śiva. (l3)

Having sprinkled [the fire] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, having struck it with that same [mantra], and having sprinkled it again with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should draw forth the consciousness of the fire by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*. (L4) Having united it with the fire of the *bindu* through the fifth inhalation (*pūraka*), and having blended it with the fire of the *jāṭharāgni* through the retention (*kumbhaka*) ending with the *bhaga*, [one should proceed].

Having contemplated the triad of fires— the elemental, the lunar, and the digestive— as one, and having drawn them outward by means of the *piṅgalā* breath and exhalation, one should cast them into the elemental fire with the *udbhava-mudrā*, reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire."

Having worshipped with the *saṃhitā* mantras, having protected with the *abhaya-śivāstra*, having fortified with the *varma*, having rendered [the vessel] nectar-like with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having honored the conch with the *hṛdaya* mantra— having meditated upon the pure seed-syllable of Śiva as the form of light, saying "Tyeja," and having circled the fire-vessel, the *kuṇḍa*, three times, one should contemplate the *kuṇḍa* and the *īśāna-śiras*.

Having cast [the oblation] toward himself by means of Vāgīśa within Vāgīśvarī, and having meditated upon... [himself as] Śiva equal to the intellect... with both knees [on the ground], the pure Śiva-fire [is established] in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of the Śiva-mantra.

One should cast [the oblation] with the *vyāhṛtis*. Having visualized the wearing of the cloth at the level of the navel, one should offer water for the *arghya*—intended for purification and sipping (*ācamana*)—into the *biṃba* with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Having covered the fire with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and ghee using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having kindled it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having worshipped it with the *saṃhitā*, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Hūṃ, obeisance to the fire of the womb-śiva," and having tied a blade of *darbha* grass for the protection of the embryo in the hand of the Goddess, and having worshipped it as it was produced for the sake of the conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. For the sake of the rite of male-conception (*puṃsavana*) in the third month, having sacrificed with the left [hand] and performed three oblations of sesame seeds with the head[-mantra], one should offer a drop of water as before.
For the purpose of parting the hair (*sīmanta*),

[this is performed] in the sixth month. Having worshipped with the *aghora* mantra, having offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the *śikhā* mantra, having assigned the faces and other limbs [of the deity], and having performed the expiation (*niṣkṛti*),
[the rite for] birth is performed by the father in the tenth month.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having offered three oblations of sesame seeds, and for the sake of removing the impurities of the womb following birth, having presented the *arghya* offering with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having protected [the child] with *darbha* grass and fuel sticks using the armor-mantra, one should remove the *darbha* bracelet from the hand of the Goddess and visualize that the Goddess has now donned a golden bracelet. Then, [one prepares] the general *arghya*.
With water ending in *huṃ phaṭ* by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), for the sake of immediately turning back the charioteer;

having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a bundle of thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*; one should meditate upon the fire as the one born from the fire.
He has two faces and a single heart, four ears, and two nostrils;
he has two mouths, six eyes, is tawny in color, and possesses seven hands.
He has three girdles and three feet, is endowed with seven tongues,
possesses four horns, is mounted upon a bull, and has a radiance equal to the rising sun;
he is equipped with a sacred thread and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
On the left side it should be four cubits, and on the right side three cubits.
In his right hands, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear; in his left hands, he holds a javelin, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiriktā, and Bahurūpā are proclaimed as the seven tongues. Of these,
the four beginning with Hiraṇyā are on the right face.
The three tongues beginning with Suprabhā are indeed located in the left face.
The tongue of Varuṇa is golden; the middle one is yellow;
the northern tongue should be red; and that situated in the southern direction is black.
The tongue of Bahurūpeśa is proclaimed to be the location of the tongue;
it is said to bestow all accomplishments and has the form of fire, O Prajāpati.
Having meditated upon [the deity] seated in the midst of the fire, facing westward...
One should offer arghya mixed with flowers to Īśāna and perform the naming ceremony.
"O Śivāgni, you are Vāgīśvarī; [unite] with Vāgīśvara by means of the Heart-mantra.

Having thus conceived the mouth and dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) extending from the northeast (*īśāna*) to the southeast (*āgneya*), and having joined the six tongues beginning with Hiraṇyā to the central tongue, one should prepare fuel of two *darbha* blades.

Having taken [the materials], having performed the *upasthāna* with the mantra "juṣṭodamūnām," having placed fuel into the fire, having prepared a seat of two *darbha* blades, and having performed the ritual placement (*sannidhāna*) of the fire, [he should worship] in the directions starting from the east with the four mantras beginning with "devasya tvā."

Having strewn ten *darbha* blades with their tips pointing east and others with their tips pointing north, [he prepares] the northern seat for the vessel, the southern seat for the *brahmā*, and the northern seat for the *praṇītā*. [He performs] the preparation of the vessels.
Upon the *kuśa* grass on the left, he places the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles (l.

4), the clarified butter pot, the *praṇītā* water vessel, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling vessel, the *caru* cooking pot, and the *yaṃ* [vessel], as well as a *darbha* garland consisting of a web of threads of various colors. [Finally, there is] pure sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Having purified [the area] so that it is free from cracks and devoid of blinking eyes, and having neutralized the dualistic forms by turning them downward with armor, one should place the kindled *darbha* grass suitable for the fire-oblation and the nine substances upon the southern space.

Having prepared two *darbha* blades as a purifier (*pavitra*), having taken up the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), having placed a *kūrca* of one span (*vitasti*) [in it], having filled it with water, and having cast flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into it, he performs three upward splashes (*utplavana*). With that [water] and while reciting the *varman* mantra, he sprinkles the vessels turned face-up and the ritual materials upon the open space to the south. Then, having taken up the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, [he places] a *kūrca* of one span [in it].

Having poured [the water] out, having filled [the vessel] with water, and having performed three leaps, he places it to the north of the fire upon *darbha* grass, saying: "Thou art Varuṇa; ghee is thy vow; thou art of Varuṇa. Having covered it with *darbha* grass and having made a cushion (*kūrca*) of seventeen *darbha* blades, (line 2)

Having placed the seat with its front facing east upon the southern throne of the Hotṛ, [one says]: "O Brahmā, obeisance to your Brahmā-seat; O Brahmā, I invoke Brahmā—*bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ*. Obeisance to Brahmā. [The seat] is worshipped with all the *rādhana* offerings. Then, taking the *caru* (sacrificial porridge): "I offer what is pleasing to Śiva. Having sprinkled what is pleasing to Śiva, [he offers] with the *sruva* ladle.

Having brought a portion of the *praṇītā* water, [he says] "I offer what is pleasing to Śiva. Having cooked it over the fire, having placed the strainers (*pavitra*) inside, having filled the vessel with clarified butter (*ājya*),
and having performed the purification beginning with inspection, [he meditates on] his own self as abiding in Brahman.

Having reflected thus, having rotated [the vessel] three times over the *kuṇḍa*, having heated it in the fire, and having placed it in the southeastern direction, one should take a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *darbha* blade and offer it to Brahmā with the mantra "Brahmajijñāna" (*brahmaṇe svāhā*). Then, having visualized one's own body as equal to Viṣṇu, one should place the vessel of clarified butter in the northeastern direction and [proceed] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade...

Having taken up a drop of clarified butter and offered it with the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ viṣṇave svāhā" while reciting "Salutation to Viṣṇu," and having again meditated upon oneself in the form of Rudra and placed the vessel of clarified butter at the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should take up a drop of clarified butter with the tip of the *kūrca* grass-bundle and [recite] "yeṣām īśa... (from the *Śatarudrīya*).

Having offered oblations with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā*, one should place [the fire] in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having removed the embers to the west and having placed [the fuel] above them, one should take two pieces of *darbha* grass broken in two and consecrated with the Heart-mantra. Having made them into a torch toward the fire and having sprinkled them with clarified butter (*ājya*), the casting of them into the fire with the Weapon-mantra (*śastra*) is the act of purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*). One should cut two finger-breadths from the tips of two *kuśa* blades with the Weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Sprinkling is the act of purification for the purpose of averting Sumbha, Niśumbha, and the Māṣakas; having cast [the oblation] with clarified butter ending in *huṃ phaṭ* while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), there is a further stirring with a blazing [fire] using a curved blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the armor-mantra,
which is free from defects.

One should cast [the offering] into the fire with the mantra "To Agni, for the armor, svāhā. Again, having performed the circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*) with a blazing oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) using the *astra-mantra* ending in "huṃ phaṭ" along with burnt *darbha* grass;

one should cast [another portion] into the fire with "To the head, svāhā. While forming the path, having moved it toward the north, having pushed back the embers, and having placed the vessel of clarified butter outside.

Having grasped with the thumb and ring finger a *kūrca* of one span (*prādeśa*) length, provided with a central knot at its root and tip, and having thrice dipped it into the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) facing the fire; having released the knot and sprinkled [it] with the *Īśāna* mantra: *Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ Śivāgne*.

Having offered with "svāhā," and having again prepared the *pavitra* as before, having likewise sprinkled it toward oneself, having released the knot, and having sprinkled [the clarified butter], one should offer it with "To Śiva-Brahman, svāhā. This is the ritual of immersion (*saṃplavana*). In the midst of that, having offered into the clarified butter with the *praṇava* a tuft (*kūrca*) made of two *kuśa* blades and measuring a span in length.
Having visualized the triad of channels—iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā—in its right and left portions;
having visualized the two fortnights, the white and the black, between the other two; having consecrated it with the *saṃhitā*; having protected it with the *kavaca* mantra;
having rendered it nectar-like; and having worshipped it with the root mantra.

Thus ends the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Thereafter, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles along with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon and the *darbha* grass, one should hold the *sruk* with its opening facing upward and the *sruva* with its opening facing downward together with the *darbha*. Placing them in the left hand while holding them with the right hand, one should sprinkle them with water using the *astra-mantra* and wash them with the *kavaca-mantra*. Then, having sealed them with the *varma-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should place them in the fire with the right hand.

Having heated the *sruc* and *sruva* with three blades of *kuśa* grass— using the tips, middles, and roots of the *kuśa*— one should touch the tips, middles, and roots of the *sruc* and *sruva* while rotating them three times, reciting the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Then,
one should invoke Śakti into the *sruc* and Śambhu into the *sruva*, reciting *hiṃ hāṃ*.

Having established [the vessels] with the word "namaḥ," one should wrap the necks of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with two threads made of three strands and measuring one cubit (*hasta*) each. Having placed them upon a seat (*viṣṭara*) in one's own left region, and having settled them there, one should invoke at their tip, middle, and base: *oṃ hūṃ*, Rudra, lord of the *śiva-tattva*; *hīṃ*, Viṣṇu, lord of the *vidyā-tattva*; and *oṃ hāṃ haṃ*, the lord of the *ātman-tattva*.

Having honored Brahmā in this manner and having stirred the sacrificial porridge with the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it into the fire as is appropriate. He should honor the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the [relevant] mantra. He lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). He lays down the enclosing sticks.

With the mantras for the armor, the eyes, and the weapons, he places the sacrificial fuel (samidh) to the north of the water-pitcher. Having placed the *anuyāja* fuel near the *praṇītā* water, and having sprinkled [the oblation] with the mantra "juṣasva naḥ samidham agne adite," and having worshipped the guardians of the world (*lokapāla*) in their respective places— (l3).

Having worshipped the fire with fragrances and other offerings, and having worshipped Ananta, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu in the east, south, west, and north respectively; then, for the purpose of removing the saliva of the devotees and for the nourishment of the fire, one should offer five palāśa fuel-sticks, wetted at both the base and the tip, into the fire with the five-pronged [mantra]: *oṃ hāṃ śivāstrāya svāhā* and *oṃ hāṃ vyomavyāpine svāhā*.

ŚLĪṂ ŚŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PĀŚUPATĀSTRĀYA SVĀHĀ | OṂ KṢAṂ KṢURIKĀSTRĀYA SVĀHĀ | Having anointed the fuel with clarified butter, [I offer it] in this fire-ritual for the purpose of contracting [the enemy's] journey, O Brahman.

He shall place the fuel on the fire. "Place [the fuel] on," is the instruction for the Brāhmaṇa. With the verse, "They have placed the fuel," he should offer the fuel consisting of fifteen pieces with its root-end downward. Meditating mentally upon Prajāpati, he does not pour the two Āghāra-libations. [He offers] "To Prajāpati, svāhā! and "To Sadyojāta, svāhā! mentally, having touched the upper junction of the enclosing sticks, [he offers] continuously to Indra in a slanting manner.

Saying "svāhā" for the heart, he makes an offering silently at the southern junction of the enclosing sticks; then, looking on, having brought [the ladle] close for the moment, he offers the two portions of clarified butter. Afterwards, taking the *sruva* ladle and taking clarified butter from the left portion during the dark fortnight, he says, "To Agni, svāhā."

Having offered into the right eye of the fire, one takes clarified butter from the left portion and offers it into the left eye of the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma. Having taken [butter] from the middle portion, one offers it into the forehead-eye of the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni and Soma.

Having taken butter from the three portions, one offers it into the central mouth of the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. In the bright fortnight, the sequence begins from the left portion; this is the rule.
Having offered twelve oblations to you,

and having offered the four [oblations] with the mantras "yuktaḥ," "catasraḥ," "ano bhadraḥ," and "virūpākṣa," as well as to Virūpākṣa, Māyā, Atiraci, Saṃsinī, Prasādhinī, and the Vyāhṛtis; then, with the seed-syllable of fire,
twenty-five oblations.

The first feeding of rice is performed with the Sadyojāta mantra with seven oblations; the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) with the Vāmadeva mantra with seven oblations; from the initiation (*upanayana*) onwards, the observances (*vrata*) with the Aghora mantra with seven oblations; [the study of the Vedas] with the Tatpuruṣa mantra with seven oblations; the return home (*samāvartana*); and the marriage with the Īśāna mantra with seven oblations. After that, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the Prāsāda mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having offered fifteen fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, each sixteen finger-breadths long, with the sixteen vowels followed by "svāhā," one should then perform the "stepping upon the horse" (*aśvakrāma*). Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the face of Sadyojāta. Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the face of Vāmadeva. Oṃ huṃ, svāhā to the face of Aghora.

(l1) Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa; oṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the face of Īśāna. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the joining of the faces: oṃ hāṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the two faces of Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva. (l2)

Oṃ hiṃ huṃ, svāhā to the faces of Vāmadeva and Aghora. Oṃ huṃ heṃ, svāhā to the faces of Aghora and Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ heṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the faces of Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the faces of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna.

Now, the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*): immediately after that, one should perform the sprinkling (*abhighāra*) of the tongue. *Oṃ ruṃ*, svāhā to the golden tongue (*hiraṇyā jihvā*) situated in the face of Sadyojāta, which has the luster of molten fire. *Lūṃ*, svāhā to the golden-yellow tongue (*kanakā jihvā*) situated in the face of Īśāna, which has the luster of silver. *Oṃ ruṃ*, svāhā to the black tongue (*kṛṣṇā jihvā*), which is red in color. *Oṃ ṣūṃ*, [svāhā] to the pearl-lustred [tongue].
To the one abiding in the *tatpuruṣa* [face], to the tongue of many forms, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ ruṃ lūṃ puṃ pūṃ ṣuṃ sūṃ hūṃ! Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiriktā, Bahurūpā.

Svāhā to the tongues! Now, the sprinkling upon the tongues—one should perform the unification of the tongues: Oṃ hāṃ ruṃ lūṃ, svāhā to the tongues Hiraṇyā and Kanakā. La ruṃ pūṃ, [to the tongues] Kanakā and Raktā.

To the two tongues, svāhā! *Vrūṃ śriṃ*, to the red and black tongues, svāhā! *Śrīṃ ṣūṃ*, to the black and radiant tongues, svāhā! *Ṣuṃ sūṃ*, to the radiant and very red tongues, svāhā! *Sūṃ hūṃ*, to the very red and multiform tongues, svāhā! *Oṃ raṃ hūṃ*, to the tongues beginning with the golden one and ending with the multiform one, svāhā! Then...

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *prāsāda* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having worshipped the *yogāsana* in the midst of the fire: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti; salutation to the Kṛta Yuga; salutation to the Tretā Yuga;
salutation to the Dvāpara Yuga; salutation to the Kali Yuga.*

Salutation to the Unmanifest; salutation to the Restrained; salutation to Keśava; salutation to the one seated upon a white lotus; salutation to the one seated upon Śiva; salutation to the embodiment of Śiva. The meditation:
He is remembered as having the form of a pillar of light, shining like ten million suns.
And its internal form is said to be both with form and without form.
Everything that has arisen in the *liṅga* is said to dissolve back into it; this divine *liṅga* is indeed called the root pillar here. Oṃ hāṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).

"Since this divine splendor of yours is supremely purifying, therefore I shall establish myself here within the lotus of your heart; I shall worship [it]. Having been thus authorized, [he performs the rites] in the fire-form: having invoked the form of Śiva with the root mantra using the Sadyojāta mantra, he [invokes] the deity appropriate for that rite together with his retinue.

Having performed worship, at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), having offered ten oblations with the root mantra, having offered one oblation for the retinue, having presented the food offering along with incense and lamps, and having given the welcoming *arghya* water, [he should offer] again with the root mantra.
Having offered ten oblations, one shall perform the expiation for the *caru*: "Homage to Agni! Svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!
May you swell, O self-same one..."

Having thus heated the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) over the fire, saying "Make the waters warm," and having sprinkled it with clarified butter (*abhighārya*), and having offered the oblation of the remnants of the *caru* (*carusaṃpātāhuti*), then follows the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood with the root mantra consisting of the *praṇava* and the *prāsāda-bīja* joined with the *śiva-bīja*. With the *Śivagāyatrī*, there shall be eight oblations of clarified butter; with the mantra "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," there shall be eight oblations. [One offers] clarified butter with the mantra "Ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe."

With the mantra, "O source of ghee, come toward the ghee; O most excellent one, come according to your own nature; rejoice; O bull, carry the oblation offered with the cry of Svāhā," eight oblations are made. This constitutes the tenth part of the Brahma-aṅgas.

Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya svāhā | Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā | Oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā | Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā | Oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ śirase svāhā | Oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai svāhā | Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya svāhā | Oṃ...

"Hauṃ, svāhā to the eyes! Oṃ haḥ, svāhā to the weapon! Having offered three oblations with the mantra: "To Kadrudra, the wise, the most bountiful, the conscious one—for he is indeed Rudra in his entirety—to that Rudra, let there be homage."

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with *dūrvā* grass soaked in honey, followed by one thousand oblations with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, and having offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *Vyāhṛtis*, one performs the *caru* oblation.
