Following that, having gone near the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), [one recites]: "The invoker of the oblation, of great majesty, the slayer of demons in battles..."

The one who enjoys [the oblation], the luminous, the shining, the fulfiller of desires—Agni, whom they call *Svakṛt* (Self-made), we invoke him with *Uktha*. O Agni, make our sacrifice well-offered; O God, overcome all hostile armies. Make for us a broad path;
strike down the enemy.
"May our life be long and undecaying—svāhā! This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; it is not mine. Having sat down silently for a moment, and having offered the remnants of the oblation, [he says]:
'To the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśve Devas who partake of the remnants, svāhā! This is not mine. Then, with the verses..."

They lead [the horse] around. Having washed the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) in the fire for Vaiśvānara, he offers it here into the fire for Vaiśvānara, the knower of the sacrifice: "May this thousand-streamed, hundred-streamed [oblation], swelling with *svadhā*, go to our father and grandfather in the heavenly world;
homage! This is for the rivers; it is not mine.

Having filled [the vessels] again with the *naṣṭapyā* waters, he pours them out outside the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), saying: "This ocean, a hundred-streamed spring, being poured out in the midst of the world— yielding clarified butter, overflowing, generating [life], O Agni, do not harm me in the highest [realm]."
"To the sky! To the oceans! This [is mine], not mine. Having touched the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the girdles (*saṃnahana*) with water, he throws them into the fire.

He offers the *jayā* oblations. Having offered with the sections beginning "Thought and Agni, the messengers" (*cittam ca agnī dūtānām*), "The upholder of Truth, O God" (*ṛtāṣāḍ yad devā deva*), and "O Prajāpati, do not abandon these" (*prajāpate nva tvadetān nyana*), he places the fuel-sticks back onto the fire.
He offers with the formula, "Prāyaścittaḥ. He offers the Jaya and subsequent oblations.

(L3) "For the sake of the success of this rite, I shall perform the Jaya and other oblations: Cittaṃ ca svāhā! This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. By the grace of that which ends in 'vauṣaṭ,' [I offer] the Pūrṇāhuti. (L4)

In accordance with the rule, he sprinkles the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *sruva* ladle; in every case, taking a small portion from the surrounding grass-strewing (*paristaraṇa*), he places the top, middle, and bottom parts [of the grass] upside down into the clarified butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*). Having set aside a single blade of grass separately, he throws it into the *kaṭutryāṇī* fire-pan with its tip facing downward, and having simultaneously cast the middle part [of the other blades], [he offers] the *āghāra* libations and the two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) while reciting the mantras for the armor (*varman*), the eyes (*netra*), the weapon (*astra*), and the heart (*hṛdaya*) and head (*śiras*).

Having cast [the offerings] with the *paridhi* sticks and the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he performs the *saṃsrāva-homa* sacrifice: "To the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśvedevas who partake of the *saṃsrāva*—this is for them, not mine. Homage to Rudra Paśupati, svāhā! (l. 7)

"To Rudra Paśupati, this [is mine], not mine. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora weapon for the sake of the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the Śiras mantra, he offers the inner and outer oblations with food.

For example—on the upper ledge (*mekhalā*) of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): in the east, in the middle and its eastern part, [one offers] *svāhā* to Sadāśiva; *svāhā* to Īśvara. In the south: *svāhā* to Rudra. In the north: *svāhā* to Viṣṇu. In the west: *svāhā* to Brahmā. On the middle ledge of the pit: in the east, in the middle and its eastern part...

*Śāntyātītakalādīn nivṛtyantakalebhyah svāhā* | [Offering] on the lower girdle (*mekhalā*). *Indrādiviṣṇvantadevatābhyaḥ svāhā*. Having offered the *bali* to the deities situated upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*viṣṭara*), [one says]: *Anantāya svāhā*.
*Rudrāya svāhā*.

*Viṣṇave svāhā! Brahmaṇe svāhā!* One should release these deities in their proper sequence. Then, having prepared two mandalas in the south-eastern quarter of one’s own [location]: in the first mandala—in the directions from the east to the north—[one offers]: *Oṃ hāṃ rudrebhyaḥ svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ mātṛbhyaḥ svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ gaṇebhyaḥ svāhā!*
Oṃ hāṃ yakṣebhyaḥ svāhā. (l6.
In the corners beginning with the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ grahebhyaḥ svāhā. Oṃ hāṃ asurebhyaḥ svāhā. Oṃ hāṃ rākṣasebhyaḥ svāhā. Oṃ hāṃ nāgebhyaḥ svāhā. (l7.)
In the center of the mandala—in the northeast, southeast, and southwest: *oṃ hāṃ nakṣatrebhyaḥ svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ rāśibhyaḥ svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ viśvebhyaḥ svāhā*.
Between the northwest and the west: *oṃ hāṃ*.
Having worshipped with "To the Guardian of the Field, svāhā! ending with *namaḥ*, and having offered the *balis* and *arghya* ending with *svāhā*,
[one worships] in the second maṇḍala— in the eight directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast— Indra and the others up to Īśa.
Svāhā! In the northeast, on the left side of Īśāna: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*. In the southwest, on the left side of Nirṛti: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave svāhā*. In the center: *nīlalohitāya svāhā*.

Having thus worshipped with the ending "namas," and having offered the bali-oblation and the arghya-water, one should dismiss all [deities] even in reverse order. And if the bali is [offered] by means of this brief [formula]:

One should offer: Oṃ hāṃ he! O Rudras, performers of fierce deeds, who dwell in fierce abodes; and whoever are gentle, dwelling in gentle abodes; the Mothers in the form of Rudras, and those who are lords of the hosts.

And others who have become obstacles, residing in the various directions—may they all, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali-offering; may they grant us success quickly and protect us perpetually from all fears. (L6) Having thus given the bali, one should place the bali-mantras within one's own heart by means of the heart-mantra. Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having performed the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making oneself complete), one sprinkles [water] as before.

O Agni, enjoy the fuel; O Aditi, be mindful of the sun. O divine Savitṛ, you have impelled [the sacrifice]. [He performs] the leading forward and the sprinkling. Having opened up the quarters from the waters led forward, he pours out the remainder on the ground.
Having purified himself with them: "In the seat, may you be mine; you are everything, everything."

May you be mine; you are full, may you be full for me. You are imperishable; may my elders purify me in the eastern direction, O God; may the officiating priests purify me in the southeastern direction;

may the months and the ancestors purify me in the southern direction; may the planets and the cattle purify me in the western direction; may the waters, the plants, and the trees purify me in the northern direction; [may they purify me] in the upward direction.
"May the sacrifice, the year, and Prajāpati purify you!

I send you forth to the ocean; go to your own source. May I possess unbroken progeny; may my vital fluid not be spilled. With these [verses], [the water] is poured upon the head of the jar and the head of the teacher.

Having performed the purification (*mārjana*), he gives a coconut along with a cow as a substitute for the Brahman priest to a Brāhmaṇa. He offers a boon to the Brahman priest and causes the Brāhmaṇa to recite the *vāja* [prayers].

"Svāhā! Whatever brilliance (*tejas*) is yours, O Agni, through that may I become brilliant. He should perform the worship (*upasthāna*) of Agni with the mantra beginning with "O Agni," and so forth. [Whatever has been done] deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion...

O God, O Consumer of Oblations, may that which has been offered by me be perfectly complete for you. [Recite] the supreme remembrance of Śiva for all [beings], and the salutation: "Śiva, Śiva, obeisance!
Having sipped water, having performed the dedication to Śiva, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.

Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of expiation according to the Kāmika-tantra, having taken the fire from the sacrificial oblation of the procession, and having taken the Saṅkoca and Ātma-kumbhakas along with the Paripāta and Vāra-kumbhas, [he should proceed] to the sacrificial pavilion.

Having delineated [the mandala], performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and established the fire, the preceptor (*deśika*) should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the rules, beginning with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), food offerings (*anna*), and clarified butter (*ājya*). At the conclusion of the invocation, having dismissed [the deity], he should perform the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*). —From the *Ajitāgama* (l2).

Having contracted the *kumbha* according to the prescribed rule, one should protect the vessel used for the *yātrā-homa* until the end of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), nor should one abandon it even in thought.
If that deluded soul should abandon [the practice], he should perform one hundred thousand oblations with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
In the Ajita [rite]—
likewise, the fire for the oblations consists of the thread from a garland of *darbha* grass.
One should collect the water from the jar and the contents of the jar for the purpose of consecration.
"Having cast [it] away, the foolish-souled one becomes an opponent of the Asuras. (L4.

According to this statement from the Śivāgama, one should first perform the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) and then place the fire into the primary pit. Immediately thereafter, one should cause the offering of food (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and the worship of sixteen lamps for the *saṃkocakumbha*s, as well as the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the four Vedas, and the sounding of hymns, dance, song, and musical instruments. (L5)
Afterward, having adorned [the image],
having summoned the preceptors and given them new garments, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon its head, having worshipped the movable seat preceded by the bull-throne,
and having placed darbha grass and flowers [thereon], one should install the water-jars.

The preceptor, holding the *vardhanī* vessel together with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), preceded by the utterance of auspicious words (*svasti*), and accompanied by the recitation of the four Vedas, the sound of bells, the blowing of conchs, the beating of dundubhi drums,

bherīs, maddalas, jhallas, dancing, singing, instrumental music, shouts of victory, and the hymns of the Bhaṭṭas, should perform a circumambulation of the temple along with a collection of flowers; then he should enter the hall immediately.

Thus ends the *Bandhatipaddhati* (The Manual on the Eightfold Bondage), which extracts the essence of the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas concerning the practice of loosening the eightfold bondage. [Composed by] Śrī Kāntimati. [Side Heading: Entry into the Sacrificial Sanctuary] (p144b, f137a)

Then the preceptor, having summoned the initiated disciple—who has been consecrated, purified, bathed, observant of proper conduct, and full of devotion—together with the guardians of the images, and having adorned him with garments, upper cloths, bracelets, and so forth; having sprinkled his head with the general *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra* from the north; and having wiped his head down to his throat with seven blades of *darbha* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*; [he should proceed] again starting from the feet...

Having wiped [the area] up to the navel with seven [blades of darbha] using the Astra-mantra; having again wiped from the navel down to the feet with seven darbhas using the Astra-mantra; having discarded the darbhas;
having again sprinkled [it] with water using the Astra-mantra; and having applied vibhūti.

Having covered the head with armor and wrapped [the body] in silken garments, one should worship upon that [seat] as follows: "Obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya; obeisance to Aiśvarya; obeisance to Padma; obeisance to Vṛṣāsana;

Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Praṇava. Having thus worshipped and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Praṇava, one should place the contracted Śiva-pitcher upon that [seat] with the root mantra.
Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel, taking it up himself and setting it in his left hand,

he should hold it with his right hand; then, having caused the eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*) to be held by the image-makers in their proper order, he [should place] the Śiva-jar [with the mantra of] the Aghora-weapon of the sixteen-fold temple.

Having performed the recitation of mantras preceded by the touching of *darbha* grass, and having circumambulated the temple (*dhāma*) together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipas*) amidst the sounding of auspicious chants and various musical instruments and lamps; and having entered through the western door leading with the right foot, one should, upon entering, carefully place the *śivakumbha* facing west upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated in the center above the altar, while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).

Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel on the left side of that deity with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having installed the *vidyeśvaras* facing toward the primary directions starting from the east, and having established the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*) and the Śiva-fire (*śivāgni*) facing westward, the preceptor (*ācārya*) [should then proceed].

Having sat upon the tortoise-seat to the south of the principal altar, facing north, and having performed the ritual identification of the self (sakalīkaraṇa), he makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day,
for this God of gods, Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his consort Śrī Kantimatī Ambā, accompanied by the Śrī Mūla-liṅga and his entire retinue."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In the sacrificial pavilion of the Lord of Sacrifice, who consists of the restoration of the dilapidated and the eightfold bond, I shall perform the worship of the firm seat (*sthirāsana-pūjā*)," one should then worship as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*). Salutation to Ananta. Salutation to Dharma. Salutation to Jñāna. Salutation to Vairāgya. (l6)

Salutation to Aiśvarya. Having worshipped [the deity] from Adharma up to Śakti; having meditated upon the body of knowledge (vidyādeha); having applied the eyes; having invoked with the root mantra and the Sadyojāta mantras; having performed the rites from installation (sthāpana) up to the lamp offering;

having offered the oblation (nivedya); having worshipped the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga); having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās; having performed the placement of the Daṇḍabhaṅgī, Muṇḍabhaṅgī, and Kalābhaṅgī; and having prayed to Īśvara.

One should perform the selection of the Brahmins for the purpose of reciting the mantras beginning with the Veda. Having invited Brahmins who are skilled and well-versed in the Vedas and so forth, having seated them upon seats, and having honored them, one should take darbha grass and [proceed] in this [rite].

For the purpose of the continuous recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the *Ṛgveda* in the eastern part of the Śiva-yāga maṇḍapa— which consists of the restoration of the ruins and the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*)— of this Lord of Devas, Sadāśiva Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his retinue, his venerable consort Śrī Kāntimatī, and his venerable primary liṅga (*mūlaliṅga*).

"I choose you along with your retinue. Having thus chosen, [he says]: "In the south, I choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the purpose of reciting the Yajurveda; in the north, I choose you for the purpose of reciting the Sāmaveda;

in the west, I choose you as the officiating priest for the purpose of reciting the Atharvaveda and the Brahma-mantras in their various forms; and in the northeast corner, [I choose you] here for the five-fold, six-fold, and eight-fold [recitations]."

I choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the purpose of reciting the *Ṣoḍaśakalā-prāsāda-mantra*. In the southeast corner— for the purpose of reciting the *Aghora-mantra* and for the purpose of reciting the *Aghorāstra*, with a daily count of more than one thousand repetitions of the *Aghora*— [End of fragment]

"I choose you as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). For the northwestern direction, I choose you, together with your retinue, for the purpose of reciting the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra more than a thousand times. For the daily recitation of each of the five weapons (*pañcāstra*) more than a thousand times in the northwest, I choose you, together with your retinue, as the officiating priest. Having thus chosen him, then the Brahmins, having been initiated, [proceeded].

Having washed their feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), with *pavitra* grass in their hands, they should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, [the worship] of this God of gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, together with the venerable Mūlaliṅga, and together with his retinue, [of the venerable Veṇu...]"

For the restoration of the ancient [shrine] of Vaneśvara Sadāśiva, consisting of the eight-fold binding (aṣṭabandhana) ritual of the Śiva-sacrifice; specifically for the protection of the Śiva-sacrifice, for the preservation of the world, for the firmness of the eight-fold binding, for the pleasure of Sāmba-Sadāśiva, and for the alleviation of the heat of the binding— [he performed] the recitation of the Śrī Rudra and other mantras the stated number of times, remaining present in those respective locations.
The avoidance of sleep, idle talk, and so forth while in the *ālaya* [state],

as well as the offering of the fruits of recitation preceded by devotion; for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of the recitation of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), one should perform the recitations of mantras such as the *Ṛgveda* and the *Śrī Rudra* in mutual cooperation.
Having made the resolve, "We shall perform [this]," one should recite the Śrīrudra, the Camaka, and likewise the Pañcaśānti,
as well as the five-syllabled mantra of Fire and the six-syllabled mantra.
The mantra of the Five Palaces, the Nīla-yakṣarī,
the nine-syllable garland mantra, the Śrīsūkta, and likewise the Āraṇa.
The Rudra-hymn, the Brahmasāman, the Bṛhatsāman, and the Rathantara.
The Puruṣasūkta, the Śivasaṅkalpa, and the Ghoṣaśāntika;
the Yavas, the Mahānāmnīs, and the Rudrahotṛ as well.
The Vālakhilya, the Pāvamāna, and likewise the Vṛṣabīja;
the Śāstādvaya, the Nīlarudra, and likewise the Rātrisūkta;
the Nārāyaṇa, the Skandasūkta, and likewise the Kavaca of Śiva.
The seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Gaurī, and the mantra of Vighnarāja.
The supreme preceptor should recite the mantra of the five palaces of Naṭeśa’s assembly, as well as the primary seed-mantras and other mantras, during the ritual recitation.
Five thousand or half of that, as is appropriate,

[should be given] at night for the protection of the sacrifice, outside the enclosure of the pavilion. Furthermore, one thousand [recitations] of the Pāvakāstra and likewise of the Aghorāstra [are required].
Half of that is the Pāśupata weapon, and likewise the Vidyāṅga weapon;
the Śiva weapon consists of six hundred [syllables], as does the Bhairavī mantra.
The Āpya mantra consists of two hundred [syllables], and the Hasta mantra is the same.
One should protect the exterior of the pavilion in all directions with these mantras.
Thus, for the sake of protecting the sky, the twice-born ones stood with their faces turned upward;
standing separately in a good formation, they should recite the hundred [verses] that pervade the atmosphere.
In that very manner, the wise one should recite according to the sequence of the Tāraka-Brahman;
likewise, for the sake of protecting the netherworld (pātāla), those with downward-turned eyes [should do so]. Thus has the Vārāha [mudrā] been proclaimed, as well as the Adhomukhī.
In the intervals, for the sake of protection, the best of Brahmins should mutter the mantras of the eight Bhairavas and other such great mantras.
Then the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Prior to the commencement of the oblation, he should prepare a well-flowing ladle,
as well as parched grain, the enclosing sticks, *darbha* grass, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
And many kinds of food, fruits, and various types of edible grains.
The most excellent of teachers should prepare everything suitable for the fire sacrifice:
fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and the vessel for the ritual substances.
Having brought the *vardhanī* vessel, unbroken rice, the *saṃpāta* remains, and the oblation vessel,
one should likewise lead them toward the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with effort.
All [the pits] should be square, but that in the southeast should be in the shape of a vulva (*bhaga*).
To the south is the Bāṇakuṇḍa, while in the southwest (Nairṛtya) is the triangular one.
In the west, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular; in the northwest, it is hexagonal;
in the north, it is shaped like a lotus stalk; and in the northeast, it has eight corners.
Between Indra and Īśāna,

having caused the primary circular *kuṇḍa* and the others to be constructed in this sequence according to rule and with their proper characteristics, [one should place them] on both sides of the principal *kuṇḍa*.

This is declared to be the station of Brahmā, with a height of four finger-breadths (*mokṣāṅgula*) and a circumference of one finger-breadth of the Lord of the World (*lokeśāṅgula*). In its center, one should draw a lotus.
Its height is one finger-breadth of the Moon (*candrāṅgula*), and it is well-spread out by one finger-breadth of Action (*karmāṅgula*).
One should arrange the place for the *praṇītā* water specifically on the left side, as it has been taught.

(The fire ritual)—having thus completed [the preliminary rites], and then having obtained permission for the fire ritual, together with the *mūrtipa*s who have offered the *praṇava* and *arghya*, one should circumambulate the fire-sanctuary (*agniketana*) from left to right, sit facing the north, and perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*). As follows: (p147b, l1)
One should perform the inspection with the Śiva-mantra, the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra,
the sprinkling with the armor-mantra (Kavaca), and the striking with the Astra-mantra.
One should then perform scratching, scattering, filling, and sprinkling;
thereafter, one should carry out pounding, and after that, sweeping.
Scratching refers to the smearing of the sacrificial pit and the circumambulation of the pit.
Then follows the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), as well as the placement of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the ritual seating mats (viṣṭara).
The wise one should fashion three lines as a vajra-pile; that is the arrangement of the *māḍhaka* mark. All of this, moreover, he should perform with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

The fivefold refinement (*pañcasaṃskāra*): purification with *sadyojāta*: *oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*. Washing with *vāmadeva*: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. Drying with *aghora*: *oṃ huṃ aghorāya namaḥ*. Cooking with *tatpuruṣa*: *oṃ haiṃ*.

Salutation to Tatpuruṣa. Sprinkling with Īśāna: *Oṃ Hoṃ, salutation to Īśāna*. In this manner, the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) should be performed even in a space that lacks room [for the full ritual].

If it is a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), it should be prepared according to the prescribed rule. Thus, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites in the primary fire-pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*) with the mantra "The earth by the earth... (*bhūmir bhūmnā...*)—[saying] "I establish"—and with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should sprinkle the pit with the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghoda*).

Having sprinkled [the site] with water, and having worshipped the Goddess of the Earth within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, saying "Laṃ, obeisance to the Earth," one should take two *darbha* blades there, each twelve finger-breadths long,
and join their roots with their tips.

One should draw lines upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*). Here, three lines are drawn with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise three extending toward the north. The mantras for the drawing and so forth follow the sequence of the Vedic and Śaiva traditions. With the *brahmajijñāna* mantra and the *hṛdaya* [mantra], one draws a single line in the center with its tip pointing east; with the *nākesuvarṇa* mantra and the *śiras* [mantra], one draws [a line] in the south; and with the *āpyāyasva* mantra and the *kavaca* [mantra], one draws [a line] in the north.

Likewise, with the mantra beginning "yo rudra" and with the Īśāna [mantra], one should place that darbha-grass in the middle; thereafter, the ritual touching should take place. "Viṣṇu strode across this; in three places he set down his foot; his footprint is gathered in the dust. (RV 1.22.17)

With this mantra, one should draw a line in the west using the Astra-mantra: "O Indra, all the songs have magnified you, you who are as vast as the ocean; the best of charioteers among charioteers, the true lord and master of spoils.

(l5) With this mantra, [one should place the darbha] at the crest in the eastern direction. Having placed that darbha in the center and sprinkled it with water using the Īśāna-mantra, one should discard it in the north.
Having recited the weapon-mantra and having sipped water, [he should worship]:
in the center—salutation to Brahmā;
on the south—salutation to Yama.
In the north—salutation to Soma.
Again, in the center—salutation to Rudra.
In the south—salutation to Viṣṇu.
In the north: "Homage to Indra.

Having worshipped these [deities] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should place a double-bundle of *darbha* grass (*kūrca*) with its tips pointing westward in the center of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of commanding Vāgīśā. Then, [one should take] fire produced from a sun-crystal, from a fire-drill (*araṇi*), or from the mouth of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*).

1) Having taken the fire in an earthen vessel or a bronze vessel and placed it before the *hotṛ*, one should gaze at the fire while reciting the mantra "mama agne," and then utter the *astra* mantra over the tips of the *darbha* grass. 2)

Having placed [the offering] in the fire; within that [fire], having taken one part from thirty-two parts; having set aside the portion for the *kavyād* in the southwest (*naiṛta*); having touched water; having recited the *astra-mantra*; having sprinkled the fire with the general *udaka* using the *aghora-mantra*; having worshipped the fire with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the *hṛdaya-mantra*; and having established the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra[-mantra]*.
Having encased [the fuel] with the Kavaca mantra and cast it into the fire, having kindled it,
[one performs] the worship of Vāgīśvara.
Homage to Vāgīśvara, whose nature is Sound, seated upon the tuft of hair in the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having meditated upon him as having five faces, three eyes, four hands, and three feet, and as being white in color, [bestowing] the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons... (l5)
The Hotṛ priest should clearly visualize the form of Vāgīśvara, holding a rosary in his right hand and a bunch of Kuśa grass in his left.

Salutation to the embodiment of Vāgīśa. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśa. Having thus invoked and worshipped [him], [one should worship] with: "Salutation to the seat of Vāgīśvarī, whose nature is the Bindu.
She is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, six-armed, and in the bloom of youth.
Adorned with all ornaments, anointed with divine unguents,
she holds in her right and left hands a rosary, a lotus, a citron, a string [of beads], and likewise the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess who has bathed after her menses, one should worship [the fire] upon the *kūrca*.

Reciting "Oṃ, salutation to the form of Vāgīśa" and "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvarī," one should invoke and worship her. Then, taking a flower with the right hand, one should lead the fire by means of the *niṣṭhura-mudrā*, the *pūraka* breath-retention, and the *astra-mantra*. That fire—

Having joined [the breath] along the path of the existent and fixed it in the fire situated at the *bindu*, having fixed both of those in the stomach-fire (*jāṭhara*), and having unified the three fires, one should meditate on the right [fire] as emerging from the tip [of the tongue]. [Reciting] the seed-syllable of fire, *oṃ hūṃ*, [one says] "Salutation to the consciousness of fire. Having placed the vessel upon that fire and consecrated it with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra* [mantra].

Having veiled [the deity] with the *kavaca* [mantra], having rendered [it] nectar-like while reciting the *pañcakalā-damana-mantra* while forming the *dhenumudrā*, and having circled the fire three times above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), kneeling upon the ground, [he says]: "O Goddess Vāgīśvarī, come here to my sacrifice through the path of the womb."

Having recited up to "asmin" [in the mantra], and having cast the fire into the center of the *kūrca* grass within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "ī agnaye namaḥ," and having visualized that fire as worthy of worship for Śiva, and having recited from "mai deva" up to "suvirāḥ," and having cast fuel together with *darbha* grass into the fire, he should worship it with "hṛdayāya namaḥ" and offer the *arghya*.

One should contemplate that the *karṇādhāna* (the rite of piercing the ears) has been performed; having offered *arghya* with the mantra "aso devāsaḥ," one should contemplate that the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child) has taken place; having offered *arghya* with the mantra "aghorebhyaḥ," one should contemplate that the *sīmantonnayana* (the parting of the hair) has been accomplished;
[then] by means of the fire-mouthed sacrifice (*agnivaktra-yajana*), one should kindle...?

l1) [No continuation] Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra; having offered seven oblations of rice (*taṇḍula*) with the *śiras* mantra for the sake of generating the fire (*agni*); and having offered the *arghya* with that same mantra; [one should perform the rite] with the *astra* mantra for the immediate cessation of birth-impurity (*sadyas-sūtaka*). l2)

Having sprinkled the two parents with the *arghya* water using the mantra, and having bathed the Mistress of Speech (*vāgīśī*) for purification with the mantra "uttha," one should again sprinkle the two parents with the *arghya* water using the tip of the *kūrca* grass. Then, having recited the mantras beginning with "yad agne" and ending with "yaviṣṭhya," one should cast fuel into the fire. Again, [one recites] "rātriṃ rātrim... and so forth.

Having recited the mantra ending with *śāniṣāmā* and having uttered the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should cast the blades into the fire. Then, one should meditate upon the fire as having two faces, three feet, and being joined by two nostrils.

He is endowed with three girdles, has six eyes, and is tawny in luster; he has four tongues on his right face and likewise three tongues on the left. He has four arms on the right side and three arms on the left.
In his right hands, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear; in his left hands, a javelin, a sacrificial vessel, and a vessel of clarified butter.
He is the fire of the mouth-oblation (*mukhahavanīyo 'gniḥ*), and the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) is said to be the tenth.
Speech is the fire of the left arm, and the other limbs are fires;
the southeast, northeast, and all the intermediate directions are proclaimed to be the limbs.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā likewise [are the goddesses].
The seven tongues are proclaimed to be excessive and multiformed.
The tongue of the west is golden, the middle one is of gold,
the northern tongue should be red, and that situated in the southern direction is black.
Suprabhā shall be the eastern tongue, and Atiriktā is situated in the southeast;
Bahurūpeśa shall be the tongue—thus is the location of the tongues proclaimed.
The tongue on the right face, however, is Hiraṇyādicutastrastu;
likewise, there are three tongues on the left face, which is Suprabhā.
The bowls are made of gold and refined gold, like royal flowers;
some are red, resembling vermilion, while others are black, like dark clouds.
Suprabhā is white-petaled; Atiraktā is like a red ruby;
Bahurūpā is proclaimed to have variegated colors and the color of the tongue.
These three are to be known as Bahurūpās, and the sixty-fourth is Galādhiṣṭhā.
Thus, the ninefold divisions of the tongues in the mouth of Agni have been declared.
Kālī, Karālī, Manoramyā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmrā, the one with another masculine form, Viśvarūpī, and Virodhikā.
That goddess with tremulous eyes is proclaimed as the Śaktis.
One should join the letters beginning with *hiraṇya* and ending with *yiḍa* to the Śaktis. [He is] four-horned, mounted upon a bull, and seated upon a lotus pedestal.
Having meditated thus: "Homage to the heart.
Having visualized [the deity] seated facing west in the midst of the fire, with the Īśāna [mantra]... (l7)

Sprinkling [the site] with *arghya* water mixed with flowers; having thus visualized the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) beginning with *puṃsavana* and ending with the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*),
and having divided the fire for the purpose of the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice— at that time.

Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) according to the rules, having poured clarified butter over it, and having set it aside, he should cover that *caru* with *darbha* grass. Then, having divided the fire while reciting the mantra "vāstoṣpate" and the ten-syllable [mantra], he should place the *darbha* grass and *palāśa* fuel-stick onto the fire and unite them with the primary fire. Taking the *palāśa* fuel-stick together with the *darbha* grass, he should worship the fire with the mantra "jiṣṇor idam".
Having cast a fuel-stick into the fire:
(l3) it is said that the knot should be one finger-breadth [in width], the tip should be four finger-breadths, and the length twenty-four finger-breadths; it should be as thick as the little finger.
The number [of blades] is one hundred and twenty-eight, and likewise for the seat (viṣṭara) in the four directions.
The characteristic of the seat has been stated; now hear the characteristic of the kūrca grass-bundles.

The number of *darbha* blades shall be thirty-six, and their length twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). There should be a knot at one finger-breadth from the tip, and the tip itself should be four finger-breadths long. Having wrapped it with that very *darbha*, one should strew it around with a tuft (*kūrca*).
Those who dwell in the northern and southern regions, as well as those in the highlands of the north.
One should place [the blades] with their tips pointing east and north in the directions beginning with the east;
one should then arrange a layer in the four directions consisting of fifty-five blades.
And for the sake of protection, the Brahma-sthāna is likewise prescribed in the outer [area].
With the mantra "devaḥ satva" [and] with the Tatpuruṣa [mantra], one performs the strewing of grass [paristaraṇa]. [Recite] "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ | aghorāya namaḥ."
To the south—spreading the sacrificial grass: "We rise up from the darkness. Homage to Sadyojāta. To the west—spreading the sacrificial grass: "O Agni, come for our enjoyment.
Homage to Vāmadeva.

To the north—fifteen darbha-blades for the strewn-covering (*paristaraṇa*). For the purpose of arranging the vessels, [one places] fifteen darbha-blades as a strewn-covering, with the southern ones to the north and the northern ones below.
To the south of the fire—(l2) fifteen darbha-blades for the place of the *brahmán* priest; [one places them] as a strewn-covering.

To the north— having strewn fifteen darbha blades for the purpose of placing the *praṇītā* water, one should place the vessels two by two: the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *praṇītā* vessel, the vessel for clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the large and small ladles (*sruk-sruva*), the fan, the wooden spoon (*darvī*), the vessel for the *caru* offering, the vessel for the *saṃpāta* oblation, the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and darbha grass,
and whatever other items are suitable for the fire sacrifice (*homa*).

Having arranged other vessels in pairs with their openings facing downward, one should place them upon *kuśa* grass using the *sammiśanti* mantra and the *astra* mantra. Having touched the vessels with the root mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship them, saying: "Salutation to Puṣkara; salutation to the Unmanifest Vessel (*avyaktapātra*). Then, [one prepares] a *kūrca* of double-stranded [grass] measuring one span (*vitasti*).
Taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel distinguished by a central knot,

having placed the *kūrca* with its tip pointing northward, and having recited the *cūlikā* mantra, one should wash the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with the *astra* mantra. Then, filling it with water from the left using the mantra "āpo vā" [RV 10.9.1], one should hold the ring finger upward.

Having purified the water three times with the *hṛdaya* mantra while holding it between the two thumbs with the mantra *śanno devī*, and having lifted up all the vessels and all the ritual substances with the mantra *tat tvā yāmi*, he should release the fuel (*idhma*). *Śanno*...

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the *deva* mantra while reciting the *kavaca*, and having taken the *praṇītā* vessel, having washed it with the *astra* mantra, and having prepared a bundle (*kūrca*) made of eighteen blades of grass; [one should say]: "O Agni, on the southern sacrificial mound, in the center of the lotus—O Brahmā, salutation to your seat! O Brahmā, we choose you as Brahmā. Having thus chosen the Brahmā—or, in the case of the *kūrca*, [having chosen] the *kūrca* as the Brahmā.

Having invoked [the deity] with the words, "I invoke [you] into this *kūrca*," he should worship it with all the offerings, saying "Salutation to Brahmā" while reciting the *culikā-mantra*. Then, having placed the *kūrca* made of seven *darbha* blades— distinguished by a knot in the middle— into the center of the *praṇītā* vessel, he should fill it with water up to the level of the *argha*.

Having purified [the vessel] with the *pavitra* and the *Trirud* mantra, and having worshipped it with "Homage to the Vessel of Nectar! Homage to Varuṇa!", one asks, "Who shall take [this] with the mantra? Having touched it with the *astra* mantra and poured out the water with the mantra "O Water, for the sake of purification," and having worshipped it with scents and flowers, one consecrates it with the *kavaca* mantra. Then, taking the *praṇītā* vessel with both hands while holding *darbha* grass upright, [one proceeds].

Lifting [the vessel] level with the tip of the nose: "Thou art Varuṇa, O thou who art firm in thy vow; thou art of Varuṇa. With "Homage to Tatpuruṣa," having placed it on the left side: "Thou art Aditi, by means of the armor. Having consecrated it with this mantra and covered it with *darbha* grass:
"Homage to Varuṇa. It is well-worshipped with all the rites of propitiation. Now...

Having taken up the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and worshipped it with the mantra, "Homage to the radiant vessel," one should cast out embers to the west with the mantra, "By speech, [I cast out] the food. Then, with the mantra, "Homage to the eyes," one should place the vessel of clarified butter upon the embers in the fire.

Having placed the *kūrca* in the middle of the vessel as previously described, having recited the *culikā-mantra*, having worshipped with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having filled the vessel with ghee using the mantra "Thou art the milk of the earth" (*mahīnāṃ payosi*) and the *aghora-mantra*, having placed the tips of two *kūrca*s [into the vessel], and having illuminated it with the *abhidyotana-mantra*: "Oṃ Raṃ, obeisance to Agni; obeisance to the armor (*kavaca*); the *rakṣas* is excluded, the *rakṣas* is excluded..."

Having performed the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) three times with the [mantra] "ārātayaḥ," he says, "Homage to the eyes! (l3). Having moved it toward the north, he says, "Homage to the weapon! (l4): "He has mixed with ghee; ghee is his source; he is celebrated by means of ghee; ghee is his path. Taste it, bring it hither, exhilarate yourself! Svāhā! To the bull, the oblation, who has been consecrated with *svāhā*. (l4)

Having thus consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra, having looked at it again with the *adaddha* mantra and the *astra* mantra, and having performed the fire-circumambulation (*paryagni-karaṇa*) three times again with the *astra* mantra, one should unite the fire with the [central] fire by saying, "Oṃ Raṃ, obeisance to Agni. Then, having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), [one should move] from east to west and from west to east using two purifiers (*pavitra*) whose tips point toward the north.

Having performed the threefold sprinkling with the mantra, "May the divine Savitṛ purify [you] with an unbroken filter, through the rays of the sun, O Vasu," and with the *sadyas* [mantra], and having rotated it three times clockwise above the fire, [one says] "Homage to the armor" (*kavacāya namaḥ*) in front of the *hotṛ*.

Having performed the placement [of mantras], having released the ancestral thread (*pitṛgrantha*), and having touched water, [one says] "Salutation to the Weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*). Having cast a bundle of grass (*kūrca*) into the center of the fire, having produced the bundle of grass as before,
and having placed it in the midst of the clarified butter, [one recites] *iḍā piṅgalā suṣumnāmayaṃ ca*.

Having visualized the clarified butter (*ājya*), then taking hold of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the right hand held upward, along with the *mekṣaṇa* stirring-spoon and the *kuśa* grass, together with the left hand, one should rotate them over the fire with the mantra "vṛttyuṣṭam" and the *tatpuruṣa* mantra. Having rotated them face-to-face while the [ladles] were facing upward and then downward, one should take hold of the *darbha* blades with the right hand, and place the *sruk*, *sruva*, and *mekṣaṇa* in the left hand.

Having placed [the vessel] in the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*) by way of circumambulation with the *kavaca* mantra, one should wipe the tip of the *sruva* ladle with the tips of the *darbha* grass using the mantra "iti. Having wiped the middle with the middle, and having rotated it again, one should wipe the base with the base using the *mūla* mantra, and rotate it once more. Then: "We choose speech, breath, and mind within ourselves. (l4)

With the mantra: "May he who is Prajāpati, the guardian of the world, protect us from death and save us from distress; may we attain long life and reach old age," and with the Astra-mantra, having wiped the ladle (*sruc*) and the *samekṣaṇa* [the vessel], one should offer oblations into those two with the formulas: "Salutation to the Ātmatattva; salutation to the Vidyātattva; salutation to the Śivatattva."

Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the *ātmatattva*; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the *vidyātattva*; salutation to Rudra, the lord of the *śivatattva*. Salutation to Śiva; salutation to Śakti. "Salutation to Aghora" [is said] over the *sruk*, *sruva*, and the *mekṣaṇa*.
Having thus assigned [these names] to the oblation (*havis*), [one says] "Salutation to the Weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*) while touching the *saṃmārjana* *darbha* grasses as before.

Having offered [the wood] into the fire, he then takes up the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Having placed one in the east with the mantra "Homage to the long-shining sun for the armor" (*jyoktasūryaṃ kavacāya namaḥ*), he places one in the south with the mantra "Thou art the arm of Indra; homage to the eyes" (*indrasya bāhur asi... netrēbhyo namaḥ*). He places one in the west with the mantra "Thou art a Gandharva; homage to the armor" (*gandharvo 'si... kavacāya namaḥ*). He places one in the north with the mantra "O Mitra and Varuṇa... (*mitrāvaruṇau tvā...*); [homage to the weapon] (*astrāya namaḥ*).

Then, above the two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in the fire and within the range of the Lord, one places the two supporting fuel-sticks with the mantra "Sūryaḥ satvā vibhābhyām," saying "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*). Then, with the mantra "Viti hotraṃ tvāgave," one says "Salutation to the Head" (*śirase namaḥ*). Finally, the after-offering fuel-stick (*anūyāja-samidh*) is placed above the *praṇītā* water-vessel, saying "Salutation to the Weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*).

Having placed a fuel-stick for the weapon-mantra (*astrāya*) and having arranged seats (*viṣṭara*) in the four directions starting from the east, one should worship them as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā" in the east; "Salutation to Rudra" in the south;
"Salutation to Viṣṇu" in the west;
and "Salutation to Ananta" in the north. Having thus worshipped them, one should place ritual grass-bunches (*kūrca*) in the directions starting from the east, and upon them—
In the east, obeisance to Śāntikalā. In the south, obeisance to Vidyākalā.
In the west, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalā. (l5)
In the north, [one should say]: "Salutation to Nivṛttikalā.

(Worship of the deities of the directions)—Furthermore, one should properly worship the deities of the directions in the four quarters, beginning with the east; and the wise one should worship them starting from Soma and ending with Varuṇa.
In the north— salutation to Kubera;
in the east— salutation to Indra.
In the south: *namaḥ vaivasvatāya*.
In the west: *namaḥ varuṇāya*. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the enclosure of the fire up to the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Regarding the enclosing sticks:
In the east— (l7) homage to Pāvaka; in the southeast— homage to Vibhāvasu.
In the south: *namaḥ* to Havyavāhana. In the southwest: *namaḥ* to Anala. In the west:
*namaḥ* to Jvalana.
In the northwest: Homage to Saptajihva.
In the north: Homage to Pāvaka.
In the northeast: Homage to Agni.

"Aditi, give your consent! Anumati, give your consent! Sarasvatī, give your consent! O God Savitṛ, impel! Having sprinkled [the water] all around, he then takes clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon:
"To the eyes of Īśāna, svāhā!"
In the south: *netrebhyaḥ svāhā*.
In the center: *astrāya svāhā*.
Then, having struck the fire eight times with two *darbha* blades in the middle of the fire, [he should cast] that *darbha* into the fire... (l3)
Having touched water and having anointed fifteen fuel-sticks with clarified butter using the root-mantra, and having uttered the sixteen names [of the deity]: "In this [place],

for the rite of the sacrificial oblation at the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the restoration of the dilapidated and the eight-fold binding, for the sake of the Brahman-priest of the venerable Vemuvaneśvara Sadāśiva— who is accompanied by the Mother Śrī Kāntimatī, joined with the venerable Mūlaliṅga, and together with his retinue."

Having offered once with the words, "I shall place the fuel," and again having offered five palāśa fuel-sticks for the purification of the two mouths [of Agni] with the mantra, "To the heart, svāhā! and having touched water with the mantra,
"Adoration to the weapon (astra)," one takes clarified butter with the *srava* spoon and [offers it] toward the northwest.

Having offered oblations ending in the southeast with "Sadyojātāya svāhā," and having offered oblations from the southwest to the northeast with "Hṛdayāya svāhā," [he offers] in the east with "Śikhāya svāhā."
In the south: *aghorāya svāhā*. In the north: *tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*. In the west: *netrebhyaḥ svāhā*.
In the center—svāhā to Īśāna. In the north—svāhā to Soma.
In the south—svāhā to Sūrya.

Oṃ raṃ agnaye svāhā | (p154a, l1) To the eyes, svāhā | To the armor, svāhā | Having meditated that this is the "facing" (*saṃmukhīkaraṇa*) of Agni, and having offered oblations in sequence with the twelve mantras beginning with *yukte* ..., [one performs] the five Brahmans and the six limbs... (l2)

One should offer oblations with the *pratimantra*. With the mantra "Aham asmi" (I am), using the *sadyojāta* [face] and food, there are seven oblations for the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*). With the mantra "Ye keśinaḥ," using the *vāmadeva* [face] and clarified butter (*ājya*), there are seven oblations for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*). With the mantra "Āyurdā deva... and the *aghora* [face], using clarified butter, there are seven oblations for the initiation (*upanayana*). With the mantra "Imaṃ stomam" and the *tatpuruṣa* [face], [one offers] to Vṛtra with clarified butter.

Seven oblations. With the mantra "Gandhadvārā" and [the deity] Īśāna, there are seven oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *samāvartana* ceremony. [One offers] "Hṛdayāya namaḥ. For the purpose of marriage, having united the two Lords of Speech (*vāgīśau*), one should meditate [on them] as having two arms and two eyes, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should visualize her seated there on the left side of the fire, wearing white garments, white in complexion, and possessing a pure smile. Then,
with the three Prajāpati mantras and the heart-mantra, one should perform the marriage ceremony with clarified butter.

Seven oblations. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the rule for the sake of completing the ritual, one should then meditate upon Agni in the form of Vṛddha. [One should offer: "Homage to the seat of Vṛddhāgni in the center of the fire; homage to the form of Vṛddhāgni. [He is] four-armed, three-eyed, single-faced, and wears matted locks.
A trident and likewise a hand-gesture of granting boons, combined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having done so, one should then divide the fire from the principal *kuṇḍa* into the individual *kuṇḍas*, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

In the case of five *kuṇḍas*, after dividing the fire in this very manner, one should worship the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śaktyanta in the principal fire. Then, having visualized the *yogāsana* within the heart of the fire—
Having meditated upon [the deity] who has five faces and ten arms, whose radiance is as white as cow’s milk,
who bestows all accomplishments, and who is seated with his face turned toward the west;
Having invoked Sadāśiva into this [liṅga] and performed the worship from the installation up to the lamps,
one should clearly visualize him as white-bodied, mounted upon a bull, and possessing an aged fire.

Having offered ten oblations of clarified butter at the place of the *nivedya* and having made a prayer, one should then offer nine oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with ghee into the principal fire for the sake of prosperity (*puṣṭi*) to Agni, accompanied by the [first] nine verses. Having again offered an oblation of clarified butter with the tenth verse, one should then place the vessel containing the remnants of the oblations to the right side of the sacrificer.
In that fire, [one should worship] with "Obeisance to the Seat of Īśāna.

[One should meditate upon] Īśāna, who is crystal-like in luster, the cause of the universe, three-eyed, crowned by the moon, gentle, serene, and holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Salutation to the form of Īśāna.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Having invoked Īśāna and worshipped him with the rites beginning from *sthāpana* up to the lamp, [one should again recite]: "Salutation to the seat of the eyes.
The eye is endowed with three eyes and adorned with four arms.
[He saw] the Lord wearing yellow garments, [holding] a noose, a trident, and a boon-granting gesture...

Salutation to the Form of the Eye (*netramūrti*). Salutation to the Eyes (*netra*). Having invoked the Eye and performed the worship beginning with the installation (*sthāpana*) and ending with the lamp, [one should again recite]: "Salutation to the Seat of the Weapon (*astrāsana*). And the Weapon itself has three eyes and is endowed with four arms.
And I worship Mahāmāyā, who holds the excellent trident and other [implements].

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the embodiment of the weapon (astramūrti). Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the weapon (astra). Having performed the worship beginning with the installation and ending with the lamp, one should worship the Vasus around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the order starting from the east: Oṃ, in the east, obeisance to Dharā.
In the southeast—to Dhruva, obeisance.
In the south—to Soma, obeisance.
In the southwest—to Anila, obeisance.
In the west—salutation to Āpāya.
In the northwest—salutation to Abhya.
In the north—salutation to Pratyūṣa.
In the northeast, [one should say] "Homage to Prabhāsa. Having worshipped the eight Vasus, one should again worship the seven Maruts in the order starting from the east.
The seven Maruts should be written elsewhere.

Then, having worshipped the fire, offered the oblation, and given the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the primary substances, beginning with the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*). Then, in the *kaṣā* vessel, one should perform a fire-oblation of tawny clarified butter (*kapilājya*) one thousand times with the root mantra using the *sruva* ladle filled with *kaṣā*.
In the case of a golden [image], one performs a hundred oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
in the case of a red [image], one performs a hundred oblations of *caru* mixed with *ārdrā*-myrobalan-sized portions with the *aghora* mantra;
and in the case of a black [image], one performs a hundred oblations of parched grain (*lāja*) in the measure of a handful with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.
In the Suprabhā [fire], one handful was offered by Vāmadeva in a number of one hundred;
in the Karakā [fire], one handful of parched grains was offered by Īśāna in a number of one hundred. Having thus offered these five substances, [he performed the rite].
One hundred *aśvattha* trees with the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra]; one hundred *audumbara* trees with the *aghora* [mantra]; a *vaṭa* tree with the *vāma* [mantra]. (l3)
One hundred [oblations] with the *sadyojāta* mantra; one hundred with the *plakṣa* tree;
one hundred fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
One hundred [strokes] with the head using khadira wood;
one hundred with the tuft using bilva wood;
one hundred with the armor using apāmārga wood.

Having offered one hundred *samidh* fuel-sticks of white *arka* with the *netra* mantra, twenty-five barley grains with the *īśāna* mantra when [the fire] is excessive; twenty-five black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the root mantra in the *kanaka* fire; and *śyāmāka* millet with the *śikhā* mantra.
And for the purpose of [the deity] Priyaṅgu...
twenty-five [offerings]; twenty-five each with the Aghora mantra; twenty-five of pure rice; twenty-five of mung-bean rice; twenty-five each of milk-rice, kṛsara-rice, and jaggery-rice.

Having thus become fivefold: in Raktā, one should offer a cake the size of one's own head with the *śiras* [mantra] twenty-five times; in Kanakā, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the *netra* [mantra] twenty-five times;
in Hiraṇyā, milk with the *īśāna* [mantra] twenty-five times.

(L7) In Kanakā, one should offer sugarcane juice and water from the Gaṅgā with the *mūla* [mantra] twenty-five times; with the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra], curd twenty-five times; in Hiraṇyā, with the *vāma* [mantra]...

Having separately offered twenty measures of these substances using the *sruva* ladle: twenty-five pieces of sugar-cane the size of a joint with the root mantra; twenty-five *gulū* fruits like *punnāga* fruits with the *aghora* mantra;
and plantain fruits with the *īśāna* mantra.

Half of a fruit is twenty-five [parts]. A mango fruit, according to its own measure, is twenty-five by its root. A *likuca* fruit, according to its own measure, is twenty-five by its root. A *panasa* fruit, divided into thirty parts and excluding the thorns, one part of a single fruit is the portion for the fire sacrifice by its root. A *badarī* fruit, according to its own measure by the root, is twenty-five. A coconut, having been split into eight parts, [is offered] by its root.
The oblation is performed with twenty-five portions.

With the root-mantra, [one uses] a powder of *sūraṇa*; having split it into pieces the size of *āmalaka* fruits, the oblation is performed twenty-five times. Likewise, with the root-mantra, [one performs the oblation] twenty-five times with *bālakaṇḍa*, *padmakaṇḍa*, and *utpalakaṇḍa*.

The *homa* [is performed as follows]: with the root mantra, sandalwood; musk; black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*); *gorocana*; saffron from Kashmir (*kāśmīrakuṅkuma*); the two types of musk (*mṛganābhi*); "moon" (*candra*), which is snow-water (*himatoya*); and fresh camphor (*ārdrakarpūra*). Having broken these into pieces the size of chickpeas (*caṇaka*), one performs the *homa* twenty-five times for each separately with the root mantra. *Bījamukhī*, *hrībera*, *ucīra*, *maru*, and *davala*—these are in the measure of two *anila*s.

The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed twenty-five times with the root mantra. Twenty-five [offerings] of *gulgulu* resin, the size of a *māṣa* bean, are offered with the root mantra. Twenty-five jasmine flowers are offered with the ten-syllable mantra; for the Pāśupata, twenty-five *bilva* fruits [are offered].

With the *aghora* mantra, one offers three handfuls of betel nut (*kramuka*), cardamom (*yelā*), cloves (*lavaṅka*), and cinnamon leaf (*patrikā*) combined; this constitutes twenty-five offerings. With the root mantra (*mūla*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*) are offered twenty-five times, and then ten offerings are made.

(L2) With the *nābhi* mantra, flat beans (*niṣpāva*) are offered twenty-five times. Bamboo shoots (*āḍhaka*), bamboo, and mung beans (*mudga*)—each of these in the measure of a *śukti*—are offered separately with the root mantra.
The twenty-five-fold oblation: twenty-five offerings of sesame with the *mṛgīmudrā* performed with the root mantra;
twenty-five [offerings] of a *māṣa*-shell measure with the root mantra; twenty-five [offerings] of white mustard seeds with the root mantra;
twenty-five [offerings] of flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) in the measure of a handful with the root mantra; twenty-five [offerings] of wheat with the root mantra.

Twenty-five [oblations] of *mātra* with the root mantra; twenty-five [oblations] of cow dung the size of a jujube fruit (*badarīphala*) with the root mantra; twenty-five [oblations] of fresh turmeric half the size of a fruit with the root mantra;

twenty-five [oblations] of [substances] the size of a jujube fruit with the root mantra. Having offered these sixty substances—beginning with *yeva* and ending with *jāti* fruit—each individually twenty-five times with the root mantra alone:

In that very fire, having offered *apāmārga* and *niṣpāva* seeds one hundred times with their roots for Īśāna; for Netra, *muñja* and *nīvāra* grains, each offered separately one hundred times with their roots;
and for Astra, three blades of *dūrvā* grass and two pieces of bamboo, [offered] with their roots.

Having offered oblations of shell-fish (*śukti*) individually one hundred times, having repeatedly taken portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering combined with all the ritual substances, and having sprinkled [the clarified butter] twice; having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa with the mantra beginning "Havyavāha"; and having offered a ladle-oblation (*sruvāhuti*) thereafter; and having performed the rites ending with the throwing of the *anuyāja* fuel-sticks, starting from the verse "Vaiśvānara" and so forth—in this auspicious sacrifice of the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana-śivayāga*).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) with the thought, "I shall offer oblations with the five-weapon mantra (*pañcāstra*) and the *vyāhṛtis* for the sake of expiation for all possible ritual transgressions," he should offer separately twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra and the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, with the *varma* mantra and the *bahurūpa* mantra, [he should perform] the consumption of sin (*pāpabhakṣaṇa*).

Having offered one hundred oblations for each [deity] with the sword-mantra *ātma-śambareṇa*, having duly given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having performed the fire-offerings distinguished by the *vyāhṛti* mantras for each substance, having prayed for the supreme state (*parama-edhi*), and having completed [the rite], (l4) having presented incense and lamps, and afterwards having offered the sacrificial food (*bali*) to those respective deities upon their girdles (*mekhalā*) with their individual name-mantras, [one should do so] briefly and with great skill on all sides of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

One should offer the bali-oblation. (L5) Having prepared a mandala and having invoked and worshipped all the deities of the bali within it—reciting the mantra beginning with "ye rudrā rudrakarmāṇaḥ" and so forth, and having offered the bali—at the conclusion of the ritual, together with the mūrtipas. (L6)

Having offered the daily full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and then having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and having presented incense and lamps, [one performs] the sprinkling of water around the north (*uttarapariṣecana*) and the release of the *praṇītā* vessel. Without the formal dismissal of the Brahman priest (*brahmodvāsana*), one takes a fuel-stick (*samidh*) in the fire, performs the salutation to the ears and other senses, and says: "O Great Lord, you are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this auspicious act performed by us. O God, may success be mine through the grace of the Sun."

Having thus offered the fruit of the *homa* to the Deity together with the *mūrtipas*, and having presented the incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, the great lamp, worship, and so forth, ending with the *ārātrika*; having restrained the Lord residing in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *aghora-mantra*; and having protected the Śiva-fire from chaff and other such things, one should pray as follows:

Thus, having posed the question, [follows] the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*) according to the *Aṣṭabandhanakāmikāgama*. Regarding the eastern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): then the presiding priest (*mūrtipa*), having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and performed the rite of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), places the vessel for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in his hand. Having purified the sacrificial pit through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, he establishes the fire—previously consecrated in the primary Śiva-pit—into the *āhavanīya* fire. Then, he sprinkles water around it (*pariṣicya*).

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] and adorned [the site], having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth, as well as the supporting fuel-sticks (*ādhāra-samit*), starting from the east and so on, and having adorned [the fire], one should worship the Āhavanīya fire: "Obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna;
obeisance to Vairāgya; obeisance to Aiśvarya."
Salutation to Padma. Salutation to the seat of the Āhavanīya fire.
[He is] one-faced and three-eyed, with three girdles and three feet;
in his right hands, he holds a rosary, a trident, and a sacrificial ladle (sruva).
In his left hands, he holds a goad, a hand-drum, and a sacrificial ladle;
he is red in color, seated comfortably, and draped in yellow garments.
One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire in the center of the eastern pit:
*Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to the form of the Āhavanīya fire; obeisance to the Āhavanīya fire.* In that fire, [one should offer] obeisance to the seat of the earth-form.

I take refuge in Lord Bhava, who has four arms and three eyes, who wears a crown of matted locks, and who is adorned with all ornaments. (2) Salutation to the embodiment of the earth; salutation to Bhava, the sovereign lord of the earth’s form.

I meditate upon the Person who is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding an axe and a trident as his upper weapons, possessing three eyes, and having a golden-yellow luster.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa; salutation to the form of Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Tatpuruṣa. Having performed the worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the lamp offering:
At the place of the food offering (naivedya), having offered ten oblations of clarified butter with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;

thereafter, having offered fifty, two hundred, or more oblations of clarified butter with that same root-mantra; then half of that [number] of Aśvattha fuel-sticks, wheat, and cooked rice (caru) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.

Having offered thus with Īśāna, one offers a black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the head-mantra (*śiras*), and millet (*śyāmāka*) with the crest-mantra (*śikhā*). With Aghora, one offers cooked rice containing *priyaṅgu* and *kulī*, as well as prepared rice with mung beans (*mudga*), rice with milk (*kṣīrānna*), and rice with sesame and peas (*kṛsarānna*). (L6) These are the five types of food, including rice with molasses (*gulānna*). One offers a cake the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit with the head-mantra, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) the size of a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) with the eye-mantra.

Milk [is offered] with Īśāna; sugarcane juice and Ganges water, in the measure of a *sruva* ladle, [are offered] with Tatpuruṣa; curd with Vāmadeva; honey, in the measure of a *sruva* ladle, [is offered]; jaggery with Aghora;
and a piece of sugarcane the size of a joint, like a *punnāga* fruit, with the Mūla-mantra.
With the Īśāna mantra, offer half a plantain fruit; an mango fruit and a *likuca* fruit according to their own size; having divided a jackfruit into three parts, perform the oblation with one part;
a jujube fruit according to its own size;

and having split a coconut into eight parts, perform the oblation with one part. With the root mantra, [offer] ginger powder, *bālakaṇḍa*, lotus-root (*padmakaṇḍa*), and blue-lotus-root (*utpalakaṇḍa*). These are the items.

The oblation (*homa*) is performed by breaking [the materials] into the size of a sacrificial offering (*āhutimātra*). With the root mantra (*mūla*), one offers sandalwood, musk (*kastūrī*), black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), *gorocana*, saffron from Kashmir (*kāśmīra*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), two types of musk (*mṛganābhi*), camphor (*candra*), snow-water (*himatoya*), and camphor the size of a chickpea (*chaṇaka*). All these are offered with the root mantra alone. With the principal seed-syllables (*bījamukhya*), one offers *hrībera*.

Taking two finger-breadths each of *ucīśīra* and *marudavana*, one performs the *homa*. With the root mantra (*mūla*), one offers a *māṣa*-sized piece of *gulgulu*; with the ten-syllable mantra (*daśākṣara*), *mallikā* flowers; with the *pāśupata* mantra, a *bilva* fruit; with the *aghora* mantra, three pieces of betel leaf and one areca nut; with *yelā* and *lavaṅga*; and with the root mantra, ten chickpeas (*caṇaka*) together with *patrikā* and *niṣpāva* beans.

With ninety [measures]. According to the *Āḍhakamata*: (6) a bamboo-measure of mung beans; these [quantities] constitute one *śukti* of sesame, a *bhrigīmudrā* of rice; one *māṣa* of white mustard, one *śukti* of black mustard; for the sake of purification, a handful of parched grain (*pṛthuka*); wheat, one *śukti*. (l7)
Cow dung the size of a jujube fruit; fresh turmeric half the size of a fruit; nutmeg the size of a jujube fruit—having offered all these with the root mantra alone;

or, having offered each of the six substances ending with the "twice-born" fruit ten times separately; having offered the *vyāhṛtis* for each substance; and having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation combined with all the substances, this is for the purpose of expiation.

Having offered oblations with clarified butter twenty-five times using the five weapons, and while seated, having offered ten oblations each with the *varman* [armor], the *bahurūpa*, the *pāpabhakṣaṇa-mantra*, the *navātman*, and the *śambara* mantras,
by the preceptor according to the rule.

Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) together [with the other offerings], he should sit down. Having presented incense and lamps, he sits facing the east: to Brahmā, svāhā; to the south—to Viṣṇu, svāhā;

to the west—to Rudra, svāhā; to the north—to Ananta, svāhā. Again, having offered the sacrificial bali to Indra and the other deities, and having offered the water of honor (*arghya*), he should conclude by making the burnt offering (*huta*). Then, having made his request and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*).

Having offered the *ārātrika* lamp, one should restrain the person representing the *āhavanīya* fire by means of the *bahurūpa* mantra. Thus ends the procedure for the *āhavanīya* oblation in the eastern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The Procedure for the Fire Oblation in the Āgneya Kuṇḍa:

Now, the presiding priest (mūrtipa), having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and executed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya). Then, after purifying the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) through inspection and other rites, he proceeds from the principal pit (pradhānakuṇḍa).

Having sprinkled water around the established fire and strewn grass around it, and having duly placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the upward-pointing fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with their respective mantras, [one should worship] with: "Obeisance to Vṛddhāgnyāsana.
[One should visualize the deity as] four-armed, three-eyed, single-faced, and wearing matted locks (*jaṭā*).

One should worship Vṛddhāgni in the southeast, having meditated upon him as white-bodied, mounted on a bull, holding a trident, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) accompanied by the boon-giving gesture. [The mantras are: "Homage to the form of Vṛddhāgni! Homage to Vṛddhāgni! Homage to Vṛddhāgni, the lord of the wind-form!"
Salutation to the fierce one, the lord of the form of Fire. Salutation to that Lord of the Form, who is the seat of the Heart.
The Heart is radiant with a white luster, three-eyed, and four-armed;
Śiva holds a noose, a trident, and the gesture of protection, and wears yellow garments.

Having meditated thus: "Obeisance to the Heart for the Lord of the Form of Fire. Having performed the worship beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the lamp (*dīpa*), and having worshipped the girdles (*mekhalā*), the Maruts, and the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should offer two hundred and fifty oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the Heart-mantra; half of that [number] of *śamī* wood, mustard seeds, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be offered with the Heart-mantra.

Having offered [the oblations], one should perform the homa with special substances: barley with the Īśāna mantra; black gram with the Śiras mantra; millet (*śyāmāka*), *priyaṅgu*, and horse-gram (*kuluttha*) with the Śikhā mantra;
and pure rice and mung-bean rice with the Aghora mantra.

Milk-rice, rice with sesame, and rice with jaggery—these are the five types of food. A cake the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit for the head; [the offering] for the self-measure [of the body]; milk-porridge (*pāyasa*) the size of a *sruva* ladle for the eyes; milk-essence (*ikṣusāra*) for Īśāna; and Gaṅgā-water the size of a *sruva* ladle. Curd for Tatpuruṣa; honey for Vāmadeva, [both] the size of a *sruva* ladle; and [an offering] for Aghora.

A *gulam* [weight] of *puṃnāga* fruit with its root; a piece of sugarcane the size of a joint; a plantain fruit or half a fruit for Īśāna; a mango fruit and a *likuca* fruit of their own natural size; having divided a jackfruit into thirty parts, one part is for the *homa*;
the *badarī* fruit... [line 2].

One's own measure [of time]. Having split a coconut into eight parts, there is one oblation for each. With the root mantra, having set aside a portion of powder made from the root of the *bālaka* lotus, the *padma* tuber, and the *utpala* tuber, the oblation is performed. With the root mantra, sandalwood, musk, black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), *gorocanā*, saffron from Kashmir, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), the two types of musk (*mṛganābhi*), camphor, snow-water, and camphor—[these] in the measure of a chickpea (*caṇaka*) are offered as an oblation.

Taking *hrībera*, *uśīra*, and *marudavana*—the primary seeds—measuring two finger-breadths each, one performs the *homa*. One *māṣa* of *guggulu* is offered with the ten-syllable mantra; *jātī* flowers with the *pāśupata* mantra; *bilva* fruit with the *aghora* mantra; and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) [with the *vāmadeva* mantra].

Three *kramuka* fruits and one *yelālavaṅga*. Combined with *patrikā*, ten *caṇaka* beans with the root-mantra, nine *niṣpāva* beans, and an *āḍhaka* of bamboo [grain]. These, along with *mudga* beans, constitute the measure of a *śukti*. *Tila* seeds are measured by the *mṛgīmudrā*; *māṣa* beans by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). White mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) are measured by a *śukti*; likewise for *sarṣapa* seeds. For the purpose of eating, *pṛthuka* grain is a mere handful; *godhūma* wheat is measured by a *śukti*. [...]

[The measure] is the size of a jujube fruit (*badarīphala*). Fresh turmeric is half a *pala*; the nutmeg fruit is the size of a jujube fruit. Having offered these with the root [mantra] alone, one should offer barley and the other substances up to the nutmeg, each ten times; for each substance...

Having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblation; having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation accompanied by all the ritual substances; having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) twenty-five times with clarified butter using the five-weapon mantra;

having offered ten separate oblations with the *varman*, the *bahurūpa*, the *pāpabhakṣaṇa* mantra, the ninefold *navātman*, the *śambara*, and the *asi* mantras; having duly presented the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); and having offered incense and lamps.
Having sat down, one should offer the *bali* oblation:

in the east—*brahmaṇe svāhā*; in the south—*viṣṇave svāhā*; in the west—*rudrāya svāhā*; in the north—*anantāya svāhā*. Again, having offered the *bali* to Indra and the others starting from the east, one should also offer the *arghya*.

Having offered the oblation (*huta*), having prayed "not for me," having sprinkled water around, having taken a fuel-stick (*samidh*) and stood before the fire, and having restrained [the deity] within the heart with water for honor (*arghyāmbhas*) in its manifold form,
one should pray for what is desired. Thus ends the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) in its mature form.
Then the presiding priest (mūrtipa), having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and sat upon a tortoise-seat (kūrma-āsana) or a gentle seat (saumya-āsana);

having performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), prepared the general offering-water (sāmānya-arghya), and sprinkled the implements for the fire-oblation (homa) as well as himself with it; and having purified [the materials] through the eighteen rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa), he established [the fire] in the southern pit (kuṇḍa) from the principal pit (pradhāna-kuṇḍa).

Having sprinkled water around the fire according to the rules, having strewn grass around it, and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the seat (*viṣṭara*), and the upright fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in their respective places with the appropriate mantras, and having sprinkled water [around them] and adorned them;
having worshipped the boundary-markers (*paridhi*) with "Salutation to Brahmā! Salutation to Viṣṇu!
Salutation to Rudra! Salutation to Ananta!", and having worshipped Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokeśa*) upon the seats (*viṣṭara*), once again—
Having worshipped the eight Vasus and the seven Maruts, [he worships] in the center: obeisance to Ananta;
obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya; obeisance to Aiśvarya; obeisance to Padma; obeisance to the seat of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
He has two faces, the luster of gold, three feet, and seven hands;
Hiraṇyā and four others are the tongues in the right face,
while Suprabhā and three others are situated in the left face.

One should meditate upon Dakṣiṇāgni in the southern sacrificial pit as mounted upon a ram, holding a Śakti, a large ladle (*sruk*), and a small ladle (*sruva*) in his right hands, and a lance (*tomara*), a fly-whisk (*cāmara*),
and a vessel of clarified butter in his left hands.
Salutation to the form of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. Oṃ, salutation to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. In that very fire, salutation to the seat of the sacrificer’s form.
[He who is] black-horned, wearing a turban of cow-dung ash, joined with Ramā, and girdled with a belt.
His body anointed with fresh butter, he is proclaimed as the sacrificer.
Salutation to the form of the Sacrificer (yajamāna). Above that—salutation to the seat of Śarva.
[He is] three-eyed, four-armed, and wearing a crown of matted hair.
One should meditate upon Śarva, adorned with all ornaments, on the right side.
Salutation to Śarva, who bears the form of the sacrificer. Above that—salutation to Aghorāsana.
He is described as having three eyes, wearing a crown, and likewise adorned with earrings.
With his eyebrows and beard aflame, he had fangs and a formidable face.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, decorated with snakes and scorpions,
[he holds] a khaṭvāṅga, a discus, a trident, a shield, and a noose.
One should meditate on [the deity] holding in his four left hands a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff that crushes enemies, and likewise in his four right hands. (l2) One should meditate.

Having worshipped [the deity] who has the luster of a fresh cloud, who is non-terrible (aghora), and who grants all desires—from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the lamp offering—with the mantra: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the form of Aghora; Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. At the time of the food offering (naivedya), having offered ten oblations of clarified butter with the Aghora mantra, one should thereafter offer fifty-two hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Aghora mantra, and half of that [number].
