Having offered an oblation of sesame and udumbara grains with the Aghora mantra, one should offer king beans (*rājamāṣa*) on the head for the Īśāna [face], and millet (*śyāmāka*), *priyaṅgu*, and *kuluttha* on the head for the Śikhā [face]. With the Aghora mantra, one offers pure food.

Mudga-rice, milk-rice, kṛsara-rice, and jaggery-rice are the five types of food. A cake the size of a fresh āmalaka fruit is offered with the head-mantra (Īśāna). [An offering] of the same measure as oneself is offered with the eye-mantra (Tatpuruṣa). Payasa is offered with the eye-mantra. [An offering] the size of a sruva-spoon is offered with the Īśāna-mantra; this includes milk, sugarcane juice, and Ganges water, each measured by a sruva-spoon. Curd is offered with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra. Honey is offered with the Vāmadeva-mantra.
The measure of the *sruva* [ladle] is as follows: with the *aghora* mantra, a *gulā* fruit the size of a *punnāga* fruit;

with the *mūla* mantra, a handful (*puṣpa-pramātra*) [of grain]; with the *īśāna* mantra, a piece of sugarcane or a plantain fruit. Half a fruit, an *āmra* fruit, or a *likuca* fruit may be used according to their own natural size. Having divided a *panasa* fruit into six parts, one part is for the *homa*. [Then there is] the *badarī*...

The fruit is of its own measure. Having split a coconut into eight parts, there is one oblation for each. With the root mantra, one offers powdered [substances] along with the *sālakaṇḍa*, the lotus-root (*padmakaṇḍa*), and the water-lily-root (*utpalakaṇḍa*). Having offered hundreds of oblations, the sacrifice consists of the root [mantra], sandalwood, musk, black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), yellow orpiment (*gorocana*), saffron from Kashmir (*kāśmīra-kuṅkuma*), the two types of deer-musk (*mṛganābhi*), camphor (*candra*), snow-water, and camphor (*karpūra*).

Taking the principal large seeds of the chickpea (*caṇaka*) size, along with *hrībera* (l3), *uśīra*, and *maruvada*—having taken these measuring two finger-breadths—one performs the *homa*. [One offers] a *māṣa*-sized piece of *gulgulu*; flowers with the ten-syllable mantra;
and *bilva* with the *Pāśupata* mantra. (l4)

With the Aghora mantra, [offer] three pieces of betel leaf; one areca nut (*kramuka*) together with cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *patrikā*; with the Mūla mantra, ten chickpeas (*caṇaka*); ... [with] nine flowers; one *āḍhaka* of bamboo, mung beans (*mudga*). These [are offered] in the measure of a *śukti*. An offering of sesame seeds (*tila*) in the form of a deer-mark (*mṛgīmudrā*); a bean (*māṣa*) in the measure of a *śukti*; white mustard (*siddhārtha*) and black mustard (*sarṣapa*), each separately in the measure of half a *śruti* and a handful (*muṣṭi*); wheat (*godhūma*).

A piece of cow dung the size of a conch-shell; a jujube fruit the size of a badarī fruit; fresh turmeric and half a nutmeg the size of a badarī fruit—one should offer these with the root mantra alone. From barley up to nutmeg, each of the sixty-three items should be offered individually and separately.

One should offer oblations ten times. Having offered the *vyāhṛti* mantras for each substance and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation combined with all the substances, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by offering twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the *pañcāstra* mantra. Then, having offered eight oblations for each with the *varma*, the *bahurūpa*, the *pāpakṣaya* mantra, the *navākana*, the *śambara*, and the *asi* [mantras], one should duly perform the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having performed the oblation and sat down, having offered incense and lamps, and then having given the *bali* offering to Brahmā and the others starting from the east upon the girdles, having offered the *arghya*, having sprinkled [water] around,
and having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), one should restrain [the deity] with the *yaghora* mantra. Thus for the southern fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The ritual procedure for the fire oblation (homa).

Then the presiding priest (mūrtipa), having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), sits upon a tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana) with a serene countenance. Having adorned himself with a turban and other ornaments, he prepares the general offering water (sāmānyārghya). With that water, he sprinkles the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the oblation materials with the weapon-mantra (astra). Then, in the triangular pit—which has been purified by the eighteen rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa)—from the principal pit...

Having sprinkled water around the established fire, having strewn grass around it, having placed the fuel-sticks for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the bundles of grass (*kūrca*), as well as the seats (*viṣṭara*) and the upright fuel-sticks (*ūrdhvasamidh*) in their respective places preceded by the appropriate mantras, having sprinkled water around it again, and having adorned it, [he places them] upon the enclosing sticks.

Having worshipped Brahmā and the others, as well as the eight Vasus, the seven Maruts on their seats, and the world-protectors; then, in the center of the fire: *namo 'nantāya*, *namo dharmāya*, *namo jñānāya*, *namo vairāgyāya*, *nama aiśvaryāya*, *namaḥ padmāya*, and *namo yadvai nāgnyāsanāya*.
Three-eyed, five-faced, with a red body and ten hands;
in his left [hands], he holds a chisel, a noose, a lotus, a discus, and the gesture of granting boons.
In the south, [she holds] the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, a vajra, a varada-mudrā, and a sword;
Hiraṇyā and Kanakā are in the southeast and northeast respectively, while the remaining two are each single [deities].
The wise one should place the Fire of Youth (*yauvanāgni*), mounted upon a bull, in the southwest.
Upon that very fire—[one should offer]: "Obeisance to the seat of the form of the Sun.
[The Sun] is mounted upon his chariot, clad in armor, wearing earrings, and bearing a banner.
Wearing a crown, holding a lotus in his hand, he was adorned with ornaments and a girdle.

Salutation to the form of the Sun; then, salutation to the seat of Mahādeva. [One should worship] Mahādeva in the southwest—three-eyed, four-armed, wearing a crown of matted hair, and fully adorned with all ornaments.

Salutation to the form of Mahādeva; salutation to Mahādeva. Above that—salutation to the seat of the crest (*śikhāsana*); salutation to the form of the crest which is the color of vermilion (*sindūravarṇa*). *Oṃ hūṃ*, salutation to Śikhāyī. Having worshipped [her] from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the lamp, at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should offer ten oblations of clarified butter with the *śikhā-mantra*.
Afterwards, [the number of oblations is] two hundred and fifty...

Having offered oblations of clarified butter with the *śikhā-mantra* according to the prescribed number; having offered half of that amount of rice cooked with *khadira* wood and *caru* with the *śikhā-mantra*; [he offers] barley with the *īśāna-mantra*, black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the *śiras-mantra*, and *śyāmaka* grain with the *śikhā-mantra*. (l6) He also offers *priyaṅgu* and *kulattha* with the *śiras-mantra*. With the *aghora-mantra*, he offers the five types of food: pure rice, mung-bean rice, milk-rice, *kṛsara*-rice, and molasses-rice. [He offers] a quantity equal to a fresh *āmalaka* fruit.
With the *Śiras* [mantra], a cake (*apūpa*) of its own size;

with the *Netra*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the measure of a *sruva* ladle; with *Īśāna*, milk, sugarcane juice, and water from the Gaṅgā, each in the measure of a *sruva*; with *Tatpuruṣa*, curd; with *Vāmadeva*, honey, in the measure of a *sruva*; with *Aghora*, molasses.

Like the *punnāga* fruit. With the root-mantra, a piece of sugarcane the size of a joint. With the *Īśāna* mantra, half a *pala* of banana fruit; an *āmra* fruit [of the same measure]. The *likuca* fruit according to its own size. Having divided the *panasa* fruit into thirty parts, one part is for the *homa*. The *badarī* fruit according to its own size. A coconut, split into eight pieces, with each piece offered as a *homa*. Gold with the root-mantra. The *bālakaṇḍa*...
The lotus-root and the blue-lotus-root.

(l3) Having offered these in the measure of an oblation, the fire-sacrifice is performed. With the root-mantra [one offers] sandalwood, musk, black fragrance, gorocana, Kashmiri saffron, and the two types of deer-musk. Moonlight, snow-water, (l4)

The oblation consists of camphor the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*). With the principal seed-mantras, one should take two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each of *hrībera*, *uśīra*, *maru*, and *vadana* (or *davana*), and perform the oblation. Guggulu the size of a black gram (*māṣa*) [is offered]. (L5) With the ten-syllable mantra (*daśākṣara*), flowers; with the *Pāśupata* mantra, *bilva* fruit; with the *Aghora* mantra, three pieces of betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) and one areca nut (*kramuka*). Also, cardamom (*elā*) and cloves (*lavaṅga*) combined with *patrikā*.

One [measure] with the root-mantra, ten with the *niṣpāva*, nine with the *āḍhaka*; likewise, a *vaiṇava* measure of mung beans; these, along with sesame in the amount of a *śukti*, a *māṣa* of mṛgīmudrā offered as a *homa*, white mustard in the amount of a *śukti*, and half a *śukti* of white *sarṣapa*—each [of these] separately in a handful.
One *mātrā* of wheat, one *śukti* of cow dung, one *badarī* fruit of fresh turmeric, half a *jātī* fruit, and one *badarī* fruit—

having offered these with the root mantra alone, one should offer each of the sixty-three substances, beginning with barley and ending with the *jātī* fruit, separately and ten times each. Having offered the *vyāhṛti* mantras for each substance, [one offers] that which is combined with all the substances.
Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation,

one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by offering clarified butter twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra; then, with the *varman* [mantra], using the *sruva* ladle, and with the sword [of] the ninefold *śambara* mantra consisting of the "consumption of evil" formula.

Having offered eight oblations for each [deity] according to the rule and having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation), one should sit down. Then, having offered the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the lamp, as well as the *bali* offering and fire to Brahmā and the others, and to Indra and the others, upon the girdles starting from the east; and having sprinkled [the site], one should worship for the sake of standing near [the deity]. One should restrain [the fire] with the *aghora* mantra. This is the procedure for the oblation in the *Nirṛti* pit. [Side Heading: Procedure for the Oblation in the Western Pit] (l1)

The presiding priest, having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and sat upon a tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) with a serene countenance; having adorned himself with a turban and other ornaments, performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and established the general offering-water (*sāmānyārghya*), he sprinkled the implements for the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) and the circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) with that water. Then, into the circular pit—which has been consecrated by the eighteen purificatory rites beginning with inspection—he [placed] the consecrated fire from the primary sacrificial pit.

Having swept around the established fire and sprinkled water around it, having placed the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*), the bundle of grass (*kūrca*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the upright fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with their respective mantras as previously stated, having sprinkled [water] around it and adorned it, [he should place] Brahmā and the others upon the enclosing sticks.

Having worshipped the eight Vasus on the seat, the seven Maruts in the surrounding space, and the World-Protectors in their proper order, [one should worship] in the center of the fire: *namaḥ anantāya* (homage to Ananta); *namaḥ dharmāya* (homage to Dharma); *namaḥ jñānāya* (homage to Jñāna);
*namaḥ vairāgyāya* (homage to Vairāgya); *namaḥ aiśvaryāya* (homage to Aiśvarya); *namaḥ padmāya* (homage to the Lotus); *namaḥ gārhapatyāsanāya* (homage to the seat of the Gārhapatya fire).
With red limbs, red garments, and face, he is endowed with the boon-granting gesture and others;
holding a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in his two upper hands, he is radiant with pearls. He is joined with seven tongues of flame, has one face, and wears matted locks.
One should meditate upon Gārhapatya mounted on a horse in the western sacrificial pit:

"Salutation to the form of Gārhapatya. In that [pit], salutation to the one who bears the form of Rudra, whose seat is the form of water. Varuṇa, whose eyes are like nooses, who is endowed with compassion, whose banner is the sea-monster, and whose nature is four-armed.
Homage to the one whose form is water, adorned with all ornaments. Above that, homage to Rudrāsana.
[He is] three-eyed, four-armed, and wears a crown of matted locks.
Complete with all ornaments.
Having meditated upon Rudra—in the west: "Obeisance to the form of Rudra. Above that (l2):
"Obeisance to the seat of the Sadyojāta form.
[He is] richly adorned with white heart, fragrance, and ornaments, wearing a white turban and white garments.
One should meditate on the [deity] complete in all limbs in the western direction.

Homage to the Lord of the Rudra-forms, to the form of Sadyojāta. Oṃ haṃ, homage to Sadyojāta. Having performed the worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the lamp, at the time of the food offering, one should offer ten oblations with the Sadyojāta mantra.

Thereafter, having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) in fifty-two hundred oblations along with its root-mantra; and having offered half of that number of oblations of *plakṣa* wood, green gram (*mudga*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with its root-mantra; [one offers] barley (*yava*) with the Īśāna mantra; black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the Śiras mantra; millet (*śyāmāka*), *priyaṅgu*, and horse-gram (*kuluttha*) at the crest (*śikhā*) with the Aghora mantra; and pure rice, green gram rice, and milk-rice with the Śiras mantra.

Kṛsarā-rice, molasses-rice, and [other] grains—these are the five foods. For the head, a cake the size of a fresh āmalaka fruit; for the eyes, milk-rice the size of a *sruva* ladle; for Īśāna, milk, sugarcane juice, and water from the Gaṅgā.

The measure of the *sruva* ladle: with the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra], it is like that; with the *vāmadeva*, honey, the measure being that of a *sruva*; with the *aghora*, a *gul̥a* fruit like a *puṇnāga* fruit; with the *mūla* [mantra], a piece of sugarcane the size of a joint; with the *īśāna*, a plantain fruit or half a fruit;
an *āmra* fruit or a *likuca* fruit according to its own natural size; having divided a *panasa* fruit into thirty parts, one part is for the *homa*.

A jujube fruit of its own size; having split a coconut into eight parts, there is one oblation for each. Having offered as many oblations as there are grains of powder from the root-mantra, [namely] *bālakadanda*, lotus-root, and water-lily-root, there is the homa.
With the root-mantra, [one offers] sandalwood and musk.

Black fragrant substance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), yellow orpiment (*gorocana*), saffron from Kashmir (*kāśmīrakuṅkuma*), the two types of musk (*mṛganābhi*), camphor (*candra*) as snow-water, and camphor in the measure of a *caṇaka* (chickpea)—this is the oblation (*homa*). With the principal seeds: *hrībera*, *uśīra*, *maru*, and *davana*—(l4) having taken these measuring two finger-breadths, one performs the oblation. Guggulu in the measure of a *māṣa*, flowers with the ten-syllable mantra, and *bilva* with the *Pāśupata* mantra.

With the *aghora* mantra, [he offers] three pieces of betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one areca nut (*kramuka*), cardamom (*elā*) and clove (*lavaṅga*), together with *patrikā*. With the root mantra (*mūla*), he offers chickpeas (*caṇaka*); with ten [repetitions], flat beans (*niṣpāva*); with nine, *āḍhaka* rice; and bamboo-seed *mudga* beans. These [are offered] in the measure of a *śukti*.

Having offered sesame with the *mṛgīmudrā* gesture; one *māṣa* of *śukti*-measure of *siddhārtha*; one handful of mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) and half a handful of rice (*śrī*); one *śukti*-measure of wheat; cow-dung the size of a *badarī* fruit; fresh turmeric half a fruit’s measure; and nutmeg the size of a *badarī* fruit—having offered these with the root mantra alone. These sixty-three substances, from barley up to nutmeg, are [to be offered] individually.

One should offer oblations ten times for each [substance]. Having offered the substance with each *vyāhṛti*, and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation combined with all the substances, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by offering clarified butter twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra (*pañcāstra*). Then, with the *varman* [mantra] of many forms...

Having offered eight oblations for each [deity] with the sword-mantra *Śambara* consisting of nine syllables, which consumes evil; having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the rule;
having sat down; having presented incense and lamps;

and subsequently, having given the bali and arghya offerings to Brahmā and the others, and to Indra and the others, upon the girdles starting from the east; and having sprinkled water and performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with the *Aghora* mantra.

One should cause [the fire] to cease. This is the procedure for the final oblation in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (l4. The image-guardian (*mūrtipa*) washes his feet, performs the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and sits upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) facing east. Having adorned himself with the *uṣṇīṣa* and other ornaments, (l5) having performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*), and having prepared the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*), he sprinkles the oblation implements and the six sacrificial pits with that water while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

In the hexagonal *kuṇḍa*, which has been consecrated by the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), [the fire] is installed according to the rule from the principal *kuṇḍa*. Then, the *parisamohana* [grass], the sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*), the spreading [of grass] (*paristaraṇa*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the *kūrca* [bunch of grass], the sacrificial seat (*viṣṭhara*),
and the upright fuel-sticks (*ūrdhasamidh*) are placed in their respective locations with their respective mantras.

Having placed [the offerings], having sprinkled [water], and having adorned [the site], one should worship Brahmā and the others in the eastern and other enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the eight Vasus on the seats (*viṣṭara*), the seven Maruts on the mats (*staraṇa*), and the Lords of the Worlds (*lokeśa*). In that fire: "Obeisance to Ananta," "obeisance to Dharma," "obeisance to Jñāna," "obeisance to Vairāgya," "obeisance to Aiśvarya," "obeisance to Padma," "obeisance to Bāla," and "obeisance to Śivāsana."
Homage! [To the deity] who has two faces and a single heart, four ears, and two nostrils;
who has four horns, is mounted upon a bull, and possesses a splendor equal to the rising sun.
In his right side, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear; in his left side, he holds a javelin, a fly-whisk, and a vessel of clarified butter.
One should meditate on the form of the infant fire (*bālāgni*) in the northwest sacrificial pit (*vāyavyakuṇḍaka*).
*Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the embodiment of the infant fire; *īṃ*, obeisance to the infant fire; obeisance to the one who bears the formidable form and whose seat is the embodiment of wind.
Four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and possessed of great strength,
he sits there exceedingly enraged, his constant movement causing the earth to tremble.
Salutation to the one who bears a terrifying form, whose form is wind; salutation to Yaṃ in the northwest. Above that (l5), salutation to the one on the Bhīma-seat.
He has three eyes and four arms, and wears a crown of matted hair.
I worship Him of terrifying form, adorned with all ornaments.

Salutation to the one of terrifying form. Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhīma. (L6) Salutation to his lord, the seat of the armor. Salutation to the form of the armor, radiant as a bumblebee. Yaiṃ, salutation to the armor. Having worshipped [the deity] from the invocation up to the lamp, at the time of the food offering, [one should perform] ten oblations with clarified butter while reciting the armor mantra. (L7)

Having offered oblations with clarified butter by means of the *kavaca* mantra fifty times, and subsequently two hundred and fifty times; and having offered half of that amount of a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) made of chickpeas and *bilva* fruits by means of the *kavaca* mantra; [one should offer] barley with the *īśāna* mantra, black gram with the *śiras* mantra, millet and *priyaṅgu* with the *śiras* mantra, horse-gram with the *śiras* mantra, pure rice with the *aghora* mantra, as well as mung-bean rice and milk-rice.
The five foods are: rice with *kṛsara*, rice with molasses, and five kinds of grain. [The portion] for Ārdrā is the size of an *āmalaka* fruit;

for Śiras, cakes of the same measure; for Netra, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) the size of a *sruva* ladle; and for Īśāna, milk, sugarcane juice, and water from the Gaṅgā, each the size of a *sruva*. For Tatpuruṣa...

Curd with the *vāmadeva* mantra; honey, the size of a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), with the *aghora* mantra; jaggery, the size of a *punnāga* fruit, with the root mantra (*mūla*); a piece of sugarcane, the length of a joint, with the *īśāna* mantra; a plantain fruit or half a fruit [with the same]; a mango fruit or a *likuca* fruit, their own natural size; a jackfruit, divided into thirty parts, one part used for the oblation (*homa*); and a jujube (*badarī*) fruit, its own natural size.

Having split a coconut into eight parts, one performs a *homa* offering for each part with the *mūla-mantra*. [One offers] powder, young tubers (*bālakanda*), lotus tubers (*padmakanda*), and blue-lily tubers (*utpalakanda*); having broken these into the measure of an oblation, one performs the *homa*. With the *mūla-mantra*, one offers sandalwood, musk, black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), yellow orpiment (*gorocana*), and saffron (*kāśmīra*).

Saffron; two types of musk; sandalwood; snow-water; and camphor in the measure of a *caṇa*. The *homa* is performed with the primary mantras beginning with *hīḍa*. Taking *hrībera*, *maru*, and *davana* in the measure of two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), one performs the *homa*. *Gulgulu* in the measure of a *māṣa*; flowers with the ten-syllable mantra; *bilva* with the *Pāśupata* mantra; and three betel leaves with one *kramuka* nut with the *Aghora* mantra.
Cardamom, cloves, and together with cinnamon. (p167b, f160a, side heading:

*Uttarakuṇḍahoma*, l1) With the root mantra, ten *caṇaka* beans, nine *niṣpāva* beans, and *āḍhaka* rice; bamboo, and *mudga* beans—these [should be] the measure of a *śukti*. ...... *Drāhṛta* beans, the measure of a *śukti*; and white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) and black mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*). (l2)

Half a *śukti* of *prathuka*, one *muṣṭi* of wheat, one *śukti* of cow dung, and half a fresh *jātiphala* fruit the size of a *badarī* fruit— having offered these with their roots (*mūla*), one should sacrifice each of the sixty-three substances, beginning with barley and ending with *jātiphala*, separately ten times for each substance. For each substance:

Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations and performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa combined with all the ritual substances, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by offering clarified butter twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra, and [then] with the *varman* [mantra], the *bahurūpa* [mantra], and the *pāpabhakṣaṇa* mantra.

Having offered eight oblations for each of the nine gems with a sword enchanted by the *śambara* mantra, and having duly performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sit down and offer incense and lamps.

Thereafter, upon the girdles at the joints [of the sword], one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) and the respectful water (*arghya*) to Brahmā and the others, as well as to Indra and the rest. Having sprinkled [the area] and performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), one should restrain [the weapon] with the *aghora* mantra using the arghya-water.
Thus ends the procedure for the fire-offering (*homa*) in the eastern pit (*vāyukuṇḍa*). (l7.

Now follows the procedure for the fire-offering in the northern pit: the image-guardian (*mūrtipa*) washes his feet, sips water for purification (*ācamana*), sits facing east upon the Brahma-Kūrma seat, and adorns himself with the turban and other ornaments. (p168a, l1)

Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* and prepared the general *arghya*, one should sprinkle the materials for the fire-sacrifice (*homopakaraṇa*) and the lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) with that water using the *astra-mantra*. Once the lotus-pit has been accepted through the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa*, one should duly establish the fire— previously consecrated in the primary pit— performing the *patisamohana*, *paryukṣaṇa*, *paristaraṇa*, *paridhi*, *kūrca*, and *viṣṭara* rites.

Having placed the upright fuel-sticks (ūrdhvasamidhaḥ) in their respective places with their respective mantras, having sprinkled [water] and adorned [the fire], one should seat Brahmā and the other [deities] upon the enclosing sticks (paridhi), the eight Vasus upon the grass seats (viṣṭara),
and the seven Maruts and the world-protectors (lokeśa).

Having performed worship, [he should offer oblations] into that fire with the following: "Homage to Anantāsana; homage to Dharma; homage to Jñāna; homage to Vairāgya; homage to Aiśvarya; homage to Padma; homage to Kevalāgnyāsana.
[He should visualize the deity as] having two eyes and two arms, endowed with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Adorned with garments having white and red lusters, it possesses a radiance equal to white and red.

One should meditate upon the God, adorned with all ornaments and seated upon a lotus throne, as the solitary fire (*kevalāgni*) correctly within the northern sacrificial pit (*uttarakuṇḍaka*). Homage to the form of the solitary fire! Oṃ Raṃ, homage to the solitary fire! Homage to the seat of the form of Paśupati... [the form of] ...!
[He is] situated in a gentle lunar chariot, bestowing the mace, the trident, and the boon;
resembling a jewel of universal form, he is joined with the nectar of the jar.
...to the image of the Lord, to the vehicle, ...to the image, obeisance! To the Moon, obeisance! Above that—to the seat of Paśupati, obeisance!
One should meditate upon Paśupati in the north as having three eyes and four arms, wearing a crown of matted hair, and adorned with all ornaments.

Salutation to the form of Paśupati. Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Paśupati. Above that—(l2) salutation to Paśupatīśa, who is seated upon Vāmadeva. One should meditate on the left [face] as having the luster of red and deep red, with garlands, garments, and a sacred thread;
and one should meditate on the left crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) as the support for the water-pot, located in the north.

Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāmadeva; Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. Having worshipped [the deity] from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the lamp, and having offered ten oblations of food and betel leaf, thereafter [fifty... (l4).
Having offered two hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Vāmadeva mantra, and having offered half of that amount of *āḍhakavaṭa* caru with the Vāmadeva mantra;

[he offers] barley with the Īśāna mantra, black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the Śiras mantra, millet (*śyāmāka*), *priyaṅgu*, and horse-gram (*kulattha*) with the Śiras mantra, and with the Aghora mantra, the five types of food: pure rice, mung-bean rice, milk-rice, *kṛsara* rice, and jaggery-rice.

An offering of *āmalaka* fruit the size of a fresh *ārdrā* leaf is for the head; a cake the size of one's own [hand] is for the eyes; milk-porridge the size of a *sruva* ladle is for Īśāna; sugarcane juice and Gaṅgā water are also the size of a *sruva*;
curd is offered with Tatpuruṣa by means of Vāmadeva.

Honey [should be] the size of a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) with the Aghora mantra; a jujube fruit (*guḷa*) the size of a *punnāga* fruit at the base, or the size of a joint (*parva*); a piece of sugarcane [likewise]. With the Īśāna mantra, half a plantain fruit, a mango fruit, or a *likuca* fruit [should be offered] according to their own natural size.

Having divided a jackfruit (*panasa*) into thirty parts, one part is for the oblation (*homa*). A jujube fruit (*badarīphala*) [is offered] according to its own natural size. Having split a coconut into eight parts, each part is for the oblation.

With the root mantra, one should offer as oblations: *sūraṇa* powder, *bālakaṇḍa*, *padmakaṇḍa*, and *utpalakaṇḍa*. Having offered these in the measure of a single oblation, the fire sacrifice (*homa*) proceeds—with the root mantra—as follows: sandalwood, musk, black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), *gorocana*, saffron from Kashmir, the two types of musk (*mṛganābhi*), sandalwood, and snow-water.

One should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with fresh camphor the size of a chickpea. With the principal seed-mantras, one should take two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each of *hrībera*, *uśīra*, and *marudavana* for the offering. One should take a *māṣa*-measure of *gulgulu* (bdellium). With the ten-syllable mantra, one offers flowers; with the *Pāśupata* mantra, a *bilva* fruit; with the *Aghora* mantra, three pieces of betel leaf and one areca nut, together with cardamom, cloves, and *patrikā*.

And with ten [parts] of *mūla*, one *caṇaka*; with nine, a *niṣpāva*. An *āḍhaka* of bamboo, *mudga*, and sesame—these are taken in the measure of a *śukti*; a *māṣa* in the measure of a *śukti*; a *siddhārtha* and mustard (*sarṣapa*) in half a *śukti*; and *pṛthuka* [is taken] in half a *śukti*.

A fistful of wheat; a *śukti* [two finger-breadths] of cow-dung; a *badarī* fruit-sized piece of fresh turmeric; half a *jātīphala* fruit; and a *badarī* fruit-sized nutmeg—having offered these with the root mantra alone, one should offer ten oblations each of the sixty-three substances beginning with barley and ending with *triphalā*, offering separately for each substance with the *vyāhṛtis*. Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation combined with all the substances... [Side heading: The Ritual for Offering in the Īśāna Kuṇḍa]

(l1) Having performed the expiation by offering clarified butter twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra; [and having offered] with the armor, the multiform mantra for consuming sin, the ninefold self, the Śambara mantra, and the sword mantra; (l2)

Having offered eight oblations for each [deity] according to the rule, having performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having sat down and presented incense and lamps; thereafter, having offered the bali and the *arghya* to Brahmā and the others, as well as to Indra and the others, in the girdles starting from the east, and having sprinkled [the area], one should worship and restrain [the deities] with the *aghora* mantra using the *arghya* water. This is the procedure for the fire-oblation in the northern pit (*uttarakuṇḍa*).
Now follows the procedure for the Īśāna-kunda.

(L4. The presiding priest (mūrtipa), having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), adorned himself with the turban and other ornaments, and sat down facing east upon a tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana), performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa) and prepared the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya). (L5.)

Having sprinkled the sacrificial implements, the eight-cornered *kuṇḍa*, and the *astras* with that water; and having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as *nirīkṣaṇa* upon the eight-cornered *kuṇḍa*;

[one should place] the fire established from the principal *kuṇḍa* into its respective places within the eight-cornered *kuṇḍa* along with the mantras, together with the sweeping, the sprinkling, the strewing of grass, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the *kūrca*, the seat (*viṣṭara*), and the upward-pointing fuel-sticks (*samidh*).

Having prepared [the fire], having sprinkled it, and having adorned it, having worshipped Brahmā and the others upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the eight Vasus upon the seats (*viṣṭara*), the seven Maruts upon the sacrificial grass coverings (*paristaraṇa*), and the lords of the worlds (*lokeśa*) in due order; then, in that fire—
Salutation to Ananta; salutation to Dharma; salutation to Jñāna; salutation to Vairāgya; salutation to Aiśvarya; salutation to Padma;
salutation to the common seat of fire (sāmānyāgnisana).
[He has] two faces, the Vedas as his horns, and holds the gestures of granting fearlessness (abhaya) and the power of the weapon (śaktihasta).

One should meditate upon the common fire (*sāmānyāgni*) in the northeastern pit (*īśānakuṇḍaka*), holding the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and a shield (*kheṭa*) in the right and left hands respectively, and bearing fire. Homage to the form of the common fire! Oṃ Raṃ, homage to the common fire! To the bearer of the form of Īśāna.
Salutation to the one whose form is the sky and who has the sky as his seat.
He has four arms and four faces;
holding a trident and a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his hands, he carries a conch and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in his right [hands]; he resembles the sky, a jasmine flower, and the moon.
Salutation to the one who bears the form of Īśāna, the embodiment of space (*vyoma*). Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Space. Above that: salutation to the seat of Īśāna.
[He is] three-eyed, four-armed, and wears a crown of matted hair.
One should meditate upon [the deity] complete with all ornaments in the northeastern direction.
Homage to the form of Īśa! Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, homage to Īśa! Homage to the seat of the head-form of Īśīśa! Homage to the head-form possessing the luster of refined gold!

"Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the head. Having thus performed the worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the lamp, at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should offer ten oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the head-mantra. Thereafter, having offered two hundred and fifty oblations of clarified butter with the head-mantra, one should then offer half of that number—namely, [one hundred and twenty-five] oblations of *arka* wood, black gram (*māṣa*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—with the head-mantra. With the *Īśāna* mantra, one offers barley.

With the *śiras* [mantra], one offers a *rājamāṣa* bean; with the *śikhā*, a *śyāmāka* grain. With the *aghora* [mantra], one offers *priyaṅgu* and *kuluttha*, as well as pure food (*śuddhānna*), mung-bean rice (*mudgānna*), milk-rice (*kṣīrānna*), *kṛsarānna*, and molasses-rice (*gulānna*)—these are the five types of food. One offers a cake (*apūpa*) the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit with the *śiras* [mantra], according to its own proper measure.

With the Netra [mantra], one should offer curd in the measure of a *sruva* ladle; with Īśāna, milk; and with Tatpuruṣa, sugarcane juice and water from the Gaṅgā, both in the measure of a *sruva*. With Vāmadeva, honey in the measure of a *sruva*; with Aghora, jaggery in the size of a *puṃnāga* fruit; and with the Mūla [mantra], a piece of sugarcane the size of a joint. With Īśāna, a plantain fruit or half a fruit; [and likewise] a mango fruit or a *likuca* fruit.

The *panasa* fruit is of its own measure; having divided it into thirty parts, there is one oblation for each part. The *badarī* fruit is of its own measure. The coconut, having been split into eight pieces, has one oblation for each piece. With the root-mantra, [one offers] *sūraṇa* powder. The *bālaganda* and the lotus-root (*padmakanda*).

And the root of the *utpala* lotus. Having offered these in the measure of an oblation (*āhutimātra*), the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) is performed. With the root-mantra, one offers sandalwood (*candana*), musk (*kastūrī*), black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*), *gorocana*, Kashmiri saffron (*kāśmīra-kuṅkuma*), the two types of musk-deer navel (*mṛganābhi*), sandalwood (*candana*), snow-water (*himatoya*), and fresh camphor (*ārdrakarpūra*). The fire-sacrifice is performed with [substances] the size of a chickpea (*caṇakamātra*). With the primary seeds, one offers *hrībera*, *uśīra*, and *marudavana*.

Having taken these [substances] measuring two finger-breadths, one performs the fire offering (*homa*). Guggulu [is offered] in the measure of a *māṣa*. With the ten-syllable mantra, flowers; with the Pāśupata mantra, a *bilva* fruit; with the Aghora mantra, three pieces of betel leaf and one areca nut. Cardamom, cloves, and *patrikā* are offered together with the root-mantra, as is chickpea, with ten recitations.

Nine *āḍhakas* of *niṣpāva* beans, one *āḍhaka* of bamboo, and *mudga* beans—these [are to be taken] in the measure of a *śukti*. Sesame is that which is brought from the *mṛgīmudrā* [measure]. *Māṣa* beans are in the measure of a *śukti*. White mustard and black mustard are half a *śruti*. *Pṛthuka* (parched rice) is one handful. Wheat is in the measure of a *śukti*. Cow dung is in the measure of a *śukti*. The fruit of the *badarī*, the mango, the *haridrā* fruit, the *arka* [flower], and the nutmeg are each in the measure of a *badarī* fruit; these are the items.

Having offered with the root mantra alone, one should offer each of the sixty-three substances, beginning with barley and ending with nutmeg, ten times individually. Having offered each substance with the *vyāhṛti* mantras,
[one performs] the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering combined with all the substances.

Having performed the *homā* expiation by offering clarified butter twenty-five times with the five-weapon mantra (*pañcāstra*), and having offered eight oblations for each [of the following]— with the armor mantra (*varma*), the multiform mantra (*bahurūpa*), the sin-consuming mantra (*pāpabhakṣaṇa*), the nine-fold *śambara*, and the sword mantra (*asi*)— and having duly offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sit down, offer incense and lamps,
and thereafter [proceed] with the girdles starting from the east.

Having offered bali and arghya to Brahmā and the others, as well as to Indra and the others; having performed the oblation (*huta*); having requested [the deities] to depart; having sprinkled [water] around; having approached the fire for worship (*upasthāna*); and having paid obeisance, one should restrain [the fire] with the *aghora* mantra using the arghya water. Thus ends the procedure for the fire-offering in the Īśāna pit.

The Great Ever-Full Oblation— now, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, having performed the fire-sacrifice in this manner, should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) by means of the path of the channel-union (*nāḍīsandhāna*), along with flowers and consecrated rice grains (*akṣata*). Just as one would fill a ladle (*sruva*) with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), place a flower at its tip, and [hold it] with the left and right hands joined like a conch shell.
Having taken [it], it is proclaimed; with feet together, the body bent,
the gaze fixed on the tip of the horn, having brought the base of the horn to the left side of the breast, with the tongue held in the air, uttering the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should hold the measure and offer all the clarified butter from every side.

Accompanied by the sound of the *dyaghoṣa*, one should cast [the offering] into the fire. Having thus performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sit down. Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* with clarified butter for half of the general expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), and having presented incense and lamps, one should offer food—or, if the *bali* was previously prepared—according to the blameless rule, first into the center above the girdle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with "To Sadāśiva, svāhā! Then, to its east—
To Īśvara, svāhā!
(l5) To the south—to Rudra, svāhā! To the north—to Viṣṇu, svāhā! To the west—to Brahmā, svāhā! In the middle girdle of Guṇḍa, to the east—to the kalā Śāntyatītā—(l6)
Svāhā! To the east—svāhā to Śāntikalā. To the south—svāhā to Vidyākalā. To the north—svāhā to Pratiṣṭhākalā.

To the west—svāhā to Nivṛttikalā. Having offered the bali-oblation below on the Meghalā to those beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu, then [to] those stationed at the enclosures, beginning with Brahmā.
In the east: *svāhā* to Brahmā; in the south: *svāhā* to Viṣṇu; in the west:

*svāhā* to Rudra; in the north: *svāhā* to Ananta. Having thus offered the water for honor (*arghya*), one should dismiss them in reverse order. Then, having prepared two mandalas in the southern direction from oneself—

In the first maṇḍala—in the directions from the east to the north—[one should offer]: *iha* rudrebhyaḥ svāhā | oṃ hāṃ mātṛbhyaḥ svāhā | oṃ hāṃ gaṇebhyaḥ svāhā | oṃ hāṃ yakṣebhyaḥ svāhā | [beginning with] Īśāna (l. 3).
In the corners: Oṃ hāṃ grahebhyaḥ svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ asurebhyaḥ svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ rākṣasebhyaḥ svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ nāgebhyaḥ svāhā | In the center— (l4)
In the northeast, southeast, and southwest [corners], one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ nakṣatrebhyaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ rāśibhyaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ hāṃ viśvebhyaḥ svāhā*.

Between the northwest and west, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ kṣetrapālāya svāhā*. Having worshipped thus with mantras ending in *namaḥ* and having offered the *bali* oblation with mantras ending in *svāhā*.

In the second maṇḍala—having offered bali in the eight directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna; then again, in the left portion of the northeast: *brahmaṇe svāhā*; in the left portion of the southwest: *viṣṇave svāhā*; in the center: *nīlalohitāya svāhā*. These [are offered] with the word "namas" at the end.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the mantra ending in *svāhā* and offered the *bali*, one should dismiss [the deities] in reverse order. Then, the rites from the northern sprinkling (*uttara-pariṣecana*) up to the final salutation (*upasthāna*) are the same. Having thus offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should restrain the water for the guest-offering (*arghyāmbu*) with the *astra-mantra*. In this manner, having restrained the fire in all the primary and other sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), one should go near the ritual jar (*kumbha*).

Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should offer them, saying: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātma-tattva; obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Vidya-tattva; obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva. Having thus offered these three handfuls of flowers, he should present the fruit of the *homa*.
O protector of the most secret of secrets, please accept this hymn composed by us;
O Maheśvara, O God, may success be ours through your grace.

Having thus offered the fruit of the fire-oblation (*homa*) together with the *arghya* water, and having again worshipped Śiva with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and having presented incense and a lamp— (the procedure for the food offering):

The procedure for the offering (nivedya) is according to the sequence to be described: having cooked [the food], accompanied by all musical instruments, near the jar (kumbha), one should offer the fivefold food (pañcānna)—consisting of what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk—to the deity according to the ritual for presenting offerings. Then again, [one performs] the worship with incense, lamps, great lamps, and so forth.

Having performed the pure concluding rite (*nṛttānta*), having offered the sacred thread (*pavitra*), and having presented the fruit of the recitation (*japaphala*), one should satisfy Śiva with hymns of praise. Such is the offering of ornaments.
(The feeding of Brāhmaṇas)—on an auspicious lunar day. (l7)

For the purpose of removing all defects arising from omissions in mantra, tantra, and ritual action that may have occurred during the rites of the restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*), the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), and the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) of this Sadāśiva, the Lord of Veṇuvana (*Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara*), together with his retinue, accompanied by the Mother Kāntimatī, and joined with the venerable *mūla-liṅga*— from the initial permission (*anujñādi*) up to the three fortnights of sacrifice, including the feeding of Brahmins at the Amitaprāhaṇa [time]— [this is performed].

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Every day, preceded by the [ritual] purification of the limbs (*aṅgapūrvaka*), and preceded by various kinds of food—namely, what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drinks such as water and cool water—I shall feed Brāhmaṇas in immeasurable numbers with the thought that they are Śiva," thus [he should act]. In this manner...
This is the procedure for feeding an infinite number of Brahmins. In this manner, one should perform it according to the rules every morning and evening for a total of ninety-six days.

Now, the principal daily worship of the western door: (l4) Then, when the dawn has become clear, on the following day, the preceptor, having performed all [the rites] such as the purification of the body as previously described; having duly performed the Śaiva twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) beginning with bathing, and the domestic fire sacrifice (*aupāsana*); and having entered the sacrificial pavilion together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*), the attendants (*paricārakāḥ*), who are bathed, pure, and adorned with garments and so forth—(l5) [he proceeds].

Having adorned oneself with the five-fold ornaments, seated upon a tortoise-posture (kūrmāsana) with the sacred thread (pavitra) in hand and a serene countenance, one should sit down; having performed the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), having prepared the general water offering (sāmānyārghya),
and having fully worshipped Vighneśvara, [one should worship] the head...

Having worshipped Vighneśvara preceded by the ritual of striking [the drum], and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): on this auspicious lunar day, for the rite of the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the restoration of what is decayed and the binding with eight [materials] for this Lord of Gods, Sadāśiva, known as Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his consort Śrī Kāntimatī, accompanied by the Śrī Mūla-liṅga, and along with his retinue.

"I shall perform the daily worship in the form of the western door-entrance, following the sequence of morning worship beginning with Saura and ending with Caṇḍa, including sacrifices, oblations, worship, offerings, daily rites, and festivals. As an ancillary part of that, for the sake of purifying all the ritual implements, I shall perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other materials. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and having duly prepared the *puṇyāha* and *pañcagavya* according to the previously mentioned procedure, [he should use] those two with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having sprinkled the sacrificial pavilion, the implements for worship, and the implements for the fire-oblation; having performed the worship of the Sun; then, having washed one's feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and applied sacred ash (*bhasman*);
[one proceeds] from the door up to the lineage of gurus.

Having performed worship as previously described, one should then go near the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*). Having removed the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), having sprinkled it with *arghya* water while reciting the Astra-mantra, and having adorned it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the purification of the Liṅga through visualization within the pitcher. Then, having bathed it with scented oil and other substances in the mirror situated before the deity, [one should bathe it] with the special *arghya* water using the Root-mantra.

Having bathed [the deity] and adorned [it], having arranged the seat for the jar beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śakti, having meditated upon the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), having applied the eyes with the Netramantra,
and having invoked [the deity] with the Sadyojāta-mantra distinguished by the root mantra, [one performs] the installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth.

Having worshipped [the deities] from the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) up to the end, one should perform the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) in the western direction. There, having specifically worshipped either Tatpuruṣa or Sadyojāta, as well as the Heart and other [limbs] as before, or alternatively the limbs of dissolution;

and having performed in the west everything from incense, lamps, and the offering of the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) up to the pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*), together with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipa*) as previously described.

Having offered oblations into all the fire-pits, beginning with the principal one, using their respective substances— from the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) up to the *jātī* fruit— namely the sixty-three substances, each accompanied by its own mantra and interspersed with the *vyāhṛti*s,
[one should perform] the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, as well as the expiation for the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Having offered the daily great full oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*) into the eastern primary fire-pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*), having presented the sacrificial offering (*bali*), and having worshipped the Blessed One residing in the fire; having restrained [the deity], having dedicated the fruit of the *homa* to the glorious Blessed Lord Veṇuvaneśvara;

having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the three principles (*tattva*); and having offered incense and lamps; accompanied by various musical instruments, one should [offer] the five kinds of food (*pañcabhakṣya*) according to the rule.

Having taken the foods to be chewed, licked, sucked, and drunk, along with mouth-fresheners and the cook, and having offered them to Śiva in the presence of the deity after first performing the purification of the ground and other preliminary rites,
[one performs] the services ending with pure dance facing west.

Having offered [the oblation], having given the *pavitra*, having recited [mantras], having presented [the offering], and having praised with hymns, one should worship the daily festival (*nityotsava*) up to the lamps while making prayers for one's desired objects;

one should also propitiate Caṇḍeśa. (Aṣṭabandhanajīrṇoddhāraṇam) This is the procedure for worship from the morning onwards. In this very same manner, at evening time as well, [one should perform] from the worship of the Sun or the worship of the Moon up to the daily festival.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),

he [found] near the primary *liṅga* a manuscript of the *Kāmikāgama*, written on twenty-nine leaves— nine fewer than one hundred— and arranged according to the previously established procedure beginning with the placement of the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*).

Having established the *śāntikumbha* according to the prescribed method, having performed the *śāntihoma* rite in accordance with the rules, having sprinkled [the area] with the water from the *śāntikumbha* while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
and having worshipped the *liṅga* with the eightfold offering of flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),
one should present ginger, sugar, coconut water, fruits, and so forth.
(The Procedure for the Eightfold Binding):

At midnight, one should perform the extraction of the decayed [substance] from the eightfold binding. (L5) Just as the Ācārya, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), having established the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), and having worshipped Vighneśvara, should pray to Vighneśvara while striking his head.

(l6) Having restrained the breath, the formal resolve: On this auspicious lunar day, [for the purpose of] this God of Gods, Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his consort Śrī Kāntimatī, accompanied by the Śrī Mūlaliṅga, and along with his retinue; (l7)

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In the rite of the Śiva-sacrifice for the restoration and re-binding of Sadāśiva’s [liṅga], I shall perform the removal of the previously installed eight-fold binding in order to install a new eight-fold binding," he should sprinkle the root-liṅga with the water from the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), perform the deposition of phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) at the locations of the Mothers (*mātṛkāsthāna*), and worship it again with the eightfold flower-offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*).
Having offered a beverage and prayed for the welfare of Śiva, and being authorized by Śiva for the purpose of restoring what was decayed, together with all the presiding priests (*mūrtipas*),
he performed the restoration of the decayed [temple] using heated iron rods and iron [tools].
By means of specific ritual methods: while reciting the *astramantra*, one should carefully extract only the decayed medicinal herbs located within other *liṅgas* or *pīṭhas* wherever they are seen,
place them in another vessel, cover them with cloth and *darbha* grass, and then smear the *liṅga* with fragrant substances along with the sprinkling of cold water.
Having worshipped with fragrant flowers,
having offered incense and lamps with the *kavaca* mantra, and having presented a coconut shell containing pieces of white sugar mixed with cardamom and cloves, together with water from a coconut;

Having offered betel and other items with the root-mantra, having performed the *ārātrika* rite, having covered the vessel containing the extracted medicinal herbs with a cloth, and having adorned it with garlands of flowers, one should place it upon the head of a palanquin or on the head of an attendant; then, preceded by the sound of all musical instruments, without letting it dry out in a great river, one should cast it into a lake while reciting this mantra. Thus.
The procedure for the extraction of the *Kāmika* [Tantra] when it has become worn out.

Now, the arrangement of the jewels and so forth: Then the preceptor, having gone together with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipa*) to the vicinity of the primary liṅga, having sat upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*), having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), and having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*).

Having worshipped Vighneśvara; having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking one’s head [three times]; having prostrated before the Guru; having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma); [making] the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the purpose of binding anew with eight bands the Śivayāga of the Lord of the Śrī Veṇuvana forest, the Sadāśiva, together with his retinue, accompanied by the primordial Liṅga (mūlaliṅga), and joined by the Goddess Śrī Kāntimatīmbā..."

For the purpose of establishing the commonality of the *liṅga*; for the purpose of attaining the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) preceded by the protection of his devotees such as ourselves; having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the placement of jewels, the installation of the *cakra*, the binding with gold threads, and so forth";
and having sipped water (*ācamana*).

Having sprinkled the *liṅga* with the water from the *śānti*-vessel while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having worshipped it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; having placed [the gems] in a washed vessel filled with water—

starting from the center and ending at the northeast (*īśāna*), according to the available size of the *māṇikā* and so forth— and having consecrated the *māṇikya* and other gems with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and having sprinkled them [with water], [one should worship] Brahmā and the others...
Having placed the World-Protectors ending with Īśāna upon the rubies and other gems,

and having worshipped them up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), one should place the gems after worshipping Brahmā and the others in their respective locations, beginning from the central *brahma-bhāga* of the *liṅga*.

Having divided the portion of the pedestal into sixteen parts, one should sequentially bind the nine-jeweled [portion] as one part, joined with ten parts consisting of the sword and so forth, and five parts.
Having drawn a square with gold according to the measurement of a trident, one should cast [the seed] into the hollow of the central aperture with the *śivabīja* mantra.

Then, having worshipped with: "Obeisance to Anantāsana; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya; obeisance to Aiśvarya; obeisance to Padma; obeisance to Śivāsana; obeisance to Śivamūrti; obeisance to Śiva. (l. 3)

Having displayed the *mukulī* mudrā, the *padma* mudrā, and the *śodhinī* mudrā; in the center—having recited the *brahmajijñāna* mantra up to the end of the *bhukti* [portion]; while muttering the root mantra: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe satyalokādhipāya daṇḍakamaṇḍaluhastāya haṃsavāhanāya saparivārāya sāstrāya namaḥ*. Thus, [place] a ruby (*māṇikya*) in the station of Brahmā.

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) in this very manner— in the direction of Indra, with the mantra "trātāra" and with the root mantra— having placed emerald (*marataka*); in the south— with the mantra "sugannāpaṃ jñāmi" and with the root mantra— an sapphire (*indranīla*).

Having performed the placement [of the gems]: in the west, having placed crystal with the mantra *tattvā yāmi* and the root mantra; in the north, having placed the vajra with the mantra *vayagug soma* and the root mantra; in the southwest, having placed lapis lazuli with the mantra *barhigo caratvanno agni* and the root mantra; and in the southwest direction, [having placed] pearl with the mantra *asanvantam* and the root mantra.

Having performed the placement [of the gems]: in the northwest (mārute), having placed a ruby with the mantra beginning with *ānoniya* and the root mantra; in the northeast (īśānadeśe), having placed coral with the mantra *tam īśānam* and the root mantra; above that, one-tenth [of the quantity] with white [substances], being pure.
Having fully completed [the rite], having made it firm, and having worshipped once again with incense, lamps, and so forth, and having offered the oblation, one should pray.

Thus ends the procedure for the placement of the jewels and other [elements] as part of the eightfold binding, as taught in the Kāmikāgama. (l3) Now, having drawn the yantra of the five syllables and so forth, either combined or alone, if it has been propitiated, that too should be placed at the base.

The Procedure for the Eightfold Binding—(l4. Now, the preceptor, having adorned himself together with the guardians of the images, and having performed the evening twilight ritual (*sāyantanī saṃdhyā*) and the special twilight ritual (*viśeṣasaṃdhyā*), [performs] the worship of the pavilion, the evening oblation, the worship, and the offering of food (*nivedana*). (l5)

At the conclusion of the daily evening festival, having prepared two equal squares on the ground with cow dung at the front of the temple, and having drawn a lotus distinguished by a pericarp and eight petals, one should arrange a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) upon it starting from the east and so forth. Having strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should prepare a square with cow dung to its north and [draw] an eight-petaled lotus.

Having drawn [the mandala] and prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice and other grains, seated upon a tortoise-seat facing north, having performed the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*), and having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules,
[he should worship him] while striking his head, [beginning with] Vighneśvara...

Having made the request, having prostrated before the Guru, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [he makes] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the sacrifice to Śiva of the God of Gods, the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva— who is accompanied by his consort the venerable Kāntimatī, together with the venerable Mūla-liṅga, and along with his retinue— preceded by the protection of ourselves and other devotees, [may there be] longevity, health, sovereignty, and so forth."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of accomplishing all my manifold desires, I shall perform the rite of binding with gold and other materials for the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara of Svāyambhuva, according to the method taught in the *Kāmikāgama*," and having sipped water (*ācamana*) in accordance with the rules.

Having established [the materials] in the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having sprinkled the binding herbs and the ritual implements with those two [substances] while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should establish nine pure vessels—ranging from gold down to earthenware—in the petals starting from the center, reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. In the central vessel, one should place three parts of conch powder with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). In the eastern vessel, two parts of sesame.

Having performed the placement with the root mantra, one should place one part of the three fruits in the vessels situated on the petals of Agni, the South, and Nirṛti, using the root mantra. In the West, one should place two parts of sugar.
In the North, one should place one part of rice and plantain fruit, using the root mantra.

In the north (saumye): having placed curd consisting of three parts with the *mūla-mantra*. In the northeast (īśāne): having placed buffalo-butter (*mahiṣa-navanīta*) in the form of the eight substances and the secondary substances (*kupadravya*) with the *mūla-mantra*. *Anantāya namaḥ* | *Dharmāya namaḥ* | *Jñānāya namaḥ* | *Vairāgyāya namaḥ* | *Aiśvaryāya namaḥ* | *Padmāya namaḥ* | *Śivāsanāya namaḥ* | *Śivamūrtaye namaḥ* | *Śivāya namaḥ* |

Having invoked Śiva with the root mantra, and having worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, within the infinite substances from the east to the northeast; and having performed the complete worship from invocation through the offering of food (naivedya); one should consecrate each [substance] separately one hundred times with its respective mantra upon the mortar and pestle situated on the northern sacrificial mound.

Having washed [the mortar] with water, having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having placed the mortar upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship it: "Homage to Ananta; homage to Dharma; homage to Jñāna; homage to Vairāgya; homage to Aiśvarya; homage to the Lotus; homage to the Brahmā-throne; homage to the Form of Brahmā; homage to Brahmā. [Then, for] the pestle...
"Salutation to Viṣṇuvāsana; salutation to Viṣṇumūrti; salutation to Viṣṇu.

Having worshipped thus, having adorned [the image] with garments, *darbha* grass, and flowers, and having offered incense and lamps, one should summon an attendant and adorn him with garments, upper cloths, and so forth. [Then, regarding] the mortar, the conch located in the central vessel...

Having taken the eight substances beginning with powder (cūrṇa) and ending with Soma along with the root mantra; having placed them in the mortar with the heart mantra; holding the pestle in his hand and pounding it himself; and having had the attendant pound it until it is well-cooked while observing it—at the time of pounding, [the officiant] together with the initiated and the Vedic scholars should recite the *saṃhitā* mantras, the root mantra, the five-weapon (*pañcāstra*) mantras, the *prāsāda* mantra, and the *rudrasūkta*.

Having consecrated and recited all the mantras— the *Trayambaka*, *Viṣṇu*, and *Brahma* sūktas, the *Pāvamāna*, the *Agni* sūkta, the beginning of the Vedas, and so forth— and having performed the recitation, one should divide [the water] into three parts purified by a cloth,
using a new earthen vessel.

Having taken [the medicine], having filled it with medicinal herbs, having wrapped the opening with a cloth, and having dried it with the rays of the sun, one should again place the medicine in a mortar, pound it,

and knowing it to be well-cooked by means of the thread-path, fashion it into the shape of a ring. Having placed the ring in a vessel, one should once more prepare the medicine through the four purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*).

Having sprinkled [the site] with the *śivabīja* mantra on the day of invocation, having worshipped up to the edge of the altar (*vedi*), and having taken the medicinal herb while reciting "Obeisance to You," one should place it upon the head of the attendant in the *śibikā* (palanquin),
amidst the sound of auspicious proclamations, various musical instruments, the royal umbrella, the fly-whisk, and the cry of "Victory! (l4–l5).

Having circumambulated the temple of Śiva accompanied [by the ritual implements], having entered, having circumambulated the sacred abode (*dhāman*), having placed [the offering] before Śiva, and having sprinkled it with drops of *arghya* water, he should again place it in the mortar. (L6) Having ascertained that it is well-cooked by means of the "thread-path" (*tantumārga*), he should divide the portion for the worship of the Liṅga into sixteen parts; one part [of these] is for the space between the Liṅga and its pedestal.
Recalling the seed-syllable of fire, one should bind firmly.

Having bound it firmly and joined it well with conch powder and other materials, the Guru, having thus bound it very securely, [should sprinkle it] again with the water from the peace-vase using the *astra*, the root-mantra, and the *pāśupata* mantra.

Having sprinkled water upon the *liṅga* and worshipped it thoroughly with the root mantra using the "eight flowers" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), for the purpose of pacifying the heat of bondage and for the sake of attaining the grace that forgives all transgressions,
[one should offer] at that very moment: ginger powder mixed with molasses,
white sugar, candied sugar, pieces of coconut, a variety of fruits such as plantains and others, refreshing drinks (*pānaka*), coconut water, and a great abundance [of other offerings].

Having offered [the oblation] with devotion and the root mantra, having presented incense and lamps, and having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony: "For the sake of protecting the devotees here, beginning with the virtuous, may my various kinds of offenses committed be forgiven; please forgive me. Thus [he says].
Having focused [the mind], one should pray for what is desired. Thus ends the procedure for the eightfold binding according to the Kāmikāgama.
The Application of Fresh Butter: Then the preceptor,

having sat upon the tortoise-seat (kūrma-āsana) on a copper vessel, having adorned himself with the [five] uṣṇīṣas and other ornaments, together with the guardians of the images, having performed the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), and having prepared the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya).

Having worshipped Vighneśvara, [having performed] the crushing of the head... (l6) and having prayed to Vighneśvara, having restrained the breath (prāṇāyāma), [he makes] the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, accompanied by the venerable Mūla-liṅga and his retinue... (l7)

In the Śivayāga consisting of the restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*) and the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of the venerable Sadāśiva, the Lord of Veṇuvana—for the purpose of performing the eightfold binding with especially firm medicinal substances for the primary rites of golden binding and triple binding; for the removal of impurity acquired by the master builder (*sthapati*) and others, and for the purification of the *nivṛtti-dvāra-liṅga*; and specifically for the protection of our own devotees and others—... [the following was performed].

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of attaining the grace of Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara and for the sake of the presence of the Liṅga, I shall perform the Great Peace Oblation (*mahāśāntihoma*) preceded by the installation of the Peace Vessel (*śāntikumbha*)," and having sipped water (*upaspṛśya*),
he should duly prepare the *puṇyāha* and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having consecrated the articles for worship and the implements for the fire-oblation (*homa*) with those two mantras and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), and having offered oblations one hundred times for each substance according to the procedure for the pacifying fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*)— in which twenty-nine leaves plus one hundred are arranged in a previously constructed square or circular pit to the west of the deity— having presented the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and so forth;
Having consecrated the primary image (*mūlaliṅga*) with the water from the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*),

and having performed the rite of surrounding it with fire (*parigni-karaṇa*) using the fire of the peace-oblation (*śāntihoma*), one should again sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, with the *Pāśupata* [mantra], and once more with the water from the peace-vessel;
then, having adorned it with sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings, [one should offer] incense.

Having offered lamps, and having prayed to Īśvara with an offering (*naivedya*) consisting of boiled milk mixed with white sugar and candied sugar, accompanied by the root-mantra, one should go outside and satisfy the architects with garments, ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth. (l7) Thus ends the dismissal of the artisans.

Now, the application of fresh butter (*navanītalepana*). Having brought pure fresh butter and consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥsaṃskāra*), one should sprinkle it with water for the *arghya* offering using the *astra-mantra* and worship it with the *śiva-bīja*. At the time of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), [this is done] by means of substances such as heated metal rods and so forth, for the purpose of strengthening the liquid medicinal paste used for the eightfold binding, and for the pacification of the sensation of heat and the binding itself.

Beginning from the base, the primary liṅga, and the pedestal, one should apply fresh butter that has sunk into a māṣa [of weight], while recollecting [the deity] as far as the top of the head; thus is the application of fresh butter.

Now, the application of the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandha-lepana*): [The] Preceptor [performs] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). For this Śiva-yāga of Sadāśiva, the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his retinue, accompanied by the venerable Mūlaliṅga, and joined by the Mother Śrī Kāntimatī—[this is done] for the purpose of restoring what is decayed and for the pacification of heat through the eight-fold binding of the root-liṅga. The root-liṅga...

Having made the resolve, "I shall smear [the liṅga] with the eight-fold fragrance (aṣṭagandha)," one should remove the butter from the liṅga with pure water, wipe it clean, and sprinkle it thoroughly with *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Then, having procured the eight-fold fragrance— namely, sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *tamāla*, water, saffron, black [fragrance], and *koṣa*— which is known as the eight-fold fragrance of Śiva (*śaivagandhāṣṭaka*), one should apply that fragrant [mixture] with cold water.

Having sprinkled it and smeared the eight-fragrance paste upon the *liṅga* and the pedestal so that it is as thick as a *māṣa* bean, one should again sprinkle it with cold water and smear it all over with fragrant flowers such as the *mallikā*, *kuṭaja*,
and *karavīra*.

The Guru should worship by completely filling both the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with other perfumes and flowers, including blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*). Having thus anointed [the deity] with the eight fragrances (*aṣṭagandha*) according to the prescribed rule, the purification of the temple (*prāsādaśuddhi*) should be performed in the manner described in the section on the "Drawing of the Leaves" (*patralikhita*).

(Purification of the Temple): Then the preceptor, having washed his feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), adorned himself with the *uṣṇīṣa* and the five ornaments, and applied sacred ash (*bhasman*),

shall sit on a tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) in the eastern part of the temple— which has been purified with cow-dung water and decorated with colored powders and garlands— with his hands holding the purificatory grass (*pavitra*) and facing the north.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya), having worshipped Vighneśvara, and having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking the head [three times], one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the purification of the temple, which is the form of the gross body, for the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the restoration of the dilapidated and the eight-fold binding of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara— who is accompanied by the primary *mūla-liṅga* and his retinue, and who is Sadāśiva"— and having sipped water (*ācamana*), having performed the rite for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) according to the rules, and having sprinkled the articles of worship with that [mantra] weapon (*astra*), [one proceeds].

Having prepared a nine-square grid on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains and other materials, one should duly place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the five squares beginning with the center. One should then place the substances for purification in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*):
in the southeast corner, [the substance] numbering one hundred...

Having placed a handful of coconut leaves; having placed śrīpatra leaves and a handful of *darbha* grass with a hundred blades in the southwest; and having placed dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, rice, and milk in the northwest—in these nine locations—having placed a garland of *darbha* grass made from threads joined by nine strings and a new cloth upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍilī*) in the northeast, while reciting the heart mantra.
Having worshipped with that very same [offering], having presented incense and lamps,

and having sprinkled the temple with the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should, while reciting the *uddhṛti* mantra, wash [it] from the base up to the pinnacle (*sthūpikā*) with pure oil using the *astra* mantra.
Having wiped the temple with the Śiva-weapon mantra from the coconut leaves at the base up to the pinnacle in the directions starting with the east;

having smeared it [with cow products]; having sprinkled it above that with the five products of the cow while reciting the Pavamāna mantras; having bathed it with pure water accompanied by mantras containing the word "water" (ab-liṅga); and having consecrated it with the arghya-water using the weapon mantra.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), and having combined a thread, a garland of *darbha* grass, and a new cloth, one should wrap [the structure] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) from the pinnacle (*sthūpī*) to the edge of the temple (*vimāna*) in a clockwise direction. (l6) Having tied a brush (*kūrca*) made of a hundred *darbha* blades to the pinnacle at the top of the temple with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), one should [sprinkle] the temple with mustard seeds and other substances while circling it clockwise with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having arranged three circumambulations for the sake of liberating the asuras, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others, and for the protection of the village people; having worshipped the palace from the spear (śakti) up to the power (śakti);
[and having performed] the placement of the Mātṛkās, the breaking of the staff, the breaking of the head, and the breaking of the digit (kalā).

Having performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās* and the *Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā* in their respective locations with their corresponding mantras; having meditated upon the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*);
having applied the eyes with the eye-mantra (*netramantra*); having filled the joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers;

having invoked the Lord Sadāśiva with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*); and having worshipped Him from the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) up to the recitation (*japa*), [one should worship] Indra or Guha in the east with perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed the worship: [one worships] Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the south;

Nārasiṃha in the west; Brahmā in the north. Then, having invoked the deities of the temple—beginning from the base and ending with the pinnacle—by means of their respective root-mantras, [one performs] the rites of installation and so forth, including incense and lamps.

Having performed [the worship] with devotion, preceded by offerings of food (naivedya), lamps, ritual service (ārādhanā), the recitation of the Vedas (vedapārāyaṇa), benedictions (āśīrvāda), the five-limbed Drāviḍa hymns, and pure dance (śuddhanṛtta)— all consisting of manifold services (upacāra) following one another— having contemplated the temple, which consists of the gross body, as pure and characterized by the individual soul (jīva), and having gratified [the deity] with hymns, one should pray for one's desired object. Thus [says] the Kāmikāgama.

The purification of the temple (*prāsāda-śuddhi*) accomplished through other means than the eight types of binding rites, as prescribed in the *Āgama* scriptures for cases where [the site] has not been obtained [through those rites]. [Side heading:
*Liṅga-śuddhiḥ*. For the purpose of purifying the *liṅga*, the *Brāhma-māya*:
(*Liṅga-śuddhiḥ*)—

Then the preceptor, having adorned himself with the *uṣṇīṣa* and other ornaments, together with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipa*), seated himself with a serene countenance in the presence of the deity. Having smeared the ground with cow dung while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), he prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having worshipped Vighneśvara according to the rules and having entreated Vighneśvara by striking his head [three times], [he honored] the Guru.
Having prostrated and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [he makes] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*):
