Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the embodiment of water; homage to Cetanā, the presiding deity of the embodiment of water.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the wind-form! Homage to Balotkaṭā, the presiding deity of the wind-form! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the moon-form! Homage to Vidyā, the presiding deity of the moon-form! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the fire-form! Homage to Kriyā, the presiding deity of the fire-form!

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one whose form is space (ākāśamūrti). Salutation to the will (icchā) who is the presiding deity of the form of space. Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and having restrained [the breath], he should say: "Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the power of action (kriyāśakti). Oṃ hrīṃ saṃ, Mahāgaurī, beloved of Rudra, svāhā! Having constructed three enclosures using these [mantras] along with ashes, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass, and having subsequently worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions, he should go near the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and [worship] the Supreme Lord in the middle of the pit and upon the girdles (*mekhalā*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) on the *nivṛtti* [kalā] and so forth, and having placed the *nāda* on the lips; having effected the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) between the fire and the linga; having visualized the channel resembling a woolen thread (*ūrṇā-tantu*) as having emerged from the risen [fire]; and having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of that union; one should worship the Śakti in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the formula: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and then offer three oblations.

Having given [the offerings], having worshipped the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), the forms (mūrtis), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras), and having gratified each with three oblations; having offered one hundred, one thousand, or half that number of oblations for each—the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, the limb-mantras (aṅgas), and so forth—along with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); and having placed the eight or four guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by assigning the principles of the self (ātmatattva) and their respective lords; having assigned the lords of their own respective forms starting from the east in due order; having offered three oblations; and having fully worshipped the mantras beginning with Tatpuruṣa.

Having offered one hundred, one thousand, or half that amount—along with the full [oblation]—in accordance with the available materials and time; having sprinkled the primary liṅga with water from the *śānti*-vessel; having touched the portion belonging to Brahmā with the root mantra using the base of a *kuśa* blade;
having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to the number of oblations; having established the presence [of the deity]; and having concealed it with the *varman* [mantra].

Having restrained [the breath], one should cause the command to be heard: "O Brahmā, Lord of the Principle of the Self (ātmatattva), you must remain right here in your presence until this *liṅga* has been purified of its defects. Having worshipped with the utterance of the *nāntanāda* (the nasalized sound ending in *ṃ*) preceded by *oṃ hāṃ hīṃ ātmatattvavidyātattvābhyāṃ namaḥ*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: *oṃ hiṃ līṃ puṃ hāṃ hauṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*. Having performed the *nyāsa* in this manner.

One should offer [oblations] with the earth and other elements, with their forms, while reciting the seed-syllables: *oṃ laṃ lūṃ saṃ lṛṃ sūṃ ruṃ rūṃ iṃ hraṃ hrāṃ kṣuṃ ṣūṃ puṃ pūṃ dhūṃ dhūṃ sūṃ sūṃ hīṃ hūṃ*. Having joined the channels (*nāḍī*) of Śiva and Agni for the sake of union, one should offer an oblation with the root mantra.

Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Tattvas, who is the essence of knowledge (vidyātattva), and having caused him to become present, one should offer oblations as before to the forms (mūrti) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara), together with their respective compendiums (saṃhitā).

(L6) Having thus offered oblations to the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ) and having gone near the liṅga, one should sprinkle it with water from the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha) and, using kuśa grass, [offer] the portion for Viṣṇu in the center of the liṅga with the root mantra.
Having touched [the linga], having recited [mantras] the number of times equal to the homa,

having sprinkled it with water for pacification (śāntyambu), and having performed the presence (sannidhi), the binding (avakuṇṭhana), and the confinement (nirodhana) with the heart-mantra, one should proclaim the command: "O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva), as long as this linga is not completely freed from its defects..."

"You must remain right here as a presence. Then, [reciting] "Oṃ hiṃ huṃ, obeisance to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva)," one should offer [oblations] to the forms (mūrti) as well. One should also present them together with the presiding deities of the forms. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should satisfy the principle of Śiva, its portion, the rudrākṣa, and the presiding deities of the forms along with those who bestow blessings. Then, having gone near the liṅga, one should sprinkle it thoroughly with the water of pacification (śāntyambu).

Having touched the portion of Rudra with the root mantra using the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, having recited [the mantra] as many times as the number of oblations, having sprinkled it with water for pacification (*śāntyambhas*), having brought it into proximity with the heart mantra, having enclosed it within the sacrificial pit, and having restrained it, one should proclaim the command:
"O Rudra! By the command of Śiva, O Lord of the principle of Śiva!"

"O Lord, you must remain here as long as this Liṅga is free from defects. Having thus prayed, [one should offer] "Oṃ Sūṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," performing one hundred oblations for each [mantra].

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having approached the vicinity of the Liṅga, having sprinkled it with water from the ritual jar (*kumbha*), and having touched the Liṅga with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass, one should recite the mantra according to the number of oblations performed. Then—

Having performed the union of the forms with the Lord of Forms, having gone [to the fire], having offered oblations, and having returned, one should pray. Having thus performed the placement [of mantras] from water up to water, and having worshipped thoroughly, one should pray. Such is the placement of the forms and the Lord of Forms.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five syllables of the root [mantra]:
on the head— *namaḥ śaṅkarātmane*.
On the strip: *namaḥ* to the self of the letter *ma*. Above the throat: *namaḥ* to the self of the letter *ya*. In the throat: *namaḥ* to the self of the letter *na*. Salutation to the throat.
"Salutation to the one whose self is the letter *ma*. Thus [it is] among the letters. "Salutation to the one whose self is the upward-facing mouth, the letter *śi*. (l. 2)

*Oṃ* vaṃ, salutation to the letter *va*, the essence of the eastern face. *Oṃ* yaṃ, salutation to the letter *ya*, the essence of the southern face. *Oṃ* naṃ, salutation to the letter *na*, the essence of the northern face... [lacuna] ...salutation to the essence of the western face. This is the gross five-syllable placement (*sthūla-pañcākṣara-nyāsa*). Having worshipped from the element water to the end of water, and having offered the oblation, [one performs] the subtle five-syllable placement (*sūkṣma-pañcākṣara-nyāsa*).
Then, on the head: *oṃ nādātmane namaḥ*.
On the arms: *va... makārātmane namaḥ*.
Homage to the self of the letter *U*—on the feet;
homage to the self of the letter *A*—on the faces; homage to the self of the *nāda*—on the face of Īśāna... (l5)
Salutation to the one with the face of a man (Puruṣavaktra).
Salutation to the essence of the letter *ma*, the essence of the Aghora face. Salutation to the essence of the letter *u*, the face of Vāmadeva.
...kārātmane sa... (l6).

Thus is the placement of the subtle five syllables (*sūkṣmapañcākṣaranyāsa*). Having performed the placement in this manner, and having worshipped [the deity] from water to water, and having offered the oblation, one should pray.
Now follows the placement of the nine syllables (*navārṇanyāsa*).
...... (l7) *haṃ* | *aṃ namaḥ* at the feet. *oṃ auṃ hiṃ saṃ namaḥ*—at the heart.
Hauṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ — on the two sides. Hauṃ hrīṃ maṃ namaḥ — between the feet. Hauṃ ...... (p208a, broken folio, c1)
Hrīṃ Vaṃ Namaḥ—on the heart;
Hau (Hauṃ) Hrīṃ Raṃ Namaḥ—on the lips;
Hau Hrīṃ Yaṃ Namaḥ—on the nose.

Hauṃ Hrīṃ Uṃ Namaḥ. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) from the water-vessel to the end of the water, having worshipped and offered the oblation (*nivedya*), one should pray. Now follows the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*). The placement (*nyāsa*): *Namaḥ* to Śiva, the Lord; *namaḥ* to the form of Śiva; *namaḥ* to Śiva. (c2.)
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the head. Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the face.
Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora, the heart.
Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva.
Oṃ huṃ (haṃ), obeisance to the Sadyojāta form. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the heart.
Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ hraṃ (or hrūṃ), vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor.
Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the eyes;

oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, and having worshipped [the deity] from water to water, one should offer a prayer. Now, by another method—(c4.)

*Tattvataraṃ nyāsa*... *Kalātattvādhipa*... *Kalādhipatvam asya*... *Vidyātattvāya*... *Vidyātattvādhipa*... *Ru kuru namaḥ*. To *Rāgatattva*... to Kāmadeva, *namaḥ*. ... (gap-filling: *kuru kuru namaḥ*). To the *Prakṛtitattva*, *namaḥ*. To Sūkṣma, the lord of the *Prakṛtitattva*, *namaḥ*.
O Lord of the principle of primordial nature... (l. 2) ...perform, perform! Homage!

Homage to the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). Homage to the Buddha, the lord of the principle of intellect. Homage to him who brings about the realization of his lordship over the principle of intellect; perform, perform! Homage!

Homage to the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*). Aha... (l3) ...homage to the one who has performed [the act]. Homage to Bhānu, the lordship over this principle of ego; perform, perform! Homage to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Homage to Candra, the lord of the principle of mind. The lordship over the principle of mind... (l4) ...a...

Homage to the reality of the ear (*śrotra-tattva*). Homage to the Buddha, the sovereign of the reality of the ear. Homage to you who effect the awakening to his sovereignty over the reality of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); perform, perform [this]! Homage to the skin... (*tvac*) ...to Vāyu; homage to you who effect his sovereignty over the limbs and his state of being the grasper of touch; perform, perform [this]!

Homage to the two eyes! Homage to Agni, the lord of the eyes! [Homage to] the sovereignty over the eyes... perform, perform, homage! Homage to the tongue! Homage to Varuṇa, the lord of the tongue! Perform, perform, homage to his sovereignty over the tongue and his capacity for perceiving taste!

Homage to the nose! Homage to the [nose-]... (l7)! Homage to him who effects the lordship of the nose and the grasping of odors; *kurukuru*! Homage! Homage to speech! Homage to Agni, the lord of speech! Homage to him who effects the lordship of speech and the utterance of speech; *kurukuru*! Homage!

Homage to the hands... (p209a, broken folio, l1). Homage to him who exercises lordship over the feet and who performs the grasping of objects; homage! Homage to the two feet! Homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the feet! Homage to his lordship over the feet; his gati... (l2).

Homage to Pāyana! Homage to Mitra, the protector and sovereign lord! Homage to him who effects the emission of his sovereignty as protector—perform, perform [this]! Homage to Upastha! Homage to Kāma, the protector and sovereign lord of Upastha... (l3) ...perform, perform bliss! Homage!

Homage to Sound! Homage to the subtle Lord of Sound! Homage to you who fulfill his lordship over sound by completing its form—*kuru kuru*! Homage to Touch! Homage to Touch... [l4] ...Homage to you who fulfill his lordship over touch by completing it with wind—*kuru kuru*!

Homage to Form! Homage to the Lord of Form, Bhānumat! May his lordship over form be fulfilled by a flood of brilliance... (l5) Homage to the Lord of Taste, Jalada! Homage to him who brings about the filling of water for his lordship over taste! Homage to Scent! Homage to the Sign of Scent! May the earth fulfill his lordship over scent... (l6)
Ya-namaḥ! Homage to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Space! Why is he the Lord of Space? Because he bestows [space]. Kurukuru namaḥ! Homage to Vāyu! Homage to Īśvara, the Lord of Wind! Va........ (l7)
Haṃ kurukuru namaḥ | To tejase namaḥ | To tejo’dhipāya rudrāya namaḥ | To tejodhipa...pākaṃ kurukuru namaḥ | To aptattvāya namaḥ | To aptattvādhipa... [Jīvanyāsaḥ] || 1 ||
"Salutation! O Sovereign of this [earth], perform the flowing [of its power], perform it, perform it!

Salutation to the Earth! Salutation to Brahmā, the Sovereign of the Earth! Salutation! O Sovereign of the Earth, perform the sustaining [of its power] for this [being], perform it, perform it! Having thus performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the *tattva-tara* (the subtle element of earth), (l2).
Having worshipped [the deity] from the water up to the end of the water, one should pray. Now follows the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa):
"The [power] has arisen in the center of the bulb (kanda) and has taken refuge in the navel of Kuṇḍalinī."
Above the *nāsīra*, it is situated like a lotus within the lotus located at the heart-center. In its center, resting upon the pericarp, are the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire.
In their midst, one should meditate on the deity by the names Ho, Hāṃ, and Heti.
That which is to be presided over by Īśāna, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
is the Suṣumnā, the middle [channel], hidden, and extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā.
The iḍā nāḍī resides in the left nostril, and the piṅgalā in the right.
Gandhārī is in the right eye, and hastijihvā in the left. Pūṣā is in the right ear, and yaśasvinī in the left ear.
Alampūṣā is in the penis, while the Hunāḍi channel is situated in the anus.
The Śaṅkhinī is located in the center of the navel; in the mouth are the vital airs, beginning with prāṇa—namely prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
"O Dhanañjaya, the serpent, the tortoise, and the boar are the *devatattva*. Having meditated thus: "Homage to Suṣumnā! Homage to the life-breath (*prāṇavāyu*) flowing through Suṣumnā!
(l7) "Homage to Iḍā! [in] the left nostril. "Homage to the downward breath (*apānavāyu*) flowing through Iḍā! Homage to Piṅgalā! [Homage to the breath] flowing through Piṅgalā!"
Homage to Samāna-vāyu; in the right nostril. Homage to Gāndharī;
homage to the flow of Gāndhārī—to this [wind], homage to Vāyu. In the right eye: homage to Asitajihvā; homage to the flow of Asitajihvā—to Vyāna-vāyu, homage.
In the left eye—*namaḥ* to Astijihvā. (l2) *Namaḥ* to the flow of Astijihvā, to the Vyāna wind. In the right ear—*namaḥ* to Pūṣā. *Namaḥ* to the flow of Pūṣā, to the Nāga wind.

In the left ear: *namaḥ* to Yaśasvinī; *namaḥ* to the flow (*pravāha*) of Yaśasvinī, and *namaḥ* to the tortoise-wind (*kūrma-vāyu*). In the penis: *namaḥ* to Alampuṣā; *namaḥ* to the flow of Alampuṣā, and *namaḥ* to the kṛkara-wind.
In the anus—to the wind Devadatta, who flows through the *kuhu*-nāḍī, obeisance!
In the center of the navel—to Śaṅkhinī, obeisance! To the wind Dhanañjaya, who flows through Śaṅkhinī, obeisance! To Māyā, obeisance! To Vṛṣāṇa, the lord of Māyā, obeisance!
O Māyīpātva, make this [substance] of one flavor with the poison; *kurukuru*, homage! Homage to Niyati! Homage to the Lord of Niyati, to Ni yāmaka! O Niyati, you too, perform its subjugation;
*kurukuru*, homage! Homage to Kāla! Homage to the Lord of Kāla!

Salutation to Kālakālarudra. Salutation to him who possesses the lordship over Kālarudra, who remains for infinite time; act, act! Salutation! Having thus performed the *nyāsa* on the *jāvanī*, and having worshipped from the ocean up to the end of the waters and offered the oblation, one should pray. (l7. The *nyāsa* of the forms and the lords of the forms:

Then, having extracted and recited the three principles—including the Lord (*seśvara*)—which consist of intellect (*buddhi*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), together with the embodied and the lord of the embodied, one should restrain them. The eight or five [principles] constitute the embodied form;
the embodied form is considered to be fixed. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the Śiva-principle. Obeisance to Soma, the lord of the Śiva-principle. *Oṃ hāṃ*.

Salutation to the Śiva-principle; salutation to the Lord of the Śiva-principle, the possessor of attributes (*dharmī*). Thus, in the portion of Rudra. (l2. Salutation to the Sadāśiva-principle; salutation to the Lord of the Sadāśiva-principle, the Unborn Lord (*ajeśa*). Salutation to the Īśvara-principle; salutation to the Lord of the Īśvara-principle, the Four-faced One (*caturānana*). Salutation to the Śuddhavidyā-principle; [salutation to the Lord of the Śuddhavidyā-principle]... (l3. Śuddhavidyā-...
"Salutation to the auspicious one, the lord of reality"—thus in the portion belonging to Viṣṇu.

Salutation to Māyātattva; salutation to Viṣāṇa, the lord of Māyātattva. Salutation to Kalātattva; salutation to Ketudhvaja, the lord of Kalātattva. Salutation to Kalātattva; (l4) salutation to Śikhivaktra, the lord of Kalātattva. Salutation to Niyatitattva; salutation to Mahādhvaja, the lord of Niyatitattva.

Salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Salutation to the lord of the principle of knowledge, Mekhalīhṛdāda. Salutation to the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*). (L5) Salutation to the lord of the principle of passion, Pallava. Salutation to the principle of the person (*puruṣatattva*). Salutation to the lord of the principle of the person, Viṣṇu. Salutation to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*).
Salutation to the lord of the principle of primordial nature, Pitāmaha. [Salutation to] the principle of intellect (*buddhi*)... (L6)

Homage to the principle of *tattva*. Homage to the wise one (*Budha*), the lord of the principle of intellect (*buddhi*). Homage to the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*). Homage to Ahaṅkṛta, the lord of the principle of egoity. Homage to the principle of mind (*manas*). Homage to Saṅkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind. (l7) Homage to the principle of hearing (*śrotra*). Homage to Vyomādhāra, the lord of the principle of hearing. Homage to the principle of touch (*tvak*). Homage to Sarvāṅga, the lord of the principle of touch.

Homage! Homage to the reality of the eye! Homage to Prakāśana, the lord of the reality of the eye! (p211a, c1) Homage to the reality of speech! Homage to Dundubhi, the lord of the reality of speech! Homage to the reality of the hand! Homage to Sāmadā, the lord of the reality of the hand!
Salutation to the principle of the feet; salutation to the lord of the principle of the feet, Cakramaṇa.

Salutation to the principle of the anus; salutation to the lord of the principle of the anus, Tūrṇabhuja. Salutation to the principle of the generative organ; salutation to the lord of the principle of the generative organ, Ghanānanda.

Homage to the reality of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). Homage to the subtle resonance (*sūkṣmanāda*), the sovereign of the reality of the subtle element of sound. Homage to the reality of touch (*sparśatattva*). Homage to the most powerful one, the sovereign of the reality of touch. (c2. Homage to the reality of the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*). Homage to Gandhakṣaya, the sovereign of the reality of the subtle element of form.

Homage to the reality of the subtle element of taste; homage to the Lord of the reality of the subtle element of taste, the Cloud-Bearer (Jalada). Homage to the reality of the subtle element of smell; homage to the Lord of the reality of the subtle element of smell, the Smell-Sign (Gandhaliṅga). Homage to the reality of space; homage to the Lord of the reality of space, the Subtle One (Sūkṣma).

Salutation to the principle of air; salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the principle of air. Salutation to the principle of fire; salutation to Tviṣāmpati, the lord of the principle of fire. Salutation to the principle of water; salutation to Jaleśa, the lord of the principle of water. (c3.)
Salutation to the Earth-principle (pṛthivītattva). Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the presiding deity of the Earth-principle. Thus, in the Brahma-sector.
In the system of the five principles (*pañcatattva*):
"Salutation to Earth, presided over by the Brahmā Sadyojāta"—thus in the west. "Salutation to the Water-principle, to Viṣṇu, presided over by the Brahmā Vāmadeva"—thus in the north.
"Salutation to the presiding Brahmā of Agni, Rudra, Aghora, and Brahmā"—in the south. "Salutation to the presiding Brahmā of Vāgīśvara, Puruṣa, and Brahmā"—thus in the east.
"Salutation to the presiding Brahmā of Sadāśiva, Īśāna, and Brahmā"—in the northeast.
First, he describes the form of the Earth:

"To the one with four faces and eight arms, who wears yellow garments, who stands upon a tortoise, whose form is gentle, and who is surrounded by mountains, oceans, and rivers; salutation to the form of the Earth."
The Fire-god is mounted upon a ram, possessing blazing flames, holding a spear in his hand;
he is shaped like a sacrificial pit, with an upward-facing mouth, intensely radiant and of brilliant luster.
*Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Fire.*
The sacrificer is proclaimed as one who has black horns, a black turban, and a black girdle, whose limbs are smeared with fresh butter. Oṃ, salutation to the form of the sacrificer.
The Sun, mounted upon a chariot drawn by horses, wearing armor, earrings, and a crown, holding a lotus in his hand, adorned and followed by a charioteer— *Oṃ, salutation to the form of Sūrya*.
Varuṇa, accompanied by his wife Pāśā, possessing the dolphin-bannered [emblem], [is seated] upon a makara.
Four-armed, his very nature being the essential form, adorned with all ornaments; homage to the embodiment of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and possessed of great strength; he always moves with a gait like that of a deer, holding a sword and a noose, with his body slightly bent.
Salutation to the form of Vāyu.
Seated in a celestial chariot as gentle as the moon, holding a mace, a conch, and granting boons,
resembling a jewel of universal form, and accompanied by the bearer of the water-pot— salutation to the form of Soma.
Salutation!

Four-armed and four-faced, holding a trident and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in his hands, and bearing a conch and a *ṭavā* in his right [hands], resembling the sky, the jasmine flower, and the moon—salutation to the one whose form is space (*ākāśamūrti*). Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [one should proceed] from the water up to the end of the waters.
Having worshipped and made the offering, one should pray:
"Now, O Great Goddess, [of her] who shines with beautiful red lotuses..."

"His body embraced by my beloved, whose shimmering ornaments are made of jewels"—having meditated thus, [one performs] the *karanyāsa* (placement on the hands). For the mantra of the *golaka-nyāsa*, Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter is the metre (*chandas*), and Umāmaheśvara is the deity (*devatā*). The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He is] the color of the *bandhūka* flower, three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon, with a smiling face, and great in stature.
With my hands, I worship Him who holds a trident and a skull-cup, who bestows boons and fearlessness, and who wears a beautiful necklace.
O lady with beautiful thighs, having placed her body [upon him], [the mantra] "oṃ namaḥ" is at the heart;
"naṃ namaḥ" is at the mouth.
*Maṃ namaḥ*—to the right shoulder; *śiṃ namaḥ*—to the left shoulder;
*vāṃ namaḥ*—to the right thigh.
Yaṃ namaḥ—on the left thigh;
oṃ namaḥ—at the base of the throat;
naṃ namaḥ—at the navel.
*Maṃ namaḥ*—on the right side;
*Śiṃ namaḥ*—on the left side;
*Vaṃ namaḥ*—in the heart.
*Yaṃ namaḥ*—on the back;
*oṃ namaḥ*—on the crown of the head;
*naṃ namaḥ*—on the face. (c4.)
*Maṃ namaḥ*—to the right eye;
*śiṃ namaḥ*—to the left eye;
*vaṃ namaḥ*—to the right nostril.
*Yaṃ namaḥ*—to the left nostril;
*oṃ namaḥ*—to the base of the right hand;
*naṃ namaḥ*—to the left hand, in the same manner.
*Maṃ namaḥ*—on the right foot, likewise. *Śiṃ namaḥ*—on the left foot, likewise.
*Vaṃ namaḥ*. *Oṃ namaḥ*—on the head. Thus at the tip of the joint.
Naṃ namaḥ—to the face;
maṃ namaḥ—to the heart;
śiṃ namaḥ—to the belly.
Vāṃ namaḥ—to the two thighs;
Yaṃ namaḥ—to the two feet;
Oṃ Haṃ namaḥ—to the heart.
Naṃ namaḥ—on the face.
Maṃ namaḥ—in the axe-mudrā. Śiṃ namaḥ—in the deer-mudrā.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: *vaṃ* namaḥ with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), and *śaṃ* namaḥ with the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*); having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with *oṃ namaśśivāya*; and having likewise performed the placement of the great spheres (*mahāgolakā*);
having worshipped [the deity] from the ocean up to the end of the waters; and having offered the oblation (*nivedya*), one should pray.
(The Vajragolakānyāsa):

Now, for the mantra of the Vajragolakānyāsa, the seer is Vāmadeva; the meter is Paṅkti; the deity is Somāskandeśvara. Having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) by means of the previously mentioned five-syllable *navaka*, one should meditate on the root [mantra] with the words "of the wish-fulfilling tree" (*kalpadrumasya*), and then meditate on the five-syllable *śakti*.
Oṃ namaḥ—at the *mūlādhāra*. Hrīṃ namaḥ—at the navel.
Hauṃ namaḥ—at the heart.
Naṃ namaḥ—to the face; Maṃ namaḥ—to the eyes;
Śiṃ namaḥ—to the middle of the eyebrows.
Vāṃ namaḥ — on the forehead; Yaṃ namaḥ — on the head;
Oṃ namaḥ — on the head.
Hrīṃ namaḥ – on the forehead. Hauṃ namaḥ – on the right eye. Naṃ namaḥ – on the left eye.
*Maṃ namaḥ*—to the right ear; *Śiṃ namaḥ*—to the left ear;
*Vāṃ namaḥ*—to the right nostril.
Yaṃ namaḥ—at the left nostril;
Oṃ namaḥ—at the right cheek;
Hrīṃ namaḥ—at the left cheek.
Oṃ hauṃ namaḥ—on the upper lip. Naṃ namaḥ—on the lower lip. Maṃ namaḥ—on the mouth.
Śiṃ namaḥ—on the tongue; vāṃ namaḥ—on the chin; yaṃ namaḥ—on the neck. (l7.)

Naṃ namaḥ, hrīṃ namaḥ, oṃ hauṃ namaḥ, naṃ namaḥ, maṃ namaḥ, śiṃ namaḥ, vāṃ namaḥ, yaṃ namaḥ—on the three joints of the right hand and on the five fingers. Likewise on the left hand. Likewise on both feet. Oṃ namaḥ—on the throat.
Hrīṃ namaḥ; Hauṃ namaḥ—on the right breast; Naṃ namaḥ—on the left breast;
Maṃ namaḥ—on the heart.
Śiṃ namaḥ — on the right side;
Siṃ namaḥ — on the left side;
Yaṃ namaḥ — on the back.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ mūlaṃ śaktipañcākṣaram | In the space between the arms— (c2)— likewise, the heart is surrounded. Oṃ namaḥ— on the head.
Hrīṃ namaḥ — on the two eyes;
Hauṃ namaḥ — on the face;
Naṃ namaḥ — on the heart.
*Maṃ namaḥ*—in the paraśu-mudrā;
*Śiṃ namaḥ*—in the mṛgīśa-mudrā;
*Bāṃ* (or *Vāṃ*) *namaḥ*—in the abhaya-mudrā.

"Yaṃ namaḥ"—in the *varadamudrā* [gesture]. Pervasive by means of the root of the *śakti*. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *vajragolaka*s, and having worshipped from the water-base (*jalādhi*) up to the end of the water, and having offered the oblation (*nivedya*), one should pray. Alternatively, the placement of the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*): (c4. the placement of the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*). In the *liṅga*, having performed the placement upon the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, from the feet to the top of the images; and in the human body—

From the feet up to the navel: *oṃ haṃ saḥ*—salutation to the Self (*ātman*). Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*). From the navel up to the throat: salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge. From the throat up to the head: salutation to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). Salutation to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva. Thus it is said.

In the *mūlādhāra*: *namaḥ* to the form of Earth (*kṣmāmūrti*); *namaḥ* to Śarva, the lord of the form of Earth. In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*: *oṃ*, *namaḥ* to the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*); *namaḥ* to Paśupati, the lord of the form of Fire. In the *maṇipūra*: *namaḥ* to the form of the Sacrificer (*yajamānamūrti*); *namaḥ* to Ugra, the lord of the form of the Sacrificer.

In the heart: *namas* to the Sun-form (*arkamūrti*); *namas* to Rudra, the lord of the Sun-form. (l2) In the throat: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namas* to the Water-form (*jalamūrti*); *namas* to Bhava, the lord of the Water-form. At the palate: *namas* to the Wind-form (*vāyumūrti*); *namas* to Īśvara, the lord of the Wind-form.
Between the eyebrows: salutation to Niśākaramūrti;
salutation to Mahādeva, the lord of Niśākaramūrti.
On the head: salutation to Vyomamūrti; salutation to Bhīma, the lord of Vyomamūrti.

At the base: salutation to Dharāmūrti; salutation to Brahmāṇī, the sovereign of Dharāmūrti. (L4) At the navel: salutation to Jalamūrti; salutation to Viṣṇu, the sovereign of Jalamūrti. At the heart: salutation to Vahnimūrti; salutation to Rudra, the sovereign of Vahnimūrti.
In the mouth: *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the wind-form (*vāyumūrti*);

obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the wind-form. In the head: *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the ether-form (*vyomamūrti*); obeisance to Sadāśiva, the lord of the ether-form. Having thus performed the placement of the specific forms (*viśeṣamūrti*).

Having worshipped [the deity] from the water to the end of the waters, having offered the oblation, and having made the prayer, then follows the ritual placement of the peaks (*śṛṅganyāsa*), which should be performed during the special worship (*viśeṣapūjā*). One should properly join [the mantras] from the head down to the feet, and at the mouth and the head; [that is,] from the head down to the feet.
Oṃ āṃ aṃ namaḥ | (l7) Oṃ hāṃ āṃ aṃ namaḥ | Oṃ āṃ namaḥ | This is the pervasive [mantra]. On the face: aṃ namaḥ |

At the crown of the head: Oṃ Āṃ Naṃ Namaḥ. In this manner, one should install the sixteen vowels from *aṃ* to *aḥ* immediately following [the previous syllables]. Having thus installed the chain (*śṛṅkhalā*), one should worship from the water-element up to the end of the water-element, present the offering, and make the supplication.
Now, the ritual placement of the constellations (*nakṣatrayāsa*):
on the head—*oṃ kaṃ* [namaḥ] to the constellation Aśvinī;
on the forehead—*oṃ khaṃ* [namaḥ] to the constellation Bharaṇī.
On the right chin: Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Kārtika. On the left chin: Oṃ Ghaṃ, obeisance to Rohiṇī.
On the right cheek: Oṃ Ṅaṃ, obeisance to Mṛgaśiras. (c2.)
On the left cheek: Oṃ Caṃ, obeisance to Ārdrā.
On the tongue: Oṃ Chaṃ, obeisance to Punarvasu. On the throat: Oṃ Jaṃ, obeisance to Puṣya.
In the heart: Oṃ jhaṃ, salutation to Āśleṣā. In the right arm: Oṃ ñaṃ, salutation to Maghā. In the left arm: Oṃ ṭaṃ, salutation to Pūrvaphalgunī.
On the right breast— (c3) Oṃ Ṭhaṃ, obeisance to Uttaraphalgunī. On the left breast— Ḍaṃ, obeisance to Hastā.
On the right wrist—Ḍhaṃ, salutation to Citrā. On the left wrist—Ṇaṃ, salutation to the Svātī nakṣatra.
At the navel—Taṃ, salutation to Viśākhā.
In the stomach—*thaṃ*, homage to Anurādhā.
In the right thigh—*daṃ*, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. In the left thigh—(c4).
Dhaṃ, salutation to Mūla;
on the right knee—naṃ, salutation to Pūrvāṣāḍhā;
on the left knee—paṃ, salutation to Uttarāṣāḍhā.
On the right calf: *phaṃ*, salutation to Śravaṇa.
On the left calf: *oṃ baṃ*, salutation to Śraviṣṭhā. On the right foot: *oṃ bhaṃ*, salutation to Śatabhiṣaj.
In the left foot: *oṃ maṃ pūrvaproṣṭhapadāya namaḥ*. At the outer edge of the right hand: *oṃ yaṃ uttaraproṣṭhapadāya namaḥ*.
On the outer edge of the left hand: *oṃ yaṃ uttaraproṣṭhapadāya namaḥ*. [Repeated?
On the outer edge of the left hand: *oṃ raṃ revatyai namaḥ*. Pervasive. *Oṃ*, in another manner (*prakārāntareṇa*):
*oṃ mūrdhni... rohiṇyai brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
On the forehead: Oṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Umā, the presiding deity of Mṛgaśiras. On the right chin: Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the presiding deity of Ārdrā.
On the left chin: Oṃ ghaṃ, [obeisance to Aditi], the presiding deity of Punarvasu.

Salutation to Aditi. On the right cheek: *Oṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to Puṣya-Bṛhaspati*. On the left cheek: *Oṃ caṃ, salutation to Āśleṣā-Sarpa*. From Maghā to Kṛttikā, [salutation] to Śiva as distinguished by each respective lunar mansion deity (*nakṣatra-devatā*). (L4)

Having thus performed the Nakṣatra-nyāsa and worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), having presented the food offering (naivedya) and made the prayer, and having likewise performed the thirty great nyāsas beginning with the Tri-tattva-nyāsa and ending with the Nakṣatra-nyāsa, and having worshipped with the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) and three handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali) as the bestower of life, one should offer incense and lamps with the root mantra, along with warm milk measuring one āḍhaka.

Having offered the powdered fragments of white sugar combined with substances such as cardamom (*elā*), and having presented everything from the betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) up until the end of the night, one should pray for one's desired object. This is the "Eightfold Binding" (*aṣṭabandhana*).
The ritual procedure for the ritual deposits (*nyāsa*).

Then the preceptor, having risen at dawn together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipāḥ*), and having completed the daily rites beginning with bathing and ending with the *aupāsana* fire-ritual, enters the temple. Having worshipped [the deities] from Sūrya up to the Guru, he approaches the sacrificial jar (*yāgakumbha*). Having worshipped the seat (*āsana*) from Śakti up to Śaktiparyanta, he performs the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Having performed the great *pūrṇāhuti* offering, and having worshipped according to the procedure for the daily rites with offerings beginning with the *nādi*, one approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having performed the worship from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the lamps according to the previously mentioned path of oblation,
[one offers] the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and so forth, as well as nutmeg (*jātīphala*), there with the sixty substances.

Having taken [the portions] separately from the image-worshippers (mūrtipas), having offered the full oblation as if it were a daily rite, and having presented the fruit of the fire-sacrifice (homaphala), one should complete the worship— including the great oblation (mahāhavis),

ornaments, offerings of incense, lamps, and the great lamp, as well as the propitiation and the ritual dance— and then, returning to the site of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍasthāna), perform the expiation (prāyaścitta). This should be done according to the *Jāti*, the *Abhyātāna*, the *Rāṣṭrabhṛt*, and the *Cakra* rites.

Having performed the *āmātyahoma* with the recitation of the *acchidra*, and having offered the *mahāprāyaścitta* beginning with "manas" and so forth, [he offers] eight oblations with "bhavāya devāya svāhā," eight with "bhavasya devasya patnī," and [eight] with "bhavasya devasya sutāya."

Having offered eight oblations with "svāhā," and having offered twenty-five oblations separately with the Weapon-mantra, then having offered one hundred oblations each with the Armor-mantra, the Bahurūpa-mantra, the Pāpabhakṣaṇa-mantra, the Navātman-mantra, the Varman-mantra, and the Sword-mantra, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Now, the Great Pūrṇāhuti (Full Oblation) is as follows: Then the Ācārya, having brought cow-derived clarified butter together with the Mūrtipas and the Brāhmaṇas,

standing to the west of the principal fire-pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*) accompanied by the sound of all Vedic recitations and the playing of all musical instruments, fills the *sruva* ladle with ghee, places a flower upon its tip,
and [offers it] along with his topknot.

Having placed [the oblation] soaked in ghee, sweet as milk, upon the tip of the *sruc* ladle— made of coconut or fine silk cloth— and having taken it with the left and right hands joined like a conch shell,

with his body erect and his feet [properly placed], bringing the base of the *sruc* to the region of the left breast, with his waist-girdle [secured] and his gaze fixed on the tip of the *sruc*, [he offers] the temple of the sixteen digits, measuring the size of a barley grain...

Uttering [the mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and again uttering [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, he offers the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the "Head" mantra, with the mantra "To the Vasus and the Rudras," and with the mantra "Seven are your [tongues], O Agni. This is the full oblation consisting of the Ṛg,
Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

Having offered oblations into the center of the fire with mantras, having sat down and performed the subsequent sprinkling (uttarapariṣecana) with the mantra "O Aditi, you are the one who grants permission," and so forth;
having taken a fuel-stick (samidh) and approached the fire with the mantra beginning "That which is your fire...

(*yatte agne...*), and having applied the ashes from that burnt offering to his forehead with the *kavaca* mantra; he should worship the deity residing in the fire with the services ending with incense, lamps, and the night-offering (*āratrika*).

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) on an auspicious lunar day: for the restoration and eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of this Lord of Gods, Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his consort Ambā Śrī Kāntimatī, accompanied by the Śrī Mūlaliṅga, and along with his entire retinue.

Having made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I offer to the Lord, the Blessed One, the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, the fruit of the recitation of mantras such as the *Mahāvrata*, *Śivarakṣitā*, and others ending with the Vedic [mantras], as well as the *Prāsāda* and other mantras; the fruit of the *Vedapārāyaṇa*; and the fruit of the oblation (*havanas*)—all of which belong to the Brahmins who perform these rites and to the image-keepers (*mūrtipās*), after having accepted them by means of a stream of water. Then, touching water.

Having summoned the Brāhmaṇas before the sacrificial pitcher (yāgakumbha) and worshipped them with the thought that they are Śiva, the word of the Brāhmaṇas is as follows: "By me, acting under your command, the recitation of the mantras for the temple and so forth has been performed along with its ancillaries, flawlessly and perfectly, [accompanied by] the eight-fold binding."

[The author] states the removal of defects arising from [the performance of] ritual actions: "May this specific recitation of mantras for the temple and so forth, performed the stated number of times, be offered to the venerable Śiva. By this, may the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara be pleased. (l.

4) Having thus taken water with flowers from the Brāhmaṇas and having received the water that was offered, [he places it] in the right hand of Yāgeśa: "You are the protector of the most secret of secrets..."

"O Lord, may there be success through your grace; may this auspicious [rite] be accomplished. Having offered it with the root mantra while the recitation has been performed with these [verses], he says again: "You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept the oblation offered by us.
May there be success."

"O Lord, by your grace, [I have realized] that the world consists of you. Having thus offered the fruit of the *homa*, he said: "Whatever good or evil deeds I have performed, O Lord, may you, who reside in the state of Śiva, consume them; utterly destroy them for me. Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer... this entire world is Śiva. Śiva is victorious everywhere. He who is Śiva, I am indeed he—whether it be good or bad."

"Whatever action has been performed by me, O Lord of Gods, accept this supreme worship. Having thus offered [the oblation] and having prayed, one should offer the *ārātrika* with the root mantra. This is the stated procedure for the offering of the fruit of the recitation (*japa*).
Then, the image-bearer [should perform] the installation of the nine fires.

(l. 2) Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire in the eastern pit, along with the Mūrtidhāraka, the Mūrti, and the Mūrtīśa, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings... having said "paramā" [and] "ita...", and having requested a blessing, [he should take] from the eastern pit the principal... (l. 3)

Having consecrated a blade of *darbha* grass up to the edge of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having filled his joined palms with flowers while reciting the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, he should extract the embodied deity residing in the *āhavanīya* fire—the form and the Lord of Form, *tatpuruṣa*—by means of the *aṅkuśa* (goad) mudrā. Then, saying "I unite him with the primary pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*) by means of its root mantra," he unites him. In the same way [he does so] in the south; in the same way in the north; in the same way [in the other directions].

In the west; likewise in the southeast; likewise in the northeast; (l5) likewise in the southwest; likewise in the northwest. Having offered [the oblation] into the principal fire-pit with its respective mantra, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ), having sacrificed into their respective fire-pits with the *bhūr* and other [vyāhṛtis], take up the Āhavanīya fire from the east and so forth. (l6)

Having placed the fuel upon the fire with the mantra *yoniḥ*, and having caused it to enter the principal *kuṇḍa* with the mantra *yā te agne*, the preceptor then honors the remaining fire— withdrawn from each respective *kuṇḍa* and situated within the principal fire—
as Sadāśiva in the form of Īśāna together with his retinue, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having offered incense and lamps, he presents the food offering (*naivedya*).

Having offered the *ārātrika* lamp, having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), and having made the request for cessation, one should pray: "May the ritual that has been performed be fruitful and complete. Then, filling the hollowed palms with flowers, one should visualize Sadāśiva together with his retinue within the principal fire by means of the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), and [having drawn him forth], one should contemplate him as being contained within those palms.

Having visualized [the deity] as consisting of light, and having joined [it] to the pitcher with the root mantra and the sixteen-fold grace, thinking "I join," and having worshipped the pitcher and the pillar up to the end with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) at the root, and having presented the *ārātrika* lamp, one should return again to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and [worship] with the *bhūr* and other *vyāhṛtis*, and with the Aghora-weapon mantra (*aghorāstra*).
Having offered oblations twenty-five times and having again performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),

he sits down and sprinkles the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *sruva* ladle. Having taken a small portion from the surrounding grass mat (*paristaraṇa*), and having placed the top, middle, and bottom parts [of the sticks] into the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*),
and having separately laid down a single blade of grass, he places the grass-bundle (*prastara*) into the fire.

Having struck [the fire] with the *varman* mantra; having struck the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with the *varman*; having struck the other two enclosing-sticks joined upwards with the *netra* mantra; having offered the residue of the clarified butter (*saṃsrāva*) with the mantra "To the Vasus, to the Rudras"; [reciting] "Obeisance to Rudra Paśupati, svāhā! This is not mine"; and having performed the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) by offering twenty-five oblations with the *aghorāstra* mantra; [he offers] with the *śiras* mantra.

Having offered the *pūrṇā* oblation, one should offer the internal and external *bali*. Just as above the altar (*kuṇḍa*), on the upper girdle (*mekhalā*): in the east, in the center, and to its east, [one offers] to Sadāśiva, svāhā; to Īśvara, svāhā;
to the south, to Rudra, svāhā; to the north, to Viṣṇu, svāhā.

Svāhā! To Brahmā in the west, svāhā! Having offered the *bali* ending in *svāhā* to the *kalās* beginning with Śāntitattva-kalā and ending with Nivṛtti-kalā—[located] in the middle girdle of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) to the east, in the center, and to the east of that—[one says]: (l2) To the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu in the lower girdle, svāhā! Then: To Ananta, svāhā! To Rudra, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā!

Having offered the bali-oblation out of sequence with "Svāhā to Brahmā," he should dismiss it. Then, having prepared two mandalas in the area to his own right, [he offers] in the first mandala: "Svāhā to the Rudras" in the directions from the east to the north, and "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Mothers."
Oṃ hāṃ to the Gaṇas, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Yakṣas, svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ in the corners beginning with the northeast—Oṃ hāṃ to the Gṛhas, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Asuras, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Rākṣasas, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Nāgas, svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, in the center of the maṇḍala—in the northeast, southeast, and southwest—oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the constellations! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the rākṣasas! (l6) Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas!
Oṃ hāṃ, in the middle of Vāyu and Varuṇa— Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Kṣetrapāla. Having worshipped thus with the ending of *namaḥ*, and having offered the bali and arghya with the ending of *svāhā*,
[one proceeds] to the second maṇḍala— (l7).

Having worshipped those beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna in the eight directions from the east to the northeast with the word "namas" at the end [of their names], and having offered the bali and arghya with the word "svāhā" at the end, one should worship with the word "namas" at the end as follows: in the portion of Īśāna, "To Brahmā, svāhā"; in the southwest, on the left side, "To Viṣṇu, svāhā"; and in the center, "To Nīlalohita, svāhā. Having thus worshipped and offered the bali and arghya, [one proceeds].
One should dismiss all [the deities] even in reverse order.

Having offered the bali-oblation with the Rudra-mantra for those Rudras who have no other place [to go], one should place the bali-mantras within one's own heart, wash one's feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), apply the sacred ashes (bhasman), perform the ritual of becoming complete (sakalīkaraṇa), and offer the oblation with the mantra: "juṣasva samidham agne" (Be pleased with this fuel-stick, O Agni).

O Aditi, you have followed after us. O God Savitṛ, impel [us] with your impulses. [Perform] the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* waters. Having poured out the *praṇītā* waters toward the various directions, and having poured the remainder upon the ground, having purified oneself with them: "May you be in my assembly; may everything be mine. You are full; may you be full for me. You are undecaying; do not decay for me. May the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves in the eastern direction."
May the months and the ancestors purify [us] in the southern quarter;
may the planets and the cattle purify [us] in the western quarter; may the waters, the herbs, and the trees purify [us] in the northern quarter;
may the sacrifice and the year purify [us] in the upward quarter.
"O Prajāpati, may they purify themselves. "I send you to the ocean; go back to your own source. May I be unbroken in my progeny; let not your water abandon me.

With these [verses], having placed [the water] upon the head of the jar and upon the head of the teacher (*ācārya*), and having given a cow as a choice gift (*vara*) to the Brahmin, saying, "I give [this]," and having placed fuel on the fire, he should worship the fire with the verse, "That which is yours, O Agni... and [worship] the fire.

Having paid homage to the fire preceded by hearing and touching, having made a request, having worshipped it with incense, lamps, and so forth, and having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra one hundred times, one should extract the retinue of the fire with the goad mudrā, visualize it as being held within the hollowed palms of the hands, and [recite] Oṃ.

With the seed-syllable *hrauṃ*, which is the seed of fire, and with *bahurūpa*, I unite Śiva’s fire along with its retinue in the jar. Having thus united it in the principal jar, and having offered the *arghya* for the "turning away" (*parāṅmukha*) with *bahurūpa*, one should then worship the Lord of the Weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāgeśa*) and the *astravardhanī*. Having extracted [the fire], one should unite it in the principal jar with its root-mantra (*tanmūla*). [Then worship] from the gatekeepers up to the Guru.

Having merged [the deities] into the principal pitcher with their respective mantras— or rather, having united all the deities situated in the pavilion, from the preceptor down to the door-keeper, into the principal pitcher—
and having offered the *arghya* water with the face turned away; (l5)

Having worshipped with the eightfold offering of flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), having presented three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) by means of the three principles (*tattvatraya*), and having offered prayers, one should observe an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*). Having correctly ascertained the auspicious time for the sacrificial jar-consecration (*yāgakumbhābhiṣeka*) together with the astrologers, and having determined it to be an auspicious moment, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). With the *pavitra* in hand, seated facing north, and having performed the ritualization of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*).

Having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking his head [in salutation], and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [he makes] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the restoration of the ancient [shrine] of Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara— this God of gods, together with the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, accompanied by the venerable Mūlaliṅga, and along with his retinue..."

In this *bandhanātmaka-śivayāga*, for the sake of protecting devotees such as ourselves and for the attainment of all desired objects, and for the purpose of entering the primary abode from the sacrificial pavilion and for the presence of the *liṅga*, I shall perform the raising of the *yāgeśa-kumbha* from the station of Brahmā. Whatever defect has arisen at the time of raising due to the lunar day, weekday, asterism, ascendant, planetary conjunction, or division (*karaṇa*), [may it be rectified].

For the purpose of averting those defects, the raising of the jar of the Lord of Sacrifice; for the sake of securing an auspicious moment for the consecration of the image; for the increase of Brahmanic luster among our own devotees and others, the gifts for processions; and for our own devotees and others, the gifts for the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*)—beginning from this point...

Especially for the sake of the increase of my lineage as long as the moon and sun endure; for the sake of achieving an auspicious moment through the gifting of ornaments and a daughter, the ritual bathing of the water-jar (kumbhābhiṣeka), the ten gifts, and the five gifts; for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects, abundant gifts, and for the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons, I shall perform the gift of fruits and the gift of betel-leaf. [I shall offer] the golden seed situated within the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha).

O Vibhāvasu, grant me peace! O you who bestow infinite crops and fruit, grant me peace! This gold, together with betel, [is offered] for the rite of the eight-fold binding of the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara; desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry of the primary liṅga from the sacrificial pavilion, the illustrious... [offers].

"O Lord of the Bamboo Grove, desiring to please you, I bestow this upon you. Thus is the auspicious gift of the vehicle. Next is the gift of the cow. Now, for the ten gifts, having brought a cow with her calf for the gift of the cow:
at the right hind leg—[for] the Ṛgveda.
Salutation!
On the left foot—salutation to the Yajurveda.
Behind, on the right foot—salutation to the Sāmaveda.
On the left foot—salutation to the Atharvaṇa Veda. On the tail—salutation to Bhairava.
On the right calf—(l2)
Salutation to Brahmā.
On the left shank—salutation to Viṣṇu.
On the throat—salutation to Godāvarī.
In the right ear—salutation to Varuṇa.
In the left ear—salutation to Kubera.
In the right nostril—salutation to Vāyu. (3)
In the left nostril: salutation to Udāna.
In the right eye: salutation to Sūrya.
In the left eye: salutation to Candra.
On the forehead: salutation to Pārvatī.
On the head: salutation to Mahādeva. On the other limbs: [as before].
Salutations to the fourteen worlds.

Having thus worshipped Kāmadhenu with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; having fully honored her with incense, lamps, food offerings, and the like; and having meditated upon and worshipped the Brāhmaṇa as the very form of Śiva, one should take betel-leaf along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). [The mantra: "In the limbs of cows reside the fourteen worlds; therefore, by the gift of this [cow], may [the worlds] be attained."

"Grant me peace. Thus, desiring the successful attainment of the auspiciousness of the moment for the entry into the Mūla-liṅga, and seeking the pleasure of the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, I bestow upon you this cow, together with her calf, adorned, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and provided with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

The Gift of Land (*bhūdāna*): Having invited a Brāhmaṇa and seated him upon a seat, one should worship him with the words, "Obeisance to the Brāhmaṇa who is the very embodiment of Veṇuvaneśvara. Then, having accepted the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and betel, one should say: "The earth, rich with all crops, was uplifted by the Boar; it is infinite and bestows the fruit of grain. Therefore, grant me peace! This land, together with its sacrificial fee, [is given] for as long as my family shall eat. *Śrī*... [text continues].

In the rite of the eight-fold bond (*aṣṭabandhakarma*) for Veṇuvaneśvara, desiring the attainment of the auspicious moment for entry into one’s own abode, I bestow this upon you. The gift of sesame seeds: two *droṇas*. Taking the sesame seeds together with gold—sesame seeds are eternally the destroyers of sin for Viṣṇu’s body.

O Keśava, born from the Sahya mountain, destroy my sins through this gift of sesame! Desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry into my own abode during the hour of non-returning karma for the Lord of Veṇuvana, I bestow upon you this sesame, together with a monetary gift and betel.

The gift of gold: Having taken three *niṣkas* of gold together with the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [one should say]: "O Hiraṇyagarbha, you who reside within the womb, the golden seed of the Sun; since you bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace. This gold, along with the ritual fee, [is offered] at the sacrifice to Śiva in the presence of Veṇuvaneśvara."
Desiring the attainment of success through this most auspicious moment of entry into the primary *liṅga*, I offer it unto you.

Clarified Butter (*ājya*)—(The offering of clarified butter): Taking four *prasthas* of it, [I say: "Born from the Wish-fulfilling Cow (*kāmadhenu*), residing in all creators, and considered the food of the gods—O Clarified Butter, grant me peace. This clarified butter, together with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and betel, is for the rite of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*).
Desiring success for the auspicious moment of the entry of the root-linga into the sacrificial sanctuary, Veṇuvaneśvara, desiring your favor, has bestowed this upon you.
The gift of cloth: the mark of modesty, a protection against cold, wind, and heat.

"O cloth that is the ornament of the body, grant me peace! Desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry into my own abode— like a rite of re-entry accompanied by a sacrificial fee— I, the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, desiring your affection, give this pair of fine garments to you along with the dakṣiṇā."
Grain (*dhānya*)—[the gift of grain]: "O you who act for the welfare of others, you make the donor prosperous in this world and the next. Grain is the life-sustenance of living beings;

therefore, grant me peace. This [gift], accompanied by its purpose and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), is for the Supreme Lord’s rite of returning [to the world], at the auspicious moment of entering the primary site.
Desiring success at an auspicious moment, I bestow this upon you.
The gift of sugar-cane: "Sugar produced from the stalk of sugarcane is like nectar; therefore, by the giving of this, grant me peace. This...

(l6) Desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the insertion of the root-linga into the eight-fold binding frame of Veṇuvaneśvara, accompanied by a sacrificial fee and sixty *ṣaṣṭiphala* measures of sugar, I [offer this] to you. (l7)
He bestowed [the gift].

Regarding the gift of silver: "Silver, born from the eye of Rudra, is dear to the ancestors; therefore, by the giving of this, grant me peace. This silver, together with the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), belongs to the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara.
Desiring success, I bestow upon you this auspicious moment for the entry into the primary *liṅga* during the Śiva-sacrifice;
[this is] the gift of salt—a provider of prosperity, the foremost and most excellent of tastes, which increases strength. (L2)
Therefore, grant me peace by giving her to me.

Desiring the successful attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry into the sacred abode during the Śiva-sacrifice of the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, I bestow upon you this salt together with a sacrificial fee.
Now, the fivefold gift:
O Goddess, you who are Sadāśiva, through whom Bhūti, Bhūmāna, Sukvāma, and Deva attained prosperity by means of your majesty; O sinless one, bound by this protection, protect me always.

Desiring the success of this auspicious moment—the entry into the inner apartments for the rite of the eightfold bond—I bestow upon you this manifestation of the Lord of the Bamboo Grove (*veṇuvaneśvara*).
[The gift of the *rudrākṣa*: It has Rudra as its deity, it is pleasing to Rudra, and it is auspicious.

Therefore, by the gift of this [rosary], grant me peace as you intend. This rosary, numbering one hundred Rudrākṣas, together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), I bestow upon you for the purpose of binding the eight [directions] of Veṇuvaneśvara, desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry into the house and its dwelling.
The Lamp-Pillar (the gift of a lamp-pillar):
"May you accept this [lamp-pillar] joined with fire by me, combined with clarified butter and *trivṛt*. (l7)
The island of Mattala, which dispels the darkness of the three worlds?

Therefore, grant me peace through the offering of this [lamp]. Desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*) during the *sudhāmapraveśa* muhūrta for the rite of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhanakarma*) of the Lord of Śrī Veṇuvana, I give this lamp-pillar, distinguished by thirty *palas* and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), unto you.
The Water Vessel (*jalapātra*)—Water is the life of living beings; they are established in the water that sustains life. Therefore, by the gift of this, may you grant me peace.

Desiring the perfection of the auspicious moment for the entry of the plaster (sudhā) during the rite of the eight-fold binding of the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, and desiring the pleasure of the illustrious Veṇuvaneśa, I give this water-vessel together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to you.
The gift of the Śiva-liṅga:
O destroyer of the Asura Andhaka, who dwells upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa;
therefore, by this gift, grant me peace as you deem fit.

Desiring the attainment of an auspicious moment for the entry of the sacred paste (*sudhā*) during the rite of the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of this *śivaliṅga* of Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), I bestow it upon you. —
The Initiation (*upanayana*).
The excellent initiation rite (*aupanayana*) is for the purpose of increasing Brahmanic splendor;
it is desired by all, bestows success, is pure, and increases the king and his kingdom.
It grants the fulfillment of desires to everyone, including the temple residents and their priests.
It is most excellent, beneficial to cows and Brahmins, auspicious, and the source of the Brāhmaṇa birth.
O Fire, grant me internal peace— that golden seed residing within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, which bestows the fruit of infinite merit.

This gold, fashioned in the measure of the initiation ceremony, I bestow upon you, desiring the attainment of the auspicious moment for entering the Sudhāma [temple] during the rite of the eight-fold binding of the Lord of Veṇuvana.
The gift of a maiden (kaṇṇi-dāna):
This gift is the most excellent merit, bestowing the increase of sons and grandsons;
it is the cause for progeny among those remaining in villages and cities,
bringing all happiness to men and granting the four aims of human existence.
The gift of a daughter in marriage is unsurpassed, bringing delight to both the ancestors and the gods.

Having uttered [the words], "A maiden endowed with gold," for the purpose of giving this maiden, adorned with ornaments, for the work of restoring the ruins and performing the eightfold binding of Veṇuśrī Vaneśvara,
he desires the increase of his lineage and so forth, lasting as long as the moon and sun, for all his devotees beginning with himself.
Desiring to achieve the perfection of this auspicious moment for the entry of the nectar of Veṇuvaneśvara, I bestow [this] upon you.
Furthermore, I shall provide my devotees with abundant ashes, sacred threads, and rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
(l5) Then follows the distribution of many gifts.

...bestow upon me that which dwells within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha. For the purpose of this extensive gift, [I give] much gold to all the Brāhmaṇas of various lineages (gotra), for the sake of removing every fault incurred through the mantra-rites— from the collection of materials for the eight-fold binding ceremony of the Lord of Veṇuvana up to the sacrificial jar-consecration— until the attainment of absolute perfection (kaivalya).
To those beginning with children and ending with the elderly, together with their mothers...

(l7) I have bestowed this desired food, accompanied by hospitality and endowed with the six flavors, upon those who partake of it. Then follows the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). The sacrificer (*yajamāna*), having come to the sacrificial seat (*yajñasadana*), with the *pavitra* grass in hand and having sipped water for purification (*ācamya*), [performs] the striking of the head (*śiraḥkuṭṭana*). (p222b, f215a l1)

Having first made the request... and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [he makes] the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the restoration of the ruins and the eight-fold binding of the Lord of Veṇuvana—together with his retinue, accompanied by the Mother Kāntimatī, and joined with the venerable *mūla-liṅga*—beginning with the permission..."

For the purpose of receiving the collective fruit of the sacrifices, pot-consecrations (*kumbhābhiṣeka*), worship, and the three fortnights of sacrifice performed by the *mūrtipā*s and other brahmins specializing in recitation, as well as the recitations, oblations, worship, and consecrations performed by the preceptor (*ācārya*)—
all as prescribed in the *Kāmikāgama* for the present restoration and eightfold binding of Śiva— [this grant is made].

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of obtaining the complete fruit of the sacrifice free from deficiency, and for the pleasure of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, I shall bestow sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others," and having touched water, he should worship the preceptor with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as garments, ornaments, earrings, and the like, perceiving him as Śiva.
A bed, a vehicle, a female slave, various kinds of jewels, a land of abundant food,
and likewise a cow with its calf.
One should give these, as well as betel and other items, as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru;

and thirty *niṣkas* or more as a fee to the Ācārya. Because this has been stated, one who desires the attainment of the complete fruit of the Śiva-sacrifice already performed—this special gold for the bed and so forth—[should act] for the auspicious moment of the Kumbha-abhiṣeka which is about to be performed.

Desiring success within a short moment, desiring the accomplishment through the grace of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, I bestow this upon you. Thus one should give it to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). For both the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the practitioner, there is one share out of eleven shares into which [the object] has been divided.

The Vāstuhoma for the image-protectors: a single portion of these [offerings] is for the Mahāśānti priest; sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Sadasyas and other learned persons for their joy. Likewise, the sacrificial fee for the ritual of the Teacher (ācārya) is as follows.

(Ācāryapūjā) — Now, having adorned the holder of the sacrificial jar, there is the worship of the Ācārya. Then the Ācārya, by means of the specific samaya-initiations and the nirvāṇa-initiation, thus well-performed, is consecrated with the five jars.
Having summoned the adorned Ācārya, who has performed his daily rites such as bathing and so forth, and is standing outside the western door of the sacrificial hall facing east,

one should wipe him three times from the navel down to the feet with seven *darbha* blades while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Again, one should wipe him three times from the throat up to the navel while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Again, with seven *darbha* blades, having wiped three times from the head— the *brahmarandhra*—

down to the throat with the *astra-mantra*, one should discard all the *darbha* blades. Having sprinkled three times from the feet up to the head with the *astra-mantra*, [one should recite] the *ab-liga* verses,
the *vāruṇa* verses, and the *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*.

Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the *pavamāna* mantras, the teacher— having given and [the disciple] having put on for him an upper garment (*upavīta*), a head-cloth, a pair of earrings, a golden sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), a pair of bracelets, and rings— and having again sprinkled him with the *astra* mantra and applied sacred ash (*bhasman*)— should cause him to enter within by the western door, leading him first by the right foot, [stroking him] from his feet up to the top of his head.

Having gazed with divine vision and having wrapped his head with a silk garment consecrated by the recitation of the *varma* mantra, and having sprinkled it with the *astra* mantra, [he should offer obeisance] therein: "Obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya;
obeisance to Aiśvarya; obeisance to Padma; obeisance to Vṛṣāsana."
The bull, possessing the form of a bull, the three-eyed one who took the daughter of Kṛttikā as his consort,
the support of all beings, with sharp horns and great strength.

Salutation to the Bull-form. Having worshipped with the Vṛṣagāyatrī, having invoked the Bull, and having performed the rites from the installation up to the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should say: "Salutation to the seat of the Praṇava" above that [image], and place the Praṇava with the finger. Thus ends the worship of the adorned Preceptor’s Bull-seat.

Now, the raising of the *dhāmaṇṭa* (or *mamaṇṭa*) jar: the preceptor, having filled his joined palms with flowers, worships above the jar, saying: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātmatattva; obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Vidyātattva. Having thus worshipped, [he offers] solid and soft foods.

Having offered the root-mantra (mūla-mantra) together with items to be licked, sucked, and drunk, or else ornaments, sacrificial oblations (havis), or fruits and the like; having given three handfuls of water;
having presented the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) ending with the words "namas," "svadhā," and "svāhā";

having worshipped with the sixteen types of service beginning with incense and lamps and ending with pure dance; having prayed for one's desired object; and having observed an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta).

Reciting the mantra of the temple of sixteen kalās, with his mind absorbed in Śiva, he carefully lifts the water-pot with both hands, places it upon the seat of the *praṇava* atop the head of the adorned preceptor, and himself holding the *vardhanī* vessel in his right hand and the [other] in his left,
[he sprinkles] from west to east, or from east to west.
Then, having carefully lifted the eight jars according to the sequence previously established, one should hold them in order upon the *mūrtipa*s of Śarva and the other deities,

preceded by the recitation of their respective names, their respective *mūrtipa* mantras, the root mantra, and the *aghora-astra* mantra; while touching the jar with one's own right hand using a brush (*kūrca*) made of a hundred blades of *darbha* grass.
Preceded by the recitation of the Aghora-weapon mantra distinguished by the root mantra,
there is the sound of auspiciousness from conchs, bells, two kettledrums, *chinnakāhala* horns, *naphaṭaha* drums, *jaghaṇṭa* drums, great bells, small bells,
and the eighteen musical instruments beginning with the *vāmā*, accompanied by dancing, singing, praise, and the like.

Meditating upon Śiva along with [his attendants], having circumambulated the altar, and having gone outside through the eastern gate with the right foot leading, slowly placing one step after another together with all the devotees,

preceded by a rain of flowers mixed with many substances— namely parched grain (*lāja*), betel, plantains, golden flowers, *kūrca* grass, fruits, and the auspicious ornaments of Gaurī— he [performed the rite].

Preceded by mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, various rows of lamps, camphor wicks, and agallochum wicks, and accompanied by a stream of water poured from the hands of Brahmins, he slowly circumambulated the abode of Śiva; then,
entering first through the right and left [doors] into the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), [he proceeded].
"One should place it nearby, in close proximity"—thus concludes the raising of the sacrificial jar.

Now, the placement of the jar in the vicinity of the root-linga: Then the preceptor, having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before Śiva with rice and other materials while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra; having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers while reciting the Kavaca mantra; and having sprinkled it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) while reciting the Astra mantra;
[he should proceed] attentively from the seat of the Bull.

Having removed the clay from the jar and established it facing the deity in the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel—having two [nozzles]—to its west. Then, beginning from the eastern side or the western side, having first consulted extensively with the wise, one should install the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the others, such as Ananta and the rest, with careful attention and a concentrated mind, [reciting]: "Homage to Ananta! Homage to Dharma!"

Salutation to Knowledge; salutation to Dispassion; (l5) salutation to Sovereignty; salutation to the Lotus; salutation to the Seat of Śiva; salutation to the Form of Śiva; salutation to Śiva. Having worshipped thus, and having offered three handfuls of flowers into the jar with the three principles (*tattva*), [one offers] to the Vardhanī: "Salutation to the seat of Manonmanī. (l6)

Salutation to the form of Manonmanī. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to Manonmanī. Having thus worshipped, [worship] from the east onwards: salutation to Ananteśa; salutation to Sūkṣmeśa; salutation to Śivottama; salutation to Ekanetra; salutation to Ekarudra;

salutation to Trimūrti; salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha; salutation to Śikhaṇḍin. Having worshipped in this manner and offered musical instruments and the like, [offer] fruits and other items with the root mantra.

Having offered [the oblation] and presented the *ārātrika* with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should pray for one's desired goal. Thus concludes the section on the installation of the jar in the presence of the *liṅga*, titled "Worship for the Presence of the *Liṅga*" (*liṅgasānnidhyapūjā*).

Now, the worship for the presence of the *liṅga*: Then the most excellent Guru, with a serene mind, having sat upon a seat near the great *liṅga* with a gentle countenance, having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, having set out the general *arghya* offering, and having worshipped Vighneśvara; having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking his head [three times], and having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, he makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) on this auspicious lunar day.

"Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): 'I shall perform the worship for the presence of the Liṅga (*liṅgasānnidhyapūjā*) in the Śiva-sacrifice of restoration and the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) of the God of Gods, Sadāśiva, known as Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his retinue, accompanied by the venerable Mother Kāntimatī, and joined with the venerable Mūla-liṅga'; having touched water and performed the *puṇyāha* rite according to the rules, [he should perform the worship] with that [mantra] and with the mantra beginning with 'O Lord of the Dwelling' (*vāstoṣpate*)."

Having sprinkled [the deity] with water, one should worship, as before, the seat— beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti— on the lower part of the pedestal beneath the *liṅga*. Having projected the form (*mūrti*), having projected the thirty-eight *kalās*, having brought about the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), and having bestowed the eyes, one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra using the previously prepared water for the feet (*pādya*).

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the [mantra] beginning with *dibhiḥ* and ending with *namaḥ svadhā svāhā*, and having presented fruits and other offerings with the root mantra (*mūla*), and having made [the deity] well-disposed through his grace,
one who has received permission from the Lord for the purpose of the sacrificial jar-consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should perform the consecration. Thus ends the worship for the presence of the *liṅga*.

Now, regarding the Great Jar Consecration (*mahākumbhābhiṣeka*) and so forth: then the supreme guru, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having prayed to Vighneśvara, and meditating upon Vighneśvara as Sadāśiva while striking his head [three times], performs three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, he makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for all living beings and our own devotees residing in this place..."

By the grace of Veṇuvaneśvara, for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects in accordance with the prayers of devotees, [this grant is made] for this God of gods, Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his mother Śrī Kāntimatī, accompanied by the Śrī Mūlaliṅga, and with his entire retinue, so that there may be no further return to saṃsāra...

In this Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*), which consists of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) for the extraction of the decayed *saṃjñika* [soul], for the sake of the long-term presence of the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*), by means of the auspicious rites— from the *anujñā* onwards— performed according to the method taught in the venerable *Kāmikāgama*,
ending with the *kumbhābhiṣeka* (the water-pot consecration), [this is] for the removal of all deficiencies and the cessation of evil.

"Having first protected us and our devotees, [the Lord] whose body consists of the mantras of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) arranged through various *nyāsa* rites such as the *jīva-nyāsa*... (l5) ...and so forth, up until "for the sake of direct vision and proximity for a long time, lasting as long as the moon and sun, I shall perform the great jar-consecration (*kumbha-mahā-kumbha-abhiṣeka*) of the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*).
Regarding the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) for the Śiva-sacrifice jar-consecration... (l6)

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the sake of accomplishing the auspicious *muhūrta*, and for the sake of attaining the grace of the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, I shall perform many offerings of fruit and betel," [he recites]: "The fruit which always bestows the fulfillment of the desires of men—for the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons, therefore grant me peace."
Betel is auspicious, bestowing prosperity, and its essence is Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
therefore, by the offering of this, grant me peace.

"These fruits, betel leaves, and ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) I have bestowed upon learned Brāhmaṇas of various lineages, together with their wives and their sons, who are distinguished by the marks of Śiva and devotion to Śiva. Having thus given these with joined palms, he then filled his hollowed hands (añjali) with flowers.

With the mind dissolved in Śiva, having recited the *ṣoḍaśakalā-prāsāda* mantra three times and offered it upon the head of the Lord, one should extract [the deity] from the water-pot along with the flower-garland using the *udbhava-mudrā*. Having extracted Śiva—who was previously invoked and consists of the form of the *ṣoḍaśakalā-prāsāda* seed-syllable—and having projected him as far as the *dvādaśānta*, one should bring him down slightly to the forehead; then, once again, he is held within the hollowed palms (*añjali*).

Having reflected: [one should meditate on] that which possesses the radiance of ten million suns, is as cool as ten million moons, white as one's own *dhā* syllable, consisting of light, and auspicious— [this] with the seed-syllable *haṃsa* of the *paramātman-mantra* and the *ghora* [syllable], at the top of the great *liṅga* by way of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇapravāha*),
using the *prasāda-mantra* distinguished by the sixteen *kalās* with the *pluta* [protracted] vowel.
