Uttering [the mantra] ending with *nāda*, having invoked [the deity] with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā] and the root-mantra *sadyojāta*, having established [him] with the *sthāpinī* [mudrā] and the left [hand],

having brought [him] near with the *sannidhāninī* [mudrā], having caused [him] to be present with the *nirodhinī* [mudrā] and the *puruṣa* [mantra], and having contemplated, "Welcome, O Mahādeva," and having contemplated the words spoken by the Lord, "Dear child, a very warm welcome," one should offer the *svāgatārghya*.
O Lord, Master of the entire world, remain present within this linga with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship.

Having prayed thus, again taking Tatpuruṣa from the jar and placing him at the eastern face, one should pray as before up to the word "welcome" (*svāgata*). In the same way, [one does so] in the south. Having invoked Aghora; in the north—having likewise invoked Vāmadeva; in the west—having invoked Sadyojāta. In the southeast, *namaḥ* to the Heart; in the northeast, the Head; in the southwest, the Topknot (*śikhā*); in the northwest, the Armor (*kavaca*); in front—

Having invoked the Eye and the All-pervading Weapon (*astra*), and having performed the rites from installation (*sthāpana*) up to the welcoming (*svāgata*), while reciting the root mantra ending in *nādānta* [namely *khastara...*], one should sprinkle everything upon the head of the *liṅga* with the water from the sacrificial jar (*yāgakumbha*) using the mantra "devassatve" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.6.2). Then, taking the seed-vessel (*vardhanī*), one should place the Great *Liṅga* on the left, invoke it, and [perform the rite] as before with the water from the *vardhanī*.

Having performed the consecration: Ananteśa in the east; Sūkṣmeśa in the south; Śivottama in the north; Ekanetra in the west; Ekarudra in the southeast; Trimūrti in the southwest; Śrīkaṇṭha in the northwest; Śiva in the northeast;
and Śikhaṇḍin—having thus invoked them, preceded by the recitation of the root mantra distinguished by their respective mantras.

Having consecrated [the disciple] in each respective place with the water from the corresponding jar, having invoked [the deity], having performed worship up to the conclusion of the welcome (*svāgata*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the root mantra ending in *svadhā* and *svāhā*, (l5) having presented incense and lamps, and having offered the food characterized by specific substances along with the mantras in the manner and sequence to be described, [one recites] the *ārātrika* and the armor (*kavaca*).
Having offered [the substance] with the distinguished root-mantra,

one should then, upon the pedestal for the daily ninefold bathing (nityasnapanavedikā), arrange the distinguished ninefold set consisting of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the procedure described for the daily ninefold bathing; and having worshipped it, either with substances such as scented oil and so forth, or with the five nectars and other materials.

Having consecrated [the deity] with the mantras ending in the ritual bath (*snāna*), having bathed [him] again with water for the *arghya* offering, and having once more presented the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the *arghya* with their respective mantras;
having wiped [him] dry with a fine cloth and,
with the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) and the "youthful weapon" mantra (*yuvāstra-mantra*), having caused Mahādeva to wear [the garments] with an unsurpassed, excellent cloth.

Having smeared the pedestal of the *liṅga* up to the depth of a *māṣa*-bean with the aforementioned fragrant water for sprinkling, distinguished by the exquisite scent of the eight perfumes (*aṣṭagandha*), using the mantra "Gandhadvārām," and having offered a pair of sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) along the Brahma-thread; [one should then adorn it] with ornaments such as the *golaka* and the two pedestals, accompanied by the Viṣṇu-sūkta.

Having adorned [it] with many garlands distinguished by the fragrant scents of *damana* grass and other perfumes; having adorned it with the root mantra and the *Rudrasūkta*; [placing] the *śūla*, *toraṇa*, and so forth held by *raṃbhā* in its presence;

having adorned it with many lamps; [performing] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*; and preceded by the nine-fold invocation (*navadūtikā*) and the placement of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvasthiti-nyāsa*), one should worship the Lord. Then, in the northwest...
One should worship Gaṇapati, who stands facing the southern direction;
one should worship Gaṇeśa, who has a protruding belly and is dark-hued, holding an axe and a rosary in his two upper hands.
I praise him who holds a *salaṭṭuka* fruit and an elephant tusk with his two lower hands, the left and the right.
Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. In the northern part of the inner sanctum:
holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus with his left and right hands.
Golden-hued, being bathed by the two gods holding maces, she who is the great refuge.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. Obeisance to the Guru Sadāśiva in the northeast. Obeisance to the Guru Ananta. Obeisance to the Guru Śrīkaṇṭha.
Obeisance to the Guru Ambikā. Obeisance to the Guru Guha. Obeisance to the Guru Brahmā.

"Salutation to Viṣṇu, the Guru. Having thus worshipped the seven gurus, he should pray: "O Gaṇeśa, O Kamala, O Pādukā of the Lord—may you, the Gurus of the World, grant permission to me who am performing this sacrifice, so that it may be successfully accomplished."
Having thus proclaimed the command of the Lord, [he beheld her] seated upon the lower part of the central pedestal,
with the head of a tortoise below, her body white as the Ocean of Milk.

Having meditated thus: "She who has the form of the root seed-syllable and the sprout, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who holds a noose and a goad, who is Power (Śakti), Action (Kriyā), and the very nature of the foundation," [one should offer salutation] with: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) upon the Brahma-stone.*
The earth is the bulbous root, the kalās are its stalk, and the bhāvas are its thorns;
pure māyā is the great lotus, crowded with many petals.

*Obeisance to Anantāsana*. Then, having meditated upon the Lord Ananteśa situated pervading the center of that [seat], one should worship him with the mantra: *Obeisance to Anantāsana*. Having thus worshipped the bright Śivāsana in the center of the Brahma-stone, [one should visualize] those resembling variegated lions, facing one another back-to-back.
Meditating upon the sandals of Śiva, which take the form of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, and which have the beautiful forms of lions colored white, saffron, and red,
[one should place them] in the corners starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast, in due order.
Homage to Dharma! Homage to Jñāna! Homage to Vairāgya! (l7) Homage to Aiśvarya! Having thus worshipped, [one should place] Kṛṣṇa in the eastern part and Śveta in the south, who is white and red.
Red and yellow in the west, and yellow and black in the northern direction.
The four limbs themselves are the powers of Ananteśa;
they have bodies resembling crystal, possess three eyes, and bear lion heads.
With their arms, heads, and necks held rigidly stiff, their heads were fixed upon their wooden sandals.

Meditating on those with human forms whose heads rest upon their forearms and feet, one should worship the presiding deities of the qualities of intellect (*buddhi*) and the factors of existence (*dharma*), etc., [as follows]: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Adharma; homage to Ignorance (*ajñāna*); homage to Non-detachment (*avairāgya*).

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Anaiśvarya," (L3) and having visualized Hunger approaching upon the upper girdle of the pedestal, one worships with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the lower cover" and "Obeisance to the upper cover" above that. In the center of that—
The bulb is like a ruby,
the stalk is the color of a diamond, the thorn has the luster of coral, and the petal resembles silver.
The filaments shine with the color of gold; at the tip is a string of pearls;

the lotus has petals like the blue lotuses of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and consists of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the bulb; salutation to the seed; salutation to the sprout; salutation to the stalk; salutation to the leaves; salutation to the petals. Thus.

Having meditated upon the petals as having the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras, [one should offer] "Obeisance to the filaments" (kesarebhyaḥ) upon the pedestal (pīṭha). In the center of the elevated portion of the pedestal,
[one should meditate on the goddess] who has the luster of molten gold and contains within her the fifty seed-syllables.
Thereafter, one should worship the sixty-four filaments of the pericarp.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kannikā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Vidyās. Having thus visualized the lotus in its complete form, one should worship it with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lotus.
[The deities] have the brilliance of the rising sun, possess three eyes, and have four arms.
Adorned with matted locks, crescent moons, and crowns, they hold chowries in their thousands;
with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, their lotus-like palms are sprinkled by Śiva.
Having meditated thus: "The Śakti Manonmanī, white as cow’s milk, [is located] upon the pericarp," [one recites]:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamani.

(Oṃ Hāṃ) Salutation to Manonmanī. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] on the circumference at the tips of the petals: Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Solar Orb (Sūryamaṇḍala). Brahmā has four faces and is adorned with four yellow staff-like arms.
Having meditated thus: "Seated upon a lotus stalk, axle, and wheels, situated in the center of the solar disc," [one should recite]:
*Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc.* On the circle at the tips of the filaments: *Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lunar disc.*
Viṣṇu has four arms; the goddess Mārī holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he resembles a dark blue cloud and is situated in the center of the lunar orb.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala.
(l6) Having thus worshipped, [one should say]:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire maṇḍala.
One should meditate upon Rudra, who stands in the midst of fire, blue-throated and three-eyed,
whose speech is the rising fire of knowledge, holding a trident in his hand and possessing four arms.

Having meditated thus: "Adorned with all ornaments, with the Naga king as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)," and having contemplated the Power (*śakti*) in the center of the pericarp with the mantra: "Obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-mandala," [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power-mandala."
Seated within the mandala of Śakti, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, three-eyed, and as pure as clear crystal.

I bow to the God who holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, and a rosary in his hands, who displays the gesture of fearlessness, who carries a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and who wears [the skin]— [of the lion and elephant]— in the order from right to left. Having thus worshipped him:

Salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala. Above that—having meditated upon [the seat] which pervades from the earth element up to Kuṭilā: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the form of Śiva. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Śiva. Having meditated upon [him] as consisting of the Śiva-tattva, one should place [him] within the encircling of the liṅga. In this form...

"Oṃ, salutation to the head of Īśāna; Oṃ Heṃ, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa; Oṃ Hūṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora; Oṃ Hiṃ, salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva; Oṃ Haṃ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*), one should then perform the six-path placement (*ṣaḍadhvanyāsa*) according to the white sequence.
"Just as the *kalā*, the world, the phoneme (*varṇa*), the mantra, and the word (*pada*)—this reality (*tattva*) has been summarized;
here the sequence of its persistence is described.

Regarding the *tattva* 36, the placement (*nyāsa*) and bathing (*snāna*): [one should place them] at the navel, the heart, the throat, the forehead, the crown of the head, the directions, the nostrils, the pervasive [center], the tongue, the hands, the ears, the genitals, the anus, the feet, and the hands. (l. 2) (c. 5)
Vāmanā is on the tongue and on the two eyes; Vyāpakā is on the two ears; Caturdaśī is on the heart;
[and] in the middle, on the head, on the hands, on the feet, and also on the heart—on the head, in a beautiful place.
Having performed the placement of the principles (*tattva-vinyāsa*), the wise one should perform the placement for each principle and its respective location:
*oṃ hāṃ pṛthivītattvāya namaḥ*— at the region of the navel.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the water element—at the heart.
Obeisance to the fire element—at the two ears. (l8) Obeisance to the wind element—at the two eyes.
Oṃ, homage to the element of space—
[this is] the nose. Homage to the element of odor— [this is] the pervasive [wind].
Salutation to the principle of taste—the tongue; salutation to the principle of form; [salutation to] the right hand—the principle of touch; [salutation to] the generative organ.
Salutation to the principle of the anus (*upastha-tattva*)—the anus;
salutation to the principle of wind (*vāyu-tattva*)—the right foot (*dakṣiṇa-pāda*); salutation to the principle of the feet (*pāda-tattva*)—the left hand (*vāma-hasta*).
Homage to the reality of the hand— (c2)—
homage to the reality of speech— [the nasal sound] ṅa.
Salutation to the principle of smell—*āghrāṇatattva*—the inner tongue. Salutation to the principle of the tongue—*jihvātattva*—the left eye (*vāmanetram*).
Salutation to the principle of sight—*cakṣustattva*—the pervasive one (*vyāpaka*).

Salutation to the principle of skin (*tvacatattva*). Salutation to the principle of the left ear (*vāmaśrotra*), the principle of hearing (*śrotratattva*). [At the heart and the directions: *Oṃ*, salutation to the principle of mind (*manastattva*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the ego (*ahaṃkāratattva*).
*Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*). 24.
Heart (hṛdayam): Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Rūpa (oṃ rutattvāya namaḥ). Head (śiraḥ): Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Rāga (oṃ rāgatattvāya namaḥ).
Both hands (hastaṃ 2): Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Niyati (oṃ niyatitattvāya namaḥ); salutation to the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattvāya namaḥ).

(c4) Heart (hṛdayam): Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Māyā (māyātattva). Kalā: 5. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Śuddhavidyā (śuddhavidyātattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Maheśvara. Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva. Oṃ...

"Salutation to the principle of Śakti (śaktitattvāya namaḥ); Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Śiva (śivatattvāya namaḥ). Thus, having performed the placement of the mantra for the thirty-six principles (tattvas), the locations, and the [deities], in this manner of established form, one performs the upward placement (ūrdhvanyāsa). Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the thirty-eight kalās.
O Maheśa, bearing the youth [Kārttikeya] with your arms, granting freedom from fear like a deer,
most gracious, adorned with all ornaments, dwelling in a lotus, and clothed in a tiger skin;

He who is the five-faced one, whose radiance is like the moon, whose forehead is adorned with a crest-jewel fashioned from millions of moons, and who possesses three eyes— he is the one who has as his crown the entire essence of the nectar of the supreme state.
All forms of the Kalās have three eyes and four arms;
they hold the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a trident and an axe.
In all these forms of the Kalās, the powers of Śaśinī are traditionally taught.
At the upper head: *oṃ hoṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ śaśinyai namaḥ*.
At the eastern head: *oṃ īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām aṅgadāyai namaḥ*.
On the southern head: Oṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of lords, the supreme lord of Brahmā, for the sake of the sacrifice.
On the northern head: Oṃ, may Śiva be mine; homage to Marīci.
On the western head: (l5)
Oṃ hāṃ sadāśivoṃ jvālinyai namaḥ.
To the upper face: Oṃ heṃ avyaktaśāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ.
To the eastern face: Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe śāntyai (l6).
Homage! To the southern face—*mahādevāya dhīmahi*, homage to Vidyā. To the northern face—*oṃ tanno rudra pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*.
In the western face: Oṃ hāṃ pracodayāt, obeisance to Nivṛtti. In the heart: Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghorāstamāyī.
On the throat—*Oṃ ghorebhyaḥ, to Ghorī, salutation*. On the right shoulder—*Oṃ ghora-jayāyai, salutation*.
On the left shoulder—*Oṃ hoṃ ghora-tarebhyaḥ, to Niṣṭhā, salutation*.
In the stomach: Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śarvataśarvabhṛtyava. In the navel: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to all the Māyās.
In the lower abdomen below the navel: Oṃ, obeisance to you, Rudra; obeisance to Kṣamā.
On the back: Oṃ, obeisance to Rūpa and [the goddess] Jarā. On the private parts: Oṃ Hīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva and obeisance to Jarā.
On the two testicles: Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to Rakṣā.
On the right thigh: Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Rudra; ...tyai salutation.
On the left thigh: *oṃ hāṃ kālāya namaḥ* | *pālinyai namaḥ*.
On the right knee: *oṃ hāṃ kalakāmāyai namaḥ*.
On the left knee: *oṃ hāṃ vikaraṇāya saṃyamanyai*.
Homage!
On the right calf—Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balakṛdhā.
On the left calf—Oṃ, homage to Vikaraṇā. Homage to Pūṣṇā.
Right buttock— Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balakārī.
Left buttock— Oṃ (l5), obeisance to Pramathana, obeisance to Buddhi.
At the region of the waist: Oṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana, salutation to Dhātrī.
On the right side: Oṃ, salutation to Unmanābrahmāṇī. On the left side: Oṃ, salutation to Unmana.
Salutation to Mohinī; salutation! On the right foot: Oṃ hāṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. On the left foot: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Ṛddhi.
In the right hand: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhavedvitī. In the left hand: Abhave, obeisance to Lakṣṇī.
At the two nostrils: Oṃ, salutation to Medhā, who is beginningless in existence.
At the head: Oṃ, accept me; salutation to Kānti. At the right arm: Oṃ, may you become [mine]; salutation to Svadhā.
On the left arm: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Udbhava; obeisance to Dhṛti*.
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the Pāśupata weapon mantra. Having thus performed the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*.
Then one should place the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkās: Vikeśā (l2) ...
[the forehead, eyes, ears, and pair of nostrils].
In the regions of the cheeks, lips, teeth, tongue, chin, and mouth;
in the joints of the arms and feet, on both sides, on the back,
the navel, the heart, and the vital organs— remove [the affliction] from these places.

In this manner, one should install each respective [deity] in its proper place. For the mantra of the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Ardhanārīśvara is the deity (devatā), *haṃ sāṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *haṃ siṃ* is the power (śakti), and *haṃ sūṃ* is the pin (kīlaka). This is the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā.
The application is in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The six-limbed [mantra] begins with *haṃ saḥ* and so forth; this is the placement (*nyāsa*). There are three types of the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa.
*Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī*: this is one position.
*Aṃ, to the self of Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī*. (L5)
"Namaḥ"—this is another view. "Aṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī"—this is yet another view. The visualization (dhyāna):
[He is] resembling the Bandhūka flower and gold, with a beautiful rosary...
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with his own staff-like arms, he wears a crescent moon as an ornament and possesses three eyes.
O Mother of the World, we eternally take refuge in your body, which brings peace.
At the hairline: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī.
On the forehead:
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aṃ, obeisance to Ananta and Virajā.
Right eye—*iṃ*, salutation to Sūkṣma Śālmali. Left eye—*īṃ*, salutation to Trimūrti Lolākṣī.
Right ear—*oṃ uṃ*, salutation to Amareśa.
Salutation to Vartulākṣī.
In the left ear—*Ūṃ*, salutation to Arghīśa, to Dīśa, and to Dīrghaghoṇā. In the right nostril—*Ṛṃ*, salutation to Bhārabhūti and to Durmukhī.
Vāmanāsi— Ṛṃ, obeisance to Nidhīśa and Gomukhī. On the right cheek— Ḷṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇu and Dīrghajihvā.
On the left cheek: *ḹṃ* salutation to Harā and Guṇḍodarī.
On the upper lip: *eṃ* salutation to Jhaṇḍīśa and Ūrdhvakeśī.
(L3) On the lower lip: *aiṃ* salutation to Bhautika and Vikṛtamukhī.
On the teeth—*oṃ sadyojātāya jvālāmukhyai namaḥ*.
On the tongue—*oṃ anugraheśāya ulkāmukhyai namaḥ*. On the chin—(l4).
Aṃ, obeisance to Akūra and Śrīmukhī; in the mouth—Aṃ, obeisance to Mahāsena and Vidyāmukhī;
at the base of the right arm—Kaṃ, obeisance to Krodheśa and Mahākālī.
At the elbow joint: *khaṃ*, salutation to Caṇḍeśa and Sarasvatī.
At the wrist: *gaṃ*, salutation to Pañcāntaka and Sarvasiddhi.
On the palm of the hand— *ghaṃ*, obeisance to Śivottama and Trailokyavidyā; on the tips of the fingers— *ṅaṃ*, obeisance to Ekarudra and Mantraśakti.
At the base of the left arm: *caṃ*, salutation to Kūrma and Ātmaśakti. At the elbow joint: *chaṃ*, salutation to Ekanetra and Bhūtimātṛ.
At the wrist: *jaṃ*, salutation to Caturmukha and Lambodarī. (L7)
On the palm of the hand—*jhaṃ*, salutation to Ajeśāstrāviṇī.
At the tips of the fingers—*ñaṃ*, salutation to Śarva and Nāgarī.
At the base of the right foot—*ṭaṃ*, salutation to Vāmeśa and Khecarī.
The knees— *ṭhaṃ*, homage to Lāṅgalinī Mañjarī. The shanks—
*ḍaṃ*, homage to Dārakarūpiṇī.
On the sole of the foot—Ḍhaṃ, obeisance to Ardhanārīśvara Viriṇī.
On the tip of the foot—Ṇaṃ, obeisance to Umākāntakāmakādarya. At the root of the left foot—Taṃ... [to ...ya].
Salutation to Pūtanā.
At the knees—to Daṇḍin and Bhadrakālī, salutation. At the shanks—to Atri and [the goddess] Nyai, salutation.
On the sole of the foot— *dhaṃ*, salutation to Mīna and Śaṅkhinī.
On the tip of the foot— *naṃ*, salutation to Meṣa and Garjinī.
On the right side—*paṃ*, obeisance to Lohita and Kālarātri;
on the left side—*phaṃ*, obeisance to Śikhin and Kubjinī;
at the back—*baṃ*, obeisance to Chakalaṇḍa and Kapardinī.
At the navel— (l4) *bhaṃ* to Dviraṇḍa and Vajraṇī, homage! At the heart— *maṃ* to Mahākāla and Jayā, homage!
In the skin: *Oṃ yaṃ*, salutation to the skin-self, to Kapālī, and to Sumukhī-Īśvarī.
In the blood: *Oṃ raṃ*, salutation to the blood-self, to Bhujaga, and to Revatī.

In the flesh—*laṃ*, obeisance to Pinākin, whose self is the flesh, who wields the *māyā* [bow], and who is Vāruṇī. In the semen—*vaṃ*, obeisance to Khaḍgīśa, whose self is fat, who wields the sword, and who is Vāruṇī. In the bone—*śaṃ*, obeisance to [the deity] whose self is the bone.
To the marrow of the back— Ṣaṃ,
obeisance to the white one, the self of marrow, and to Rakṣopasāriṇī. To the semen— Saṃ, obeisance to the white one, the self of semen, and to Bhṛgavī Sahajā.
In the heart: *haṃ* to Lakulīśa, the self of breath (*prāṇātman*), and to Lakṣmī, obeisance. At the base of the *liṅga*: *ḷaṃ* to Śiva, the self of the *liṅga*, and to Vyāpinī, obeisance.

At the tip of the *liṅga*: "KṢAṂ! Obeisance to Saṃvartaka, whose nature is wrath, and to Māyā. [Then follows] the sequence of syllables at the base of Śiva and Śakti. Having thus performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha, one should then perform the deposition of the spheres (*golaka-nyāsa*). The deposition of the spheres is said to be upon the heart, the face, and the pair of shoulders. This is the deposition of the spheres.

For the mantra: Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandas*), Umāmaheśvara is the deity (*devatā*). Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Hrīṃ is the power (*śakti*), and Hroṃ is the pin (*kīlaka*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the placement of the spheres (*golaka-nyāsa*). The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) begins with Hrām and so forth. (L3) Meditation (*dhyāna*):

I worship Him who has the luster of a conch shell, three eyes, and wears the crescent moon; who bears a smiling countenance, holds a trident and a skull-cup in His hands, grants boons and fearlessness, and is adorned with beautiful necklaces.

Having meditated thus: "May the body of my beloved—who has cast herself down upon my left thigh, whose beautiful red lotus shines in her palm, and who is adorned with shimmering jewel ornaments—be destroyed by [my] hand," one should recite:
Oṃ namaḥ to the heart.
Naṃ, salutation to the face; Maṃ, salutation to the right shoulder; Śiṃ, salutation to the left shoulder. (L5.)
... Oṃ namo to the right thigh; yaṃ namo to the left thigh;
oṃ namo to the base of the throat.
Naṃ, salutation to the navel;
Maṃ, salutation to the right side;
Śiṃ, salutation to the left side.
*Vaṃ* namaḥ at the heart;
*yaṃ* namaḥ at the back of the body;
*oṃ* namaḥ on the head.
Naṃ, obeisance to the mouth; maṃ, obeisance to the right eye; śiṃ, obeisance to the left eye.
Vaṃ, obeisance to the right nostril; yaṃ, obeisance to the left nostril;
oṃ, obeisance to the base of the right hand.

Naṃ namaḥ; śiṃ namaḥ; vaṃ namaḥ; yaṃ namaḥ—thus at the tips of the fingers of the right hand. (l7) In the same manner for the left hand. In the same manner for the right foot. In the same manner for the left foot. Oṃ namaḥ on the head.
Naṃ, obeisance to the face; maṃ, obeisance to the heart; śiṃ, obeisance to the belly.
VĀṂ, homage to the two thighs;
VAṂ, homage to the two feet;
OṂ, homage to the heart.
Naṃ, obeisance to the face; Maṃ, obeisance to the axe mudrā; Śiṃ, obeisance to the deer mudrā.
Vaṃ, homage to the Abhayamudrā;
Yaṃ, homage to the Varadamudrā. Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa).
"Oṃ namaśśivāya"— this is the pervasive [mantra]. Having thus performed the placement of the spheres (*golaka*),
[one performs] the placement of the three principles (*tattvatrayanyāsa*).

At the head: Naṃ, salutation to the supreme Śivatattva; salutation to its essence. In the mouth: Uṃ, salutation to the supreme Vidyātattva; salutation to its essence. In the heart: Aṃ, salutation to the supreme Ātmatattva; salutation to its essence.
"Namaḥ"—thus is the placement of the three principles.

Now follows the placement of the five principles (*pañcatattvanyāsa*). The placement of the "Staff-breaker" (*daṇḍabhaṅgin*) is as follows: on the head—*oṃ hauṃ*, salutation to the self of the *śāntyatīta-kalā*;
*oṃ haiṃ*, salutation to the self of the *śānti-kalā*.
In the heart: Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the self of the vidyā-kalā. In the navel: Oṃ hvīṃ, salutation to the self of the pratiṣṭhā-kalā.
On the two knees: *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalātmane namaḥ*. Thus is the placement of the five principles (*pañcatattvanyāsa*).
On the head—(l5) Oṃ Hoṃ, homage to the self of Īśāna, the head.
On the mouth—Oṃ Heṃ, homage to the self of Tatpuruṣa, the face; Oṃ, homage to the self of Aghora, the heart.
At the navel: Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to the self of the left secret organ.
At the feet: Oṃ haṃ, salutation to the self of the Sadyojāta foot. Thus is the Daṇḍapaṅkti-nyāsa.
Now, the placement of the rows of shaven-headed ones (muṇḍapaṅktinyāsa):
"To Īśāna, the self of the upper face"— thus, on the upper face.
Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the essence of the eastern face—in the east. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora, the essence of the southern face—in the south.
Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva—in the north.
"Salutation to the one whose self is the eastern face"—in the north;
"Salutation to Sadyojāta, whose self is the western face"—in the west. Having thus performed the placement of the row of skulls.
Then one should meditate upon the body of knowledge—
the Lord consisting of the knowledge of accomplishment (*siddhi*), situated above the *śivaliṅga*,
endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās*, and having assumed a form composed of the limbs of Brahmā.
The form of Sadāśiva is here described for the purpose of meditation:
five-faced, ten-armed, white as crystal, with three eyes;
peaceful, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, and with matted hair beautifully bound and smiling.
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantras, he stands atop a white lotus.
In the mandala, [it is adorned] with jewel necklaces, waist-bands, upper-ties, armlets, bracelets,
and joined with severed hero-scarves.
He is sixteen years of age, handsome, very serene, and has a smiling face.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and fire;
and with [his left] hands, he displays the gesture of fearlessness, a noose, a bell, and a goad.

One should meditate with the five [senses] upon the Lord of auspicious form, who bestows boons to the left. The Lord is like crystal in the center; he is saffron-colored in the east; he is fierce in the south; and he arises as gentle on the left.
One should meditate upon the orb of the moon’s rays, suddenly appearing in the western direction.
[Therein is] the lion-nose...; on the forehead in the east is an auspicious eye.
Devoid of eyebrows, with a prominent nose and radiant cheeks, it is beautiful for smiling.
Indeed, despair has a harsh form, terrifying with its side-long glances.
With a wide-open mouth, most terrible, tawny-eyed, and licking his lips;
adorned with serpent ornaments, having a skull as his crest-ornament;
shaped like a flame, with matted locks, fierce arms, and a topknot rising upward.
Full-bodied, composed of water, serene, with a beautiful nose and a lovely forehead,
three-eyed, adorned with a crown and earrings, and auspicious.
Resembling the form of a bumblebee, adorned with golden ornaments,
marked with a tilaka upon his forehead, and possessing a mind as reflective as a mirror;
endowed with a mass of curls, he was gentle and possessed of tranquility.
The Mistress of Speech is said to be situated on the face, adorned above and above with beautiful ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon the faces and the form of Sadāśiva—adorned with earrings, three-eyed, and decorated with the moon upon his crown—one should worship him, saying:
"Homage to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādehāya namaḥ*). Then, [one worships] the five faces, saying: "Homage to the eyes" (*netrebhyo namaḥ*).
Having offered the eyes, and then having filled the joined palms with flowers, and having brought [the visualization] as far as the heart-lotus,
[one meditates on] Śiva— the eternal, perpetual, whose nature is the bliss of knowledge,
all-pervading, the object of valid cognition, incomparable, and beyond description.

Having visualized [the deity] in his joined palms— devoid of designations, worthy of worship, beyond the reach of mind and speech, partless, whose nature is light, and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns— and while reciting the mantra of the temple of the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśakalāprāsādamantra*), having led [the breath] to the *dvādaśānta* and meditated upon it as being as intensely cool as ten million moons, he should again bring it down to the center of the earth, then lower it slightly to the forehead, and once more...
Having visualized the one consisting of light as being held within the hollowed palms,

[one should invoke] Śarva with the mantra "ā tvā vaha" and with the mantra "tryambakam. O Supreme Lord, I invoke you, who are established within my own self, stainless and pure, like a sacrificial fire in the fire-drills, assuming a manifest form.

Reciting this mantra, [one should think]: "With the *sadyojāta* mantra, I invoke Sadāśiva together with Ambā into the target image. Having invoked him with the *āvāhinī* [mantra], having established him with the *vāmadeva* and the *saṃsthāpinī*, having brought him into proximity with the *aghora* and the *sannidhānī*, and having confined him with the *tatpuruṣa* and the *nirodhinī*, one should utter: "Welcome to you, O Great Goddess! "Child..."
Having perceived that "A most welcome greeting" was spoken by the Lord, and having offered a welcoming *arghya* with the root mantra:
"O Master, Lord of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship..."
"Until then, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of affection.
(L5. Then one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*: "Of this great mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*).
The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda are the meters (*chandāṃsi*). (L6.)

Obeisance to the one who effects the creation of the entire world; the supreme deity is the power of life (*prāṇaśakti*). *Hrāṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kroṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the Lord of the Bamboo Forest (*Veṇuvaneśvara*).
Oṃ. (l7)
Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅam | To the self consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether:
Āṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ | To the self consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose: Ī, salutation to the two index fingers.

Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ | To the essence of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell: ūṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers (madhyamā). Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ | To the essence of speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ: aiṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers (anāmikā).

Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ | To the self consisting of speech, giving, movement, excretion, and pleasure: Oṃ, salutation to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ). Oṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ (l3) ḷaṃ kaṣaṃ | To the self consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta). Oṃ ahaḥ āḥ, [to] the palms of the hands (karatala).
Salutation to both palms and backs of the hands. Such is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. The visualization (*dhyāna*):

Seated upon a lotus that shines like a red water-lily floating on a sea of blood, she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a bow made of sugarcane, a bowstring made of bees, a goad, and the five arrows.

May the Goddess, the supreme power of life (*prāṇaśakti*), who bears a garland, a skull, and three eyes, and who is adorned with a resplendent, thick bow and lotus feet, and whose color is like the rising sun, be the bestower of happiness upon us.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one recites]: *Āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom* | *Haṃsaḥ so’ham* | "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of this person, the life-force (*jīva*) of this person, which reside here; all the sense faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of this person, together with the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*), having come here, may they remain happily for a long time, *svāhā*. Klīṃ. (l6–l7)

Paralyze! Paralyze! O Asunīti, [you who are] one's own sister! Āṃ hrīṃ! Kroṃ! Kroṃ hrīṃ! Ām! Ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom! O messenger of nectar, come, come! Having entered the heart of such-and-such a person, having bound his kinsmen together, forcibly [seize] from such-and-such a person! Yaṃ! Bring, bring that which has your form! Cause it to enter the image and so forth, cause it to enter! Establish, establish! Return again!

Come! Be firm in your own place. Vauṣaṭ. (l2) Namaḥ. Oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom. Yaṃ: May the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the skin-self of such-and-such a person be here as vital breaths; may the life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such a person remain here; [may] all the sense-faculties and the mind (*manas*) of such-and-such a person [remain here]. (l3)

Having arrived together with the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*citta*), may they remain happily for a long time, *svāhā*. *Kauṃ*, paralyze, paralyze! *Oṃ hāṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīm*. *Ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom*. *Īṃ*, O messengers of Vaivasvata, come! Having entered the heart of such-and-such a person, having seized even those of his own kin, forcibly [seize] such-and-such a person. *Īṃ*, bring him in the form of blood; cause the image (*bimba*) and so forth to enter.

Enter! Be established! (l5) Be established! Return again! Return again! Be firm in your own place! Vauṣaṭ! Namaḥ! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīm! Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hom! Īṃ! Here are the vital breaths of the soul of such-and-such a person; here are the vital breaths! (l6)

O life-force of such-and-such a person, remaining here! O all his senses, together with the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*), come and dwell happily for a long time, *svāhā*! *Klauṃ*, paralyze, paralyze! *Oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom*. *Laṃ*, O messenger of the life-force, come, come! Having entered the heart of such-and-such a person, even though he be of the same kind...

Having seized it, forcibly bring forth its form of flesh! Enter the image and so forth! Stabilize, stabilize! Return again, return! Be firm in your own place! Vauṣaṭ! Namaḥ! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hom! Laṃ, of the nature of flesh! Prāṇa! (l2)

Here are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). Here abide the life-force (*jīva*) of that person, along with all his sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*), together with mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). May they remain here happily for a long time, *svāhā*. *Klauṃ*, paralyze, paralyze! *Oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīm*. *Ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom*. *Vaṃ* to the vital breaths. O messenger of the vital breaths (*prāṇadūtī*), come! Having entered the heart of that person.

By force, bring this one’s fat-form! *vauṣaṭ*! *namaḥ*! *oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīm*. (l4) *ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom*. *vaṃ*, to the self of fat, *namaḥ* + *svāhā*. *klauṃ*, paralyze! Paralyze! *oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīm*. *ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hom*. O messenger, attract [it]! Come, come! O you whose form is auspicious (*svastirūpa*). (l5)

Honour! Bring! Be! Vauṣaṭ! Namaḥ! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! Sah-oṃ-śā-hastya-ātmanaḥ! Svāhā! Klauṃ! Paralyze! Paralyze! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! Sa Hom! Ṣaṃ! O Grathinī, messenger, go, go! Ṣaṃ! Bring the form of Majjā! Be! Vauṣaṭ! Namaḥ! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! Sa Hom! Oṃ Ṣaṃ!

Of the middle self: Svāhā! Klauṃ, paralyze, paralyze! Oṃ Āṃ Krīṃ Hrīṃ! Ya Ra + Sahom! Saṃ, O messenger of joy, come, come! Saṃ, O pure form! Nāya + Bhava Vauṣaṭ! Namaḥ! Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! Ya Ra + Sahom!
Saṃ, of the white self: Svāhā! Klauṃ, paralyze, paralyze! Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ.

Ya ra sa hom | Haṃ visphuliṅganī āgaccha ccha | Haṃ prāṇarūpam ānaya ya bhava vauṣaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ ya ra sa hom | Haṃ prāṇātma namaḥ svāhā | Klauṃ stambhaya stambhaya | Āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ ya ra sa hom | Ḷaṃ kṣetrapratihāri dūti āgaccha gaccha | Ḷaṃ jīvarūpam ānaya ya – bha.

*vauṣaṭ* *namaḥ*. *ḻaṃ* to the individual self (*jīvātman*), *namaḥ*. *svāhā*. *klauṃ*, paralyze (*stambhaya*) [it] three times, *stambhaya namaḥ*. Having thus established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), one should pray:
"O All-pervading One, whose nature is indivisible existence, consciousness, and bliss; partless and immutable!"
O Lord of all that is to be known, I pray for Your lotus feet, which are of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and are free from beginning, middle, and end;
O Mahādeva, stay, stay! Grant Your presence in this *liṅga*.
Having gathered all the deities through the path of the suṣumnā channel,
together with the deities of the inner sanctum and those residing in the celestial chariot;
O Maheśvara, when the Liṅga has been offered by me along with the Goddess, together with the deities of the gates and all the surrounding retinues.
Enter, O Mahādeva; be present in your own abode.
O Vikrama, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Self, O Teacher of the World!
Since this Liṅga has been fully worshipped by me upon the earth, just like [the sun] remaining for a period within the constellations, remain for a long time in this Liṅga; O Vidvila, stay here now.
Having stayed happily in this Liṅga, [accept] the offerings made by me to you both.
O Lord, [reveal] to me, who have become the mantra, the body consisting of the six paths.
O Lord, how is there an invocation, and likewise, O All-pervading One, how is there a seat?
Even the discernment between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done does not exist in me in the slightest.
Therefore, O Lord, may all that be forgiven; have compassion for me, your servant.

"O Blessed One, although you are indeed all-pervading, even as one invokes you... [just as] fire [is found] within fuel, or as sugar [is found] in fire through churning, so do I invoke you here; therefore, O Acyuta, depart! Having thus prayed, [one should place the mantras] in the locations starting from the heart and ending with the hands, beginning with the heart.

Having performed the placement of the mantras (*nyāsa*), having established oneness with the root mantra, having protected [the deity], having bound [the limbs] (*avakuṇṭhana*), and having performed the rites of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), having tied the five-faced [noose], and having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, one should present the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā* respectively. Then, having offered *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth with the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the root mantra, one should offer salutation upon the head with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Self whose nature is the crest-jewel (*śikhā-ratna*)."

On the forehead (paṭṭikā): homage to the one whose self is the syllable *ma*. On the two ears: homage to the one whose self is the syllable *ra*, which is Rudra. On the throat: homage to the one whose self is the syllable *na*.
Below the throat: homage to the one whose self is the syllable *ma*. Now, regarding the faces: on the upper face, homage to the one whose self is the syllable *śi*.

Salutation to the letter *va* (*vaka*), the essence of the eastern face. Salutation to the letter *ya*, the essence of the southern face. Salutation to the letter *na*, the essence of the northern face. Salutation to the letter *ma*, the essence of the western face. Thus ends the gross placement of the five syllables (*sthūla-pañcākṣara-nyāsa*). (The subtle placement of the five syllables, *sūkṣma-pañcākṣara-nyāsa*:)

On the head: *namaḥ* to the self of *nāda*. On the face: *namaḥ* to the self of *bindu*. In the heart: *namaḥ* to the self of *makāra*. In the two arms: *namaḥ* to the self of *ukāra*. In the two feet: *namaḥ* to the self of *yakāra*. Again, on the faces: *namaḥ* to the face of Īśāna, the self of *nāda*; *namaḥ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, the self of *bindu*; *namaḥ* to the face of Aghora, the self of *makāra*; *namaḥ* to the face of Vāmadeva, the self of *ukāra*.

"Obeisance to the one whose self is the letter *a*, whose face is Sadyojāta. Thus is the subtle placement of the five syllables (*sūkṣmapañcākṣaranyāsa*). Again, "on the two feet"—this is the water for the feet (*pādya*). On the faces: "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, svadhā"—this is the water for sipping (*ācamana*). "Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the head"—this is the water for respectful offering (*arghya*).

Oṃ hauṃ namaḥ. Having mentally visualized the preliminary rites for the bath— such as anointing with oil, rubbing with unguents, and wiping— and having bathed [the deity] with the water-drop from the *arghya* vessel, having offered the *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya*,
and having wiped [the deity] with a fine cloth.

With the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ namaḥ gandhadvārāyai," I offer fragrance. Having offered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *dūrvā* grass, auspicious flowers, sacred thread (*upavīta*), earrings, ornaments, and so forth, with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one offers three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātma-tattva; obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Vidyā-tattva; obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva."

Having worshipped with the root mantra and with flowers, and having worshipped with the eight names beginning with Bhava, while sounding the bell with the *astra* mantra—reciting the mantra: "Thou art the burner; burn him who burns us, burn him who burns others; O God, thou art the protector"—and [protecting] with the *kavaca* mantra.

I offer incense at the nose; I cause it to be smelled. Having kindled the lamp with the clarified butter of a tawny cow, which is joined with the activity of curds, O Jātavedas, protect my person and grant me cattle, waters, and life from the ten directions. O Jātavedas, do not harm my cow, horse, man, or the world. O destroyer of sin, come hither and bestow prosperity upon me. *Oṃ hauṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* to the eyes.

Thus, having displayed the *manoratha-mudrā*, I show the lamp within the eyes. Then, having worshipped the limbs of Brahmā in their respective places of dissolution (*layasthāna*), and having made known one's desires, one displays the *mahāmudrā* and the *amṛtamudrā*. Then, in the presence of the deity—

Having lit various other kinds of lamps, beginning with the unbroken five-faced lamp, the archway lamp, and ending with the trident lamp; then the preceptor shall perform the formal ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) in the presence of Śiva: "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of gods, the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva, together with the Mother Kāntimatī, accompanied by the venerable Mūla-liṅga, and along with his retinue..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the daily offerings in the Śiva-sacrifice for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple] first established according to the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, and for the eightfold binding," he should summon a Brāhmaṇa,

worship him with the thought that he is Śiva, using the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*), the image-mantra (*mūrti-mantra*), and the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and [give him] along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Reciting the mantra preceded by the offering of betel-leaf,
and having worshipped the cow— (the gift of a cow)— [one should recite:
"In the limbs of cows reside the fourteen worlds."
Therefore, by the giving of this, grant me peace from this [misfortune].
Desiring the pleasure of Viṣṇuvaneśvara, I bestow upon you, who are of the nature of Śiva, this milch cow, together with her calf and adorned; thus is the gift of a cow.

(The Gift of Sesame Seeds: Taking sesame seeds filling a copper vessel measuring two *prasthas*, and having honored the Brahmins with [this] intention; taking betel-leaf together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): "Sesame seeds are eternally the destroyers of sin, born from the body of Viṣṇu.
By the gift of sesame seeds, may my sin here [be destroyed]."
O Keśava, destroy [my sins]! Desiring the pleasure of Veṇuvaneśvara, I offer this sesame seed along with its vessel and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). I bestow it upon you, who are Śiva in form.
Regarding the gift of gold:
O Fire, you whose seed is gold, you who reside within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha... (verse 3).
"Grant me peace from this [act], which yields the fruit of infinite merit. Thus he offered it. This concludes the ritual of the gift of gold.

(Godāna 2) — Then, having brought five cows together with their calves, and having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, having presented threefold measures of black sesame seeds along with fruits and water, having applied sacred ash, having re-entered [the inner sanctum], having offered incense and lamps, and having made supplications, one should request [permission] for the sake of the worship of the protective deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*).

Taking Īśāna from the upward-facing [face], one should worship him at the top-knot (karṇikā). Taking Tatpuruṣa from Tatpuruṣa—[placing him] in the east. Taking Aghora from Aghora—[placing him] in the south. Taking Vāmadeva from the northern [face]—[placing him] in the north. Taking Sadyojāta from the western face—[placing him] in the west; one should perform the worship.
All are endowed with five faces and adorned with ten arms;
they are arrayed in various ornaments and embellished with diverse scents of blood.
They have the appearance of sixteen-year-olds, possessing the natural beauty of youth.
They have serene faces, are gentle, possess three eyes, and are seated upon auspicious seats.
Having thus honored these [deities] with seats and other offerings, one should take [the mantra] from heart to heart:
the head in the southeast, the crest-lock in the northeast, the armor in the southwest, and the kavaca in the northwest;
the heart has the luster of a pearl, while the head is the lord, having the color of yellow orpiment.
One should properly contemplate the crest-lock, which resembles a girdle at the waist;

having contemplated the armor, radiant as a bumblebee, and having contemplated the eye in front, shining with the form of light; and having contemplated the weapon, tawny in color, on all sides—[one should offer] these:
the seat, water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings: "Obeisance to the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, together with the deities of the first enclosure beginning with Īśāna.
Second enclosure worship:
In the east—Ananteśa (l4).

Homage! To the South—homage to Sūkṣmeśa. To the West—homage to Śivottama. To the North—homage to Ekanetra. To the Northeast—homage to Ekarudra. To the Southeast—homage to Trimūrti. To the Southwest—homage to Śrīkaṇṭha. To the Northwest—homage to Śikhaṇḍin. This is their visualization:
These gods all have four faces, ten arms like Hara, crescent moons upon their crests, and they abide upon lotuses; they possess various forms and hold swords,
shields, bows, arrows, water-pots, and rosaries.
They are endowed with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and hold tridents and lotuses in their hands.

Having worshipped these [deities], who resemble the sun at the end of an eon and whose sphere is Śiva, with the rites of invocation and so forth; having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra; [one should offer salutation] to the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara together with the second enclosure:
*namaḥ*.
Now, for the third enclosure at the neck of the pedestal:
in the north—salutation to the Goddess; in the northeast—salutation to Caṇḍeśvara; in the east—salutation to Nandīśa; in the southeast—salutation to Mahākāla;
in the south—salutation to Vṛṣabha; in the southwest—salutation to Gaṇeśa; in the west—salutation to Bhṛṅgīśa.
Salutation! To Vāyu—salutation to Guha. Their meditations are as follows:
the Goddess, Śiva, Caṇḍeśa, Mahākāla, and likewise the Bull;
Nandīśa, the leader of the Gaṇas, Bhṛṅgīśa, and Skanda.
"One should meditate upon [the deities] following that, unimpeded and possessing a luster like that of rubies.
Having thus meditated and having worshipped them with the rites of invocation and so forth, [one offers salutation]: "Salutation to the glorious Veṇuvaneśvara, together with the third enclosure."
In the fourth enclosure, on the pedestal-base: in the east—*namas* to Indra.
[He is] mounted upon a double radiance, yellow in color, and holding a thunderbolt.
One should worship Indra, the thousand-eyed, situated in the eastern quarter.
Homage to Indra on the path...
[to him] who is surrounded by a garland, who wields a spear, and whose seat is fire.
Homage to Agni.
To the south, [one should worship] Yama, who is black, stands upon a buffalo, and holds a staff in his hand;
*aṃ* to Yama, *namaḥ*. To the southwest... [Nairṛta].
[Nairṛti] is blue, holding an excellent sword, and seated upon a man. (l6.
Oṃ, obeisance to Nairṛti. (In the western direction—)
In the western quarter, one should worship Varuṇa, who is white, seated upon a large fish, and holding a noose in his hand;
[the mantra is] "Vaṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa.
And in the northwestern quarter, one should worship Anila (Vāyu), who has a smoky luster, holds a banner in his hand, and is mounted upon a deer.
Salutation to Vāyu.
[The mace-bearer] ... [the mace-bearer] Kubera also in the north.
Salutation to Kubera.
One should worship Īśāna in the form of Śaṅkara— tawny-hued, with a trident in hand, mounted upon a bull, three-eyed, with a gracious countenance, and joyful.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna.
Then [one should visualize] Viṣṇu, dark-complexioned, with a sword in one hand and holding a discus in the other;
homage to Viṣṇu.

The wise one should worship Brahmā, who has the luster of the dawn and rides upon a swan, holding a lotus in his hand and moving upwards, with offerings of his own [inner] self and its constituent elements. (2) *Namaḥ* to Brahmā. Having worshipped these two with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, [one offers] *namaḥ* to the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, together with the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*).

Now, the fifth enclosure: one should place upon the head of Brahmā (l3), in the eastern direction, a yellow six-pointed vajra; *vajrāya namaḥ*. In the southeast, a spear (*śakti*) with a deep red luster; *śaktaye namaḥ*.
A black staff in the south; *namaḥ* to the staff. In the southwest—(l4.
on the blue portion, *namaḥ* to the sword. A white noose in the west; *namaḥ* to the noose.

In the northwest, one should worship Citradhvaja with "Homage to the Banner" (*dhvajāya namaḥ*). [One should worship] Hemābha, who holds a conch, a mace, and a sword, with "Homage to [Hemābha]. In the northeast... [one should worship] the trident held aloft with "Homage to the Trident" (*śūlāya namaḥ*). The discus—one possessing a radiance equal to the sun—with "Homage to the Discus" (*cakrāya namaḥ*). Above that, the wise practitioner should visualize a white lotus with "Homage to the Lotus" (*padmāya namaḥ*).
Having worshipped these [deities] with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, [one should offer obeisance]:

"Obeisance to the glorious Veṇuvaneśvara, together with the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). Alternatively, having mentally recollected [the deities] from the invocation up to the altar (*vedī*), [one should worship] with their respective root-mantras (*mūla*).
One should offer the *arghya* oblation. This concludes the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
(l7) One should perform the worship of the fifth enclosure of one’s own power (*svaśakti*) in another manner.
Now, in the northeast of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), [one says]: *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. To his left: *ambikāyai namaḥ*. In the east— (p246a, l1)

Salutation to Puruṣa; salutation to Gaṇāmbikā. To the south—salutation to Aghora; salutation to Gaṅgā. To the north—salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Gaurī. To the west—salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Umā. To the southeast—salutation to Hṛdayā; salutation to Pāśāmbā. To the northeast—salutation to Śiras.

Salutation to Nīlāmbā in the west; salutation to Śikhāyī in the southwest; salutation to Kavaca in the northwest; salutation to Pāśāmbā in the north; salutation to Netra at the front [east]; salutation to Khaḍgāmbā; salutation to Astra in all directions starting from the front;
salutation to Jṛmbhiṇyambā. These are the deities of the first enclosure.
Salutation to the Accompanied Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara. On the petals, starting from the east: salutation to Ananteśa; salutation to Bhūtyambā; salutation to Sūkṣmeśa; salutation to Svadhāmbā.
Salutation to Śivottameśa; salutation to Kṣāntyambā; salutation to Ekanetra; salutation to Prabhāmbā; salutation to Ekarudra; salutation to Puṣṭyambā;
salutation to Trimūrtīśa; salutation to Śrutyambā; salutation to Śrīkaṇṭheśa; salutation to Kīrtyambā.
Salutation to Śimmeḍhīśa. Salutation to Medhāmbā. Salutation to Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara together with the second enclosure.

On the northern side of the pedestal: salutation to Umāyī; salutation to Bhadrāmbāyī. In the northeast: salutation to Caṇḍeśa; salutation to Devadhānyambāyī. In the east: salutation to Nandīśa; salutation to ...nalyambāyī. In the southeast: salutation to Mahākāla.

Salutation to Bhṛṅgiṇyambā. To the south—salutation to Vṛṣabha; salutation to Badānyambā. To the southwest—salutation to Gaṇeśa; salutation to Hlādinyambā. To the west—salutation to Bhṛṅgīśa; salutation to Rūpiṇyambā. To the northwest—salutation to Guha.

Salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara together with the third enclosure. At the base of the pedestal: salutation to Indra in the east; salutation to Śacīdevī on the left and right; salutation to Vipulā; salutation to Agni; salutation to Svāhā; salutation to Svadhā.

Homage to Yama; homage to Kāḷakaṇṭhī; homage to Nīlī; homage to Nirṛti; homage to Jātāyī; (l3) homage to Sukeśinī; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Hlādinī Ambā; homage to Harṣaṇī Ambā; homage to Vāyu; homage to Mahiṣī;
homage to Maṅgalī Ambā; homage to Soma; homage to Ṛddhi Ambā; homage to Samṛddhi Ambā. (l4)

Salutation to Īśāna; salutation to Jitāmbā; salutation to Svarūpiṇyambā. In the southwest (Nirṛti): salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Śrīdevyambā; salutation to Bhūdevyambā. In the northeast (Īśāna): salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Sāvitryambā. (L5)

Salutation to the deity of the fourth enclosure, Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara. Upon the head of Brahmā: Salutation to Vajra in the east; salutation to Prasannātmikā; salutation to Śakti; salutation to Gopātmikā; salutation to Daṇḍa. (L6)

Homage to Guṇātmikā! Homage to Khaḍga! Homage to Komalātmikā! Homage to Pāśa! Homage to Viṣātmikā! Homage to Aṅkuśa! Homage to Vikṛtātmikā! Homage to Gadā! Homage to Mohātmikā! Homage to Triśūla! (l7)
Homage to Maṅgalātmikā! Homage to Cakra! Homage to Lakṣmī! Homage to Padma! Homage to Sarasvatī!
Homage to the deity of the fifth enclosure, Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara!
These [deities], from the invocation up to the offering of food (naivedya), [are to be visualized] in the mind.

Having recollected [the deities] with their respective root mantras, one should offer the *arghya*. Having displayed the *mudrās* of the cow (*dhenu*), the lotus (*padma*), the trident (*triśūla*), and the crocodile (*makarī*) for Īśāna and the others, and having shown the *namaskāra-mudrā* for the limbs (*aṅga*s), one should offer incense and lamps to them. For the sake of the food offering (*naivedya*), there is the purification of the site;
having sprinkled it with "Oṃ hāṃ astrāya phaṭ," one should smear it in the shape of a square.

Having arranged perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth upon that [vessel], and having placed water purified by the *astra-mantra* on top of it; then, having worshipped once more with "Obeisance to Brahmā," "Obeisance to Viṣṇu," and "Obeisance to Rudra" upon the vessel purified by the *astra-mantra*; [he places] pure rice, rice with jaggery (*gulānna*), rice with sesame and peas (*kṛsarānna*), milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), and rice with mung beans (*mudgānna*) separately in those vessels and so forth.

Having cooked those foods according to the rules, numbering [them] with the *śiva-saṅkhyā*, and having taken up the dishes along with their side-dishes— consisting of items to be chewed, licked, sucked, and drunk— and placing them upon his head,
he brought them from the kitchen to the sacrificial ground accompanied by song, instrumental music, dance, and chanting.

Having placed [the vessel], having consecrated it once more with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) while reciting "Oṃ," having sprinkled it with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ," and having protected it with "Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ" while taking water in the right hand, having written [the mantra] "...", and having sprinkled it, one should contemplate it as dried. Again, taking water in the right hand, having written "Raṃ," and having sprinkled it, one should contemplate it as cooked. Taking water in the left hand, having written "Saṃ," and having sprinkled it... (Note: The ellipses indicate the omission of specific mantras or syllables that would be written on the vessel during the ritual.)

Having visualized [the vessel] as overflowing with nectar (*amṛta*), having recited the root mantra eight times, and having performed the *surabhi-mudrā* [with]: *Oṃ yeṃ (eṃ) aiṃ sauṃ sauṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvarī amṛtavarṣaṇi amṛ...*.
Make it flow! O God Savitṛ, impel! I sprinkle thee with truth by means of truth. *Oṃ*, having consecrated [the food] with the *Brahma-gāyatrī* mantra, [reciting] "I am this...

with the hymn (*sūkta*), may all partake of the rice-mess (*odana*). ... "The rice-mess is indeed Parameṣṭhin; may it not fail to reach my highest goal. "The winds are sweet for the sake of Truth; the rivers flow with sweetness; the honeyed..."

May the source of contentment, the honeyed night, and... like the earthly dust, may the sky be honeyed for us, our father; may the lord of the forest be honeyed for us, and may the sun be honeyed. May our cows be full of sweetness. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva.
"Thou art the under-layer of nectar. Taking water with flowers in both hands and placing it in the vicinity [of the deity], one recites: "Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā; to Brahmā svāhā.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. (l6) "I offer pure rice. "Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; I offer rice cooked with jaggery. "Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Aghora. [I offer] *kṛsara* rice.
I offer: Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. (l7) I offer mung-bean rice. Oṃ Hoṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta; I offer milk-rice. I offer this to you, O Maheśvara; may you accept it with pleasure.

Having thus offered fivefold food, along with condiments, solid refreshments, and drinks, together with the deities of the five protective enclosures, saying: "Svāhā to the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara," one should then give water three times for the sake of drinking in the center.

"You are the lid for the nectar. Having offered water three times again, [he says: "I offer water for rinsing the mouth; I offer water for washing the hands; I offer water for washing the feet. Having given water for sipping (ācamana) once more, [he gives] hand-rubbing powder. The bridegroom, having wiped [his hands], [takes] betel-leaf. 380 (Section 120)

Having offered betel leaf together with nutmeg (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), nutmeg fruit (*jātiphala*), and cinnamon leaves (*jātipatri*)—saying, "I present this betel to the Lord of Veṇuvana"—and then, preceded by incense and lamps, [offering] many...
hundreds of... on the [specified] day.

Having offered a chariot and other items accompanied by *geya* songs, along with three *ārā* [arrows], while reciting the respective mantras; then, having honored the Lord (*Īśvara*) with mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, the recitation of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*), benedictions (*āśīrvāda*), the five-limbed Dravidian hymns (*pañcāṅgadrāviḍastuti*), pure dances, praises, and stotras; and having meditated upon Him as being exceedingly joyful; one should fill the hollow of the hands (*añjali*) with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), [offering] that which is born of speech, mind, and body for the sake of those who are measured...
The *Nityā*...

(l7) ...is for the purpose of removing the sins acquired through deficiencies in mantra-rites and meditative cultivation during the remaining consecrations, worship, festivals, and so forth; it is for the completion of the rites already performed...

Having recited the Prāsāda mantra— "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of all principles"— and having placed the *pavitra* upon the top of the *liṅga*, and again having offered the *ārātrika* lamp, and having displayed the *prarocana* [light-show], and having prayed to Śiva, one should take up the rosary (*akṣamālā*) counted at one hundred and eight and perform purification with the *bahurūpa* mantra.

Having drawn [the deity] with the middle finger... (l3) having recited the root mantra one hundred times and having recited a tenth part of its limbs, taking [the materials] in both hands together with *kuśa* grass, flowers, unbroken rice, and water for the *arghya* offering:
*oṃ hāṃ guhyādigu...* (l4)

Therefore, O Maheśvara, accept this recitation performed by us; may success be mine through your grace. Whatever action there may be, O God, whether always well-done or ill-done, that [action], O Śivapada, consume and destroy for me.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere—he who is Śiva is indeed myself.

Reciting thus, having performed the recitation (*japa*) and worship with devotion, and having offered himself into the boon-granting hand of Śiva by means of the heart-mantra and the *udbhava* mudrā, he should thereafter perform three circumambulations and five prostrations, and satisfy [the deity] with hymns of praise.
Having praised [the deity] with numerous hymns such as "O Lord of Suras, homage to you," and having meditated upon him as joyful, sweet-voiced, and satisfied,

one should perform the daily fire ritual (*nityāgnikārya*). Having requested the auspicious instrument for the sake of the fire ritual, saying, "You have become qualified for the fire ritual," and having received permission, one should take the *arghya* vessel and other implements toward the southern, southwestern, and western directions, or in another direction.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, (l2) ...

having swept it with *darbha* grass, having placed [the materials] there, having prepared a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having sprinkled it with the general *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*, one should bring about the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with pieces of brick, as before. (l3)
Having sat down on the northern side, one should perform the inspection of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) with the eye fixed upon the root-mantra; the sprinkling with the *Śiva-mantra*;

the striking with *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; the scattering, filling, and pounding with the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*; and having performed the sweeping and smearing with a sword-like *kuśa*, one should discard the *darbha* grass and [proceed with] water...

...at the moment. Having performed the scattering, filling, and pounding [of the site], as well as the sweeping and smearing, with the *kavaca* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, using the sword and the *kuśa* grass; having discarded the *darbha* blades; having performed the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*);

and having again taken up a *darbha* blade, one should draw three lines pointing eastward in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *astra* mantra using the *kuśa*, and likewise fashion one line pointing northward.

(l6) If it is a Rāśya [offering], one should prepare it by means of the reverse procedure. Having placed a blade of *darbha* grass there and sprinkled it with water while reciting the *kavaca* mantra, one should discard the *darbha* in the north (*saumya*). Having performed the ritual touching of water (*upasparśana*), one should manifest the perfection of all the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*). (l7)

In the center, having offered a seat (*viṣṭara*) made of *kūrca* grass with the heart-mantra, [the wise one] should invoke the Goddess according to the ritual rules, saying: "Homage to the seat of Vāgīśvarī. He should meditate upon the Mother of the Universe, who is dark-complexioned, in her fertile state, adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments, possessing a serene countenance and three eyes resembling lotus petals.

She is dark-complexioned, beautiful, six-armed, and in the prime of youth; she is adorned with all ornaments and stands upon two lotuses. She holds a pomegranate fruit and a lotus in her left and right [hands] respectively.
And [the hands hold] a rosary, a noose, as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Then, having meditated upon her who has bathed after her menses, one should place [the seed-syllables] with the *kūrca* [mantra].

(L3) Having thus meditated: "Obeisance to the form of Vāgīśvarī; obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Having worshipped in this manner: "Obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvara," one should invoke the Deity: "O Wise One, according to the rule, O Viśva... (L4)
Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara are known as Bindu and Nāda;
Bīja is declared to be Vāgīśvarī, and Nāda is remembered as Vāgīśvara. He has five faces, three eyes, four hands, and three feet. (L5)
He should be known as white in color, bestowing fearlessness and granting boons;
he holds a rosary in his left hand and a brush in his right hand.

"Having meditated thus: 'The meditation on Vāgīśa alone shall extinguish even the weapon,' she should invoke Vāgīśvara and worship him. Afterwards, having brought fire produced from a forest or elsewhere, or obtained from a pure dwelling, into a clean vessel, she should place it on the right side of the Hotṛ, [casting away] the flesh-eating portion belonging to Nirṛti..."

Having abandoned [the external fire], having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), having worshipped it with the heart-mantra, and having performed the binding of the directions with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and the veiling with the armor-mantra (*varman*), one should take up the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) using the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of fire" while employing the *saṃhāramudrā*. Then, by means of retention (*kumbhaka*), one should unite it with the fire of the navel and the fire of the *bindu*, merging them into one.
By means of exhalation (*recaka*) through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], [one should recite]:

"Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire (*vahnicaitanya*). Having thus cast the seed-syllable of fire (*āgneyabīja*), which resembles the flame of a lamp, into the fire within the vessel by means of the *udbhava-mudrā* while reciting the fire-mantra; ||| 3 ||

Having worshipped with the *saṃhitā* mantra and contemplated [the fire] as the virility (*vīrya*) of the Supreme Lord, one should perform the protection rites and display the *avaguṇṭhana*, *dhenu*, and *mudrās*. With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should rotate the fire three times clockwise over the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), contemplate it being cast into the womb-channel of Vāgīśvarī by means of Vāgīśvara, and then, with the knees resting on the ground, one should cast the face toward the root-mantra. Having poured a little water into that vessel and gathered [the ashes], [one should offer] the garment to the parents.
Having put on [the garments],

performed the purifications and ritual rinsings with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, covered [the fire] with fuel sticks, worshipped it with the *brahma-mantras* beginning with *sadyojāta*, offered five oblations of sesame seeds with the root mantra,
and strewn it around with *kuśa* grass.

Having worshipped in the east, west, south, and north with: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; and having requested the protection of the child [saying], "O Agni, protect the infant," and having given him the name "Agni Śiśu" (the Child Fire), one should say: *vāgīśvarī vāgīśvarābhyāṃ namaḥ*.

Having dismissed the two parents, then, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— which are wrapped here with the *varman* [mantra], together with *kuśa* grass, turned face-downward and then upward— having sprinkled them with the *astra* [mantra], having concealed them with the *kavaca* [mantra], having heated them in the fire, and having touched them in front of the fire, he should rotate them again.

Having again rotated [the vessel] from the middle to the middle and from the base to the base, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the *śivatattva*, at the tip; obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the *vidyātattva*, in the middle; obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the *ātmatattva*, at the base. Having thus performed the placement, one should place Śakti in the *sruca* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* spoon. Then, on the left side of oneself, upon *kuśa* grass, with the root-mantra...

Having performed [the preliminary rites], then having purified the cow-derived clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of inspection and other [purificatory acts], having meditated upon one’s own body as consisting of Brahman, having placed the vessel of clarified butter in front, having placed a bundle of *darbha* grass within it with the *śikhā-mantra*,
and having filled it with ghee, one should take two blades of *darbha* and apply them to the fire.

Having performed the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) over the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *astra-mantra*, having released [the thread] toward the north, and having touched water; having performed the threefold sprinkling (*utplavana*) with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] situated in the *ājya*-vessel using the *astra-mantra*; having untied the knot; having touched water with the *astra-mantra*; having cast the *darbha* into the fire; and having sprinkled water starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and ending at the northwest (*vāma*), [he recites]: "O Fire, in the lotus, [I invoke] Śiva."

Having worshipped [the deity] especially with the *ādhāraśakti*, having invoked [the deity] as before, and having performed worship, one should offer fruit-wood fuel-sticks (*phalāśasamidh*) one hundred times with the root mantra (*mūla*). Having offered oblations for the limbs (*aṅga*) at one-tenth that amount, one then performs the *vyāhṛti* oblation. The principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*) consists of clarified butter (*ājya*) one hundred times with the root mantra; the oblation for the limbs is one-tenth of that.

Then the *vyāhṛti* oblation. The principal offering (*pradhānahoma*) is performed with the *caru* in a number of one hundred; the subsidiary offerings (*aṅga*) are offered in a tenth part of that number. Then the *vyāhṛti* oblation. The sesame offering (*tilahoma*) is performed with the root mantra (*mūla*) in a number of one hundred; the subsidiary offerings are offered in a tenth part of that number. Then the *vyāhṛti* oblation. Then the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra in the number of one hundred and eight for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Having offered betel-leaf, having given the *arghya* water,

having worshipped with the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), having applied the sacred ashes (*bhasman*), having raised Śiva residing in the fire and joined him with the [deity in] the image, and then having performed oblations with the *vyāhṛti*s both individually and collectively, one should offer the *bali* for the enjoyment of Brahmā and the other deities.

Having paid homage to the fire with the prayer, "The oblation has been consumed by the Supreme," and having dismissed the fire with "Oṃ Āṃ Hrūṃ, obeisance to Śivāgni," one should dismiss Brahmā and the others in reverse order with "Oṃ Hāṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the Heart. Then,
having prepared three maṇḍalas in the south-eastern direction from oneself...

In the first maṇḍala—in the four directions starting from the east: *namaḥ* to the Rudras; *namaḥ* to the Mothers; *namaḥ* to the Gaṇas; *namaḥ* to the Yakṣas. In the corners starting from the northeast (*īśāna*): *namaḥ* to the Planets (*graha*); *namaḥ* to the Asuras; *namaḥ* to the Rākṣasas; *namaḥ* to the Nāgas.
In the inner maṇḍala—in the directions starting from the east up to the northeast corner: *namaḥ* to the Lunar Mansions (*nakṣatra*); *namaḥ* to the Zodiac Signs (*rāśi*); *namaḥ* to the Viśvedevas.

(l1) Between the wind and fire [directions]—having worshipped with "Salutation to Kṣetrapāla" and having offered the bali and arghya ending in *svāhā*—in the second maṇḍala, from the east to the northeast: *Indrāya svāhā*; *Agnaye svāhā*. (l2)

Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Nirṛti! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Vāyu! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Īśāna! Again, in the northeast: Svāhā to Brahmā! In the southwest: Svāhā to Viṣṇu! In the center: Svāhā to Nīlalohita! Having thus worshipped and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), [one should proceed].

In the third circle: "Svāhā to the crows and others! Svāhā to those who violate the samaya! Svāhā to all the lords of the dwellings... Having thus offered the bali and the arghya separately for each, one should dismiss all the bali-deities situated within the three circles.
Then follows the northern sprinkling (*uttarapariṣecana*).

Having performed [this], one should stand before the fire. This is the rule for the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*). Then the teacher, having approached the vicinity of the root-liṅga and offered the fruit of the *homa*, and having displayed the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), should raise the deities of the enclosure and so forth with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) by means of the withdrawal-mudrā (*saṃhāramudrā*). Having joined them to the liṅga with the form-mantra (*mūrtimantra*), and intending "Forgive me," he should recite the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) together with the root-mantra.

Having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva, one should pray: "Whatever has been done by me and whatever I shall do—all that is your good deed. O Śiva, you alone are the protector of the universe; today you are my lord. [Then follows: *sāyuvāsāyuvā*.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, accept all this action performed by me as my supreme worship. Having prayed thus,
one should perform the daily festival according to the prescribed rules in the presence of Śiva, followed thereafter by [the rite of] Ananta.

Having summoned the artisan, having purified him through the rites of inspection and so forth, having wiped him with *darbha* grass, having sprinkled him with *arghya* water, and having applied sacred ash, one should wrap his head with a silk cloth over which the *kavaca* mantra has been recited.
Having adorned his neck with a fragrant garland of *damana* flowers, one should offer upon a leaf coconut fruit, betel, and other items dedicated to the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara.

Having taken up [the ritual], accompanied by various musical instruments, songs, and the sound of conchs, filled with the heart-mantra of the palace, and preceded by many benedictions: "May he be long-lived like Mārkaṇḍeya,
possessing health and prosperity."

"May you be as fortunate as Indra; may you be as radiant as the sun; may you be as healthy as Saubhari; may you possess a virtuous lineage like one of good character; may you have a worthy wife; may you be as devoted to Śiva as Agastya; may you be as fortunate as Indra. (l6) "...May you be a practitioner of dharma like Tāpi. Thus he should offer [the gift]. This is the bestowing of grace (*prasāda*).
