Now, the procedure for the Great Consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*): On the day of the Great Vase Consecration, at midday or in the evening, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipa*), having performed the *brāhmī* and *śaivī* rites as prescribed for the time of bathing and so forth, shall smear [the area] all over with cow dung in the presence of Śiva using the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having adorned it with colored powders, garlands, and other ornaments, he shall hold the sacred thread (*pavitra*) in his hand.

Having sat upon the seat with a serene countenance, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having prepared the general arghya offering, having worshipped Vighneśvara, having prayed to Vighneśvara while striking the head [of the image], and having performed three rounds of prāṇāyāma, [he makes] the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, for this God of Gods, together with the Mother Śrī Kāntimatī, accompanied by the Śrī Mūlaliṅga and his retinue, the Śrī..."

In accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Kāmikāgama for the Śivayāga consisting of the eight-fold binding (aṣṭabandhana) and the restoration of what was worn out, performed today for Lord Veṇuvaneśvara Sadāśiva— preceded by the pacification of the heat of the binding— for the purpose of bringing about the presence of the Liṅga and for the protection of many devotees,
[to] Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara...

"I shall perform the consecration by means of the primary jar-abhiseka preceded by the ritual bath with twenty-five substances for the sake of attaining grace. As a constituent part of that, I shall perform the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*). Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and touched water, and having duly prepared the auspicious day, the five products of the cow, the five nectars, and so forth, [the rite is performed] by the preceptor of the daily worship (*nityapūjācārya*).
Having caused [the ritual] to be performed up to the placement of the nine jars as described in the *Nirukti*, one should,

on the permanent altar (*nityavedikā*) or at another location, [draw] eight lines with their tips pointing east using flour and turmeric powder for the purpose of the ablution with the jar of twenty-five substances.
Having likewise struck the lines, there are forty-nine squares. Having designated a nine-square square in the center,
in the first enclosure— one having consecrated [the site] with the Vāmadeva mantra in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
and having prepared the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) from rice and other grains with the Aghora mantra, one should strew it around with *darbha* grass and flowers.
In the second enclosure— in the cardinal and intermediate directions— one should install eight jars with the Aghora mantra; then,

having installed eight jars on the side-pads adjacent to those, one should wrap the primary and other *vardhanī* jars with the cord of the Śrīsūtra using the Tatpuruṣa mantra, and with the Astra mantra, [one should perform the rite] by means of Sadyojāta.

Having washed [the vessels] and having again established all the primary and other jars upon the sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) with the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should place the central jar with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*),
the *vardhanī* vessel, the five jewels (*pañcaratna*) with the root mantra, and the substances for the jars of the first enclosure.
One should place water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the arghya offering, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
water with kuśa grass, milk, curd, and ghee in the first enclosure.
Having thus deposited [the substances] with the root mantra, if one wishes for the materials for the vases of the second enclosure, they are as follows: milk, *gocaka* powder, turmeric powder,
parched rice (*lāja*), sesame, and mustard seeds, as well as parched rice powder.
Likewise, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in the eight directions with the *mūla-mantra*, one should place the substances for the eight jars at their sides:
a plantain tree, a citron, a pomegranate, and likewise a jackfruit; as well as a lotus, a blue water-lily, *tulasī*, and a *bilva* leaf.

Having placed the ritual substances upon all the corners starting from the southeast with the root mantra, and having then performed the rites beginning with the purification of oneself up to the purification of the mantras; having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste and having worshipped the head with the mantra "Obeisance to the Śiva-self in the form of flowers," [one should contemplate] "I am Śiva."

Having visualized [the deities] and worshipped the two hells, [one should take] one [portion] from the substance-flask... (l2) ...and afterwards one into the principal jar. Having worshipped the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, having performed the worship starting with the thirty-eight-fold nyāsa and ending with the Jayā-rite including the invocation and so forth, and having likewise worshipped in the *vardhanī* jar as well—(l3)

In the first enclosure, [one should worship] the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas); in the second enclosure, the World-Protectors beginning with Indra, and at their sides, the [weapons] beginning with the thunderbolt (vajra). Having performed the worship from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the end of the recitation (japa), and having caused the recitation of the Rudra-hymns and so forth preceded by the great placement (mahānyāsa) according to the previously mentioned method; then, according to the previously mentioned path, in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), following the purification of the pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra), [one should perform the rites] from the kindling of the fire (ādhāna) up to the marriage ceremony (vivāha).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], having invoked Śiva into the midst of the fire, and having offered oblations according to the procedure for the *śānti*-homa— preceded by the recitation of the mantras over the substances and their respective counts— and having completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites,
as well as the dismissal of the fire, the offering of the *bali*, and the final oblation... having thus established [the ritual].

Having performed the worship beginning with the adoration of the door and ending with the bath and the seat as prescribed for the daily rite; having removed the previous day's floral offerings (*nirmālya*); having worshipped [the deity] with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings; having returned again to the vicinity of the *kumbha* and worshipped it with the offering of food (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth; having worshipped the bull-throne (*vṛṣāsana*); and having first established [the deity] in the *kumbha*, one should circumambulate the temple accompanied by all musical instruments, [and then perform the same for] all the principal *kumbhas* and other vessels.

Having consecrated each respective location with its corresponding mantra, having adorned them with garments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items with their respective mantras, having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) with the root mantra, and having performed the *ārātrika* rite,
[one prepares] all substances such as oil that have undergone the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*).

One should perform the consecration preceded by the respective authorities and mantras. One hundred bhāras of water for the consecration—equivalent to one bhāra in measure—should be set out in the number of *kuḍabas*.
Having mixed these together: cloves (*lavaṅga*), *yela*, dried *caṅkaśuka* flowers, *pārārijātaka* blossoms, *koṣṭha*, and *uśīra*, [one should prepare] four *prasthas* of fragrant oil.

With the five-syllable [mantra], one should grind *likucasāra*... with the six-syllable [mantra], ground *āmalaka* and *rajanī*. Separately, in the quantity of four *prasthas*, having formed a handful with the eight-syllable [mantra], one should purify the root of the *darbha* grass, the *liṅga*, and the pedestal with the *praṇava*.

A pure bath with wet garments [performed] with the nine-syllable mantra; the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); one *droṇa* [of water]; having recited the *brahmamantra*; five *bhāra* of milk with the five weapon-mantras (*pañcāstramantra*);

five *bhāra* of curd; ghee with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra; lukewarm water with the *bahurūpa* mantra; and the *ekaśiva* [mantra]; five kinds of fruit and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); ten thousand plantains.
Five hundred mangoes;
one hundred mātulaṅgas; ... nāgalipa fruits; five hundred wood-apples (kapittha); one thousand nāraṅgas; five hundred tamarīs; five hundred *gostanī* fruits;
one hundred large nāraṅgas; [and] coconuts.

Fifty *gula* of fruit; two hundred [units] of cow-ghee; one *āḍhaka*; fifty *yela*; one *karṣa*. With the *pañcaprāsāda* mantra, there is also the fivefold nectar (*pañcāmṛta*) of substances. One hundred *nāra* of the essence of fruit; two hundred mangoes; one hundred large oranges (*bṛhannāraṅga*); five small oranges (*kṛcaśanāraṅga*); one hundred grapes; fifty *tamarī* fruits; fifty [more].

The essence of fruits with the Rudrasūktas; two *droṇas* of bilva and other pure sacrificial tree wood collected by ants with the [Puruṣa-sūkta]; a load of sugarcane juice with the Puruṣasūkta; three thousand coconuts with the Pāvamāna mantras;
and [the offering] for worship.

With the mantra, [one should offer] one *āḍhaka* of cooked rice, one *āḍhaka* of red *śāli* rice grains, cow’s fresh butter, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), cardamom (*yelā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and camphor—each weighing one *karṣa*. With the *trayambaka* mantra, [one offers] *bilva*-water and one thousand *bilva* fruits. Fifteen *candana* [sticks], fresh camphor weighing two *karṣas*, and twenty-five conch shells with the *Śrīrudra* mantra.

And having duly worshipped the Dakṣiṇāvṛtta [mantra] with the *camaka-praśna* over a thousand recitations, [he offers] fragrant water, perfume consisting of a hundred fruits, fresh camphor, ten parts of black [sandalwood],
black fragrance, musk, saffron flowers, yellow orpiment, musk-powder, and *korpara*.

Each leaf [should weigh] five *karṣas*. The consecration with the water-pitcher (*kumbhābhiṣeka*) should be performed with the *ambaramantra*, while recollecting the *śivamantra*. Thus, in this sequence and according to the rule, there is the consecration with sixteen [pitchers]. At the end, having consecrated [the deity] with the water-drop from the *arghya* vessel, and having offered the three beginning with the *pādya*, one should present the mantra-consecrated food that has been cooked according to the rule. Again, having offered the *pādya* and so forth.

Having wiped the pedestal of the *liṅga* with a fine cloth using the *aghora* mantra, and having offered a pair of priceless fine garments with the *yūṃ vastra* mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra, and having offered protective sacred ash (*vibhūti*) with the root mantra,
[one should worship] with the *gandhadvārā* mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra.

Having offered the secondary articles (*upadravya*), having offered the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the *yajñopavīta* mantra, and having adorned [the deity] with the *brahmajijñāsa* mantra, with the heart mantra, and with ornaments such as the seat of light (*prabhāpīṭha*),

one should adorn [the deity] residing in the inner sanctum with fragrant flowers and garlands of *damana* grass using the mantra "devassatve" and also with the *bhogaśakti* [mantra] by means of its root mantra.
Having consecrated [the deity] and adorned [it],

one should worship Veṇuvaneśvara situated in the northwestern direction facing south; having worshipped Śrīma in the north and Saptaguru in the northeast, and having made the formal request, [one should worship] from the base of the pedestal upward,
ending with the Śaktiyādi-śaktis.

The offering of the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*) consisting of five types of food and other items, distinguished by the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) preceded by the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*); the recitation of the four Vedas (*caturveda-pārāyaṇa*), the benediction (*āśīrvāda*), and ten thousand lamps (*ayutadīpa*) such as the chariot-lamps; the *śivakumbha* [offering]; the *śivadaśaka*; one *bhāra*; twenty-one *bhāras* for Śiva—these [are performed] according to one's means, relying upon that doctrine.

Five loads; the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) with twenty-five condiments; ten thousand betel leaves; five cakes (*apūpa*); [ten thousand] grains of rice and vegetables; at the time of offering, ghee from a tawny cow (*kapilā-goghṛta*); one thousand lamps for the thousand-fold rite; eight hundred for the general lamp; four hundred for the *pākku*? (Mahākumbhābhiṣeka, side heading).

The Drāviḍa-stuti, pure dance (śuddhanṛtta), and the daily offering of oblations (nityahavana) should be performed according to the rules until the conclusion of the daily festival worship (nityotsavapūjā), following the previously described procedure for the worship of the long-standing presence of the Liṅga. Thus ends the Mahābhiṣeka-vidhi of the Kāmika [Tantra] concerning the eight-fold binding (aṣṭabandhana). On the evening of the day of the Mahākumbha-abhiṣeka, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, [one should worship] Mahāgaṇapati, Skanda, Somāskanda, and Devī...

One should cause a festival to be performed according to the rules at night, beginning with the midday ritual bath, for the Lord of the Chariot (Rathamāhātmya), extending as far as the devotees and Caṇḍeśa. Now, the worship of Caṇḍa: then the preceptor, having gone to the temple of Caṇḍeśvara, [should offer] "Obeisance to the Sound-Caṇḍa Seat."

Having worshipped with the mantra: "Salutation to Caṇḍamūrti, who is fierce, red, with a gaping mouth, and whose two hands display the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness," and having honored him with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, as well as with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), garments, scents, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth— [one should offer] the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consisting of things to be licked, sucked, drunk, and the like, from that which has been offered to Śiva.

Having taken whatever [is available] and placed it within reach, having offered it to Dhvanicaṇḍa, and having presented the *ārātrika* lamp, one should pray: "O Caṇḍanātha, by your command, may this entire web of ritual actions be accomplished."
Surely it attains completion;
may that be fulfilled for me.

Having prayed thus, having washed the feet again, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and having applied the sacred ash (*bhasman*), one should bow to Śiva in his presence. Having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra (*aghorāstra*) one hundred times for the sake of fulfilling the previous purpose, and having offered it, one should pray for one's desired goal. This is the worship of Caṇḍa.

Now follows the procedure for the Great Bathing (mahāsnāpanavidhi), to be performed on the day following the sacrificial pot-consecration (yāgakumbhābhiṣeka). The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipāḥ), having completed the daily rites beginning with the bath and ending with worship, shall enter the temple. Having adorned himself with the fivefold ornaments beginning with the turban (uṣṇīṣa), he shall sit upon his seat with a serene countenance.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having prepared the general arghya offering, having worshipped Vighneśvara, and having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "On this auspicious lunar day, according to the method prescribed in the Kāmikāgama, for this God of Gods, Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his consort Śrī Kāntimatī Ambā, accompanied by the Śrī Mūlaliṅga and his entire retinue..."

In this Śiva-sacrifice, consisting of the restoration of what has decayed and the binding of the eight [limbs], performed today— preceded by the presence of the Liṅga at the gateway through the application of fragrant unguents for the pacification of heat— and preceded by the protection of devoted people such as ourselves, for the sake of attaining the grace of Veṇuvaneśvara,
[this is] in the form of a most excellent great ablution (*mahāsnāna*).

"I shall perform the consecration with one thousand and nine jars of substances, together with all its primary and secondary limbs; and furthermore, I shall perform the bathing and consecration with one hundred and nine [jars], together with its preliminary and concluding limbs. Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), he performs the great bathing (*mahāsnapanam*) according to the procedure for the thousand-jar ritual as set forth in the *Kāmikāgama*, beginning from Saura and ending with Caṇḍa.

The ritual task, if it consists of one hundred and nine [verses], is to be performed according to the procedure (*paḍḍhati*) that will be explained; thus ends the *Kāmika-mahāsnāpana-vidhi*. The *Kāmika-mahāsnāpana-vidhi* is complete. The *Kāmika-mahāsnā
The liberation from views—
for the sake of liberating all views, and especially those of the wicked—
and for the purpose of pacifying the remnants of the eyes: neem leaves and mustard seeds.
Reciting the mantra of the weapon (*astra*) over ashes mixed with cotton seeds,
he should encircle [the disciple] three times from the head down to the feet with the armor mantra (*kavaca*).
Having placed water for the sake of the *nirmālya* vessel and touched it with water,
the *deśika*, having likewise performed the preliminary rites and washed his hands,
then proceeds to the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) accompanied by the *praṇava* and the *arghya*.
And having offered arghya to the deities of the doors and so forth, [he should face] away from them.
Outside the gate of the gopura, one should designate the bali-maṇḍala;
with powders of five colors, one should scatter the accumulated bali offering.
Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes,
those who reside at the junctions of day and night (saṃdhyā), O gentle one, as well as those who do not so dwell;
those who inhabit the surface of the earth and those who dwell in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla).
The Mothers who have the form of Rudra, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas.
And others who exist as obstacles, dwelling constantly in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may you all, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering.
May they nourish my intellect and protect me constantly from perpetual fears.
May whatever exists within the universe, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, including all that is moving and unmoving,
go to its satisfaction through this offering given by me.

Having thus offered the *bali* oblation, having dismissed [the deities], having washed one's feet, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), having applied the sacred ash (*bhasman*), and having performed the rite of complete protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should recite the *Aghora-astro* mantra one hundred times. Then, having recited the *Āyuḥ-sūkta* and the *Abhayaṅkara-mantra*, one should pray for one’s desired goal.
This is the procedure for the liberation of the gaze. [Side heading: Maṇḍalābhiṣeka] (p. 257b, f. 250a)

(The Maṇḍala Consecration: Then the preceptor, having performed all the preliminary rites such as the morning bath and so forth, enters the temple. Having first offered a prayer to Vighneśvara, he makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the restoration of the ancient [shrine] of the God of Gods, Śrī Sadāśiva Veṇuvaneśvara—who is accompanied by the Mother Śrī Kāntimatī, together with the Śrī Mūla-liṅga, and his entire retinue—"

In the Śiva-sacrifice consisting of the eight bonds (*aṣṭabandhana*), as taught in the *Kāmikāgama*, for the purpose of pacifying the heat of the bondage incurred on that very day, beginning from the day immediately following the jar-consecration (*kumbhābhiṣeka*) and lasting for forty days or up to three fortnights; 13–14.

For the sake of attaining the grace of Śrī Veṇuvaneśvara, there shall be a sacrifice lasting three fortnights, preceded daily by worship including the Mahārudrābhiṣeka, the ninefold *pañcagavya*, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the ritual invocation of merit (*puṇyāvācana*), the propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*), and the worship of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvārcana*), as well as the worship with the Thousand Names (*sahasranāmārcana*) distinguished by offerings of milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), the five grains (*pañcānna*), and great oblations (*mahāhavis*), followed by the feeding of Brahmins.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) with the words "I shall perform [it]," one should carry out the three-fortnightly worship (*tripakṣārcana*) in this very manner every day, according to the procedure for daily worship, beginning from Saura and ending with Caṇḍa.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the three-fortnightly worship according to the Kāmika [Tantra].

Then, on the forty-fifth day, at the conclusion of the mandala, one should perform the festival for the specific *mūlaliṅga* and the *utsavamūrtis* together with their retinues— beginning from Saura up to Caṇḍa—
preceded by the great ceremonial bath (*mahāsnāna*). Thus,

in accordance with the scriptural injunctions regarding the procedure for the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) as taught in the *Kāmikāgama*, [the ritual proceeds] from the worship of Gaṇapati up to the great festival of the mandala.

The *Phalasulocanapaddhati*, consisting of one hundred and fifteen verses and freed from the eight bonds of form, is complete. It is offered to the venerable Veṇuvaneśvara, together with his retinue, the venerable Mūlaliṅga, and the venerable Kāntimatī. Of this—

May there be auspiciousness! Victorious is the illustrious Veṇuvaneśvara, distinguished by his splendor and wisdom. Homage to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. (L4)
Salutations to the Guru of all worlds, the physician for the diseased, the treasury of all sciences— Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Śrī Kāntimatī is pleased.

Regarding *śuddhanṛtta* (pure dance): Now, the preceptor should cause the *śuddhanṛtta* to be performed at the conclusion of the great festival of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), the great ablution (*mahāsnapana*), and so forth; as well as at the great consecration of the solar and other *liṅgas*, the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*), the offering of the great oblation (*mahāhavi-nivedana*), the propitiation of lamps (*dīpārādhana*), the recitation of the four Vedas (*caturveda-pārāyaṇa*), and the Dravidian hymns and lute-songs to Rudra—at the front pavilion of the deity.
Having smeared a square measuring two cubits with cow dung, and having adorned the mandala with flour and turmeric powder, one should worship it there with flowers.
Having sprinkled it with the general *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā; Oṃ hvīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalā; Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Vidyākalā."
Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Śāntikalā. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītakalā. (L2) ...

having worshipped the maṇḍala and meditated upon the maṇḍala of the Kalās, one should place a golden vessel in its center with the Heart Mantra. Within that [vessel]: obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya; obeisance to Aiśvarya. (L3)

Salutations! Salutations to Padma! Salutations to Naṭeśvarāsana! Salutations to the form of Naṭeśvara! Oṃ Heṃ, salutations to Naṭeśvara! Having invoked Śrī Naṭeśvara, together with Pārvatī and distinguished by the deities of the enclosure, using the root mantra, saying: "I invoke [him] here," and having worshipped from the rites of installation up to the lamp, [one offers salutations]: "Salutations to Nandin in the east; salutations to Brahmā in the south; in the west..."
"Salutation to Skanda! Salutation to Viṣṇu in the north!

Having thus worshipped, outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, starting from the east. Outside of that, one should worship the *vyāhṛti*-mantras of the thunderbolt and so forth, starting from the east and ending with Īśāna. [Then] incense and lamps...

Having worshipped with the food offering (*naivedya*), he should then summon a young woman who has bathed and is adorned with a rosary of beads (*akṣamālā*) and other ornaments. Having sprinkled her with *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*, and having placed [the substance] in her hand, he should have her apply it as a mark (*uddhūlana*) on her forehead. Then, having given water into her hand and having washed her hands, he should place a flower in her joined palms (*añjali*) while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*). By means of her...
Having caused a handful of flowers to be offered to the Guru,

and having washed his hands again, and having taken up a flower again while reciting the root mantra, he offers a handful of flowers to Śiva in his presence. Then, the worship [is performed] in the eastern part.

One should perform the *śuddhanarta* dance, known by such names as *prajaghāti* and so forth, as taught by Bharata; it is pleasing to Śiva and bestows happiness. At the time of beginning the dance, the dancer (*nartaka*) and the drummer (*mardakoṭa*) should stand to the right of the mandala. First, with the mandala...

The singer known as Vaṃśaka should stand [there], and the *maurvika* should stand in front. In the north, accompanied by the playing of the muraja drum, he should perform the *śuddhanṛtta* while contemplating the meaning of verses appropriate for the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). At dawn, Brahmā is the presiding deity; at midday, Viṣṇu; and at the evening twilight, Rudra—these are the lords of the three twilights.

May this offering of flower-clusters at the hour of dawn— accompanied by the sweet sounds of songs sung by swarms of intoxicated bees amidst the various fragrances of *brāhmī* flowers, *śloka* verses, and *mandāra* blossoms; and increasing through various types of bodily movements—
be for your sake.

To the one seated upon the lotus, accompanied by the Lord, with the most excellent *rasa*, dancing, born from the tradition of dance, and surrounded by bees intoxicated by fragrance— to that Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), let there be an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). May this offering of flowers be for my sake, performed with various dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) by the daughters of Rudra who have been made into a lineage (*santāna*), and celebrated with heaps of various blossoms for the prosperity of the king and his realm.

O Supreme Lord, I praise the southern direction, which is illuminated by the sun of the ultimate supreme syllable, which possesses the fierce form of Yama, the lord of the asuras, which is ordained for the sake of accomplishment, O Lord, which has Varuṇa as its presiding deity, and which is resorted to by the Lord of Wealth.

Furthermore, when the recitation of the verses of the *Uttarāśā* has been completed without omission, the Ācārya, having bid farewell to Naṭeśvara with a display of prowess (*vikrama*) and weapons (*heti*), [should perform] ... for the sake of turning away [the obstacles].

Having uttered [this], he should contemplate his desired goal preceded by a prayer for blessings. Thus ends the ritual procedure for dance (*nṛttavidhi*) as taught in the *Kāmikāgama*. End of manuscript.
